When the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude. All remained silent, except for Mahākāśyapa, who broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the subtle and wonderful Dharma-gate of the true mark that is formless.
It does not rely on words and letters; it is a separate transmission outside the teachings. I now entrust it to Mahākāśyapa."
A verse by Miaoxi says: "Holding up a single branch of flowers, the true style flows forth from within the house.
If one speaks of transmitting the Dharma of the mind, matters throughout the world are as numerous as hemp seeds.
Long ago, when the World-Honored One arrived before the Many-Sons Stupa, he bade Mahākāśyapa share his seat and wrapped him in the saṃghāṭī robe.

He then declared: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye; I transmit it secretly to you. You must uphold and maintain it, transmitting it to future generations so that it shall never be severed."
One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat and sat in silence. Ānanda struck the gavel and said, "I request the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said, "In this assembly there are two bhikṣus who have violated the Vinaya. For this reason, I do not preach the Dharma.
Ānanda, using his supernormal power of reading others' minds, examined these bhikṣus and then had them expelled. The World-Honored One remained silent once more. Ānanda spoke again.

"Venerable One, these two bhikṣus have already been sent away; why do you not preach the Dharma? The World-Honored One said, "I vow never to preach the Dharma for those of the Śrāvaka or the Two Vehicles. Having said this, he descended from his seat.
As the World-Honored One was walking together with Ānanda, he saw an ancient stūpa of a Buddha. The World-Honored One paid homage to it.
Ānanda asked, "Whose stūpa is this? The World-Honored One replied, "It is the stūpa of the Buddhas of the past. Ānanda then asked, "The Buddhas of the past..."
"Whose disciple are you? The World-Honored One replied, "I am his disciple. Nan replied, "It should indeed be so.
One day, when the time for the meal was approaching, the World-Honored One instructed Ānanda, "You should enter the city with your alms bowl. Ānanda responded with assent.
The World-Honored One said, "Since you are carrying the bowl, you should follow the ritual procedures of the seven Buddhas of the past. Ānanda then asked:
"What is the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past? The World-Honored One called to Ānanda, and Ānanda responded.
The World-Honored One said, "Take this bowl and go.

When the World-Honored One was practicing as a bodhisattva, he spread his hair upon the mud to cover it and offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha. Dīpaṃkara saw the place where the hair had been spread.
He then signaled for the assembly to withdraw. Pointing to the ground, he said, "On this plot of land, a Brahma-shrine (Buddhist monastery) ought to be established.
Among the assembly was an elder named Xianzi, who took up a marker and, at the spot where he had pointed, planted it, saying, "The construction of the Brahma-shrine is now complete.
Thereupon, the devas scattered flowers and praised him, saying, "This younger son possesses great wisdom!"
The World-Honored One remained in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for ninety days, preaching the Dharma for his mother.

When he took his leave of the celestial realm and descended, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all went into the air to welcome him. There was a bhikṣuṇī named Utpalavarṇā who thought to herself:
"I am a female monastic; I will certainly be placed behind the great monks. It would be better to employ my supernormal powers and transform myself into a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
The King, surrounded by his thousand sons, was the first to see the Buddha; thus his vow was fulfilled. As soon as the World-Honored One saw him, he rebuked him, saying:
"Utpalavarṇā Bhikṣuṇī, how could you bypass the great monks to see me? Although you see my physical body (rūpakāya), you do not yet see my Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Subhūti, sitting in meditative absorption within the mountain cave, sees my Dharma-body."
The World-Honored One was asked by a seer possessing the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā): "The World-Honored One possesses six supernormal powers, whereas I possess only five.

What is this one supernormal power? The World-Honored One called out, "Seer of the five supernormal powers! The seer responded, "Yes. The World-Honored One said, "That one supernormal power—ask me about it."
Xuedou said, "The Old Barbarian originally did not know that one stroke; instead, he used the heterodox to strike the orthodox.
Yunfeng Yue said, "Great Gautama was exposed by the heretics.
Is there anyone here who does not accept this? Come forward! I wish to ask you: what is that one stroke?"
Baoning Yong’s verse says: "Throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have never encountered it before; how could I reach its midst without moving?
Do not say that the Buddha-dharma has little substance; most grievous is that Gautama has not yet mastered it."

The World-Honored One was approached by the Brahmin Dīrghanakha, who sought to debate the meaning of the Dharma. They made a prior agreement, saying: "If my doctrine falls into error, I shall cut off my own head as an apology.
The World-Honored One asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine? The Brahmin replied, "My doctrine takes the non-acceptance of all things as its tenet.
The World-Honored One then asked, "Is this view itself accepted? At this, the Brahmin brushed out his sleeves and departed. As he was walking along the road, there appeared—
Xing said to his disciples, "I shall return home to behead myself as an apology to the World-Honored One.
His disciples said, "Since you were victorious in the presence of the assembly of devas and humans, why should you behead yourself?
Zhi replied, "I would rather be beheaded before those who possess wisdom than achieve victory before those who lack it. He then sighed, "In both respects, my doctrine has suffered defeat. This is it.
If one accepts the view, the point at which the burden is incurred is coarse; if one does not accept the view, the point at which the burden is incurred is subtle.
No humans, devas, or followers of the Two Vehicles can know where my meaning falls; only the World-Honored One and the great Bodhisattvas know where my meaning falls.
Returning before the World-Honored One, he said, "I have been defeated and fallen in two matters regarding my doctrine; therefore, I shall cut off my head to offer my apology.
The World-Honored One said, "In my Dharma, there is no such thing as this. You should turn your mind toward the Path.
Thereupon, together with his five hundred followers, he simultaneously threw himself upon the Buddha, left the household life, and realized arhatship.
The Verse by T'ien-i Huai says: "If this view accepts it, one's family line is ruined; If this view does not accept it, with whom can one debate?
When the扁担 (pyan-t'an) is snapped, both ends are released; Within a single hair-tip, heaven and earth appear."
The World-Honored One, because of a question from a bhikṣu, said: "In the Buddha-dharma, you say that while the place of seeing exists, the place of realization does not yet exist;
what, then, would the World-Honored One point out to you? The Buddha said: "Bhikṣu so-and-so, what would I point out to you? That is precisely what you have asked."
Because the World-Honored One was skilled in discerning sounds and voices through Jīvaka, they went together to a cemetery and saw five skulls.

The World-Honored One struck one skull and asked, "To which realm was this person born? Jīvaka replied, "He was born into the human realm. He struck another and asked, "To which realm was this person born?
Jīvaka replied, "He was born into the heavenly realm. He struck yet another and asked, "To which realm was this person born? At this, Jīvaka was at a loss for an answer.

The World-Honored One, for the sake of the brahmin Kālakarṇin, exercised his supernatural power and, with his left and right hands, held up two stalks of *saṃyukta* and *pīlu* flowers to offer them to the Buddha.
The Buddha called to the rishi, who responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "Put it down. The rishi put down the flower in his left hand.
The Buddha again called to the rishi, "Put it down," and the rishi put down the flower in his left hand. The Buddha again—
The Buddha summoned the immortal and told him, "Let go. The immortal said, "I am now standing here empty-handed; what more could I let go of?
The Buddha said, "It was not for you to let go of that flower. You should let go of the six external sense objects and the six internal consciousnesses."
Relinquish the six sense-faculties within simultaneously, until you reach a state where there is nothing further to relinquish; this is the place where you escape birth and death.
As soon as your resolve is released upon these words, you will awaken to the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because Devadatta slandered the Buddha, he fell alive into hell. The Buddha commanded Ānanda to inquire after him, saying, "Are you at peace within hell?
Devadatta replied, "Though I am in hell, it is as joyful as the Third Dhyāna Heaven.
The Buddha again commanded him, asking, "Do you intend to leave? Devadatta replied, "I shall leave as soon as the World-Honored One comes. Ānanda said, "The Buddha..."

"This is the Great Teacher of the Three Realms; how could he have any portion that leads to entry into hell? Da said, "Since the Buddha has no portion for entering hell, how could I have any portion for exiting hell?"
Cuiyan Zhen said: "The words of the Master came from his own mouth.
Once, when a heterodox practitioner asked the World-Honored One, 'Are all phenomena permanent? the World-Honored One did not answer. He asked again, 'Are all phenomena impermanent?
and the World-Honored One likewise did not answer. The heterodox practitioner said, 'The World-Honored One possesses all-encompassing wisdom; why do you not answer?'"
"I, World-Honored One, say that what you have asked is all mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
One day, the World-Honored One took a *cintāmaṇi* jewel that reflected the colors of its surroundings and asked the kings of the five directions, "What color is this jewel?
The kings each spoke of it as having different colors. The World-Honored One then hid the jewel and raised his hand, asking, "What color is this?"
The Heavenly King Varuṇa said, "The Buddha has no pearls in his hand; from where could color arise? The World-Honored One sighed and said, "How can you be so utterly deluded?
When I show you a worldly pearl, you insist on saying it has blue, yellow, red, or white. When I show you a genuine pearl, you do not know anything at all.
At that time, when the Heavenly Kings of the five directions heard these words, they all attained enlightenment.
The World-Honored One was asked by King Prasenajit: "Within the Noble Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), does the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) exist?
If one says it exists, then wisdom should not be single; if one says it does not exist, then wisdom should not be dual. What is the meaning of this duality and unity? The World-Honored One replied:
"Great King, in the past, under the Dharma of the Buddha Dragon-Light (Nāgaprabha), you once asked about this very matter."
"I now have nothing to say; you also have nothing to hear. This absence of speaking and hearing is called "one meaning" and "two meanings.
Cuiyan Zhen said: "King Prasenajit asked well but answered poorly; the World-Honored One answered well but asked poorly.
In one case, there was a deficiency in principle; in the other, a deficiency in fact. At that time, Cuiyan...
If you see [him], light a torch and examine this "yellow-faced old fellow" to see how thick his skin is.
While the World-Honored One was seated, he saw two men carrying a piglet past and asked, "What is this?
The man replied, "The World-Honored One possesses all-encompassing wisdom, yet he does not even recognize a piglet. The World-Honored One said, "I must ask about it anyway."
Dayang Yan said: "It was not because of the World-Honored One’s question that [Kāśyapa] remained in a state of forgetfulness.
It was because when the Gandharva King presented music, at that moment the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all became the sound of the lute.
Kāśyapa rose from his seat, and the King asked: 'Kāśyapa, are you not indeed an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted? How can there still be [this sound]? "
"Regarding the residual habits," the Buddha said, "In truth, there are no residual habits. Do not slander the Dharma.
The King then played the lute three times, and Kāśyapa likewise performed a dance three times. The King said, "Kāśyapa has danced; is this not so? The Buddha said, "In truth, he never danced.
The King said, "World-Honored One, how can you speak falsely? The Buddha said, "I do not speak falsely. When you play the lute, the mountains, rivers, and great..."
The earth, the grasses, and the trees all produced the sound of lutes. "Is this not so? [the King asked]. The Buddha said, "It is. The King said, "It is.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa is also like this; he truly never danced. Thereupon, the King believed and accepted it.

Xiu Shan-zhu asked Chan Master Chengyuan: "When the Gandharva King performs music, it causes Mount Sumeru to tremble and the waters of the ocean to surge in waves, such that Kāśyapa breaks into dance. How do you understand this?
Yuan said, "Kāśyapa was once a musician in a past life; his habitual tendencies have not yet been eliminated. Xiu said, "Mount Sumeru trembles!"
"The waves surge upon the sea. Again, how is this? Yuanxiu departed.
Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying, "This is precisely habitual tendency (*vāsanā*).
Once, when a non-Buddhist asked Shizhi, "What Dharma did you preach yesterday? he replied, "I preached the Dharma of concentration (*samādhi*). The non-Buddhist said, "Today..."
"What dharma do you teach? Why do you teach the indeterminate dharma? The outsider said, "Yesterday you taught the determinate dharma;
why do you today teach the indeterminate dharma? Yesterday it was determinate; today it is indeterminate."
Daguang Zhe said, "This is not the realm of ordinary people.
Once, when an outsider asked the World-Honored One, "I do not ask about speech; I do not ask about silence," the World-Honored One remained seated.

The outsider praised him, saying, "The World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, has cleared away the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter [the Way]," whereupon he prostrated himself.
He then departed. Ānanda said to the Buddha, "What realization have these outsiders attained that they claim to have entered? The World-Honored One replied, "They are like fine horses of the world:
upon seeing the shadow of the whip, they immediately gallop forward."
Cuiyan Zhi said: "The Great and Small World-Honored Ones were smeared with mud by the outsider right before their faces.
As for the outsider saying, 'Let me enter,' [the Buddhas] had never even dreamed of it. Since they had never dreamed of it, why did they attain awakening?
Cuiyan Zhen said: "Throughout the six directions and nine realms, among those in black and yellow robes and those in blue and purple..."
In one instance of mutual engagement, everyone said that after a long while he took his seat and remained silent; yet, fundamentally, this was not it.

He further cited the various approaches used by masters of all quarters, and then said: "Alas! Even if Śāriputra and Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra were to employ their wisdom, compose their words, and exert their mental faculties, what benefit would there be?
Xuedou said: "When the heterodox and the orthodox are not distinguished, the fault lies with the whip."
Ying Miaoxi said: "The heterodox and the orthodox are distinguished from one another;
the orthodox arises from the shadow of the whip. Tianyi Huai’s verse says: "The double blades cover and protect, yet both are shattered;
The clouds of delusion are from this moment suddenly dispersed. Having recovered the bell-handle from the beginning of the kalpa, A light shake sends forth thunder and lightning."
The World-Honored One, because of the Seven Virtuous Women, was traveling through the Śītavana cemetery. One woman pointed to a corpse and said, "The corpse is here;
where is the person? Another woman said, "How? How? Sisters, observe closely! Each of them attained realization.
Moved by this, Śakra devānām indra scattered flowers and said, "I pray only that the Noble Sisters may tell me what they require; I shall provide for you for the rest of my life. The women—
He said, "In my home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all fully provided. However, I require three things: first, a single rootless tree;
second, a patch of ground where neither sun nor shade exists; and third, a mountain valley that echoes not when one calls.
Śakra replied, "Of everything you require, I have it all. As for these three things, I truly..."
"There is nothing to be attained. The woman said, "If you have nothing of this kind, how can you save others? Śakra was at a loss for what to do and went together with her to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Kauśika, even my disciples, the great Arhats, do not all understand this meaning."
Only the great Bodhisattvas can understand this meaning.
After the World-Honored One attained enlightenment, he sat cross-legged beneath a tree in the Jeta Grove. At that time, two merchants were passing by the edge of the grove with five hundred wagons.
Two of the oxen pulling the wagons would not move, which the merchants found strange. Then the mountain deity...
He replied, "There is a sage in the forest who has attained the Way; more than forty-nine days have passed, yet he has not eaten. You should make an offering to him.
The merchant entered the forest and indeed saw a man sitting upright and motionless. He then asked, "Are you the Brahma King?"
"Is it Śakra? Is it a mountain deity? Is it a river deity? The World-Honored One smiled and raised his *kāṣāya* robe to show them.
The merchants prostrated themselves and presented their offerings.
One day, at the assembly for the Great Parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored One stroked his chest with his hand and addressed the great multitude, saying:
"Behold well my body, which is the color of purple-gold; gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied, lest you later feel regret.
If you say that I have entered extinction, you are not my disciples; if you say that I have not entered extinction, you likewise are not my disciples. At that time, there were hundreds of billions...
The entire assembly attained realization of the Way.
Yunfeng Yue said, "In that case, the gate of the incurable is insufficient to administer medicine.
Today, Yunfeng shall act as a physician for a dead horse. Do you all have any blood beneath your skin?"
When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, Mañjuśrī requested that the Buddha turn the wheel of the Dharma once more. The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, for forty-nine years I have dwelt in this world, yet I have never spoken a single word. You ask me to turn the wheel of the Dharma again;
have I ever turned the wheel of the Dharma?"
The World-Honored One had already entered *nirvāṇa*. Kāśyapa arrived later, and the World-Honored One revealed his two upturned feet from within the outer coffin to him.
Kāśyapa prostrated and requested that the Tathāgata cremate himself by means of the fire of *samādhi*. Immediately, the golden coffin—
Rising from his bed of the seven treasures, he circumambulated the city of Kuśinagara seven times, then returned to his original place and,
entering the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi), spontaneously cremated himself.
The Great Sages and Holy Ones of India (twenty-five in total):
One day, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī instructed Sudhana to gather medicinal herbs, saying, "Bring back whatever is medicine. Sudhana gathered them everywhere;
there was nothing that was not medicine. He returned and reported, "There is nothing that is not [medicine]. Mañjuśrī said, "That which is medicine..."
Having gathered them, Sudhana plucked a blade of grass and handed it to Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī held it up and showed it to the assembly, saying:
"This medicine can kill a person, and it can also bring a person to life."
Daguang Zhe said: "Sudhana was able to gather; Mañjuśrī was able to employ it.

Not only while he was bedridden in Vaiśālī, but even if every person throughout the entire earth were suffering from a terminal illness and came to Mañjuśrī’s place—if Mañjuśrī were to instruct them, each would depart having cast off their physical body.
Why is this? To understand its employment, one need not have a sword with a frost-sharpened blade; to prolong one's life, why indeed..."
The Ninth Elixir of Reversion.

The Great Being Mañjuśrī addressed the Devaputra Susīma, saying: "If you were now able to go against all Buddhas and slander the Dharma and the Saṅgha, I would then practice such a holy life (brahmacarya) together with you. The Devaputra said: "Great Being, for what reason now..."
Thus he spoke. The Mahāsattva said: "Son of Heaven, according to your understanding, what do you take to be the Buddha? The Son of Heaven replied:
"The suchness (tathatā) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu)—I say this is the Buddha. The Mahāsattva asked: "What do you think? Can suchness and the dharma-realm be stained or attached to?
The Son of Heaven replied: "No. The Mahāsattva said: "For this reason, I speak thus. You now..."
"If you can reject and turn your back on the Buddha-dharma, I shall practice this holy life together with you.
Mañjuśrī asked the woman Aṅgulimālā, "What is the meaning of birth? The woman replied, "The meaning of birth is that which is born from non-birth.
Mañjuśrī asked, "In what way is the meaning of birth that which is born from non-birth? The woman said, "If..."

One can clearly know that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never themselves attained any state of combination, yet they are able to function according to their suitability as the principle of arising.
Mañjuśrī asked again, "What is the meaning of death? The woman replied, "Death takes the non-death of death as its meaning.
Mañjuśrī asked, "How is it that death takes the non-death of death as its meaning?"
The woman said, "If one can clearly understand that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never themselves experienced separation or dispersal,
yet can, according to what is appropriate, take this as the meaning of death."
When the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu descended from Maitreya’s inner palace, Asaṅga asked him: "The sutras state that four hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for those devas.
During a single period, Maitreya brings five billion devaputras to accomplishment and leads them to realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
I do not yet know what dharma he preaches. Vasubandhu replied: "He preaches only this very dharma; it is simply this."
The Brahma-voice was pure and elegant, making it a joy to hear.
Tianyi Huai said, "Maitreya has already spoken erroneously; Vasubandhu has already transmitted erroneously.
Today, this mountain monk shall follow error with error and annotate it for all of you. After a long silence, he said, "Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
Listen. The subsequent text is extensive; it shall be entrusted for another day.
Beneficial Bodhisattva addressed Dīpaṃkara Buddha: "I wish to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I pray only that the World-Honored One will instruct me so that I may swiftly achieve enlightenment. The Buddha said to Beneficial: "Observe this dharma. What is this dharma? It is...
Regarding your question:
There was once a preeminent bodhisattva in India who acted as a mendicant.
As he entered the city to beg for food, there was a bhikṣu named Gaṅgā who asked the mendicant, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from reality. Again he asked:

"What is meant by 'reality' (tattva)? "It is called reality because it is quiescent (śānta). He asked again: "Within the state of quiescence, is there anything to be sought, or is there nothing to be sought?
"It is said that there is nothing to be sought. He asked again: "If there is nothing to be sought, for what purpose does one seek?
"It is said: 'Within that which has nothing to be sought, I wish to seek it. He asked again: "Within that which has nothing to be sought, for what purpose does one seek? The answer was: "There is."
That which is sought is entirely empty; the attainer is also empty; the one who clings is also empty; the reality is also empty; the seeker is also empty;
the speaker is also empty; the questioner is also empty. Even nirvāṇa, the state of quiescent extinction, and all divisions of the realm of space are likewise entirely empty.
Yet, for the sake of such empty dharmas, I have sought what is real and true.
In the assembly at Vimalakīrti’s dwelling, thirty-two bodhisattvas each expounded the gate of non-duality. Mañjuśrī said, "Regarding all dharmas, there is no speech and no discourse;
there is no indication and no cognition; it is free from all questioning and answering—this is the bodhisattva’s entry into the gate of non-duality.
Mañjuśrī then questioned Vimalakīrti, and Vimalakīrti remained silent. Mañjuśrī sighed in admiration, saying, "Even unto..."
There is no speech or written words; this is the Bodhisattva’s true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Baofu Zhan said, "Great or small, Vimalakīrti was pinned down by Mañjuśrī with a single sitting, and until this very day he cannot rise.
Xuedou asked, "What did Vimalakīrti say? He further remarked, "He has been thoroughly seen through."
Langya Jue said: "Mañjuśrī’s praise of the good was merely divining with a ladle by listening to empty sounds.
Vimalakīrti’s silence—do not you all go about boring through tortoise shells and striking tiles."
Vimalakīrti, because of Subhūti, took his bowl to the gate, filled it with fragrant food, and said to the Venerable One:
"If one can be equal regarding the Dharma, one is also equal regarding food; even entering into all false views, one does not fail to reach the other shore."
You dwell in the eight difficulties and do not attain freedom from them; you are identical to afflictions and separated from pure dharmas.
As for you who have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention, all sentient beings likewise attain this samādhi. Those who give to you cannot be called fields of merit;
those who make offerings to you fall into the three evil realms. You act in concert with the various māras, serving as their companions in toil. You and the multitude...
"Māra and all the afflictions (*kleśa*) are equal and without distinction. Toward all sentient beings, you harbor a mind of enmity; you slander the Buddha and disparage the Dharma;
you do not enter the ranks of the assembly and shall never attain *nirvāṇa*. If you are thus, only then may you take this food.
When Subhūti heard these words, he was bewildered and did not know how to respond; setting down his bowl, he wished to depart.
While Subhūti was preaching the Dharma, Śakra rained down flowers. Subhūti then asked: "From where did these flowers come?
Did they come from heaven, from the earth, or from humans? Śakra replied to each question, "No.
Subhūti asked, "Then from where were they obtained? Śakra raised his hand. Subhūti said, "So it is, so it is."
Subhūti was sitting in meditative seclusion among the crags. The devas rained down flowers and offered praise. The Venerable One asked, "Who is it that offers praise from the air?
The deva replied, "I am Brahmā. Out of reverence for the Venerable One, I have praised the excellent exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Venerable One said, "Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, I have never uttered a single word. Why do you praise me? The Devaputra replied, "It is so.
The Venerable One has not spoken, and I have not heard. This state of no speaking and no hearing is the true teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā."
Xuedou said: "To avoid clamor and seek a place of stillness—there has never been such a method in the world.
Even while sitting in meditation amidst the crags, one is smeared by this pack of fellows. Furthermore, there is this old fellow who cannot hold himself together;
when asked about the rain of flowers falling from the sky, he utters words of praise. Who is it that has already brought about this failure? I deeply revere him."
This person speaks well of Prajñāpāramitā, yet evil water is splashed over his head. It is also said: "Regarding Prajñāpāramitā, I have never spoken a single word.
You grass-blade man! The Venerable One has nothing to say, and I have nothing to hear; you clearly recognize what is good and what is evil.
"All are like such people. Where would there be a 'today' for them? He then called to the assembly again, saying, "Xuedou is fortunately a man of no affairs.
What are you seeking by coming here? With his staff, he drove them all away at once.
Śāriputra asked the goddess, "Why do you not transform away this female body? She replied, "For twelve years I have sought the mark of a woman and have been unable to find it at all;

what, then, is there to transform? Immediately, the goddess used her supernormal powers to transform Śāriputra into a goddess and herself took on a form like that of Śāriputra. She then asked Śāriputra, "What [do you seek to transform]?"
She did not transform away from her female body. Śāriputra said, "I do not know now by what wheel this has been transformed into a female body.
Then, as Śāriputra entered the city, he saw the girl Candrottarā coming out of the city from afar. Śāriputra reflected both mentally and verbally:
This elder sister saw the Buddha and did not know whether he had attained *kṣānti* (patience/endurance). I shall try to ask her. As soon as she drew near, I asked, "Where are you going?
The woman said, "I am going just as Śāriputra goes. Śāriputra said, "I have just entered the city; you should be leaving the city.
Why do you say you are going just as Śāriputra goes? The woman said, "As for the disciples of the Buddhas, upon what should they rely?"
Śāriputra said, "The disciples of all Buddhas should dwell in accordance with the Great Nirvāṇa.
The woman said, "Since the disciples of all Buddhas dwell in accordance with the Great Nirvāṇa, I shall go in such a manner as Śāriputra."
Śāriputra asked Subhūti, "Is the teaching of the six pāramitās within a dream the same as or different from that when one is awake?
Subhūti replied, "The meaning of this is profound and far-reaching; I am unable to explain it. There is the Great Being Maitreya in this assembly;
go to him and ask."
Xuedou said: "Had he not let him pass at that time, he would have followed up with a written decree. Who is Maitreya?
Who is it that is Maitreya? At these words, all traces would vanish like ice melting and a fortress collapsing."
Pūrṇa asked the Buddha, "If [the nature of reality] is fundamentally pure and serene, how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Langya Huijue said, "I, this mountain monk, do not say so. If [the nature of reality] is fundamentally pure and serene, how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Jianfu Xian said, "The beginning was not reached; the end went too far."
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: "When I do not see, how can you not see the place where I do not see?
If you see my non-seeing, it naturally is not that characteristic of non-seeing. If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, it naturally is not a thing."
"How is it not you? Xuedou’s verse says: "The whole elephant and the whole ox are no different from the cataract; from of old, the masters have shared this model.
If you wish now to see the old man Huangtou, every land and every speck of dust lies halfway there."
When Venerable Piṇḍola was questioned by King Aśoka, who asked, "I have heard it said that you, Venerable One, personally saw the Buddha; is this true or not?

the Venerable One raised his eyebrows with his hand and said, "Do you understand? When [the King] replied, "I do not understand," he said, "The Nāga King of Lake Anavatapta once invited the Buddha for a meal; at that time, I was included among those present."
Cuiyan Zhen said, "Tell me, where do you see it? Even if the snow falls in vast drifts and the lake’s light is serene and expansive, do not speak of such things as dreams.
Daopi Zhe said, "Although King Aśoka provided food for thirty thousand great arhats, even so—"
He recognized Piṇḍola. At that time, [the Master] waited for him to raise his eyebrows and said, "Do you understand? He then prostrated to him.
Not only did he recognize Piṇḍola, but he also participated as a fellow student with the ancient Buddha.
When the seer Viśvāmitra took Sudhana by the hand, Sudhana saw himself traveling to the abodes of Buddhas in as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in the ten directions,
even passing through unspeakably unspeakable numbers of eons as numerous as atoms.
When the seer released his hand, Sudhana immediately saw himself returned to his original location.
Sudhana visited fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Finally, he arrived before the pavilion of Maitreya and saw that the doors of the multi-storied tower were closed.

He gazed up at it with reverence and offered praise. Seeing Maitreya approaching from another direction, Sudhana prostrated and said, "I pray that the doors of this pavilion may open so that I may enter.
Immediately, Maitreya came before Sudhana and snapped his fingers once; the tower—
The gate of the pavilion opened; as soon as Sudhana had entered, the gate closed.
He saw hundreds of thousands of millions of pavilions, and within each pavilion stood a Maitreya leading his retinue, with a Sudhana standing before him.
Because of Wuzhuo’s question, “I wish to see Mañjuśrī; which one is he? Sudhana said, “If you give rise to a single thought of pure mind, that is he.
Wuzhuo said, “I have given rise to a single thought of pure mind; why do I not see him?
Sudhana said, “This is truly seeing Mañjuśrī.”
The Devaputra Sunirmita addressed Mañjuśrī, saying, "We should go together to the presence of the Tathāgata to seek resolution regarding what has not yet been received;
we shall likewise inquire and debate according to the Dharma at this very time. Mañjuśrī said, "Do not engage in conceptual discrimination or attachment toward the Tathāgata. The Devaputra said:
"Where is the Tathāgata now, so that I may not become attached to him? Mañjuśrī replied, "He is right before your eyes.
The Devaputra asked, "If this is so, why do I not see him? Mañjuśrī said, "If you do not see anything at all, this is called truly seeing the Tathāgata.
The Devaputra said, "If he is seen right before me, why do you admonish me not to grasp or be attached to the Tathāgata?"
Mañjuśrī said, "What do you see before you now? The devaputra replied, "There is the realm of empty space. Mañjuśrī said, "The Tathāgata is this realm of empty space;
the realm of empty space is itself the Tathāgata. Within this, there is not a single thing that can be conceptually distinguished."
Aṅgulimāla, while carrying his alms bowl, arrived at the house of an elder. He encountered a woman in difficult labor whose child and mother had not yet been separated.
The woman said, "Gautama’s disciple, you are considered a most holy one; what dharma do you possess that can deliver one from the hardships of childbirth?
Aṅgulimāla said to the elder, "I have only recently entered the Way and am not yet acquainted with this dharma. Wait until I return and ask the World-Honored One. He then departed.
He came to inform [the Buddha], and upon his return, he reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla, "Go quickly and tell her:
'Since I followed the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones, I have never killed a living being. Aṅgulimāla went and informed her; upon hearing this, the woman was immediately relieved of her burden.
A verse by Miaoxi says: Before the mountains of Huayin lies a hundred-foot well; Within it, cold spring water pierces the bones with its chill.
Whose daughter comes here to reflect her image? She does not look at anything else, but gazes at her tilted neck.
The King of the Yuezhi heard that in the kingdom of Kaśmīra there was a venerable one named Jīvaka, who possessed great renown.

He immediately set out for that country with his ministers to pay his respects, inquire about the Dharma, and offer his veneration. Having completed these acts of respect, he requested the venerable one to expound the teachings for him.
The Venerable One said, "Great King, it is good that you have come at this time. Know that when you depart now, it shall be as when you arrived.
The Kinnara King then performed music of non-arising (*anutpāda*) as an offering. The Buddha then commanded that both sentient and insentient beings should all follow the King;
if there were even a single thing that did not follow the King, it would not be permitted to go to the Buddha’s place.
King Anala entered the Great Samādhi of Tranquility and issued a decree that all sentient and insentient beings must obey him;
if there were even a single thing that did not obey the king, he would not be able to enter the Great Samādhi of Tranquility.
The Mara Śambara, leading his retinue, followed the Bodhisattva Vajrāgra for a thousand years, searching for the place where he had arisen but could not find it.
Suddenly, one day, he beheld him and asked: "Upon what do you rely for your dwelling? For a thousand years..."
When searching for the place where you arise, it cannot be found. Qi said: "I do not dwell by relying on dwelling; I do not dwell by relying on non-dwelling. I dwell in this manner."
Fayan said: "The Obstructing Demon King does not see the Diamond Boundary; that may be granted for now.
But as for the Diamond Boundary itself—does it see the Obstructing Demon King?"
To the east of the city there was an old woman who had been born at the same time as the Buddha, yet she did not wish to see him.
Every time she saw the Buddha approaching, she would immediately turn away to avoid him; nevertheless, wherever she looked toward the east or west, everywhere was the Buddha.
She then covered her face with her hands, but even within the palms of her ten fingers, it was all the Buddha.
The woman Āmrapālī asked Mañjuśrī, "If you clearly understand that birth is the principle of non-birth, for what reason are you still subject to the cycle of birth and death?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Because my power is not yet sufficient."
There was a village inhabited by a venomous dragon. At that time, five hundred venerable ones went there but were unable to subdue it.
A venerable one from another region merely snapped his fingers once, and the dragon was immediately subdued.
Langya Jue said: "If one were to rely on the scriptural vehicles, there would naturally be a formal classification and judgment. But I, this mountain monk, am not like that;
even this single snap of the fingers is unnecessary. Nevertheless, do not let the weary fish rest at the bamboo screens, nor the sluggish birds settle among the reeds."

The First Patriarch of the Western Heaven, Mahākāśyapa (three times): sharing his seat, transmitting the robe, witnessing the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, presiding over the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka, and expelling Ānanda for not yet having exhausted all outflows. Subsequently, at the Piṭhara Rock, before the Paṇḍava Stone...
The Master sat until midnight, at which time he attained the fruit of the Way. He immediately manifested supernatural powers and passed through a stone to enter [the cave].
Later, Kāśyapa transmitted the Eye of the Dharma to him and spoke this verse: "The dharmas are originally the Dharma; There is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
Why, within a single dharma, Should there be both dharma and non-dharma?"
A non-Buddhist asked, "What is this 'self of mine'? The Patriarch said, "The one who seeks the self is your self.
The non-Buddhist said, "This is my self; where is the master's self? The Patriarch said, "You ask me while seeking it."
While the Patriarch was treading in the mud, a śrāmaṇera asked him, "Venerable Sir, why do you do this yourself? The Patriarch replied, "If I do not do it myself, who will do it for me?"
Fayan said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have dragged him away to tread in the mud.
Regarding the Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda (three times): One day the Patriarch said to the Buddha, "Today I entered the city and saw a most extraordinary thing.
The Buddha asked, "What extraordinary thing did you see? The Patriarch replied, "As I was entering the city, I saw a troupe of musicians."
[The Buddha] performed a dance and left the city; [the Patriarch] saw that all were subject to impermanence. The Buddha said, "Yesterday when I entered the city, I also witnessed a remarkable event.
The Patriarch asked, "I do not know what remarkable event you witnessed. The Buddha said, "When I entered the city, I saw a group of musicians performing a dance;
when I left the city, I also saw a group of musicians performing a dance."
The Patriarch asked Kāśyapa, “Elder brother, besides the golden-brocade *kāṣāya* robe that the World-Honored One transmitted to you, what else did he transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, “Ānanda! The Patriarch responded, “Yes? Kāśyapa said, “Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate.”
Fenyang Shanzhao said, "If you do not ask, how can one know?
Cuiyan Zhi said, "A thousand-year-old tree without a shadow; a bottomless boot of the present age.

Since the Great Matter of the Patriarchs was accomplished, he went to the Changshui River, which transformed into a golden land, where he gathered the assembly of holy ones and looked upon those who had attained the Way.
The disciple Śāṇakavāsin was entrusted with the Eye of the True Dharma. He spoke a verse, saying: "The Dharma that was originally entrusted exists; Once entrusted, it is said to be non-existent.
Each must awaken to this for themselves; Upon awakening, there is neither existence nor non-existence."
The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śaṇavāsa (Section One), asked Upagupta, "How old are you? He replied, "I am seventeen years old.
The Patriarch said, "Is it your body that is seventeen, or is it your nature that is seventeen? He replied, "My teacher’s hair has already turned white;
is it his hair that is white, or is it his mind that is white? The Patriarch said, "It is only the hair that is white; it is not the mind that is white. [Upagupta] said, "As for my body..."
Seventeen. Non-nature Seventeen. The Patriarch knew he was a vessel for the Dharma and later transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, speaking this verse:
"Neither dharma nor mind; No mind and no dharma. When speaking of this mind-dharma, This dharma is not a mind-dharma."
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta (Part Two). The Patriarch visited a bhikṣuṇī; as soon as he entered the gate, he bumped and knocked over her alms bowl.
The bhikṣuṇī said, "In the days when the Buddha was alive, the group of six bhikṣus were extremely coarse in their conduct.
Even when they came to my quarters frequently, they did not behave like this. You are one who has succeeded to the Patriarchal position; how can you act with such coarseness?"
Fenyang Shanzhao said: "I already know this is an error.

When the Patriarch preached the Dharma to save sentient beings, his tally sticks filled the stone chamber. There was the son of an elder named Zhongxiang, who left home to become a monk under the Patriarch."
The Patriarch asked, "Do you leave home with your mind, or do you leave home with your body? He replied, "I leave home as neither mind nor body.

The Patriarch said, "If it is for neither mind nor body, then who is it that leaves home? He replied, "As for leaving home, because there is no self or 'mine,' the mind is neither born nor extinguished.
That the mind is neither born nor extinguished is itself the eternal Way; therefore, the Buddhas are also eternal. The mind has no form or appearance."

The nature of his body was likewise so. The Patriarch said, "You shall attain great enlightenment; your mind will naturally penetrate through. He then performed the tonsure for him and changed his name to Dīpamkara.
He subsequently entrusted him with the Eye of the Dharma and spoke this verse: "The mind is itself the original mind; The original mind is not a dharma that exists.
If there were dharmas, there would be an original mind; But since it is neither mind nor dharma, it is the fundamental reality."
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Tīṭibha (1): There was one named Mucilinda who, upon seeing the Master’s compassionate countenance, immediately awakened to his past causes.
He then abandoned his immortal arts to seek the fruit of sainthood. He questioned the Patriarch, saying, "In the Way of the Immortals, I have made no further progress;

I merely maintain emptiness and stillness, yet I do not penetrate the ultimate principle. The Patriarch said, "The Buddha taught that those who cultivate immortality revere and study only the minor path."
"It is like being pulled by a rope; you may know this for yourself. If you abandon the small stream and suddenly return to the great ocean, you shall realize the Unborn.
Upon hearing these words, Mīchaka attained sudden and profound enlightenment. Later, when he was entrusted with the Dharma-eye, he spoke this verse:
"Having penetrated the mind of the fundamental Dharma, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Awakening is the same as non-awakening; even without awakening, there is no dharma."
The Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Mīchaka (one instance), was transforming through the Way in Northern India.
There was one named Vasumitra who, carrying a wine vessel in his hand, met him and asked, "From where do you come, Master? Where do you wish to go? The Patriarch replied, "I come from my own mind."
The Master said, "Where do you wish to go? He asked, "Does the Master recognize the object in my hand? The Patriarch said, "This is a vessel for contact, yet it carries purity.
He asked, "Do you still recognize me? The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize you; if I were to recognize you, I would no longer be myself.
You should state your name, and later I will show you your original cause. He replied, "My surname is Bharadvāja and my given name is Vāsūmitra. The Patriarch said, "Buddha..."

"I record you: you shall succeed to the ancestral position. He immediately granted him the tonsure and ordination, whereupon [the recipient] suddenly awakened to his past causes. Later, he transmitted the Dharma-eye and spoke this verse:
"No mind, nothing to be said; If one speaks, it is not called the Dharma. If one realizes that mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand the mind and its dharmas."

The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra (one fascicle), traveled through various kingdoms, preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings. There was a man of wisdom who called himself Buddhanandi;
he said to the Patriarch, "I wish to debate the meaning of the teachings with you. The Patriarch replied, "If it is the meaning, there is no debate; if there is debate, it is not the meaning.
If you intend to debate the meaning, in the end it will not be a discussion of the meaning. At these words, Buddhanandi immediately awakened to his original mind.
He entered the monastic order under National Teacher Touzi and later received the Dharma-eye from him. He then spoke this verse: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space;
It manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When the realization of empty space is attained, There is neither 'is' nor 'non-is'."
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi (1): His wisdom was as deep as a vast abyss, and his swift eloquence was unimpeded.
A man named Upagupta paid him homage and asked: "If parents are not my kin, who is the most intimate kin?
If the Buddhas are not my Way, who is the ultimate Way? The Patriarch replied: "That which you speak of is more intimate than the mind; it cannot be compared even to one's parents."
"Your practice accords with the Way; the minds of all Buddhas are identical to yours. To seek externally for a Buddha with form is not compatible with you.
If you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate. Upon hearing these verses, Vovada suddenly awakened to the principles of the Buddha.
The Patriarch conferred ordination upon him and subsequently transmitted the Dharma-eye, saying in verse: "Space has no interior or exterior; the nature of the mind is likewise so."
It is so. Because he thoroughly comprehended empty space, he attained the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra (1), from birth until fifty years of age, sat upon a single mat;

his mouth never spoke, and his feet never trod the ground. Upon hearing a verse, he awakened to the Way and transmitted the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. There was one named Nansheng who... [sought refuge].

The Master left the household life and sat perpetually without reclining. He attained thorough penetration of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). The Patriarch entrusted him with the Eye of the Dharma and spoke this verse:
"The True Principle is originally nameless; Through names, the True Principle is revealed. Having received the most authentic Dharma, It is neither true nor false."
The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta (one instance): He remained in the womb for sixty years. A divine pearl manifested as a response in a dream.

On the day of his birth, the entire room was filled with radiance. Having left the household life and attained the Way, he arrived at a forest grove where a man named Pūrṇayaśas stood before him, reverently joining his palms.
The Patriarch asked, "From where have you come? He replied, "My mind does not go anywhere. The Patriarch said, "You..."
[The student] asked, "Where do you dwell? [He replied], "I say my mind does not abide. The Patriarch said, "Are you not settled? [He replied], "All Buddhas are likewise.

The Patriarch said, "You are not the Buddhas. [He replied], "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas]. The Patriarch knew he was a vessel for the Dharma and immediately granted him the tonsure and ordination.

He transmitted the Dharma and spoke this verse: "The true essence is naturally true; Because it is true, there is the principle of explanation. Having realized the Dharma of true truth, There is no..."
Practice also has no cessation.
*Lian deng hui yao*, Scroll One;
*Lian deng hui yao*, Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Chan monk Wuming, a successor to the patriarchs at Suilue Sui Fu Chan Temple:
The Eleventh Indian Patriarch, Venerable Pūrṇāśa (Funa Yeshi). (One scroll) He traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. There was the Great Master Aśvaghoṣa...

The layman went to meet the Patriarch and paid his respects, asking, "I wish to recognize the Buddha; what is it that is the Buddha? The Patriarch said, "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, it is that which does not recognize.
The layman asked, "Since I do not recognize the Buddha, how can I know that it is so? The Patriarch replied, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha," [it is precisely that which does not recognize].
"How do you know it is not so? [Bodhidharma] said, "This is the meaning of the saw. The Patriarch said, "That is the meaning of the wood. The Patriarch asked again, "What is the meaning of the saw?

He replied, "It emerges level with the Master. Bodhidharma then asked, "What is the meaning of the wood? The Patriarch said, "You have been cut down by me. At these words, Aśvaghoṣa attained sudden and great enlightenment. Later, he was entrusted with the Dharma-eye and spoke this verse:

"Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; The nature of the mind is neither deluded nor awakened. When the mirror of wisdom is polished bright, All phenomena are seen as they truly are."
Light and darkness are inseparable; now I entrust you with the Dharma of concealment and manifestation. It is neither one nor two.

(One) After the Twelfth Patriarch, the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa, had attained the Dharma, there was in the city of Pāṭaliputra one Kambala who possessed great supernatural powers and a retinue of three thousand followers. The Patriarch asked him: "Exert all your supernatural powers and manifest transformations."

[The disciple] asked, "If so, I could transform the great ocean; that would be a very minor matter. The Patriarch said, "Can you transform the ocean of nature (xinghai)? He asked, "What is meant by the 'ocean of nature'?
[The disciple] replied, "I have never known it. The Patriarch said, "As for the ocean of nature: the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all depend upon it for their establishment.
The three samādhis and the six supernormal powers are manifested from it. Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāra realized his own fundamental nature.

Xin, together with three thousand disciples, left home to follow the Patriarch. Later, he was entrusted with the Dharma-eye, and the Patriarch spoke this verse: "Concealment and manifestation are the fundamental Dharma;
light and darkness are originally non-dual. Now I entrust you with the Dharma of complete awakening—it is neither grasped nor abandoned."
The Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāṇadeva (1): Originally he practiced the non-Buddhist paths, but later turned his heart toward the Buddha-vehicle.

While traveling through Western India, he arrived at a deep mountain where the Venerable Nāgārjuna came out to meet him. He asked the Patriarch, "This deep mountain is solitary and desolate, inhabited by snakes and pythons.
Great Virtue, why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet to come here? The Patriarch replied, "I am not one who seeks supreme honor; I have come..."
He went to visit the Sage. Nāgārjuna thought silently to himself: "Has this master attained the definitive nature and the eye of clear insight?
Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle? The Patriarch said: "Though you speak with your mind, I already know your intent. Simply prepare for the renunciation of the household life;
why worry that I am not a sage? Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. The Patriarch granted him the tonsure and later transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, speaking this verse:

It is said: "The dharma that is neither hidden nor manifest is called the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). To awaken to this dharma of the hidden and the manifest is to be neither foolish nor wise.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Nāgārjuna, possessed great knowledge and vision, was unimpeded in all matters, and traveled through Western India.

He went to the country of P'o. The people there mostly believed in meritorious deeds. Upon hearing the Venerable One preach the sublime Dharma, they said to one another, "The meritorious deeds of humans are supreme in this world;
as for the Buddha-nature, it is merely a word— who can perceive it? The Patriarch said, "If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your pride.
The assembly asked, "Is the Buddha-nature large or small? The Patriarch replied, "It is neither large nor small."

Neither broad nor narrow; without merit and without retribution; neither dying nor being born. Having heard this superior principle, they all returned to their original resolve and realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
There was one named Kanadeva who visited the Patriarch. The Patriarch, knowing him to be a man of wisdom, first ordered an attendant to fill a bowl with water and place it before his seat.
Kanadeva took a single needle and advanced to cast it into the water, whereupon he joyfully attained accord with the truth.
Later, he transmitted the Dharma-eye to Huì and spoke this verse: "To clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, I have now explained the logic of liberation.
Regarding the Dharma, the mind does not realize it; There is neither anger nor joy."
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva (Part One). Widely learned and possessed of discerning wisdom, his fame spread throughout many kingdoms.
Later, while traveling through the city of Pāṭaliputra, he heard that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma; they had been plotting this for some time.
The Patriarch took up a long banner and entered their assembly. They said, "Why do you not come forward? The Patriarch replied, "Why do you not stay behind? They said, "You..."
[The monk] said, "I am like a thief. The Patriarch said, "You are like a good person. [The monk] asked, "What Dharma do you understand?

The Patriarch said, "You do not understand a hundred things. [The monk] said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood. The Patriarch said, "I say you will certainly attain Buddhahood. [The monk] said, "It is not right for you to attain it.
The Patriarch said, "Originally I said I would attain it; you truly have not attained it. [The monk] said, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have? The Patriarch said, "You have..."
"It is because of me that [the Dharma] could not be obtained. Since I am without self, I shall obtain it myself.
When he was thus reduced to silence, the other asked, "What is your name? The Patriarch replied, "My name is Kanadeva.

Among that assembly was the leader Rāhulabhadra, who, upon hearing these words, repented his errors and attained immediate awakening. The Patriarch transmitted the Eye of the Dharma to him and spoke this verse: "Fundamentally..."
To those who transmit the Dharma, he expounds the principle of liberation; yet regarding the reality of the Dharma, there is no realization—neither end nor beginning.
The Sixteenth Patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata (1), after attaining the Dharma, benefited sentient beings wherever he went.
Upon reaching the city of Śrāvastī, at the source of the Golden Water River, he saw Saṃghanandin entering meditative absorption. The Patriarch waited for him for seven days.
Just as he was rising from meditative absorption, the Patriarch asked him, "Is your body in absorption, or is your mind in absorption? He replied, "Both my body and mind are in absorption.
The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind are in absorption, what is there to enter or exit? He replied, "Although there is entering and exiting, it does not lose the characteristic of absorption.
It is like gold in a well, or gold taken out of a well; though worldly phenomena come and go, the essence of the gold remains eternally still. The Patriarch said, "If the gold is in [the well]..."

The Well. If gold comes out of a well, the gold itself has neither movement nor stillness; how could there be coming and going? If one says that the gold moves or is still, what is it that comes and goes?
If one speaks of the gold coming and going, the gold is not moving or still. The Patriarch said: "If the gold is in the well, what is this gold that comes out?"
"If gold comes out of the well, what remains? If you say that when the gold comes out of the well, what remains is not gold;
and if the gold remains in the well, what came out is not the object," the Master said, "This interpretation is not so. [The other] said, "That principle is not established.

The Master said, "This interpretation must fall. [The other] said, "That meaning is not accomplished. The Master said, "That meaning is not accomplished; my meaning is accomplished. [The other] said, "My meaning..."
"Even though it is established, the dharma is not the self. The Patriarch said, "The meaning of 'self' is already established, because the self is non-self.

[The monk] asked, "If the self is non-self, what further meaning is established? The Patriarch said, "Because the self is non-self, your own position is thereby established. [The monk] asked, "Whom do you, O Virtuous One, take as your teacher?"
[The Master] attained this non-self (*anātman*). The Patriarch said: "My teacher, Kāṇadeva, realized this non-self.
Saṃghanandin praised him with a verse, saying: "I bow my head to Teacher Deva, Who has emerged from you, O Benevolent One.
Because you, O Benevolent One, are without self, I desire to take you as my teacher. The Patriarch replied with a verse: "Since I am already without self, You must see my self. You..."
If you take me as your teacher, you will know that "I" is neither self nor non-self. At this, Nandi suddenly attained sudden enlightenment and immediately requested ordination.

Later, [the Master] transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, saying in verse: "In the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; Neither grasped nor abandoned. The Dharma has no marks of existence or non-existence;
How could it arise internally or externally?"
The Seventeenth Patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin (Part One), was the son of King Ratnavyuha.
Once, while visiting a mountain hermitage, he saw a young boy holding a round mirror in his hand who went straight before the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "How old are you?"

[The monk] said, "I am now one hundred years old. The Patriarch said, "Your age is still young; why do you say you are a hundred? That is not reasonable. [The monk] said, "I do not understand the principle;
I am truly a hundred years old. The Patriarch said, "Are you skilled in the kōan? [The monk] said, "The Buddha said:
'If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not understand the kōan of the Buddhas, it would be better to live for a single day and attain decisive realization. The Patriarch said, "You..."
"What does this object in my hand signify? he asked. [The master] replied, "It represents the great perfect mirror of all Buddhas, which is without flaw or obscuration within or without.
Two people can see it together; the eye of the mind is identical for both. Thereupon, he entered the monastic order under the Patriarch and was named Gayāśata.

He was then assigned to serve him. One day, the wind blew against the corner of the hall and the bell rang. The Patriarch asked, "Is it the wind that makes the sound, or is it the bell? [Gayāśata] replied, "Neither."

The wind chimes rang. [Nanquan] said, "It is my own mind that rings. The Master asked, "And who is it that possesses this mind? He replied, "Because all things are utterly tranquil. The Master said, "Excellent, excellent! Who else but you could succeed to my Way? He then transmitted the Dharma-eye to him and spoke this verse: The wind chimes ring; My mind rings too.
