The mind-ground is fundamentally without birth; the ground arises from conditions. Condition and seed do not obstruct one another; so too it is with flower and fruit.
After the Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayāsata (one instance), attained the Dharma, he traveled extensively through various kingdoms.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Mahāśaka, he saw the house of a Brahmin. As the Patriarch was about to enter the gate, the master of the house, Kumāralata—

The questioner asked, "Whose followers are you? The Master replied, "We are the followers of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, his spirit was struck with awe, and he immediately closed his door.
After a long while, the Master knocked on the door. The man said, "There is no one in this house. The Master asked, "Who is it that answers 'there is no one'?"

Upon hearing these words, he was moved; he opened his door to welcome him and, with sincere devotion, left the household life. Later, [the master] transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, speaking this verse:
"When there is a seed and the ground of the mind, Through causes and conditions, a sprout can emerge. If one does not obstruct the conditions, Then birth will arise, yet ultimately remain unborn."
The Nineteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata (one instance): He was a lord of the Īśvara Heaven. When the time arrived for him to succeed to the Patriarchate, he descended to be born among humans.
After he had attained the Dharma, he went to the kingdom of Central India. There was one named Jayata who asked:

"My family has long been devoted to the Triple Gem, yet we are constantly beset by illness and suffering. Our neighbors, the Caṇḍālas, achieve all their desires as they wish. How can they be so fortunate?"
"But what fault have I committed? Zu said, "Why is there any need for doubt? Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil occurs across three periods.

Ordinary people see only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious meet with good fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune; they then claim there is no causality and that merit and retribution are empty.
Little do they realize that like and shadow follow one another, without the slightest deviation. Even through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, this never perishes. At that time, the Kṣānti...
Yatuo, upon hearing these words, his doubts were instantly dispelled. He was further told:

"You have already gained faith in the three karmas, yet you do not yet understand that karma arises from delusion, delusion exists because of consciousness, and consciousness depends upon non-awakening (abodhi). Non-awakening depends upon the mind. The mind is fundamentally pure;
it is without birth or extinction, without creation or action, without retribution or response, and without victory or defeat. It is profoundly still and luminously aware."
"If you enter this Dharma-gate, you shall be equal to all Buddhas. All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions.
At these words, he suddenly realized non-arising (*anutpāda*). Later, when the Dharma-eye was transmitted to him, he spoke this verse:

"In the fundamental nature, there is originally no arising; It is spoken only in response to those who seek it. Since nothing can be attained within the Dharma, Why harbor doubts about being resolved or not?"
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Jayata (one entry). The patriarch was in the city of Rājagṛha, where he extensively promoted the Buddha’s work and expounded the teachings of the Sudden Dharma.

Among his disciples, there was a particular fondness for debate. There was a chief disciple named Vasiṣṭha who ate but once a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods of the day;
he was pure, free from desire, and held in high esteem by the assembly. The patriarch wished to deliver him.
He questioned the assembly, saying, "This Ubhaka-Kaccāyana practices the dhūta austerities and diligently cultivates the pure conduct;
can he attain Buddhahood? The assembly replied, "Our teacher is so diligent; why should he not attain it? The Patriarch said, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way.
Even if he were to practice asceticism for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it would all be the root of delusion. The assembly asked, "What virtues does the Venerable One possess?"
[The monk] slandered my Master. The Patriarch said: "I do not seek the Way, nor am I inverted.
I do not eat only one meal a day, nor do I eat mixed foods. I am not content, nor am I greedy. My mind has no expectations; this is what is called the Way.
When Biexing heard these words, he gave rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). After a short while, the Patriarch asked him again: "Just now, when I was addressing the assembly..."

"To have been humiliated by a benevolent person—could this not cause distress? Since I have been reproaching myself and repenting my transgressions, even when hearing harsh words from others, they have been like the wind or an echo;

how much more so now that I have obtained the drinking of the unsurpassed nectar of immortality—would I instead give rise to feverish affliction? I only pray, O Great Being, [to grant me your compassion]."

He instructed him with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said, "You have long planted the roots of virtue; you shall succeed to my lineage. Later, he transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, speaking this verse:
"Under these words, one accords with non-arising, Identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can understand in this way, One will fully penetrate both principle and phenomena."

The Twenty-first Patriarch, Vasiṣṭha (one fascicle): Having received a prediction while in the womb that he would surely become a lamp for the world, he practiced asceticism from birth and realized the fruit of the Way.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Nādikā, there was a son of the king named Maṇḍara who entered the patriarch’s order as a renunciant.
He attained great supernormal powers and suddenly awakened to the essence of the mind. As he was to succeed the patriarch, the Dharma-eye was transmitted to him. And...
A verse was spoken: "Bubbles and illusions are equally unimpeded; why do you not awaken to this? To penetrate the Dharma within it is neither of this age nor of antiquity.
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Maṇḍara (1), renounced the pleasures of the royal palace, left the household life, and realized the Way. He went...
In the country of Yuezhi, there was one named Helena who asked, "Why are the dragon sons so wise, while the flock of cranes is so deluded?

The Patriarch explained their past causes and conditions to him, and his mind immediately attained awakening. He then asked, "What karma should I now cultivate so that this flock of cranes may be transformed and attain human bodies?
The Patriarch replied, "The Buddha possesses the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure, which has been transmitted from one to another; I now entrust it to you. Spread it widely."
He delivered sentient beings. Through this, the assembly of cranes attained liberation. Later, he transmitted the Dharma-eye and spoke a verse, saying:
"The mind turns according to the myriad objects; In the place where it turns, reality is profoundly subtle. If one recognizes one's nature while following the flow, There is neither joy nor sorrow."
The Twenty-third Patriarch, Venerable Hòulènná (one fascicle). At the time of his birth, heavenly flowers scattered in brilliant colors and golden coins were spread upon the ground.

He was taken in and raised within the royal palace, where he extensively manifested miraculous transformations. Later, he arrived in Central India. There was a bhikṣu named Siṃha who asked: "I wish to seek the Way;
how should I apply my mind? The Patriarch said: "If you wish to seek the Way, there is no place for the mind to be applied. [The bhikṣu] said:
"If there is no application of mind, who performs the Buddha-work? The Patriarch said, "If you apply your mind, it is not a meritorious deed;
if you are without fabrication, that itself is the Buddha-work. As the Sūtra says: "The meritorious deeds I have performed are without the notion of 'mine'.
Upon hearing this, Siṃha immediately entered the Buddha-wisdom. The Patriarch transmitted the Dharma-eye to him and spoke this verse: "When the ground of the mind is recognized..."
He spoke of the inconceivable; it is utterly ungraspable. When it is attained, one does not speak of knowing it.
(Three times total) The twenty-fourth patriarch, Master Siṃha, arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra. He asked the master of dhyāna, Dharmada, saying:
"Virtuous one, you practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*); from where have you come here? Now that you have arrived here, why do you say you practice concentration? [Dharmada] replied: "I..."
"Although I have come here, my mind remains undisturbed. Concentration (samādhi) follows one's cultivation; how could it depend on a particular location?

The Patriarch said, "Since you, O worthy one, have come, your concentration has also arrived. Since it has no fixed location, how could it depend on personal cultivation? You say that concentration cultivates the person, rather than the person cultivating concentration.
Although I have come here, my concentration is constantly cultivated. The Patriarch said, "It is not that the person cultivates concentration; rather, concentration cultivates the person."
When you come here of your own accord, what state of concentration (*samādhi*) do you practice? [The Master] says: "It is like a pure, bright pearl, with no obscurations inside or out.

If one penetrates concentration, it must necessarily be like this. The Patriarch said: "If one penetrates concentration, it is just like a bright pearl. Now that I see you, you are not of the 'pearl' type. [The Master] said:
"Since the pearl is clear and transparent, both inside and out are entirely settled; my mind is undisturbed, just like this purity."
The Patriarch said, "That pearl has neither interior nor exterior; how can you, O worthy one, determine it? Impure things do not cause it to waver;
this concentration is not of the nature of purity. Upon hearing these words, his mind became clear and radiant.
One day, the Patriarch encountered an elder who led his son before him and asked, "This boy is named Vashistha.
At birth, he clenched his left hand in a fist; though he has now grown to adulthood, he is still unable to open it. I pray that the Venerable One will reveal the karmic cause from his past life.
The Patriarch gazed at him intently and then said, "Give me back my pearl. The boy immediately opened his fist and presented the pearl. The assembly was amazed.
Everyone was struck with wonder. Sengzhu said, "In my previous life, I was a monk who attended a vegetarian feast for the Dragon King of the Western Sea and received this pearl as an offering.
I have now returned it to the pearl to this youth, Vasiṣṭha; this is but natural. The elder may now give up his son."
Having left the household life and received ordination, the Patriarch was about to repay his karmic debts from past lives and thus entrusted the Mind-Dharma to him, speaking this verse:
"When one speaks of knowing and seeing, knowing and seeing are themselves the mind. When the mind is present, there is knowing and seeing; knowing and seeing are right here and now."
In Kaśmīra, there were two non-Buddhist practitioners who studied various magical arts and falsely claimed to be śrāmaṇeras.

They broke into the royal palace, but when their treachery was exposed, the King of Kaśmīra grew enraged and destroyed the monasteries. He then personally took up a sword and asked the Patriarch, "Have you realized the emptiness of the aggregates?

The Patriarch replied, "I have realized the emptiness of the aggregates. The King asked, "Have you transcended birth and death? The Patriarch replied, "I have transcended birth and death. The King said:
"You may give me your head. The Patriarch said, "The body is not mine; how much less so my head? The king then brandished his blade, whereupon white milk surged up more than a zhang high.
The king's right arm also fell to the ground immediately, and he died seven days later.
Xuansha said, "The Great Master Śāriputra did not even know how to take charge of his own head.
Xuedou said, "A master sovereign has a natural presence."
The Twenty-fifth Patriarch, Venerable Vasishṭha (in two parts). His mother dreamed of a divine sword; upon waking, she became pregnant.
Once born, he encountered the Venerable Siṃha, who revealed his past causes and secretly transmitted the Mind-Seal to him.

When he arrived in the kingdom of South India, the King of Central India, named Kṛṣṇa, established rites of worship and made offerings to him. There was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Nairātmya who served as the king’s [advisor].

He was deeply envious of the Patriarch. Thereupon, before the King, he said to the Patriarch: "I shall debate with you in silence, without resorting to words. The Patriarch asked, "Who will know who has won or lost?
He replied, "We do not contend for victory or defeat; we seek only the meaning. The Patriarch asked, "What do you take to be 'meaning'? He replied, "I take 'no-mind' (amūrchā) to be the meaning.

The Patriarch said, "Since you have no mind, how can you obtain its meaning? He replied: *Note: This excerpt is from the famous encounter between Bodhidharma and the Emperor Wu of Liang, recorded in the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*.*
I say "no-mind" (wúxīn); this should be called "not meaning" (fēiyì). The Patriarch said: "You say 'no-mind'; this should be called 'not meaning. I say 'not mind' (fēixīn);
this is 'meaning' (yì) and not 'name' (míng). He asked: "'Meaning and not name'—who can discern the meaning? The Patriarch said:

"Your 'name is not meaning'—what name is this name? He replied: "It is for the purpose of discerning what is not meaning; thus it is called 'the nameless name' (wúmíng). The Patriarch said: "If the name is already not a name..."
"Principle is also not principle. "Who is this debater? What is it that should be debated? Thus they exchanged words fifty-nine times, until the non-Buddhist was silenced and submitted in faith.

Bajiao said: "It is like an elephant or a horse that is unruly and difficult to tame; only when subjected to various forms of pain and torment that penetrate to the very bone will it finally be subdued.
Dayang Yan said: "The clam and the heron hold each other fast, yet both fall into the hands of the fisherman.
Miaoxi said: "Venerable sir, why use such elaborate words? Wait for him to say, 'Please, Master, remain silent.'"
The Master did not rely on verbal explanation, but simply said, "The meaning has been realized.
Because Prince Amṛtodana of South India had come to the Master to seek ordination, the Master asked, "For what purpose do you seek ordination?
He replied, "I seek ordination for the sake of performing the Buddha’s work. The Master sighed and said, "Prince..."
When the Deva of Wisdom arrived, it was surely because various sages had descended to manifest their traces; he immediately received [the transmission], shaved his hair, and took full ordination.

The Dharma-eye treasury was entrusted to him, and a verse was spoken: "The Sages speak of knowledge and vision; within the objective realm, there is nothing that is not thus. I have now awakened to the true nature."
There was neither worldly path nor principle.
The twenty-sixth patriarch, Vajramitra (one instance), renounced his status as a crown prince to transmit the Dharma and save sentient beings.
Upon arriving in Eastern India, there was the son of a Brahmin who wandered through the streets and alleys without ever staying in one place.
The Patriarch asked him, "Why do you travel so fast? He replied, "Why does the Master travel so slowly? The Patriarch asked, "What is your surname now? He replied, "It is the same as the Master's.
The Patriarch asked, "Do you remember past events? He replied, "I recall that in distant kalpas, I lived together with the Master. The Patriarch said, "Together..."
"For what reason? [The Master] replied, "The Master is expounding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and I am turning the profound *Sūtra*.

The Patriarch said, "What you have discussed today deeply accords with your past causes. You are indeed the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. He immediately ordained him as a monk and named him Prajñātara.
Later, he transmitted the Dharma-eye to him and spoke this verse: "The treasury of the true nature within the mind-ground, Without head and without..."
He was without a tail. Adapting to conditions to transform sentient beings, his skillful means were termed "wisdom.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra (in two parts): Having already attained the Dharma, he traveled to South India.
King Xiangzhi venerated the Buddha-vehicle and honored it with offerings. He bestowed a priceless jewel upon his grandfather. The king had three sons;
taking the jewel he had received, the grandfather asked the three princes, "This jewel is perfectly bright;
is there anything that can equal it? The first and second princes both replied, "Among the seven treasures, this is the most honored; certainly nothing surpasses it."
The third prince said, "Bodhitāra, this is a worldly treasure, yet it is not the supreme one; among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme.
This is a worldly light, yet it is not the supreme one; among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This is a worldly radiance, yet it is not the supreme one; among all radiances, the radiance of the mind is supreme. [He spoke thus regarding] the luster of this jewel.

Brightness cannot illuminate itself; it must rely upon the light of wisdom to discern it. Once it has been discerned, one knows it is a pearl; once it is known to be a pearl, one recognizes its value as a treasure.
If the treasure were not recognized as such by itself, it would not be a treasure; if the pearl were not discerned by itself, it would not be a pearl.
One must rely upon the "wisdom-pearl" to discern the worldly pearl. If the treasure were not a treasure by itself, it must rely upon wisdom—

"O Jewel! By means of the Dharma-jewel, you illuminate it. Thus, when the Master possesses the Way, his jewels manifest of themselves; when sentient beings possess the Way, their mental jewels are likewise so.
The Venerable One marveled at his eloquence and wisdom, finding none who could equal him."
The Patriarch asked again: "Among all things, what thing is formless? He replied: "Among all things, non-arising is formless. The Patriarch said:
"Among all things, what thing is highest? He replied: "Among all things, the self (ātman) is highest. The Patriarch said:
"Among all things, what thing is greatest? He replied: "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is greatest. The Patriarch knew [he had understood].
He was a vessel for the Dharma. Consequently, he received the full precepts of renunciation and was entrusted with the True Eye of the Dharma, whereupon [the Master] spoke this verse:
"The seeds produced within the ground of the mind, Through conditions, give rise once more to principle. When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; When the flower blooms, the world arises."
Miaoxi said: "The reasoning you have articulated is excellent. Take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The Twenty-eighth Patriarch, Bodhidharma (13): He was the third son of the King of Southern India.

Because of his ability to resolve doctrinal disputes with his pearl-like eloquence, he was revered and submitted to by all. In his native land, there were two masters: one named Buddhajaya and the other named Buddhabhadra.
The Great Radiance was titled the Two Gates of Ambrosia (*amṛta*). His great and eminent disciples divided into six schools: first, the School of Phenomenal Marks; second, the School of Non-Marks;
third, the School of Samādhi and Prajñā; fourth, the School of Preceptual Practice; fifth, the School of Non-Attainment; and sixth, the School of Quiescence.
Each adhered firmly to their own understanding and propagated their teachings to many followers.
The Patriarch asked a follower of the Saṃlakṣaṇika school, "Regarding all dharmas, what is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?
Among the assembly was a leader named Sarvarā who replied, "Among all marks, that which does not intermingle with other marks is called the true mark.
The Patriarch said, "If all marks do not intermingle and this is called the true mark, by what means would you establish it? [Tell me] regarding these various marks..."

"In truth, there is no fixed [nature]. If all characteristics were fixed, how could they be called 'real'? The Patriarch said, "The fact that all characteristics are not fixed is precisely what is called the 'Real Characteristic' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
You are currently not fixed; how then can you attain it? [The monk] said, "When I say 'not fixed,' I am not speaking of characteristics;

I am speaking of the characteristics themselves, and their meaning is likewise so. The Patriarch said, "Your statement that 'it is not fixed' should itself be the Real Characteristic. Whether fixed or not fixed—"
Therefore, it is not the true mark (*dharmatā*). Since that which is fixed is not fixed, it is not the true mark. Because one knows "I am not," it is neither fixed nor changing. The Patriarch said:
"If you are now unchanging, how can it be called the true mark? That which has already changed and passed away is likewise so."
[The Master] said, "If it were unchanging, it would have to exist; because it both exists and does not exist, it changes its true nature (*dharmatā*). This is used to determine its meaning.
The Patriarch said, "If the true nature were unchanging, then change would not be real. Within the realm of existence and non-existence, what could be called the true nature?

Sāvala understood that his teacher’s profound understanding reached deep into the mysteries. Pointing to the sky with his finger, he said, "This is the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*); yet it is also capable of being empty."
"You should know whether this body can be made to resemble that," he asked. The Patriarch replied, "If you understand the true mark (*dharmatā*), you will see that it is not a mark.
If you realize it is not a mark, its form is likewise so. Within form, do not lose the essence of form; within the absence of marks, do not be obstructed by existence.
If you understand in this way, this is called the true mark. When the assembly heard this, their minds became clear and bright.

The Patriarch asked the followers of the Formless School (Wuxiang Zong), saying, "You speak of the formless; by what do you realize it? Among that assembly was one named Pratītya, who replied, "I clearly perceive the formless because the mind does not manifest.
The Patriarch said, "If your mind does not manifest, by what means do you clearly perceive it? He replied, "I clearly perceive the formless because the mind neither grasps nor rejects.
At the very moment of this clear perception, there is also no one who 'should' perceive. The Patriarch said: [The Patriarch said: "... (The text continues with the Patriarch's further instruction.)
Regarding existence and non-existence, the mind neither grasps nor rejects; furthermore, there is no one who shall attain them, for all luminous wisdoms are absent. He said:
"Even when entering the Buddha-samādhi, there is nothing to be attained, let alone desiring to know the signless. The Patriarch said: "Since the sign is not known," [how can it be realized?]

Who says there is existence or non-existence? Since even that which is attained does not exist, what can be called *samādhi*? When I say I do not realize it, it is because realization has nothing to be realized;
it is not [ordinary] *samādhi*, therefore I speak of *samādhi*. The Patriarch said: "If it is not *samādhi*, how can it be named?
Since you do not realize it, what is there to be realized in this 'non-realization'? Upon hearing the Patriarch’s analysis, Pratibhānu immediately awakened to his original mind.
The Patriarch asked Zongding Hui: "In your study of concentration and wisdom, are they one or two? A man from the assembly named Póluántu replied:
"This concentration and wisdom of mine are neither one nor two. The Patriarch said: "Since they are neither one nor two, why call them concentration and wisdom?"

It is said that concentration is neither fixed nor non-fixed; wisdom is neither wisdom nor non-wisdom. One is not one, and two is not two. The Patriarch said: "When it is one, it is not one; when it is two, it is not two.
Since it is neither fixed concentration nor wisdom, by what means could concentration and wisdom be defined? It is said: "Neither one nor two."
"Concentration and wisdom can know; that which is neither concentration nor wisdom is likewise so. The Patriarch said, "Because wisdom is not concentration, how then can it be known?
Neither one nor two—who is concentrated and who is wise? Having heard this, Bharadvāja’s doubts were suddenly dispelled.
The Patriarch asked Jie Xingzong, "What is called 'precept' (jie)? What is called 'practice' (xing)? Regarding these precepts and practices, are they one or two?
Among that assembly was a worthy man who replied, "'One-two' and 'two-one'—both are produced from them. To rely on the teachings without defilement is what is called precept and practice.
The Patriarch said, "Your statement that one 'relies on the teachings' is itself defiled. Both 'one' and 'two' are thus violated. Why?"
Regarding the reliance on teachings: these two [aspects] are contradictory and do not reach the level of practice; being neither clear internally nor externally, how can they be called precepts?

To say "I have internal and external" is something he has already fully understood. Once one attains such thorough penetration, that itself constitutes the practice of the precepts. If one speaks of contradiction, [it is only in relation to this].
"Both 'is' and 'is not' are spoken of as being pure; this is both precept and practice. The Patriarch said, "If it is both 'is' and 'is not,' how can it be called pure?
Since one has attained penetration, why speak of internal and external? Upon hearing this, the worthy man immediately felt ashamed and submitted.
The Patriarch asked Wude Zong, "You speak of 'non-attainment. What is attained through non-attainment? Since there is nothing to be attained, there is also no attainment of attainment.
A man named Baojing from that assembly replied, "When I speak of non-attainment, it is not the attainment of non-attainment.

It should be called the attainment of attainment; non-attainment is itself attainment. The Patriarch said, "If you have already attained non-attainment, then attainment is also not attainment. Since you say it is the attainment of attainment—"

"What is obtained by the 'obtainment of obtainment'? How can one see that which is both obtainment and non-obtainment? Non-obtainment is itself obtainment; if one sees it as non-obtainment, this is called the 'obtainment of obtainment. The Patriarch said:
'Since obtainment is already non-obtainment, the obtainment of obtainment is non-obtainment. Since there is nothing to be obtained, what could possibly be obtained?
Upon hearing this, Baojing was suddenly freed from the net of doubt."
The Patriarch asked Jijingzong, "What is meant by 'quiescence'? Among all phenomena, what is quiescent and what is tranquil?
He replied, "This mind is unmoving; this is called quiescence. To be unstained by phenomena is called tranquility."

The Patriarch said, "The fundamental mind does not move; it merely relies upon stillness. Since it is originally still, what need is there for stillness? He continued, "All dharmas are fundamentally empty.
Because they are empty even of emptiness, within that emptiness of emptiness, they are called 'still. " The Patriarch said, "Emptiness itself is already empty; all dharmas are likewise so.
Being still and signless, what is there to be stilled and what is there to be quieted? When the guide heard these instructions from the Patriarch, he was enlightened.

He attained sudden and complete enlightenment. Subsequently, the six groups of disciples all returned to him, and his transformation spread throughout Southern India, delivering immeasurable multitudes.

Thereupon, the Patriarch reflected that the conditions were ripe and the time had come to propagate the teaching abroad. His secular nephew, King Hīranya, prepared a great ship and filled it with various treasures.

He was escorted to the coastal marshes. The Master voyaged across the vast ocean for three seasons, reaching the South Sea and arriving at Guangzhou on the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the eighth year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty.
The Regional Inspector, Xiao Ang, received him with hospitality and submitted a memorial to Emperor Wu.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy with an imperial decree, and on the first day of the tenth month, he arrived in Jinling. The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne..."
...and arrived. He built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting. "What merit does this entail? the Patriarch asked. The Emperor replied, "How can there be no merit?
The Patriarch said, "These are merely the minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas; they follow one like a shadow follows a form. Though they exist, they are not real.
The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Patriarch replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence..."
"Self-empty and tranquil. Such merit cannot be sought through worldly means. The Emperor asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?
The Patriarch replied, "Vast and empty; there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not grasp the meaning.
On the nineteenth day of this month, the Patriarch secretly crossed to the north of the river. On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month...
He arrived in Luoyang during the tenth year of the Tahe era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Later Wei dynasty.

He took up residence at Shaolin on Mount Song and sat facing a wall all day long; people called him the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin. A monk named Shenguang came to pay his respects, but he received no instruction or encouragement.
Shenguang thought to himself: "When the ancients sought the Way, they would break their bones to extract the marrow and pierce their skin to draw blood..."
He relieved the hunger of others; he spread his hair to cover the mud; he threw himself from a cliff to feed a tiger. If the ancients were already like this, who am I to be otherwise?
On the night of the ninth day of the twelfth month of that year, it snowed heavily. Daoguang stood beneath the courtyard eaves; by the break of dawn, the accumulated snow had risen above his knees.
The Master took pity on him and asked, "Standing in the snow, what do you seek? Guang shed tears and said, "I pray that the Master will open the gate of ambrosia to widely deliver all beings.
The Patriarch said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort through vast eons;

one must be able to practice what is difficult to practice and endure what is difficult to endure. How can you, with such meager virtue and limited wisdom, and with a frivolous and arrogant mind, desire it?"

To succeed in the True Vehicle, one must labor diligently and undergo hardship. Upon hearing the words of the Patriarch, Sengcan secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Patriarch.
The Patriarch, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, said: "The Buddhas sought the Way; for the sake of the Dharma, they forgot their bodies.
Since you have now severed your arm before me, your seeking is permissible. He then changed his name to Huike and proceeded to preach the Dharma to him, saying:
He said to him: "You need only cease external conditions and let the inner mind be free from agitation; when the mind is like a blank wall, you may enter the Way.
Although Huike had spoken variously about the mind and nature, he had never yet realized the principle. Suddenly, one day, he attained awakening and ran to inform the Patriarch, saying:
"I have now ceased all conditions. The Patriarch asked: "Have you not fallen into annihilationism? Huike replied: "It is not annihilationism. The Patriarch [said]: "... (The text here ends).
[The student] asked, "What is the proof? [The Master] said, "It can be said that because it is constantly and clearly known, words cannot reach it.
The Patriarch said, "This is the essence of mind transmitted by all Buddhas; do not harbor further doubts."
The Patriarch has a Dharma-gate for settling the mind which says: "In delusion, the person pursues phenomena; in awakening, phenomena pursue the person.

In awakening, consciousness subsumes form; in delusion, form subsumes consciousness. Whatever involves mental activity, discrimination, or calculation—whatever is the manifestation of one's own mind—is entirely a dream.
If one realizes that the mind is quiescent and extinguished, such that there is not a single place where a thought moves, this is called Right Awakening. Question: What is meant by this?

"It is the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind. [The interlocutor] replied: "One perceives all phenomena as existent; yet existence does not exist of itself—it is the mind itself that conceives it as existent.
One perceives all phenomena as non-existent; yet non-existence does not exist of itself—it is the mind itself that conceives it as non-existent.
This applies to all phenomena in the same way: they are all conceived as existent or non-existent by the mind itself. Furthermore, if a person commits all manner of transgressions..."
One who sees the Dharma-king within oneself immediately attains liberation. One who attains liberation through the practice of activities possesses great vigor;
one who sees the Dharma within the activities does not lose mindfulness in any situation; whereas one who understands through words and letters possesses weak vigor.

That which is "immediate phenomenon is immediate reality" is profound. From your various activities—whether leaping, bounding, falling, or stumbling—all do not transcend the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
If one were to enter the dharma-realm by means of the dharma-realm, one would be a deluded person. Whatever actions or endeavors there may be, they all do not transcend the mind of the dharma-realm.
Why is this? Because the essence of the mind is the dharma-realm. [He] asked the people of the world: "Regarding their various studies, what..."
"Why is it that one does not attain the Way? He replied, "It is because of seeing the self. For this reason, one does not attain the Way. 'Self' refers to the ego.
The Perfected Person encounters suffering without sorrow and meets joy without delight. Because they do not see the self, they do not perceive suffering or joy.

Because they have extinguished the self, they reach the state of non-being (*xūwú*). If even the self itself is extinguished, what further thing could there be that is not extinguished? [Question: "..."
Since all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty, who is it that cultivates the Path? The answer is: if there is "who," one must cultivate the Path;

if there is no "who," then there is no need to cultivate the Path. "Who" refers to the self (*ātman*). If there is no self, then upon encountering objects, one does not give rise to notions of right and wrong.
What I consider right is not what others consider right; what I consider wrong is not what others consider wrong.
When the mind is such that there is no mind, this is called penetrating the Buddha-way. When one encounters objects without giving rise to views, this is named reaching the Way.

Encountering things directly and penetrating them, one knows their original source; such a person’s eye of wisdom is opened. The wise person relies on things and does not rely on themselves. Thus it is said:
There is no grasping or rejecting, nor opposition or compliance. When a fool follows his own will rather than the Way, there is grasping and rejecting, as well as opposition and compliance.
Not seeing a single thing is called "seeing the Path. Not practicing a single thing is called "walking the Path. Thus, in all places, there is no place.
It is the very place of action, the non-place of action, and the non-action of phenomena; therein one sees the Buddha. When seeing signs, one sees ghosts in all places;
because of grasping at signs, one falls into hell, but by contemplating phenomena, one attains liberation. If one sees conceptualization and discrimination...

One immediately experiences such matters as the boiling cauldrons and burning coals, which are the manifest signs of birth and death. If one perceives the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, that is the nature of *nirvāṇa*.
It is free from recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination; this itself is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. Because the mind is not form, it is not existent;

because its function is never abandoned, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because it functions while being eternally empty, it is not existent; because it is empty while functioning constantly, it is not non-existent.
Yang Xuanzhi, the Grand Governor of Qicheng, exhausted his sincerity in seeking instruction and requested that the Master reveal the essential principles. The Master spoke this verse:
"Neither seeing evil does one give rise to aversion; Nor observing good does one exert effort to pursue it. Neither abandoning wisdom does one draw near to folly."
Nor does one cast aside delusion to attain enlightenment. Reaching the Great Way, one transcends measure; penetrating the Buddha-mind, one goes beyond calculation.
Not sharing the same orbit as ordinary beings or sages, such a person is transcendently named an Ancestor (Patriarch).
As the Patriarch was about to return to the West, he addressed his disciples, saying, "The time has come; each of you should speak of what you have attained.
Dao Fu said, "As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters, yet I do not depart from words and letters, but take them as the functioning of the Way. The Patriarch said:
"You have obtained my skin," said the Patriarch. Niti Zongchi replied, "My understanding is like that of Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha:
having seen it once, one never sees it again. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my flesh. Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist.
Yet in my own field of vision, there is truly not a single dharma that can confront the mind. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my bones."
Huike performed three prostrations and stood in his place. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my marrow.
Tianyi Huai remarked, "When the Patriarch speaks in such a manner, it turns into a calculated maneuver even within the absence of calculation."

In that which has no path, one nevertheless creates a path. If they were taught to tread upon the ground of Deshan and Linji, they would have avoided sitting coldly for nine years, being called a "wall-gazing barbarian monk" by others.
Even if it were so, it still could not avoid bringing calamity upon their descendants. Dayang Yan said: "Tell me, is there yet another?"
A man came forward. [The Master] asked, "What have you attained? The man replied, "Nothing attained, nothing attained.
Cuiyan Zhi said, "The Second Patriarch was hoodwinked by him right before his eyes. Let alone the marrow, he had not even touched the skin.
Why, then, did he succeed to the Patriarchal seat?"
The Patriarch looked toward Huìkě and said to him: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa;
it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must uphold and protect it.

I also grant you this robe as a token of the Dharma, each of which symbolizes something specific. Huìkě said, "I pray that the Master will point out and explain them for me. The Patriarch said, "Internally..."
He transmitted the Dharma-seal to certify the realization of the mind; externally, he entrusted the *kāṣāya* robe to establish the fundamental principle.

Two hundred years later, the transmission ceased. The Dharma had encompassed the entire realm of sand-grains; those who clarified the Way were many, but those who practiced the Way were few. Those who discoursed on principles were many, but those who mastered the principles were few.
There were more than ten million who secretly conformed to and silently realized [the truth]. Listen to my verse: "I originally came to this land..."
He transmitted the Dharma to save those lost in delusion. One flower blooms and five petals unfold; the fruiting occurs naturally.
The Patriarch passed away sitting upright on the fifth day of the tenth month in the nineteenth year of the Taihe era of the Later Wei dynasty, the year of Bingchen.
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month, he was buried at Xiong’er Mountain. Three years later, Song Yun was dispatched as an envoy to the Western Regions.

Upon his return, he met Bodhidharma at the Pamir Mountains. The Master was walking alone, his single sandal fluttering in the wind. Baoyun asked, "Where are you going now? Bodhidharma replied, "To the Western Heaven.
He then said to Yun, "Your master has already grown weary of the world. Baoyun set out toward the east in a state of bewilderment. When he returned to report, Emperor Ming had already passed away.
After Emperor Xiaozhuang ascended the throne, Baoyun submitted a memorial detailing these events, and an imperial decree was issued.
When the tomb was opened, there was only an empty coffin with a single shoe remaining.
Regarding the Second Patriarch of the Eastern Land, Grand Master Huik’e (three times): the Master asked Bodhidharma, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas?"
Mozhao said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from others. The Master said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to pacify my mind.
Mozhao said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will pacify it for you. The Master reflected for a moment and then said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unattainable."
Moyun said, "I have finished granting you peace of mind.
Bajiao said, "A diamond rubbing the back of a clay figure.
Baizhang Wendeng’s verse says: "Searching from beginning to end, the mind cannot be found; in vast stillness, Shaolin is nowhere to be seen."
"A person fills the courtyard; the old snow is known once more for its chill. The nostrils remain as before, resting upon the upper lip.

The Master was once traveling north through Qi when a lay practitioner, over forty years of age, came before him and paid his respects, saying: "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a chronic wind-ailment.

I pray that the Master will perform a rite of repentance for my transgressions. The Master said: "Bring forth your transgressions, and I shall repent them with you. After a long silence, the layman said: "I search for them..."
"The nature of sin is utterly unattainable. The Master said, "I have finished repenting your sins for you; you should dwell in accordance with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The layman said, "Now that I have seen the Honored One, I already know what the Sangha is; what then is meant by 'Buddha' and 'Dharma'? The Master said, "This very mind is the Buddha."
"This mind is the Dharma; the Buddha and the Dharma are not two. It is the same with the Sangha Jewel.
The layman said, "Only today do I know that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha and the Dharma—they are non-dual."
The Master held him in high esteem.
Langya said, "He still lacks the realization of what it means to say 'Brahma exists.
The Master immediately granted him the tonsure for ordination and changed his name to Sengcan. He transmitted the Dharma to him, speaking this verse: "Originally, conditions exist."
The ground: flowers grow from seeds in the earth, yet originally there were no seeds, nor have the flowers ever been born.
Later, on the sixteenth day of the third month in the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era (the Gui-chou year), he manifested parinirvāṇa at the age of one hundred and seven.
The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan (Part II): When the śrāmaṇera Daoxin came to him, he prostrated and said, "I pray that the Upādhyāya will grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation.
The Master asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me. The Master said, "Why then do you seek liberation?
At these words, Daoxin attained great enlightenment. He served the Master diligently for nine years, after which the Dharma-eye was transmitted to him, and the Master spoke this verse:
It is said: "Although the seeds of flowers depend upon the earth, it is from the earth that the seeds produce flowers. Yet, if no one sows the seeds, neither flowers nor earth will ever grow.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Daye era (the Bingyin year) of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty, the Master [Dayan] proclaimed this for the fourfold assembly.
Having finished preaching the essentials of the Dharma, he stood with palms joined beneath a great tree until his end. His stupa was enshrined at his home mountain.
The Fourth Patriarch, Chan Master Daoxin (1), was the son of the Sima family of Henei. The Master asked the Third Patriarch, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddhas?
The Patriarch said, "What mind do you have right now? The Master replied, "I have no mind right now. The Patriarch said—
He said, "Since you have no mind, how could the Buddhas possibly have one? At these words, the Master’s doubts were instantly extinguished.
From that time on, he restrained his mind and slept no more; for sixty years, his side never touched the mat.

One day, in Huangmei County of Qizhou, he encountered a young boy whose skeletal features were extraordinary and beautiful, unlike those of ordinary children. The Master asked him, "What is your surname? He replied, "My surname is..."

"It exists, yet it is not of a permanent lineage. The Master asked, "What is its lineage? He replied, "It is the Buddha-nature. The Master asked, "Do you have no lineage? He replied, "Because my lineage is emptiness.
The Master silently recognized his potential and accepted him into the monastic order, shaving his head and having him serve as an attendant.
Later, he transmitted the Dharma-eye to him, speaking this verse: "The seeds of flowers have a place of birth; Depending on the ground, the flowers grow. The Great Condition..."
He was sixty-two years old when he passed away on the fourth day of the ninth month in the *xinhai* year of the Yonghui era of Emperor Gaozong. He sat peacefully and entered nirvana.
His stupa was enshrined at his native mountain.
The Fifth Patriarch, Great Master Hongren (1), was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou. He had no father; he followed his mother’s surname, Zhou.
After receiving the Dharma, he resided at Mount Poutou. A lay practitioner named Lu Huineng came to visit him. The Master asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "From Lingnan. The Master said, "What do you seek? He replied, "I seek only to become a Buddha. The Master said, "Lingnan..."
"Ordinary people have no Buddha-nature; how then could they attain Buddhahood? People may come from the north or the south, but how could it be so with Buddha-nature?

The Patriarch silently marveled at this, yet rebuked him, saying, "Go and work in the stable. Huineng entered the rice-pounding hall, where he wore a stone around his waist to pound the grain and served the assembly.

When the Master was about to transmit the Dharma, he commanded his disciples to present verses; he would bestow the transmission upon whoever had realized their own nature. Among them was the chief disciple, Great Master Shenxiu, who composed:
A verse was inscribed on the wall of the corridor, which said: "The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is like a bright mirror stand.
At all times diligently wipe it clean; Do not let dust and grime collect. The Master sighed and said, "If one practices according to this, one will also attain a supreme fruit."
The assembly was all reciting it and could hear him. They then asked, "What chapter or verse is being recited? Neng’s fellow student recounted the matter in detail.
Neng said, "It is beautiful indeed, but its meaning is not yet fully understood. His fellow student rebuked him, saying, "How can a commoner like you know this? To utter such mad words!
Neng replied, "If you do not believe me, I wish to harmonize with it by adding a verse. The fellow student looked at one another and laughed.
He was able to stay until late at night. Holding a candle himself and employing a young attendant, he wrote a verse beside Xiu’s verse, saying:
Bodhi originally has no tree; The bright mirror is likewise not a stand. From the beginning there has been nothing at all; Where, then, could dust and grime settle?
The Master knew that Neng was capable of this, yet he remained silent in his heart. He then said to the assembly, "This verse also does not yet reveal one's nature.
Deep in the night, he secretly summoned Neng into his room and instructed him, saying, "I entrust to you the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous True Dharma, along with the robe I have transmitted.
Guard and uphold it well; pass it on to future generations so that it shall never be severed. Listen to me..."
The verse says: "When sentient beings come to plant seeds, the fruit arises from the ground; since insentient things have no seeds, that which lacks nature also has no arising.
Regarding the method for receiving the robe while kneeling, it says: "Now that the Dharma has been received, to whom shall the robe be entrusted?

The Master said: "When Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him; therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest the reality of having attained the Dharma. Now that faith has matured..."
"The robe is the root of contention; let it remain with your person and shall not be passed on further.
Four years after the Master’s transmission of the Dharma, in the second year of the Shangyuan era, he addressed the assembly, saying, "My work is now finished; the time has come.
He then sat upright and entered nirvana at the age of seventy-four. His stupa was erected on East Mountain in Huangmei.
The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng (8th entry), was a native of the Lu clan from Xinzhou. After he had attained the Dharma, he lived in seclusion at Faxing Monastery in Nanhai.
Once, as the wind blew the temple banner, two monks engaged in a debate; one said it was the wind that moved, while the other said it was the banner that moved.
Their back-and-forth discussion failed to accord with the truth. The Master said, "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves. It is your own minds that move."
At this, his mind was moved; the two monks were struck with awe.
Xuefeng said, "The Patriarch has a dragon's head but a snake's tail; he deserves twenty blows.
As the attendant Taoyuan Fu stood by, he unconsciously gnashed his teeth. Xuefeng said, "I have spoken thus; he too deserves twenty blows."
Baling Jian said: "The Patriarch said, 'It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. Since it is neither, where do the wind and the banner reside?
If there is someone who can act as the Patriarch’s advocate, let them come forth and meet Baling.
Xuedou said: "The wind moves, the banner moves. Since they are the wind and the banner, where [do they reside]?"
He remained stuck there. Someone acted as a patron for Baling and came forth to meet Xuedou.
Baoning Yong’s verse says: "A vast, open imperial highway, Where people pass unimpeded day and night.
It is not that the whole family fails to advance; It is simply that thorns grow before the gate."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Good friends, each of you should quiet your minds and listen to my teaching of the Dharma.
You all, sirs, your own minds are the Buddha; do not harbor any further doubt. There is not a single thing externally that can be established;

everything arises from the fundamental mind, which gives birth to the myriad kinds of dharmas. Therefore, a sutra says: 'When the mind arises, the myriad dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, the myriad dharmas cease.'"

If one wishes to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one must attain the samādhi of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇasamādhi*) and the samādhi of a single practice (*ekavyūhasamādhi*).
If, in all places, one does not dwell upon characteristics, does not give rise to hatred or love toward those characteristics, and neither grasps nor rejects them;

and if one does not contemplate matters such as benefit, success, or failure, but remains at ease, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and serene—this is called the samādhi of a single characteristic. If, in...

In all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—one maintains a purely upright mind; this unmoving site of practice is the true accomplishment of the Pure Land, and it is called the Samādhi of Single Practice.
If a person possesses two or three such samādhis, they will be like the earth with seeds, able to contain, nurture, and bring to fruition their results.
This single characteristic and single practice are also like this. My current preaching of the Dharma is like a timely rain, falling universally.
It moistens the great earth. Your Buddha-natures are like seeds; encountering this soaking moisture, they shall all sprout.
Those who receive my intent will certainly attain Bodhi; those who follow my practice will surely realize the wondrous fruit.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "I have an object that has no beginning and no end, no name and no characters, no back and no front.

How much less so, then, regarding the fundamental Buddha-nature? Even if this person were to cover his head with a thatched roof in the future, he would only become a follower of the school of intellectual understanding.
Fayan said, "The person who received the prediction in ancient times was ultimately not mistaken. Now, those who establish intellectual understanding as their school are the followers of Heze.

The monk asked, "I do not yet understand how this is so. The Master replied, "The Way is realized through the awakening of the mind; why should it depend on sitting? A sutra says:

"It neither comes nor goes. If there is no arising or ceasing, this is the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna. All dharmas are empty and quiescent; this is the Tathāgata’s pure sitting.
Since ultimately there is nothing to be realized, how much less is there 'sitting'? Jian said: "When your disciple returns to the capital, His Majesty will surely question me.
I pray that you, Reverend, will instruct me on the essentials of the mind so that I may transmit them to the Sage and to the scholars of the capital."
It is like a single lamp that kindles hundreds of thousands of lamps; those in darkness all become bright, and this brightness is inexhaustible.
The Master said: "The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the meaning of succession and replacement. That brightness is inexhaustible is itself also finite. Jian said:
"Light refers to wisdom, and darkness is used as a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*). If a person who cultivates the Way does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter their afflictions,"

"In beginningless birth and death, by what means can one attain liberation? The Master said, "If one uses wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, this is the view of the Two Vehicles—the capacity of those such as the sheep and the deer. Those of superior intelligence and great root are not like this.
Jian asked, "What is the view of the Mahāyāna? The Master said, "Luminosity and ignorance—ordinary people see these as two; the wise person realizes them as one."
Its nature is non-dual. This non-dual nature is the true nature. As for this true nature: it does not diminish when dwelling among the ignorant and foolish;
it does not increase when present among the worthy and sages. It is not disturbed while abiding in afflictions; it is not quiescent while residing in meditative concentration.
It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes; it is not in between, nor within or without. It is neither born nor extinguished. This is its nature.
"Phenomena are suchness; eternally abiding and never shifting—this is called the Way. Jian said, "The Master speaks of non-arising and non-extinction; how does this differ from the heterodox?
The Master said, "What the heterodox speak of as non-arising and non-extinction involves using extinction to stop arising, and using arising to manifest extinction.

Though they speak of extinction, it is not truly extinguished; though they speak of arising, it is said to be non-arising. What I call non-arising and non-extinction is that which is fundamentally non-arising from the beginning."

Now there is likewise no cessation. This is why he differs from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever;
you will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, its wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

Having received this instruction, he attained sudden and great enlightenment. He took his leave by prostrating and returned to the capital, where he reported the Master’s words to the Emperor. By imperial decree, he was granted a *kāṣāya* robe and silk fabrics.

On that day, his secular age was seventy-six. His remains were enshrined in a stupa at Baolin Monastery in Shaozhou. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dajian.

The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained within the source of the mind. All gates of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations, are entirely and spontaneously complete within you;
they do not depart from your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are, by their very nature, empty."
"Ji: All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world from which to escape, and there is no bodhi to be sought.
Humans and non-humans are equal in their essential nature and characteristics. The Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation.
Such a Dharma you have now attained; there is not the slightest thing lacking. How does this differ from the Buddha? There is no other dharma. You need only let the mind be as it is."
"Be present. Do not practice contemplative exercises; do not clarify the mind. Do not give rise to greed or anger; do not harbor sorrow or anxiety. Vast and unimpeded, move freely as you wish.

Joyful and free from worry, it is for this reason called 'Buddha. The Master said, "Since the mind already possesses..."
[Suzong] asked, "What is the Buddha? What is the mind? The Patriarch said, "If it is not the mind, do not ask about the Buddha; if you ask about the Buddha, it is not apart from the mind.
The Master said, "Since one does not engage in contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), when objects arise, how does one apply the antidote?

The Patriarch said, "Objects and conditions have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise in the mind. If the mind does not insist on naming them, from where would deluded sentiments arise? [Deluded sentiments...]
Since it does not arise, the true mind is naturally all-pervasive and all-knowing. You need only follow the mind with freedom; there is no further need for antidotes.

This is precisely what is called the eternally abiding Dharmakāya, which is without change or variation. I have transmitted the Dharma-gate of the Sudden Teaching to Master Can; I now entrust it to you.

Chan Master Yunchu Zhi of Tiantai, the dharma successor of Chan Master Weize of Fuku Yan at the seventh generation of the Niu-tou lineage in Jinling (one instance).
A monk named Jizong asked: "Regarding 'seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha'—"
"What is the meaning? The Master said, "The nature of purity is originally serene and still, without movement or fluctuation.

It does not belong to existence or non-existence, purity or impurity, long or short, nor to grasping or rejecting. Its essence is naturally carefree. To see clearly in this way is called 'seeing one's nature.
Nature is the Buddha; the Buddha is nature. Therefore, it is said that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha. The monk asked, "If nature is pure, it does not belong to existence..."
[The monk] said, "There is nothing. How can there be seeing? The Master said, "Seeing is without anything seen. The monk said, "If there is nothing seen, how can there still be seeing?
The Master said, "Even the place of seeing is non-existent. The monk said, "When seeing occurs in this way, who is it that sees?
The Master said, "There is no one who is able to see. The monk said, "Ultimately, what is the principle of this like? The Master said, "Do you know? You falsely calculate it [to be so]."

There is existence; that is, there is the subject and the object, which is what is called delusion. Following one's perceptions to give rise to conceptual understanding, one then falls into birth and death.
For one who sees with clarity, it is not so: though seeing all day long, they have never truly seen. If one seeks the locus of this seeing, its essence and characteristics cannot be found.
When both subject and object are utterly transcended, it is called "seeing one's nature. A monk asked, "Does this nature pervade all places? The Master said, "There is nowhere it does not pervade.
The monk asked, "Do ordinary people possess it? The Master said, "Since you have already said it pervades everywhere, how could there be an ordinary person who does not possess it?
The monk asked, "For what reason are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not constrained by it, while ordinary people alone [are]..."

[The monk] said: "Ensnared in suffering, how could one ever attain universality? The Master said: "Ordinary beings, within the nature of defilement and purity, calculate the existence of subject and object;
they thus fall into birth and death. The Buddhas and Great Beings well know that within the pure nature, there belongs neither to existence nor non-existence;
thus, subject and object do not arise. The monk said: "If it is explained in this way, then there must be people who understand and those who do not. The Master said: "Even 'understanding'..."
"It is unattainable. How could there be anyone who can fully comprehend it? The monk asked, "What is the ultimate principle? The Master said, "I shall tell you the essential point:
you should immediately reflect that within the nature of purity, there are neither ordinary beings nor sages, nor is there anyone who can comprehend or fail to comprehend."
Ordinary person and sage—both are merely names. If one generates understanding based on these names, one falls into birth and death.
If one knows that provisional names are not real, then there is no one who truly corresponds to those names. It is further said: "This is the state of ultimate consummation.
To say 'I can understand' while 'he cannot understand' is a great sickness. To perceive distinctions between purity and defilement, or ordinary persons and sages, is likewise a great sickness."

There is no mind that clings or grasps; there is a mind that acts for the sake of things, yet no mind that conceives of a body.

If one can be thus, then though born before heaven and earth, one does not become a vital essence (*jing*); though dying after heaven and earth, one does not become old. Though changing all day long, one does not become active;
though ultimately silent and still, one does not become at rest. To awaken to this, even if one marries, it is not a wife; even if one partakes of feasts, it is not [a meal].
It is taking [the Way]. Though the handle is not the pivot, though the action is not the original intent, though one is intoxicated, it is not delusion.

If one can be without mind toward the myriad things, then even if caught in desire, it does not become lust; even if fortune follows from lust, it does not become theft; even if there is confusion, error, suspicion, or entanglement, it does not become killing;
even if one’s actions precede or follow Heaven’s way, it does not become falsehood; even if one is muddled, chaotic, or inverted, it does not become intoxication. This is what is called—
"There is no mind. Where there is no mind, there is no precept; where there is no precept, there is no mind. There is no Buddha and no sentient beings.
There is no you, and thus there is no self. What, then, is a precept? The spirit said, "My supernatural powers are second only to those of the Buddha.

The Master said, "As for your supernatural powers, of ten items, five you can do and five you cannot. As for the Buddha, of ten items, seven he can do and three he cannot. The spirit was struck with awe and withdrew from his seat.
Kneeling, he asked, "May I hear it? The Master said, "Can you cause the Supreme Deity to turn eastward while the Seven Luminaries travel westward? He replied, "I cannot.
The Master said, "Can you seize the Earthly Spirits, melt the Five Sacred Peaks, and bind the Four Seas? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Then how can you understand the Way?"

[The interlocutor] said, "I cannot. The Master said, "This is called the five things that cannot be done. The Buddha can empty all phenomena and realize the wisdom of all dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma.
The Buddha can know the nature of all beings and exhaustively understand the events of an eon, yet he cannot transform and guide those who lack the karmic affinity.
The Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot bring the realm of sentient beings to an end. This is it.

This means that the three [conditions] are incapable [of producing the result]. Even determinate karma (*niyata-karma*) is not fixed or eternal. Even in the absence of conditions, it constitutes a single lifetime.

The realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*) is fundamentally without increase or decrease. Furthermore, there is not a single person who can preside over this Dharma. Where there is a presider but no Dharma, this is called "the non-existence of the Dharma."
"Without method and without master—this is called 'no-mind. As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*);

he is simply able to penetrate all phenomena through no-mind. The Divine One said, "I am truly shallow and ignorant; I have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). I shall uphold the precepts you have received.
Now I wish to repay your compassionate virtue by demonstrating what I am capable of. The Master said, "I observe the body..."
"There is nothing. Contemplating that all phenomena are impermanent, what further desire could there be for this mere lump of flesh?

The spirit said, "Master, you must surely command me to perform a worldly task and display my minor divine powers, so that these five classes of people—those who have already resolved their minds, those who have first resolved their minds, those who have not yet resolved their minds, and those who lack faith—may certainly gain faith.
Let them behold my divine traces and come to know that there are Buddhas and spirits, and that there is both capability and incapability."
[The Master] said, "It is possible. There are those that are natural, and there are those that are not natural. The Master said, "The Unconditioned (wuwei) is it. The Unconditioned is it.
Shen said, "Even the Buddha had spirits protect the Dharma; how could you, Master, dare to rebel against the Buddha? He requested, "I pray you will instruct me according to your will.
Reluctantly, the Master spoke, saying: "The barrier of Dongyan Temple is vast and treeless. While the northern peak has trees, its back is not a screen."

Master Yong said, "Can you move the northern tree to the eastern ridge? The spirit replied, "I have received your command. However, there will surely be a great commotion during the darkness of night;
I pray that the Master does not be alarmed. He paid his respects and took his leave. The Master saw him off at the gate and watched him go.
He beheld the ceremonial guards winding along in a procession like those of a sovereign, amidst swirling mists and vapors, with banners, streamers, and tinkling ornaments intermingling in profusion.
The sky became obscured. That evening, there was indeed a violent storm with thundering peals, rushing clouds, and flashing lightning;
the buildings shook and swayed, and the birds roosting there clamored noisily. The Master said to the assembly, "Do not fear, do not fear! The deity has entered into a covenant with me.

At dawn, the weather cleared and brightened, and the pines and cypresses from the northern cliff had all been moved to the eastern ridge, standing there in dense, orderly rows. The Master said to his disciples, "I..."

Chan Master Weizheng of Zhongnan Mountain (1). A native of the Zhou clan from Pingyuan, he was a disciple of the Tang Emperor Wenzong.

Because the Emperor was fond of eating clams, the coastal officials were burdened with the task of presenting them in succession. One day, among the imperial dishes, there was one that would not open even after being pried.
The Emperor considered this extraordinary and burned incense to pray for its opening. When it was opened, he beheld the form of a Bodhisattva, complete with the marks of a Brahma.

He immediately placed it within a casket of gold, grain, and sandalwood, covered it with fine brocade, and bestowed it upon Xingshan Monastery, ordering the assembly of monks to gaze upon and worship it.

Thereupon, he questioned his ministers: "What auspicious omen is this? Some replied that on Mount Taiyi there was the Chan Master Weizheng, who possessed a profound understanding of the Buddha's teachings.

The Emperor issued an edict to request an audience with him. The Emperor summoned the Master and questioned him about the matter. The Master said, "Your servant has heard that no phenomenon responds in vain;
this is merely to inspire Your Majesty’s faith. Thus, a sutra states: 'Those who are to be saved by this body shall have this very body appear before them to preach the Dharma.
The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva’s body has indeed appeared, yet I have not yet heard him preach the Dharma. The Master replied:

"Your Majesty, observing this, do you consider it permanent or impermanent? Do you regard it as real or unreal? The Emperor replied, "This is a most extraordinary matter; I believe it with deep conviction.
The Master said, "Your Majesty has already heard the teaching of the Dharma to its conclusion. The Emperor’s heart was filled with great joy, such as he had never experienced before.
He subsequently issued an imperial edict that every temple throughout the realm must establish an image of Avalokiteśvara.

The Master then addressed the great assembly, saying: "A Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter; the True Dharma is difficult to hear. Each of you listen attentively!
This capacity for hearing is not something that arises through hearing; it is not contingent upon the faculty of hearing. It is fundamentally unarisen—how could it ever cease?

When there is sound, it is the object of sound (*śabdaviṣaya*) that arises of itself; when there is no sound, it is the object of sound that ceases of itself. Yet this nature of hearing does not follow after sound."

"How is it that there is no extinction? And how is it that there is liberation? The Master said: "When the mind does not arise upon encountering objects, this is called non-arising.

As for the true mind: when thoughts arise, it does not follow them in arising; when thoughts cease, it does not rely on stillness.
It neither comes nor goes; it is neither fixed nor distracted; it neither grasps nor rejects; it neither sinks nor floats. It is unconditioned and signless—vibrant and agile."
Flickering. This essence of mind is ordinarily free and at ease; ultimately it cannot be apprehended, and there is nothing to be known or perceived. Everything encountered by the eyes is thus;
there is nothing that is not the manifestation of the nature of seeing.

The Sixth Patriarch, Zen Master Huineng’s Dharma heir, Tripitaka Master Xitian Jueduo (1), was a native of India. After receiving the Dharma, he traveled to Mount Wutai, where he encountered a monk who had built a hermitage and sat in meditation.
The Master asked, "For what purpose do you sit alone? The monk replied, "I am contemplating stillness. The Master said, "As for 'contemplating'—"

Why do you not go to Caoxi to resolve the essential truth? The monk bowed in gratitude and subsequently went to Caoxi.

The Patriarch said, “When the preceding thought does not arise, that is the mind; when the succeeding thought does not continue, that is the Buddha.

"The very mind is originally the Buddha; failing to realize this, one remains self-subdued. Now I know the cause of concentration and wisdom."
Cultivating both [wisdom and means] while remaining detached from all phenomena.

When the Master arrived at Caoxi, he circumambulated the meditation platform three times, struck his staff once, and stood there with solemn composure.

The Master replied, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize the state of non-arising?"
“Is it not too fast? The Master said, “The essence is unborn; since it is fundamentally unborn, how could there be speed? The Patriarch said, “So it is, so it is.
The Master then assumed the full ceremonial demeanor and paid his respects. After a short while, he took his leave. The Patriarch said, “Is your departure too hasty?

[The Master] said, "It is different. The Patriarch said, "You have thoroughly grasped the meaning of non-arising. The Master said, "How can non-arising have a meaning?

The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who is it that makes distinctions? The Master said, "Distinction itself is not a meaning. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! Stay for one more night."
