Chan Master Benjing of Sijiang Mountain (fourth in the series), a native of the Zhang family from Jiang, was asked by a monk:
"What is the Way? The Master said, "Mindlessness is the Way. The monk said, "The Way arises because of the mind; how can you say that mindlessness is the Way? The Master said:

The Way is fundamentally nameless; it is because of the mind that the Way is named. If the mind were to have a name, the Way would not be empty. Since the mind, when investigated to its limit, is non-existent, upon what could the Way rely to be established?
Both are equally empty and false; they are all merely provisional names. You say you see the existence of body and mind—have you already attained the Way?
The Master said, "This mountain monk’s body and mind are, from the very beginning, the Way. [The student] said, "Just now you spoke of no-mind being the Way; now again..."
The monk said, "If you say that body and mind are fundamentally the Way, does this not contradict [your previous statement]?
The Master said, "A mindless state is the Way. When the mind is extinguished, the Way is non-existent. Mind and the Way are one and the same; therefore, it is said that a mindless state is the Way.

Body and mind are fundamentally the Way, and the Way is also fundamentally body and mind. Since body and mind are fundamentally non-existent, how could the Way exist when its source is exhausted? The monk said, "I observe meditation..."
The Master’s physical form was very small, yet he thoroughly understood this principle. The Master said, "Virtuous One, you see only the mountain monk’s form;

you do not see the mountain monk’s formlessness. That which sees form is what you, Virtuous One, perceive. The Sutra says: 'All that has form is entirely illusory. If one sees that all forms are no-form, then one sees the Way.

If one takes form to be real, even after an eon..."* *(Note: The source text appears to be truncated. The standard continuation of this famous passage from the Diamond Sutra is: "...one would not be able to attain the Buddha-way.")*
[The Master] was able to see the Path. [The student] asked, "How is it that the various masters speak of 'signlessness' (animitta) upon the basis of signs?
The Master said, "The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* states: 'The four great elements have no master; the body likewise has no self. To be without the view of 'mine' is to be in accord with the Path.

Venerable sir, if you hold that the four great elements have a master which is the 'self,' or if you harbor the view of a self, you will not encounter the Path even at the end of an eon. He then pointed this out with a verse, saying: "The four great elements have no..."
The Master, moreover, is like water: meeting curves or encountering straightness, he makes no distinction between self and other; whether in purity or filth, he gives rise to no thought.

Whether obstructed or flowing freely, he never possesses two intentions. When encountering objects, he is simply like water, without a mind of his own. Moving through the world with such spontaneity—what affairs could there be?
Chan Master Zhiming asked: "If you say that 'no-mind' is the Way, then tiles and pebbles are also no-mind; they too should be the Way.
Furthermore, if you say that body and mind are fundamentally the Way, then since all beings of the four births and ten categories possess body and mind, they too should be the Way. The Master said:
"Virtuous One, if you understand this through the conceptualization of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, you are worlds apart from the Way; you are merely seeking to see and hear it."
As for "perceiving through awareness," this is not the seeking of the Way. A sutra says: "There are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

Since even the six sense faculties do not exist, from what could seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing arise? When one exhaustively investigates the source and finds it does not exist, where can the mind abide?

How could one not then be the same as grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles? With his resolve firm, he closed his mouth. The Master further showed him with a verse: "Seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing are unobstructed."
Obstruction. Sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch are the Samādhi of Constancy. Like a bird flying through the air, there is neither grasping nor rejecting, neither aversion nor attachment.
If one is fundamentally without mind regarding these sensory objects, only then can one be called Avalokiteśvara.
The Chan Master Zhen asked: "If the Way is indeed mindless, does the Buddha have a mind? Are the Buddha and the Way one or two?
The Master said: "Neither one nor two. [Zhen] asked: "The Buddha delivers sentient beings because he possesses a mind; why is it that the Way does not deliver people?"

Because there is no mind, how can there be duality? The Master said: "If one says that the Buddha delivers sentient beings while the Way does not deliver them, this is a Great Virtue who falsely gives rise to dualistic views. It is not so for one such as this mountain monk. 'Buddha' is a hollow name;
'the Way' is also falsely established. Both are unreal; they are all merely provisional names. Within a single provisionality, how can one distinguish two? To speak of 'Buddha'..."
"Buddha" and "the Way"—these are provisional names. At the moment these names are established, who is it that establishes them? If there were three [entities], how could one say they do not exist?
The Master said: "Buddha and the Way are established based on the mind. When one investigates to the ultimate the mind upon which they are established, the mind itself is also non-existent.
Since the mind is non-existent, one realizes that both are unreal. Knowing them to be like dreams and illusions, one awakens to their original emptiness. [This is] merely..."
The establishment of two names for the Buddha-way is the perspective of those of the Two Vehicles; they thus speak of neither cultivation nor realization.
As the verse says: "One cultivates the Way only after seeing the Way; if one does not see it, what is there to cultivate? The nature of the Way is like empty space; what can empty space cultivate?"
One who universally observes the cultivation of the Way is like one who beats out fire to seek a bubble; they merely watch a puppet being manipulated, which ceases all at once when the strings break.
Chan Master Fakong asked, "If both Buddha and the Way are merely provisional names, then the twelve divisions of the teachings must also be unreal.
Why have the venerable masters of the past all spoken of 'cultivating the Way'? The Master said, "You have misunderstood the intent of the scriptures. The Way is fundamentally non-existent."
Cultivation. You, Venerable Sir, cultivate with effort. The Way is fundamentally without action; you, Venerable Sir, act with effort.
The Way is fundamentally without affairs; you create many affairs where there are none. The Way is fundamentally without knowing; within it, you insist on knowing. Such a view is contrary to the Way.

It is not as the venerable masters of old practiced. This is simply because you, Venerable Sir, have not understood. Please reflect upon this. He further pointed this out with a verse, saying: "The Way..."
The essence is fundamentally without cultivation; by not cultivating, one naturally accords with the Way. If one gives rise to a mind that cultivates the Way, this person does not understand the Way.
They abandon their single true nature and instead enter into a state of chaotic turmoil. If you encounter a person who has attained the Way, first of all, do not speak of the Way.

Chan Master Xuance of Wuzhou (Case 1) was a native of Jinhua. While traveling throughout the land, he arrived at Heshuo, where he heard that Chan Master Zhihuang had visited the Fifth Patriarch and claimed to have attained *samādhi*.
He subsequently lived in a hermitage, sitting in meditation continuously for twenty years.
The Master knew that what the student had attained was not yet genuine. He went to the hermitage and asked, "What are you doing here? The student replied, "I am entering meditative absorption.
The Master said, "When you say you enter meditative absorption, do you enter it with a mind or without a mind? If you enter it without a mind—"
"All insentient things—grass, trees, tiles, and stones—should likewise be able to enter samādhi.

If there were such entry for those with mind, then all sentient beings and the multitude of conscious creatures would also be able to enter samādhi. Huang said, "When I am entering samādhi, I do not perceive a mind of existence or non-existence.
The Master said, "Not perceiving a mind of existence or non-existence is precisely constant samādhi. How could there be entering or exiting?"
"If there is coming and going, it is not the Great Samādhi. After a long silence, Huáng asked, "Whom do you follow as your teacher? The Master replied, "My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi.

Huáng asked, "What does the Sixth Patriarch take to be meditative concentration? The Master replied, "According to what my teacher has taught: 'It is wondrously profound, perfectly still, and quiescent; its essence and function are suchness.

The five aggregates are fundamentally empty; the six sense-objects do not exist. It neither emerges nor..."* (text continues). *Note: The source text appears to be an excerpt from the *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch*. The final phrase "不出" (not emerging) likely refers to the state of non-arising or non-manifestation within the context of the Great Samādhi.*

He does not enter; he is neither fixed nor distracted. The nature of dhyāna has no abiding; it is free from the dwelling in meditative stillness. The nature of dhyāna has no arising; it is free from the conceptualization of dhyāna as arising.
His mind is like empty space, yet even the measure of empty space does not exist. Upon hearing this teaching, Xuangui traveled to Caoqi to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked, "Virtuous one, where have you come from? Xuangui recounted his previous circumstances in detail. The Patriarch sighed and said, "Truly, it is just as Subhūti said."

When he spoke thus, the Patriarch took pity on his journey from afar and granted him an explanation. Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment; the mental states he had cultivated over twenty years vanished entirely, leaving no trace.
That night, the common people and officials of Hebei heard a voice in the air saying, "Today Master Huáng has attained the Way.
He shall return to Hebei to transform and guide the fourfold assembly; this is truly due to the power of the Master."
Chan Master Shenhui of Heze (in four parts): A native of the Gao clan from Xiangyang. The Master went to visit the Sixth Patriarch.

The Patriarch asked, "Worthy one, you have come from afar with great hardship; have you brought your original nature? If you possess this original nature, you ought to recognize its master. Try to speak of it.
The Master replied, "Taking non-abiding as the original nature, seeing is itself the master. The Patriarch said, "How can you, a novice monk, presume to..."
While they were conversing in a casual manner, [Nanyue] struck him.

The Master (Xitang) then served him with diligent devotion. Later, the Master visited Qingyuan Xingsi. Xingsi asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Caoxi. Xingsi asked, "What is the essential meaning of Caoxi?
The Master straightened his body and stood there. Xingsi said, "You still carry some rubble with you. The Master said, "Preceptor, do not..."
"Is there any real gold for you? He thought: "Even if there were, where would you put it? Cuiyan Zhi said:
"Real gold and rubble—these are mistaken names and phrases. What would you call them now?"
One day, the Master received news from his hometown that both his parents had passed away. He entered the Sangha hall and struck the gavel, saying: "Both my parents have perished;

I ask the assembly to recite the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. As the assembly prepared to recite, the Master suddenly struck the gavel again and said, "I trouble you, assembly," and they immediately dispersed.
A monk asked, "Does the Dharma of non-thought still possess existence or non-existence? The Master said, "I do not speak of existence or non-existence.
The monk asked, "At such a time, what is it like? The Master said, "There is also no such time. It is like a bright mirror:
if it does not reflect an image, one will never see an image. If one sees that there is nothing, that is true seeing."
Chan Master Zhichang of Xinzhou (1 total): He was originally from Guixi in this province. He went to visit the Sixth Patriarch, who asked, "Where have you come from?
What do you seek? He replied, "I recently went to Mount Baifeng to pay my respects to Chan Master Datong."

I have received your instruction on the meaning of “seeing one’s nature and attaining Buddhahood,” yet my doubts remain unresolved. I humbly hope that the Venerable Master will compassionately provide me with guidance.
The Patriarch asked, "What words did he say? Try reciting them for me, and I shall verify them for you.

[The student] replied, "When I arrived there, I spent three months without receiving any instruction. Because of my intense longing for the Dharma, I went alone to the abbot’s quarters and prostrated myself before him."
He asked, "What is the original mind and original nature of such-and-such a person? The other replied, "Do you see empty space? He said, "I see it.
The other asked, "In seeing empty space, do you see any form or appearance? He said, "Empty space has no shape; what form or appearance could it have?
The other said, "Your original nature is like empty space. Observe your own nature, and you will find there is not a single thing."
That which can be seen is called right view. To realize that not a single thing exists that can be known is called true knowledge.

When there is no longer blue or yellow, long or short, but only the vision of the fundamentally pure source and the perfectly luminous essence of awakening, this is what is called "seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood.

It is also called the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and it is also called the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision. Although students hear these explanations, they have still not reached a definitive understanding.

"I beg the Master for instruction so that I may be free from stagnation. The Patriarch said, "What he has shown you still involves views and cognition, which prevents you from attaining full realization.
I shall now show you a verse: 'Not seeing a single dharma, yet maintaining the view of non-existence, Is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun.
Not knowing a single dharma, yet clinging to the knowledge of emptiness, Is like lightning flashing within the vast void. This—
A flash of cognition and view suddenly arises; how could such mistaken recognition ever be the understanding of skillful means?

Now, in a single thought-moment, you know for yourself that it is wrong; your own numinous light is constantly manifest. Hearing this verse, his mind was suddenly enlightened, and he composed a poem saying:

"Groundlessly giving rise to cognition and view, One clings to appearances while seeking Bodhi. If the mind harbors even a single thought of awakening, How can it transcend its former delusion? The source of self-nature is awakening..."
As for the essence: following illumination, one wanders through deluded flux; failing to enter the patriarch’s chamber, one is bewildered, pursuing two extremes.

Chan Master Zhītōng of Shòuzhōu (Case 1): He was a native of Ānfēng in his home commandery. Although he had read the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* more than a thousand times, he did not understand the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
He paid obeisance to the Sixth Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning. The Patriarch said: "As for the three bodies..."
The pure Dharma-body is your nature. The perfect Reward-body is your wisdom. The thousand-billion transformation-bodies are your practice.
If you were to depart from your original nature and speak of the three bodies separately, they would be called "having a body but lacking wisdom.
If you realize that the three bodies have no self-nature, they are called the four wisdoms of Bodhi. Listen to my verse: "The original nature is endowed with..."
The three bodies manifest and give rise to the four wisdoms; without departing from seeing and hearing conditions, one transcends and ascends to the ten stages.
I shall now explain this for you: believe it with certainty and without doubt. Do not follow those who rush about in pursuit, speaking of *bodhi* all day long.
Tong said, "May I hear the meaning of the four wisdoms? The Patriarch said, "Since you have already understood the three bodies, you naturally comprehend the four wisdoms. Why ask again?"
Yes. If one speaks of the four wisdoms separately from the three bodies, this is called "having wisdom but no body.
Thus, that which possesses wisdom actually becomes a state of non-wisdom. Furthermore, a verse says: "The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure;

The Wisdom of Equality has a mind free from affliction. The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; The Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror. Five, eight, six, and seven..."

The transformation of cause and fruit consists merely of conventional designations and lacks any real nature. If one leaves no attachment to this process of transformation, then amidst all profuse activity, one dwells eternally in the *nāga-samādhi*.
[He] offered a general prostration of thanks and praised him with these verses: "The three bodies are originally my own substance; The four wisdoms are fundamentally the clarity of the mind.

Body and wisdom merge without obstruction; In responding to things, they take forms as they will. To initiate cultivation is entirely deluded movement; To cling to a state of preservation is not true."
Essential. The wondrous meaning arises from the teacher’s instruction;
ultimately, one forgets even the name of defilement. Chan Master Fada of Hongzhou (Case 1). When the Master prostrated before the Sixth Patriarch, his head did not touch the ground.

The Patriarch rebuked him, saying, "If you do not prostrate yourself fully to the ground, how is that any different from not prostrating at all? Within your mind, there must be some object; what have you been habitually cultivating? [Fada] replied:
"Such-and-such a person has recited the *Lotus Sūtra* three thousand times," [the disciple] said.

The Patriarch said, "If you were to recite it ten thousand times and attain the meaning of the sūtra, yet still not consider yourself superior, then you may walk with me. You are currently burdened by this task, yet you do not recognize your own fault.
Listen to my verse: The essence is fundamentally to break the banner of pride; why has your head not yet reached the ground? If there is a self, then sin immediately follows."
[He] was born. His merit and blessings were beyond compare. The Patriarch asked again, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Fada. The Patriarch said, "Your name is Fada;
when have you ever mastered the Dharma? He then spoke a verse, saying: "You now bear the name Fada, Diligently reciting without ceasing.
You recite in vain, merely following the sounds; To understand the mind is called a Bodhisattva. Because you now possess the karmic conditions, I shall now act for your sake..."

He said, "I speak only because I trust that the Buddha is beyond words; yet the lotus flower issues from his mouth. Upon hearing this verse, the Master repented and said, "From this day forward, I shall treat all with humility and respect.
I only pray that the Preceptor, out of great compassion, will briefly explain the principles and meanings within the sutras. The Patriarch said:
“You recite this sutra; what is its essential principle? The Master said, “I am a dull-witted student who merely recites it according to the text;
how could I know its fundamental purport? The Patriarch said, “Recite it for me once, and I shall explain it for you.

The Master then recited it aloud until they reached the "Chapter on Expedient Means. The Patriarch said, “Stop, stop! This sutra fundamentally takes the appearance in the world through causes and conditions as its core.”
This is the central tenet. Even if there were many kinds of parables, they would not exceed this. Why?
Because the causal conditions consist solely of the One Great Matter, and the One Great Matter is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

You must be careful not to misinterpret the meaning of the sutra by seeing it as saying that "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" belong exclusively to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, while we have no share in them. If you interpret it in this way, you are slandering [the teaching].
This scripture disparages the Buddha. Since he is already a Buddha, having fully perfected his knowledge and vision, why would he need to open [his eyes] again?
You should now believe that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is nothing other than your own mind; it has no separate essence.

It is simply because all sentient beings obscure their own radiance, greedily craving external objects, and being disturbed within by external conditions, that they willingly submit to being driven about. Thus, they trouble others to emerge from samādhi.
He rose. [The Master] spoke various harsh words, urging him to rest and not seek outside, for he is no different from the Buddha. Thus it is said, "Opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If you merely exhaust yourself with fixated thoughts, claiming them to be your daily practice, how is this any different from a yak that loves its tail?
The Teacher asked, "If that is so, would it not suffice to understand the meaning alone, without the trouble of reciting the sutras? The Patriarch replied, "What does the sutra have..."
[The Master] said: "This is not so. How could it obstruct your mindfulness? It is simply that delusion and awakening depend on the person; loss and gain depend on you. Listen to my verse:

When the mind is deluded, the *Lotus Sūtra* turns [against] the mind; When the mind is awakened, the mind turns the *Lotus Sūtra*. If one recites for a long time without clarifying oneself, One becomes an enemy to the meaning of the text.

Without thoughts, every thought is correct; With thoughts, every thought becomes deviant. When neither existence nor non-existence is reckoned, One forever drives the white ox-cart. The Master [said].

Upon hearing the verse, he spoke again, saying: "The sutras state that even all the great śrāvakas, up to and including the bodhisattvas, cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom despite exhausting their thoughts and measurements.
Now, you claim that an ordinary person need only awaken to their original mind to be called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Unless one possesses superior faculties, such a teaching cannot avoid being met with doubt and slander. Furthermore, the sutras speak of the three vehicles; how can this [teaching] be compared to the Great Ox-Cart? He then presented a white ox-cart.
“The ox-cart. How are they to be distinguished? I pray that the Venerable Master will grant me further instruction. The Patriarch said:

“The meaning of the sutras is clear, yet you yourself are deluded and turn your back upon it. That the followers of the three vehicles cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom lies in their reliance on intellectual measurement.

Even if they were to exhaust all their thoughts to investigate it together, they would only find themselves increasingly distanced from it. The Buddha originally taught this principle for the sake of ordinary beings; he did not teach it for the sake of Buddhas.”
If you are unwilling to believe, then withdraw from this seat. You do not realize that you have already sat upon the White Ox Cart, yet you still seek the three carts outside the gate!
Moreover, the sutra text clearly tells you: "There is neither two nor three. Why do you fail to comprehend this?
The three carts are provisional, for they belong to the past; the One Vehicle is real, for it belongs to the present.
I teach you only to leave the provisional and return to the real. Once you have returned to the real, even the "real" has no name. You should know that all precious wealth belongs entirely to you;
as you enjoy it, you should no longer harbor the thought of a father, nor the thought of a son, nor even the thought of "use. This is so.
He was named Chih Fa-hua (Holder of the Lotus Sutra). From kalpa to kalpa, he did not let go of the scroll from his hand; from day to night, there was no moment when he did not contemplate it.
Upon receiving this inspiration, the Master leaped for joy and praised him in verse: "Three thousand sections of the sutra have been recited, yet a single phrase of Caoqi has been lost.

If the ultimate meaning of transcending the world is not clarified, how can the madness of successive lives be stilled? The metaphors of the sheep, deer, and ox were provisionally established; at first..."
In the middle and at the end it is excellent; who would have known that within this burning house there was originally the King of the Dharma?
The Patriarch said, "From now on, you may truly be called a monk who recites the sutras."
Chan Master Zhiche of Jiangxi (Volume One), whose secular name was Xingchang, was a young man who had been a knight-errant.

Since the division between the Northern and Southern schools, although the two Patriarchs themselves had no sense of "self" versus "other," their disciples nonetheless gave rise to feelings of attachment and aversion.

The followers of the Northern school established Huineng as the Sixth Patriarch, yet they harbored resentment toward Great Master Huineng’s transmission of the robe, which became known throughout the world. The Patriarch foresaw this matter in advance.

He immediately placed ten taels of gold in the abbot’s quarters. At that time, Xingchang, having been commissioned by followers of the Northern School, entered the Patriarch’s room with a blade hidden about him, intending to do him harm.
The Patriarch extended his neck toward him; though Xingchang brandished the blade three times, it did not inflict even the slightest injury.
The Patriarch said, "The true sword is not crooked; the crooked sword is not true. I owe you only the gold, but I do not owe you your life."

Xingchang was so startled that he fell prostrate. Only after a long time did he regain consciousness; he begged for mercy and repented his transgressions, immediately vowing to leave the household life.
The Patriarch then gave him gold, saying, "Go for now; I fear that your fellow disciples might instead bring harm upon you. On another day, you may come in a different guise, and I shall accept you.

Having received these instructions, Xingchang fled under the cover of night and joined the monastic order to receive full ordination. There he practiced with diligence, yet one day he remembered the Patriarch.

He spoke these words. Having traveled from afar to pay his respects, he said, "The Master has long thought of me; why have you come so late? [Baizhang] replied, "Yesterday I was granted the Master’s pardon of my transgressions.

Although I have now left the household life and practice asceticism, it will be difficult to ever repay such profound kindness. Is it not only through the transmission of the Dharma and the saving of sentient beings that one may do so?
Your disciple has previously read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, yet I do not yet understand the meaning of 'permanence' and 'impermanence. I beg the Master’s compassionate guidance."
To explain it briefly: the Master said, "That which is impermanent is the Buddha-nature; that which is permanent is all dharmas of good and evil—the discriminating mind.
[The interlocutor] said, "What the Master has said greatly contradicts the scriptural texts. The Master said, "I transmit the Mind-essence school of the Buddhas;
how would I dare contradict the Buddha's scriptures? [The interlocutor] said, "The scriptures state that the Buddha-nature is permanent, yet the Master says..."
"All dharmas, whether good or evil, up to and including the bodhicitta, are impermanent. Yet the Preceptor claims they are permanent;
this is a contradiction that causes students to become increasingly confused. The Patriarch said, "In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, I once heard the nun Wujinzang recite it once and then expounded upon it;
not a single word or a single meaning accorded with the text of the sūtra."
"Even unto you, I have never had two words of teaching. You say that as a student your capacity for understanding is shallow and dim;
I pray that the Master will explain this to me in detail. The Patriarch said, "Do you understand? If Buddha-nature were permanent, what further need would there be to speak of good and evil dharmas?
Even until the end of kalpas, not a single person would ever give rise to the Bodhi-mind. Therefore, I speak of impermanence; this is precisely the Buddha."

This is to explain the Way of True Permanence (*tathatā*). Furthermore, if all dharmas were impermanent, then every individual thing would possess its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) that undergoes birth and death, and there would be places where True Permanence does not pervade. Therefore, when I speak of "permanence," it is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the true meaning of impermanence.
This is because ordinary people and non-Buddhists cling to false permanence, [and this teaching is intended for those] who are attached to such dualistic views.
Those who ride upon the vehicle [of the teachings] calculate the permanent as impermanent; together, these constitute the eight inversions.
Therefore, within the definitive teachings on Nirvāṇa, those biased views are refuted, and the true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity are clearly expounded.

You now rely on the words while turning your back on the meaning, asserting annihilationist impermanence and fixating on death as permanence; thus you have erroneously misunderstood the Buddha’s perfect and subtle final subtlety.
He said, "Even if you were to read this a thousand times, what benefit would there be? At these words, Xingchang suddenly felt as if he had awakened from a drunken stupor. He then spoke a verse:
"Because of guarding the mind of impermanence, The Buddha spoke of the nature of permanence. Those who do not know the skillful means Are like those picking pebbles from a spring pond.
Now, without applying effort, The Buddha-nature appears before me. It was not bestowed by my teacher, Nor is there anything I have attained. The Patriarch [Huineng] said:
The Master said, "You have now attained thorough penetration. You should be named Zhiche (Thorough Penetration).
He bowed in thanks and departed. Chan Master Zhicheng of Jizhou (1). He was a native of Taihe in that same province. Initially, he studied under Shenxiu.

Shenxiu’s disciples mocked Huineng, the Great Master, saying, "He does not recognize a single character; what excellence can he possibly possess? Shenxiu replied, "He has attained teacherless wisdom."
"In his profound realization of the Supreme Vehicle, he is my superior. That the Fifth Patriarch personally entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma was by no means in vain.
I regret that I could not go far to attend upon him; thus I have received the bounty of the state in vain.

You all, do not remain stagnant here. You may go to Caoxi to resolve your doubts. When you return in the future, tell me what you have learned. Upon hearing these words, the Master took his leave and departed for Caoxi.

He followed the assembly to seek instruction, yet did not mention his place of origin. The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying, "There is currently a person who steals the Dharma, secretly present at this gathering.
The Master stepped forward, paid his respects, and fully explained the matter. The Patriarch said, "How does your teacher instruct his disciples?

He says he constantly teaches the assembly to dwell the mind in quiet contemplation and to sit for long periods without lying down. The Patriarch continued, "'Dwelling the mind in quiet contemplation' is..."
"Sickness! This is not meditation. To sit for long periods and constrain the body—what benefit does this provide for the Principle? Listen to my verse: 'In life one sits and does not lie;
In death one lies and does not sit. Originally it is but a stinking skeleton; Why then establish merit and fault?

The Master said, 'I do not yet understand, Great Master, by what Dharma you instruct people. The Patriarch said, 'If I were to say that I have a Dharma to give to others, I would be deceiving you. However,' "
Furthermore, according to the circumstances, he was released from his bonds and given the provisional name Samādhi. Listen to my verse: "The self-nature precept is entirely without mind;
The self-nature wisdom is entirely without obstruction. Neither increasing nor decreasing, it is the true vajra; The body departing and the body arriving are fundamentally samādhi.

Upon hearing the verse, the Master repented and apologized, presenting this verse in return: "This illusory body of the five aggregates—how can illusion reach its ultimate end? I shall turn back toward the True."
The Master [Huineng] replied, "As for the Dharma, it is originally impure. The Patriarch agreed with this. He then returned to Yquan.
Chan Master Zhītōng of Guǎngzhōu (entry one). A native of Nánhǎi, he first visited the Sixth Patriarch and asked:
"Since I left home to become a monk, I have studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for over ten years, yet I have not yet understood its great meaning. I pray that the Upādhyāya will deign to instruct me."
The Patriarch said, "What is it that you have not yet understood? He replied, "I am doubtful about this: 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the nature of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss. The Patriarch asked, "How do you doubt this? He replied, "All sentient beings..."
All possess two bodies, namely the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The form-body is impermanent; it has arising and ceasing. The dharma-body is permanent;
it is without cognition and without awareness. As the Sutra says: "When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss.

I do not yet understand which body is in quiescent extinction and which body experiences bliss. If it is the form-body, then when the form-body perishes, the four great elements disperse entirely. [The text here breaks off.]
However, this is suffering. Suffering cannot be called pleasure. If the Dharma-body were quiescent extinction, it would be identical to grass, trees, tiles, and stones;
who then would experience pleasure? Furthermore, the Dharma-nature is the substance of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates are the function of arising and ceasing.

With one substance and five functions, arising and ceasing are constant. When there is arising, the function emerges from the substance; when there is cessation, the function is withdrawn back into the substance. If you listen...
If there is rebirth, then the categories of sentient beings are neither interrupted nor extinguished.

If rebirth were not permitted, then one would forever return to quiescent extinction, becoming identical to insentient things. In such a case, all dharmas would be suppressed by *nirvāṇa* and could not even arise;
what joy would there be in that? The Patriarch said: "You are a son of the Śākya; why do you practice the annihilationism of the non-Buddhists?"

You hold constant wrong views while discussing the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle. According to your understanding, you claim that apart from the physical body (rūpakāya), there is a separate dharma-body (dharmakāya) that transcends birth and death, seeking a state of quiescent extinction.
Furthermore, you infer the permanence and bliss of nirvana and speak of one who experiences it through a body.

You should know that this is merely to cling to the cycle of birth and death out of stinginess and to be addicted to worldly pleasures. You must now understand that the Buddha, for the sake of all deluded people who identify with the five [aggregates]...
The aggregation of the *skandhas* constitutes the aspect of one's own self-nature, while the differentiation of all phenomena constitutes the aspect of external objects.
Clinging to life and fearing death, they flow on and change from moment to moment; unaware that these are like dreams, illusions, or falsehoods, they undergo saṃsāra in vain.

Taking the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa* to be, on the contrary, a mark of suffering, they spend their days in frantic pursuit. Out of compassion for them, the Buddha revealed the true bliss of *nirvāṇa*, which is non-existent even for a single *kṣaṇa*.

There is the characteristic of arising, yet in each moment there is no characteristic of cessation; since there is nothing further to be extinguished through arising and cessation, this is the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śānti*).
At the time of this manifestation, there is even no measure of "manifestation. This is what is called "eternal bliss" (*nitya-sukha*).
This bliss has no experiencer, nor is there anyone who does not experience it. How could there be such designations as "one substance with five functions"? How much less need one speak of *nirvāṇa*?

To claim that all phenomena are suppressed so as never to arise again is to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Listen to my verse: The unsurpassed Great Nirvana is perfectly luminous, eternally tranquil, and illuminating.
The ignorant call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as annihilation. Those seeking the two vehicles regard it as non-action.
All these belong to the calculations of the deluded mind, the root of the sixty-two views. They falsely establish what is empty...
This is a provisional name. What is the meaning of ultimate reality? Only those of transcendent capacity penetrate it without grasping or rejecting.
By knowing the phenomena of the five aggregates and the "self" within the aggregates, one perceives all external forms and every characteristic of sound as equal to dreams and illusions.

One does not give rise to views of sage or ordinary person, nor does one form a conceptual understanding of nirvana. With the two extremes and the three temporal limits severed, one should always respond to all beings.
The faculty functions, yet one does not give rise to the thought of functioning; one discerns all phenomena, yet does not give rise to the thought of discernment.
When the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and the winds strike the mountains together, the bliss of true, eternal quiescence—the characteristics of nirvāṇa—are thus.
I now speak these words by force, so that you may abandon your false views; do not follow the literal meaning of my words, for I permit you to know but a small portion. The Master heard this verse.
He leaped for joy, prostrated himself, and withdrew.
(Twenty-five in total. National Teacher Huizhong of Guangzhai in the Western Capital was the son of the Ran family from Zhuji in Yue Province.
He first visited the Sixth Patriarch and attained sudden enlightenment into the essence of the mind.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who study the Chan school should follow the Buddha’s words. That which is the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle accords with the source of one's own mind;
that which is not definitive is not mutually permitted. This is like the worms within a lion’s body.

Now, if one who acts as a teacher for others becomes entangled in fame and profit, or opens up heterodox paths, what benefit is there for oneself or others? It is like a master craftsman of the world whose adze and axe do not injure his own hand."
What a fragrant elephant can carry, a donkey cannot endure.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The green creeper winds its way up to the very summit of the cold pine; the white clouds drift and flow, appearing and disappearing within the great void.
All phenomena are fundamentally at rest, yet it is people themselves who create the clamor."
Huanglong Nan raised [the case] and said: "What is all this fuss? *Du*! Xuedou said: "The National Teacher has run inside the pillar.
Do you see him? Do you see him? After a long pause, he said: "To show his head is to die."
The Master asked a monk, "From which direction have you come? The monk replied, "I have come from the South. The Master said, "What kind of teachers (knowledgeable ones) are there in the South?
The monk said, "There are quite many such teachers. The Master said, "How do they instruct their disciples? The monk said, "The teachers of that region directly point out to people:
'This very mind is Buddha. 'Buddha' has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*). You now fully possess the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; this nature is good."

It is able to raise the eyebrows and blink the eyes; it moves through coming and going and through stillness and activity throughout the entire body. When the head is touched, the head knows; when the foot is touched, the foot knows.
Therefore, it is called the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (Samyak-saṃbuddha). Apart from this, there is no other Buddha. This very body is subject to arising and ceasing.
The nature of the mind has, since beginningless time, never undergone arising or ceasing.
As for what arises and ceases, it is like a dragon shedding its bones, like a snake sloughing off its skin, or like a person leaving an old house; the body is impermanent, but its nature is eternal.
This is roughly what is taught in the South. The Master said: "If that were so, there would be no difference between this and the non-Buddhist Sāṃkhya heretics. They say: 'I..."
"This body and this nature are able to perceive pain and pleasure; when the body perishes, the spirit departs. It is like a house that is burning:

the master of the house departs, while the house itself is impermanent, yet the master of the house is eternal. If one examines it in this way, there is no distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox; which of these could be considered correct?
In my recent travels, I have frequently encountered such views, and they have become even more prevalent lately. They gather together and... [text ends]... three.
The assembly of five hundred [monks] looked up at the heavens and said: "This is the fundamental doctrine of the South.

They have altered the *Platform Sūtra*, interpolating vulgar talk and excising the sacred intent, thereby deluding and confusing later followers. How can this constitute the verbal teaching? Alas! Our school is lost.
If seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing were themselves Buddha-nature, then Vimalakīrti should not have said: 'The Dharma is free from seeing and hearing.'"

"Perception. If one perceives through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing while in the midst of conditioned activity, then that is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
The assembly asked again, "The *Lotus Sūtra* is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). How is this so?

The Master said, "When it says 'revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,' it does not even mention bodhisattvas or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha*), let alone ordinary sentient beings who are deluded and inverted. How could it be that they immediately become identical to the Buddha?"

"Is it knowledge and vision? The Sangha asked again, "Which one is the Buddha-mind? The Master said, "The walls, the tiles, and the rubble. [A monk] said, "This greatly contradicts the scriptural texts.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: 'Because it is apart from walls and insentient things, it is called Buddha-nature. Now you say..."

"This is the Buddha-mind. I do not yet understand whether the mind and nature are distinct or not. The Master said: "In delusion they are distinct; in awakening they are not distinct. [The student] asked:
"The sutras state that Buddha-nature is eternal and the mind is impermanent. Now you say they are not distinct. Why is this? The Master said:
"You merely rely on the words and do not rely on the meaning. It is like the cold months when water freezes into ice, and then upon reaching warmth..."
At that time, when the ice melts, it becomes water. When sentient beings are deluded, the nature of the knots forms the mind; when they awaken, the mind dissolves and returns to its nature.
If you insist that insentient things lack Buddha-nature, the Sūtra should not have stated that "the three realms are but mind. This would clearly be a contradiction on your own part.
"I do not contradict it. [The monk] asked, "Since that which is without emotion already possesses the nature of mind, does it also understand how to preach the Dharma?

The Master said, "It preaches incessantly and without interruption. [The monk] asked, "Why is it that I do not hear it? The Master said, "You yourself do not hear it. [The monk] asked, "Who is able to hear it?
The Master said, "All the sages are able to hear it. [The monk] asked, "Would this mean that sentient beings have no share in it? The Master—

[The monk] said, "I speak for the sake of sentient beings; I do not speak for the sake of the sages. [You] say that such-and-such a person is deaf and blind and does not hear the insentient preaching the Dharma, yet the Master ought to hear it.
The Master said, "I also do not hear it. [The monk] said, "Since the Master does not hear it, how do you know that the insentient are able to preach the Dharma?
The Master said, "It is fortunate that I do not hear it. If I were to hear it, you would not hear what I have heard."
[The student] asked: "When the Dharma is preached, do sentient beings hear it? The Master said: "If sentient beings were to hear it, they would no longer be sentient beings. [The student] asked:
"What scriptural authority is there for 'insentient things preaching the Dharma'? The Master said: "Have you not seen that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

'The lands preach, the sentient beings preach; all things of the three periods of time preach'? Are sentient beings not sentient? [The student] asked: "Master, you only speak of insentient things having Buddha-nature. The Master said: "..."
"How then is it with sentient beings? The Master said, "If even insentient things are thus, how much more so sentient beings?

If that were the case, as the teachers of the South previously claimed—that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the Buddha-nature—then they should not be judged the same as the non-Buddhists. The Master said: [This concludes the passage.]
It is not that one says others lack Buddha-nature. Do non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) not possess Buddha-nature? It is simply because their views are mistaken;

within a single dharma, they give rise to two views, and for that reason, it is incorrect. [The questioner] asks: "If both possess Buddha-nature, then when one kills a sentient being, there is the mutual repayment of karma through the commission of the act;

yet when one harms a non-sentient thing, no retribution is heard of. The Master said: "Sentient beings are the primary retribution (*vipāka*), whereas [non-sentient things] are what one reckons as 'self' and 'mine.'"

If one harbors resentment toward that which is insentient, there will be a retribution for the offense. Insentient things are the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment resulting from karma). Since there is no mind of resentment toward them, it is said that they do not receive retribution.
You say that within the teachings we only see sentient beings attain Buddhahood and do not see insentient things receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Yet, among the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, which one is insentient? The Master said: "It is like a Crown Prince; before he has received the throne..."
It is but a single body. After one has received the position [of Buddhahood], the entire realm belongs to the King; how could there be a separate reception of the position for a realm?
Now, it is only sentient beings who receive the prediction (vyākaraṇa). At the time they become Buddhas, the realms of the ten directions are entirely the body of Vairocana Buddha.
How could there be further insentient things that receive the prediction? Thus, all sentient beings dwell entirely within the body of the Buddha.
[Question: "If one defiles the Buddha’s body with excrement and urine, or pierces and tramples upon the Buddha’s body, would there not be sin?
The Master said: 'Sentient beings are entirely the Buddha; whom do you wish to make guilty? [Question: 'The sutra says that the Buddha’s body is without obstruction.
Now, to take conditioned, obstructive things as the Buddha’s body—does this not contradict the holy intent? The Master said: 'The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*...'"
[The student] said: "One cannot speak of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) apart from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Do you believe that form (*rūpa*) is empty? [The Master] said:
"These are the sincere words of the Buddha; how could I dare not believe them? [The student] said: "If form is already empty, how can there be any obstruction? [The student] said:

"Since the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is identical, if only one Buddha were to practice, all sentient beings should be liberated at that very moment. Since this is not the case now, [how can it be so? [The Master] said: "It is identical."

"Wherein does the meaning lie? The Master said: "Have you not seen the meaning of the Six Characteristics in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*? It says that within the same there is difference, and within difference there is sameness;

so it is with formation and destruction, and with the general and the particular. This applies to all categories. Although the various patriarchs and the Buddha share the same nature, it does not prevent each from practicing individually and attaining realization for themselves.
One has never seen another eat and be satiated by it. He asked: "How many teachers have you served? [The Master] replied: "I have shown my studies to them."
People say: "When one simply realizes the nature of consciousness, at the time of impermanence, one casts aside this 'shell-and-leak' body to one side;
the numinous mind and wisdom-nature depart in a transcendent manner—this is called liberation. How is this so? The Master said: "I have already explained this before;
it is still merely the measure of the Two Vehicles and the non-Buddhists. The Two Vehicles loathe and depart from birth-and-death, while delighting in Nirvana..."
The Way also says: "I have a great affliction: it is because I have a body. Thus, one proceeds toward the Ultimate Truth (*tattva*). A *srotāpanna* remains for eighty thousand *kalpas*;
those who have attained the other three fruits remain for sixty-four and twenty thousand *kalpas* respectively; a *pratyekabuddha* remains for ten thousand *kalpas*.

They abide in the state of non-attainment (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), as do the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) for eighty thousand *kalpas*, abiding in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). When these two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) have completed their *kalpas*, they are still able to turn back [from their state].

"The mind is directed toward the Way; those of external paths return to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). You say that Buddha-nature is of one kind—is it distinct [from them]? The Master said: "It cannot be said to be of one kind.
"How so? The Master said: "Some are entirely without arising or ceasing; some are half-arising and half-ceasing; some are half-arising and half-non-arising.
"Who provides this interpretation? The Master said: "In my place here, Buddha-nature is entirely without arising or ceasing. In the South..."
"Buddha-nature is half-born and half-extinguished; half is neither born nor extinguished. How do you distinguish between them?

The Master said, "In this state, body and mind are as one, with nothing remaining outside the body; therefore, it is entirely neither born nor extinguished. As for you in the South, the body is impermanent."
“Divinity is eternal; therefore, half of it arises and perishes, while the other half neither arises nor perishes.

How can the Master’s physical body be the same as the Dharma-body, which is neither arising nor perishing? The Master said, “How have you fallen into a heterodox path? He replied, “When did I fall into a heterodox path?
The Master said, “Do you not see that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: ‘To see by form or to seek by sound’?”

All practice deviant paths. Is what you have now seen not like this? You say that such-and-such a person once studied the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna and also saw their path—the state of the Middle Way and True Nature, which is neither arising nor ceasing.

You also saw texts stating that while these aggregates cease and those aggregates arise, and the body undergoes transformation, the consciousness does not perish. How can you utterly dismiss them all?
[This is] the same as the two views of permanence and annihilation held by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The Master said: "You have studied the unsurpassed, truly correct Way that transcends the world;
do you instead study worldly birth-and-death and the two views of annihilation and permanence? Have you not seen what Master Zhaopeng said: 'To discuss the Truth is to oppose the conventional;

to follow the conventional is to deviate from the Truth. Because one deviates from the Truth, one is deluded regarding one's nature and cannot return. Because one opposes the conventional, one speaks of the flavorless [emptiness], yet...'"
"It has no flavor. Those of middling capacity are as if they exist and yet as if they have perished; those of inferior capacity clap their hands and pay it no heed.
Do you now wish to emulate the inferior capacity and laugh at the Great Way? The Master also said, "The mind itself is Buddha.
A teacher of the South also says, "The mind itself is Buddha. How can there be difference or agreement? You, Master, should not consider yourself right and others wrong. The Master said:
Some say that names differ while the substance is the same; others say that the substance is the same while the names differ. It is on this account that confusion arises.

For instance, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, *tathatā*, and *buddha-dhātu* differ in name but are identical in substance. Conversely, the true mind and the deluded mind, or Buddha-wisdom and worldly wisdom, are identical in name but differ in substance.
In the south, there are those who mistakenly take the deluded mind to be the true mind, identifying a thief as their own son;

they grasp at worldly knowledge and call it the Buddha-mind, like confusing fish eyes with bright pearls. These cannot be treated as the same; matters must be carefully distinguished. [The questioner] asked:
"How can one avoid this error? The Master said: "You need only minutely observe each of the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)."

[The Master] said, "When you investigate to the very limit, is there even a hair’s breadth that can be apprehended? He replied, "If I observe closely, I do not see a single thing that can be apprehended.
The Master asked, "Do you destroy the characteristics of body and mind? He replied, "Body and mind are by nature detached; what is there to be destroyed?
The Master asked, "Apart from body and mind, is there still anything else? He replied, "Since body and mind have no exterior, how could there be anything further? The Master said, "You..."
"Does one destroy the characteristics of the world? Since the characteristics of the world are themselves non-characteristics, why use further destruction?
The Master said, "If that were so, you would have transcended all faults."
The Master asked Nanquan, "Where have you come from? Nanquan replied, "From Jiangxi. The Master said, "Have you brought back the portrait of Master Ma?
Nanquan said, "This very one is it. The Master said, "What about the one behind it? Nanquan then desisted.
Changqing Ling said, "It is very much like not knowing.
Baofu Zhan said, "He has simply not yet arrived here at this monastery.
When Danxia visited the Master, he happened upon him while he was sleeping. Danxia asked the attendant, Tanyuan, "Is the National Teacher in? Yuan—
Yunzai said, "I am here, yet I simply do not see the guest. Changxia said, "That is too profound and remote. Dongshan Liangjie said, "Do not say that; even the Buddha’s eye cannot see it.
Changxia said, "The dragon gives birth to a dragon; the phoenix gives birth to a phoenix. When Master [Shishuang] woke from his sleep, Dongshan recounted the previous conversation.
The Master struck him with twenty blows and drove him out. Upon hearing this, Changxia remarked, "He is truly no false heir to the National Teacher of Nanyang."
One day Danxia came again; as soon as he spread his sitting mat, the Master said, "No need, no need. Danxia stepped back three paces.
The Master said, "So it is, so it is. Danxia stepped forward three paces. The Master said, "Not so, not so. Danxia circled around.
He circumambulated the meditation seat once and departed. The Master said, "The time since the Sage has passed; people are mostly indolent.
Thirty years from now, it will be difficult even to find a single monk."
Daguang Zhe said: "Danxia may truly be said to harbor a supreme treasure; when he encounters one of wisdom, its brilliance increases.
National Teacher Huiguo’s great gate stands wide open—only those who are the right person can ascend it.
Is there anyone present now who can act as Danxia’s advocate? Come forth and meet with Daguang! Is there such a person? After a long silence, he said: "No."
This is a guest from Dragon Gate; one must strictly avoid having one's forehead marked with a dot.
Chan Master Xitang Zang arrived there on a mission for Mazu. The Master asked, "What Dharma does your teacher preach?
Zang walked from west to east and stood there. The Master said, "Is that all? Is there anything else? Zang walked from east to west and stood there. The Master—
Xuefeng said, "This belongs to Master Ma. How do you understand it, worthy one? Zang replied, "I have already presented it to the Master long ago.
Baofu Zhuan remarked, "The Xutang has not failed Master Ma by a small margin."
When Magu arrived, he struck his monk’s staff once and stood there upright. The Master said, "Since you have already done so, what need is there to see me?
Magu struck his staff once again. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Wild fox spirit! Get out!"
Xuedou said: "Had he not reached this point...
One day the Master called his attendant; the attendant responded. He called him thus three times, and the attendant responded three times.
The Master said: "I thought it was I who had failed you; who would have known that it was you who had failed me?"
Zhaozhou said, "It is like a person writing characters in the dark; though the characters themselves are not formed, the traces of the brushstrokes are already manifest.
Xuedou then gave a shout. Touzi said, "Why do you force people so? Xuedou said, "You rootless fellow!"
Xuansha said, "In fact, it was the attendant who understood. Xuedou said, "This stops the prisoner but increases his cleverness.
Yunmen asked, "What is the place where the National Teacher betrayed the attendant? If you can understand this, it is still groundless.
Xuedou said, "It turns out he did not understand. Yunmen asked, "What is the place where the attendant betrayed [the National Teacher]?"
"Regarding the place where he owed the National Teacher: even grinding one's bones to powder would not suffice to repay him.
Xuedou said, "Pointless, pointless. Fayan said, "Go for now; come back at another time. Xuedou said, "You cannot deceive me.
Xinghua said, "One blind man leading a crowd of blind men. Xuedou said, "Truly blind. When someone asked Xuedou, he then—
Strike! This too must be scrutinized by those from all quarters.
Xuedou’s verse says: "The meeting of teacher and disciple is no trivial matter; without cause, they walk together through the weeds."
"I owe you; I owe you. Let no one ask about it. Let the world compete for it as they will.
Cuiyan’s true verse says: "The attendant was never once called back. The National Teacher raised wind and thunder on dry land.
Had we met him at that moment, The nine-fold elixir would have turned to ash."
There was a Tripitaka Master named Daren who had attained the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others. Emperor Suzong invited the Master [Baizhang] to test him.
As soon as the Tripitaka Master saw the Master, he prostrated and stood to his right. The Master asked, "Have you attained the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others?
The Tripitaka Master replied, "I dare not say so. The Master asked, "Tell me, where is this old monk right now? The Tripitaka Master replied, "The Master is the teacher of the entire nation."
"How can you go to Xichuan to watch the boat races? The Master remained silent for a long while and then asked again, "Tell me, where am I right now?
Zang replied, "The Master is the teacher of an entire nation; how can you go to Tianjin Bridge to watch a monkey being entertained?
The Master remained silent for a long while and then asked again, "Tell me, where am I right now? Zang was at a loss.
Cuo. The Master rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit! Where is his supernormal power of knowing others' minds? Cuo had no reply.
Xuansha said, "Tell me, did you see him during the previous two instances? Yangshan said, "The previous two instances involved engaging with external objects;
later, he entered the Samādhi of Self-Enjoyment, which is why he was not seen."
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "The Third Time the Great-Eared Tripitaka Master Could Not See the National Teacher—where, then, was the National Teacher?
Zhaozhou replied, "He was inside the Tripitaka Master’s nostrils. Later, the monk asked Xuansha about this.
"Since it is already inside the nostrils, why can one not see it? Sandou said, "It is precisely because it is too close.
Baizhang Wenyuan said, "If National Teacher [Huikong] were within the 'nostril-roar' of the Tripitaka Master, what would be difficult about seeing him?
One simply does not realize that the National Teacher is within the eyes of the Tripitaka Master."
The Master asked Imperial Attendant Zilin, "What is the practice upon which you, Great Virtue, have focused? He replied, "I lecture on the *Qinglong* commentary.
The Master asked, "Is that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? He replied, "It is. The Master said, "Regarding the first two characters of the sūtra text, what word do they form?
He replied, "'Thus' (*evam*'). The Master said, "What is this?"
Mingzhao spoke on his behalf, saying: "What was seen at Vulture Peak in the past is what is being seen directly today.

The Master asked the Palace Attendant, "What is the meaning of 'Buddha'? He replied, "It means 'awakening' (jue). The Master said, "Has the Buddha ever been deluded? He replied, "He has never been deluded.
The Master said, "If so, what use is awakening? The Attendant was speechless.
The Palace Attendant said, "I request that you, Master, establish a thesis; I shall refute it. Or, I shall establish a thesis; you, Master, shall refute it.
First, I request that you, Master, establish a thesis. The Master said, "The thesis has been established. The Attendant asked, "What is this thesis?
The Master said, "Indeed, you do not see it. The Attendant was speechless. The Master said, "This is not within your sphere."
The Master asked the Palace Attendant, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From south of the city. The Master said, "What color is the grass south of the city?
He replied, "It is yellow. The Master then asked a young boy, and the boy also said, "It is yellow.
The Master said, "This very boy could also be granted the purple robe before the imperial curtain and discuss the profound mysteries in the presence of the Emperor."
Fengfu wished to comment on the *Siyi jing* (Sutra of Mindfulness). The Master asked, "In general, when one comments on a sutra, one must first understand the Buddha’s intent;

if you do not understand the Buddha’s intent, how can you possibly explain it? The Master then ordered his attendant to bring a basin of water, place seven grains of rice in the water, and lay a single chopstick across the top. He then asked, "What is the meaning of this? Fengfu was at a loss.

[The Master] said, "I do not yet understand the old monk’s own meaning, let alone the Buddha’s meaning. Furthermore, how could you possibly annotate the sutras? The Master asked the Dharma Master, "What sutra are you lecturing on?
He replied, "The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only). The Master said, "'The triple world is mind-only; all phenomena are consciousness-only.
How do you understand this? The Dharma Master had no reply. The Master pointed to the curtain and asked, "What dharma is this? [The Dharma Master] replied, "..."

[The Master] spoke of the dharma of form. The Master said, "The Great Master was granted the purple robe before the imperial curtain and discussed the profound mysteries before the Emperor; yet he did not even observe the five precepts. The Dharma Seat Master asked, "In the School of the Patriarchs, what is it that is transmitted and maintained? The Master replied, "And what is it that you, Master of the Dharma Seat, transmit and maintain? [The Master] said, "The Three Sutras and Five Treatises. The Master said, "They are all but cubs of the lion. The Master of the Dharma Seat bowed and departed. The Master called out, "Master of the Dharma Seat! The Master of the Dharma Seat turned back. The Master said, "I have already let you go; why do you turn back? The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "To ask for the meaning of the previous words. The Master said, "If you had not turned back, I would have hit you. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I am not afraid of being hit. The Master said, "I do not strike those who are not afraid. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I am not afraid of those who do not strike. The Master said, "I do not speak to those who are not afraid. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not listen to those who do not speak. The Master said, "I do not teach those who do not listen. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not learn from those who do not teach. The Master said, "I do not know those who do not learn. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not understand those who do not know. The Master said, "I do not see those who do not understand. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not perceive those who do not see. The Master said, "I do not hear those who do not perceive. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not experience those who do not hear. The Master said, "I do not encounter those who do not experience. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not meet those who do not encounter. The Master said, "I do not greet those who do not meet. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not salute those who do not greet. The Master said, "I do not bow to those who do not salute. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not pay homage to those who do not bow. The Master said, "I do not prostrate to those who do not pay homage. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not perform the full prostration to those who do not prostrate. The Master said, "I do not offer incense to those who do not prostrate. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not scatter flowers to those who do not offer incense. The Master said, "I do not make offerings to those who do not scatter flowers. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not make merit to those who do not make offerings. The Master said, "I do not cultivate virtue to those who do not make merit. The Master of the Dharma Seat said, "I do not practice the Way to those who do not cultivate virtue. The Master said, "I do not attain Buddhahood to those who do not practice the Way.
