"What instruction [should I give]? The Master said, "Tell him it is not a thing.
Layman Pang asked, "Water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a ten-thousand-hu vessel; how is this principle so? The Master said:
"I have no water here, nor do I have a boat. What need is there to speak of sinews and bones?
This is from the lineage of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi of Jiangxi, the third generation of Mount Nanyue.
Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan of Chizhou (14th in the lineage), a native of the Wang family in Zhengzhou, addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Way of Dīpaṃkara Buddha is already exhausted. If one gives rise to all phenomena through the thoughts of the mind, they are all empty, false, and unreal. Why is this?"
If the mind itself does not exist, how can it give rise to all phenomena? It is like a shadow following a form, or discriminating within empty space;
it is like a person attempting to capture sound and place it inside a chest, or like blowing into a net, wishing to make it full of air.

Therefore, the ancient masters said: "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not a thing. This is merely to instruct you brothers in your practice. According to the teachings, even a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground...
Abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they attain the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
Spontaneously obtaining all meditative concentrations, liberations, and the wondrous applications of supernormal powers, they reach all worlds and universally manifest form-bodies.

They may manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, or enter parinirvāṇa. They cause the immeasurable to enter a single pore; by expounding a single phrase, [they reveal the infinite].

Even after immeasurable kalpas, its meaning is not exhausted. Though one may teach and transform immeasurable billions of sentient beings and attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), this is still termed the ignorance regarding the knowable (jñeya-āvaraṇa-moha).
This most subtle ignorance regarding the knowable is utterly at odds with the Way; it is a great difficulty, indeed a great difficulty.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "To call it 'suchness' (tathatā) is already to have altered it. These days, teachers and monks must walk among the heterodox classes.
Guizong said, "Though one performs the deeds of an animal, one does not receive the retribution of an animal. The Master said, "Old fellow Meng, you go about in such a manner again!"
Deshan Mian said, "Nanquan has been poisoned. Langya Huijue said, "When meeting water, drink the water;
when meeting grass, eat the grass. How could one know the conduct of a beast?"
He addressed the assembly, saying: "All you venerable sons of the Buddha, when I was eighteen years old, I already knew how to make a living.
Is there anyone here now who knows how to make a living? Come forward and let us deliberate together. After a long silence, he looked around at the great assembly and said:
"One must indeed be such a person before it can be achieved. Take care!"
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra fought each other at the third watch last night;
I gave each of them thirty blows of the staff and sent them out of the monastery. Zhaozhou stepped forward from the crowd and asked, "Whom does the Master intend for the staff to strike?
The Master replied, "Where is the fault of Old Wang? Zhaozhou then prostrated himself.
Yunmen spoke on his behalf, saying: "I deeply appreciate the Master’s compassion; I shall return to the shelter of your robes and bowl to attain peace and happiness.
He also spoke on his behalf, saying: "To eliminate harm for the sake of the assembly."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Old Teacher Wang is selling himself; is there anyone who will buy him? At that time, a monk came forward from the assembly and said, "I will buy him.
The Master said, "Neither as something precious nor as something cheap—how will you buy him? The monk was speechless.
Zhaozhou said, "Next year, I will make a cloth robe for you, Master.
Wolong Qiu said, "The Master belongs to me.
Xuedou said, "Although these masters compete to buy it, they nonetheless do not understand the turning of the pivot. Now tell me, South..."
"Does Nanquan still consent? Xuedou also intended to offer a price for this; he would have had Nanquan with no way to advance and no door to retreat through.
After a long silence, he said: "The Master cannot be accommodated elsewhere."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Since my youth, Old Master Wang has raised a water buffalo. If I intend to pasture it on the east bank of the stream, I cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass;
if I intend to pasture it on the west bank of the stream, I cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass."
"It is not as good as taking a little bit according to one's capacity.
[The monk] said, "In that case, it is not seen at all. Yunmen said, "Now tell me: do you take it inside the ox, or do you take it outside the ox?
Even if you can explain it so that the place of 'taking' is clear, I will ask you further: where is the ox to be found?"
Daguang Zhe said, "Yunmen only knows how to seek out the ox; he does not know how to pass the needle through its nostrils.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "The Great Master Mazu of Jiangxi says, 'This very mind is Buddha. Old Teacher Wang does not speak thus:
'It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. In speaking thus, is there any fault? At that time, Zhaozhou came forth."
They prostrated themselves, and the Master then descended from his seat.
Miaoxi offered this verse: "I have emptied my belly and turned over my guts to speak to you; I know not for what reason you still hesitate.
Now is the very time to take it up with fierce resolve; Entrust it to those in the world who are free from affairs."
Later, there was a monk who asked Zhaozhou, "After the Senior Monk has finished his prostrations and departed, what is the meaning of this?
Zhaozhou said, "You should go ask the Abbot. The monk then asked the Master (Zhaozhou), and the Master said, "He, however, understood my meaning."
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The Way is not outside of things; that which is outside of things is not the Way. When Zhaozhou came forward and asked, "What is the Way outside of things?
the Master struck him. Zhaozhou grabbed hold of the staff and said, "Master, do not strike me; you may strike others in the future.
The Master threw down the staff and said, "It is easy to distinguish dragons from snakes, but it is difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk."
The Master was with Luzu, Guizong, and Shanshan while drinking tea. As they were doing so, Guizong lifted up his cup and said, "When the world had not yet been formed, there already was this.
The Master said, "Nowadays people recognize only this, yet they do not recognize the world. Guizong said, "Yes.
The Master asked, "Does my elder brother share this same view? Guizong lifted up his cup and said, "Into the world!"
"Before it is accomplished, can you say it? The Master made a gesture with his palm. Zong made a gesture with his face as if receiving the palm.
The Master, together with Guizong and Magu, went to pay his respects to National Teacher Zhong.
On the way, the Master drew a circle on the ground and said, "If you can say something, then we shall go; if you cannot say it, we shall not go. Zong sat down inside the circle. Magu—
He performed a woman’s bow. The Master said, "If that is so, then you will not go. Zong asked, "What kind of mental activity is this?
Thereupon, he turned back.
Cuiyan Zhi said, "Had I seen him at that moment, I would have given each of them a blow of the staff, so as to ensure peace throughout the world."
Foyin Yuan said: "Guizong and Magu possessed a majestic bearing like that of kings, yet they fell into Nanquan’s trap.
At that time, when they saw him draw a circle, they simply brushed their sleeves and departed. Even if Nanquan had possessed supernatural powers, [they would have been beyond his reach]."
It was also three thousand *li* away.
The Master, along with Luzu, Shanshan, and Guizong, took leave of Mazu and each planned to dwell in a hermitage. As they parted ways midway, [Mazu said]:
The Master planted his staff on the ground and said, "If you can speak, you are obstructed by this; if you cannot speak, you are also obstructed by this.
Yunmen Zong dragged the staff and struck him, saying, "It is just this very thing. What does Old Master Wang mean by 'obstructed' or 'unobstructed'?
Luzu said, "This single phrase alone spreads throughout the world. Yunmen Zong said, "Is there anything that does not spread?"
[The Master] asked, "How? The Patriarch said, "There is. Dongshan asked, "What is that which does not scatter? The Patriarch made the gesture of clapping his hands.
While the Master and Xiangshan were warming themselves by the fire, the Master said, "Without pointing east or marking west, speak directly of your fundamental matter.
Xiangshan thrust a fire-tongs into the brazier. The Master said, "Even if it were exactly like this, you would still fall short of Wangshi."
The Master said, "A single thread from Wáng Lǎoshī. He then asked Zhàozhōu. Zhàozhōu drew a circle and placed a dot within it.
The Master said, "Even if you were to do so, you would still fall short of Wáng Lǎoshī by a single thread."
The Master asked Shenshan, "Where have you come from? Shanshan replied, "I have come from beating a sieve. The Master said, "Do you beat it with your hands or with your feet?
Shanshan had no reply. The Master said, "Ask me that question yourself. Shanshan repeated his previous question. The Master said, "Memorize this clearly and present it to those with the clear eye."
The Master sent a letter to Zhunyu, saying: "Principle changes according to phenomena; its vastness is not external. Phenomena attain harmony with principle;
their stillness is not internal. A monk asked Zhunyu, "What is meant by 'vastness is not external'? Zhunyu said, "It does no harm to answer a hundred for one question.
The monk asked, "What is meant by 'stillness is not internal'? Zhunyu said, "To perceive forms and hear sounds is not it."

"Excellent hands," [the Master] said. He then questioned Zhaozhou; Zhaozhou made the gesture of eating a meal. The monk followed up with his subsequent remark, and Zhaozhou made the gesture of wiping his mouth.
He then questioned Changsha Cen; Cen stared at him with wide-open eyes. The monk followed up with his subsequent remark, and Cen closed his eyes to indicate his understanding.
When the monk reported these instances to the Master, the Master said, "These three men are not mistaken; they truly deserve to be my disciples."
One day, the Master closed the door of his quarters and surrounded the exterior with ashes, saying, "If anyone can speak a word that hits the mark, I shall open the door.
The assembly offered various responses, but most failed to accord with his intent. Zhaozhou said, "Heaven! Heaven! Thereupon, the Master opened the door.
Zhaozhou asked, "After the Master passes away, where will you go? The Master said, "I shall go to become a water buffalo on the mountain below.
Zhaozhou said, "Thank you for the instruction, Master. The Master said, "Last night at the third watch, the moon shone through the window."
The Master was holding a memorial feast for Master Ma. He asked the monks, "Tell me, will Master Ma come? No one in the assembly could answer.
Dongshan said, "He will come when he has a companion. The Master remarked, "Although this boy is young, he is quite capable of being refined.
Dongshan replied, "Master, do not treat a person of quality as if they were common."
The Master was cutting thatch when a monk asked, "Where does the road to Nanquan lead?
The Master held up his sickle and said, "This sickle of mine was bought for thirty coins. The monk said, "I am not asking about this;
where does the road to Nanquan lead? The Master replied, "It works most efficiently."
The Master asked the rector, "What are you doing today during the communal labor? The rector replied, "We are hauling the millstone.
The Master said, "You may haul the millstone as you wish, but you must not move the central pillar. The rector was left speechless.
The Master held up a ball and asked a monk, "Which of these is like this one? The monk said, "It is not like it.
The Master said, "Where did you see that one, that you say it is not like this? The monk said, "If you ask about my own realization, I ask the Master to set down the object in his hand.
The Master said, "I grant you a single eye."
The Master was once confronted by a dispute between the two halls over a cat. He then picked up the cat and said, "Monks, if you can speak, I shall not kill it;
if you cannot speak, I shall kill it. The assembly remained silent. The Master then killed it.
Xuedou’s verse says: Both halls are filled with Chan monks; Stirring up dust and smoke, there is no help for it.
Fortunately, Nanquan was able to issue the command; With one stroke, he cut them both in two, regardless of bias.
After a short while, Zhaozhou came from outside. The Master brought up the matter for him; Zhaozhou took off his sandals, placed them on his head, and went out.
The Master said, "If you had been here, you would have saved the cat."
Cuiyan Zhi said: "The Great and the Small Zhaozhou can only save themselves.
Xuedou’s verse says: "When the public case is brought to completion, one asks Zhaozhou; he wanders at leisure through the city of Chang'an."
"Straw sandals on the head—no one understands this. Upon returning to the mountain home, one simply rests.
When the Master was staying at his hermitage, a monk came to visit. The Master said, "I am going up the mountain to perform manual labor. At mealtime, you, Venerable One, should prepare the rice.
After you have eaten, please send a portion back for me. At the time of the meal, the monk prepared the rice, ate it himself, and then took the cooking utensils.
He broke everything at once and lay down upon the bed. The Master waited for him to leave, but when he returned and saw the monk lying prostrate, the Master also went and lay down beside him.
The monk then rose and departed. The Master said, "How remarkably sharp and quick-witted!

Later, after the Master had established his own residence, he remarked, "When I was staying at my former hermitage, there was a certain sharp-witted practitioner; even until now, I have not seen him again."
Cuiyan Zhi said: "Those two fellows did not even reach the village, much less the inn.
The Master entered the garden and saw a monk; he threw a piece of tile or rubble at him. The monk turned his head, and the Master stood on one leg. The monk was speechless.
The Master returned, and the monk followed him to request further instruction, saying: "Master, when you just now threw a piece of tile or rubble at me, was it not..."
[The Master] was not alerting someone in particular. The Master said, "What about when [a monk] stands on one foot? The monk had no reply.
The Master asked another monk, "There was a fine wind last night. The monk said, "There was a fine wind last night. The Master said, "It blew down a pine tree in front of the gate.
The monk said, "It blew down a pine tree in front of the gate. He then asked yet another monk, "There was a fine wind last night. The monk said—
"What wind is this? The Master said, "It blows down a pine tree in front of the gate. [The monk] asked, "What kind of pine tree is it?
The Master said, "One gains, one loses."
Cuiyan Zhen said: "Among the assembly, some deliberate thus: 'In the first instance, he answered according to reality, which is why it is called a gain;
in the latter instance, he ought not to have asked, "What wind is this? Therefore, it is called a loss.
They know only that the chariots and books are unified and that jade and clay are of one substance, yet they do not understand the source of the Way or the depth of its principle."
Do you understand? When meeting a swordsman on the road, one must present one’s own sword;
if one is not a poet, one does not offer a poem. There was a hermit who lived in a hut; people said to him, "Nanquan has recently appeared in the world; why do you not go to pay him homage?
The hermit replied, "It is not only Nanquan—it would be the same even if the thousand Buddhas were to appear. When the Master heard this, he ordered Zhaozhou to go [to see the hermit].
Kan-zan examined him. As soon as the Governor saw the Master of the Hermitage, he prostrated himself; the Master paid him no heed.

The Governor walked from west to east and from east to west, standing there, yet the Master still ignored him. The Governor said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated," and pulling down the curtain, he departed.
He presented this to his teacher. The teacher said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
Xuedou said, "How great were Nanquan and Zhaozhou, yet they were exposed by this fellow carrying a wooden board!"

One day, the Master went down to a village estate. The headman had prepared offerings in advance to welcome him. The Master said, "I have lived here as usual and have never let anyone know of my movements;
why have you made such preparations in advance? The headman replied, "Last night, the local tutelary deity informed me. The Master said, "..."
Master Wang was weak in his practice. He was spotted by a ghost and spirit.
An attendant asked, "Great Good Friend, why were you spotted by a ghost and spirit? The Master said, "Offer another portion of rice before the local deity."
Daguan Ying said, "When Nanquan was questioned by this monk, he could not help but make his living inside a ghost cave.
While the Master was playing with the moon, a monk asked, "When will I be able to become like this? The Master replied, "Master Wang has been so for twenty years."
[The Master] said, "Previously, I too came in this very way. The monk asked, "And how is it now? The Master then returned to his quarters.
A monk, having finished his greeting, stood with his hands folded. The Master said, "Too worldly! The monk joined his palms.
The Master said, "Too monastic! The monk was speechless.
A monk asked, "When Niutou had not yet met the Fourth Patriarch, why did the hundred birds bring flowers to offer him?
The Master said, "Because he was treading the steps of the Buddhas at every step. [The monk asked,] "After he had seen him, why did they no longer bring flowers to offer him?
The Master said, "Even if they had not come at all, they would still have been one thread's breadth behind Old Wang."
A monk asked, "One cannot attain 'this very mind is Buddha,' yet one cannot attain 'neither mind nor Buddha. What is your intention, Master?
The Master said, "You simply take it as 'this very mind is Buddha' and that is enough. Why speak further of attainment or non-attainment?
It is just like when you have finished eating and walk up and down the east and west corridors; you do not need to ask everyone whether you have attained it or not."
The Master asked Liangqin, "In the void eon (*śūnyakalpa*), is there still a Buddha? He replied, "There is. The Master said, "Who is he?
He replied, "Liangqin. The Master said, "In what land does he dwell? Qian was speechless.
The Master asked a monk, "When you do not think of good, do not think of evil, and do not think of anything at all—bring me back your original face.
The monk said, "There is nothing that can be revealed."
Dongshan said, "Have you ever used this to instruct others?
A monk asked the Master, "When residing in the master's quarters, what do you use as a guide? The Master said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox;
when I rose at dawn, I had lost my fire."
The Master asked the presiding lecturer, "What sutra are you lecturing on? He replied, "The Sutra of Maitreya’s Descent. The Master said, "When will Maitreya descend?
He replied, "He is currently in the heavenly palace and has not yet come. The Master said, "There is no Maitreya in heaven, and there is no Maitreya on earth."
Dongshan raised this question to Yunju. Yunju said, "There is no Maitreya above the heavens; there is no Maitreya beneath the earth.
I wonder who gave him his name? When Dongshan was thus questioned, his meditation seat shook violently, and he said:
When I was at Yunyan, I asked [the Master], and the old man caused the brazier to tremble.
Today, when I am questioned by you, my whole body breaks into a sweat.
There was a presiding lecturer who took his leave; the Master asked him, "Where are you going? He replied, "Down to the mountain. The Master said, "First of all, you must not..."
[The Master] slandered his royal teacher, saying, "How would one dare? When the Master sneezed, he asked, "How much is it? The host had no reply.
A monk asked, "At the top of a hundred-foot pole, how does one advance further? The Master said, "Advance one step further. He then questioned Yanguan.
The Official said, "At the top of a hundred-foot pole, what need is there to advance further? The monk did not approve and left, shaking his sleeves.
The Official then struck him. Chengtian Zong said, "If you would study Nanquan, you must take a step forward;
if you would study Yanguan, you must take a step back. Discern this with clear eyes."
Dafu Lu Xun asked the Master, "Master Zhao is truly extraordinary; he explains that 'Heaven and earth share the same root as I, and the myriad things are one body with me.
The Master pointed to a flower in the courtyard and said, 'Dafu, when people of this age see this single stalk of a flower, it is like being in a dream.'"

The Master was with a high official when they saw someone playing *shuanglu* (double-sixes). The official picked up the dice and asked, "Whether it is so or not so, what is it like when one simply trusts the outcome?
The Master picked up the dice, threw them, and said, "A set of stinking bones, eighteen in total.
The official asked, "In my home there is a piece of stone; sometimes I sit upon it, sometimes I lie upon it. Now I intend to carve it..."
"Can one become a Buddha? Can one not? The Master said, "One can. The Grand Councilor said, "Can one not? The Master said, "One cannot.

The Grand Councilor asked the Master, "The Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā possesses so many hands and eyes; what does he do with them? The Master said, "It is like a state employing a Grand Councilor; what would he do [without them]?"

The Great Officer said to the Master, "I, your disciple, also have a modest understanding of the Buddha-dharma. The Master asked, "Great Officer, how do you conduct yourself throughout the twelve periods of the day?
The Officer replied, "I am not attached to even a single thread of silk. The Master said, "You are still a man standing below the steps. He added further, "Have you not heard it said:
'A sovereign who possesses the Way does not admit ministers who possess mere cleverness'?"
The Great Officer returned to his administrative seat in Xuancheng. The Master asked him, "When you leave that place, how will you govern the people?
The officer replied, "I shall govern the people with wisdom. The Master said, "If that is so, then all the living beings in that land will surely suffer the calamities of fire and water.
The officer was speechless.
Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai of Hongzhou (sixteen fascicles). He was a native of Changle, Fuzhou. The Master attended upon the Great Master Mazu as his attendant.

Whenever a donor brought offerings of rice for the midday meal, as soon as the Master lifted the lid of the serving tray, the Great Master Mazu would pick up a piece of *hubing* (a flat, unleavened cake) and show it to the assembly, asking, "What is this? This occurred every day. After three years had passed, the Master [attained realization].
At that moment, he had an awakening.
While the Master was attending upon Mazu Daoshi, they were out walking in the mountains when they suddenly saw wild ducks fly past.
The Patriarch asked, "What is that? The Master replied, "Wild ducks. The Patriarch asked, "Where have they gone? The Master said, "They flew away. The Patriarch then grabbed the Master.
Nitou was struck by the Master, who, in his agony, cried out in a broken voice, "Ayaya! Ayaya! The Patriarch said, "You say it flies away again?
At these words, the Master attained awakening; sweat poured down his back. He returned to the attendant's quarters and wept bitterly.
A fellow practitioner asked, "Do you remember your parents? The Master said, "No. He asked, "Have you been scolded by someone?
The Master said, "No. He asked, "Then why are you crying? The Master said, "My nostrils were pinched by the Great Master; the pain is unbearable.

The fellow practitioner said, "What karmic conditions prevent you from being in accord with one another? The Master said, "Go ask the Abbot yourself. The fellow practitioner then went to question the Abbot.
Master Ma said, "Attendant Hai, what is the reason you have not attained realization? Go into the quarters and weep, and tell the Abbot to explain it for you.

The Master said, "He has understood; you should go ask him yourself. After they returned to the quarters together, the attendant said, "The Abbot said, 'You have understood,' and told me to ask you myself. The Master then laughed heartily, saying, "Ha ha! The attendant then departed.
[The Master] said, "Just now you were weeping; why do you laugh now? The Master replied, "Just now I was weeping; now I am laughing. His colleagues were left bewildered.
Miaoxi composed a verse on this: Sometimes laughing, sometimes weeping, Sorrow and joy intermingled, silently urging one on.

The next day, when Master Mazu ascended the hall and the assembly had just gathered, the Master [Baizhang] stepped forward and rolled up his sitting mat. Mazu immediately descended from the seat and returned to his quarters.
He then asked the Master, "Just now when I ascended the hall, I did not say a single word. Why did you roll up your mat?"
The Master said, "Yesterday, I was pinched by you, O Patriarch, until my nose ached with pain.
The Patriarch said, "Where did you direct your attention yesterday? The Master said, "Today, my nose does not ache anymore.
The Patriarch said, "You have deeply grasped the matter of today. The Master bowed and withdrew.

In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he once dwelt on this mountain. When a student asked him, "Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect?
he replied, "I do not fall within cause and effect. Consequently, for five hundred lifetimes, he fell into the body of a wild fox.

Now he requests the Master to provide a turning word in his stead. He then repeated the previous question. The Master said, "One does not obscure cause and effect. At these words, the old man was enlightened.

He attained great enlightenment. He prostrated and said, "I have already cast off my wild fox body. I reside behind the mountain; I beg that you grant me the funeral rites accorded to a deceased monk.
The Master ordered the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) to strike the gavel and announce: "After the meal, we shall escort the deceased monk.

The assembly was all astonished and asked, "Since no one has passed away, why are we to escort a deceased monk? After the meal, the Master led the assembly to the base of a cliff behind the mountain. With...
Taking up his staff, he pulled out a dead fox and performed its cremation according to the rites. That evening, the Master ascended the hall and recounted the preceding circumstances.
Huangbo stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "If an ancient master gave a single erroneous response, he fell into the body of a fox for five hundred lifetimes;
had he not erred at each turn, what would he have become? The Master said, "Come closer, and I will tell you. Huangbo approached him. The Master said:
The Master gave him a slap with his palm. Clapping his hands, he laughed and said, "I thought the beard was red;
here is yet another red-bearded barbarian. Dharmatā Sīmā asked Guishan about this. Guishan shook the door panels three times. Dharmatā said, "That is too crude.
Guishan said, "The Buddha-dharma is not a matter of this kind. Guishan then raised the same question for Yangshan.
Yangshan said, "Huangbo often used this device. Miaoyan asked, "Is it obtained from Heaven, or is it obtained from man?
Yangshan said, "It is both received through the lineage of the teacher and the realization of one's own nature. Miaoyan said, "So it is, so it is. Zhenjing Wen’s verse says:
"Not falling into the storehouse, not missing the division; He must, from this, cast off the fox."
[The verse says: "Everyone they meet says they have retired from office; yet in the forests below, not a single person has ever been seen.
Daguang Zhe’s verse comments: "In the great furnace of the forge, Buddhas and Patriarchs are smelted. When the mold has been completely melted away, those who seek to recognize it are at a loss."
A monk asked, "What is the Mahayana teaching of sudden enlightenment? The Master said, "You must first bring all conditions to rest and cease from all affairs.
Regarding all dharmas—whether good or not good, mundane or supramundane—do not recall them, do not give them thought.
Let go of body and mind so that they may be free; let the mind be like wood or stone, without discrimination. Let the mind have no..."
Practice. If the mind-ground is empty, the sun of wisdom will manifest of itself, like the sun appearing when the clouds disperse.

Cease all攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to objects of thought), and exhaust all defilements of greed, anger, craving, and grasping. Facing the five desires and the eight winds, one is not bound by seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing;
one is not deluded by various external conditions. Spontaneously endowed with supernatural powers and wondrous functions—this is liberation.

A person whose mind is neither still nor distracted toward any object, who is neither constrained nor dispersed, and who penetrates all sounds and forms without obstruction, is called a "Way-person" (*daoren*).
However, when one is not fettered by any good or evil, defilement or purity, nor bound by the conditioned world of merit and wisdom, that is called "Buddha-wisdom.
All perceptions of right and wrong, like and dislike, principle and non-principle—these various views and cognitions [are thus transcended].

Exhausted [of delusions], they are no longer bound; dwelling with mastery over the mind, they are called Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds. They immediately ascend to the stage of Buddhahood.
All dharmas are fundamentally not empty of themselves, nor do they call themselves "form," nor do they speak of right or wrong, defilement or purity.

Furthermore, there is no mind that binds people; it is only that people themselves falsely conceptualize and cling, producing various kinds of interpretations and giving rise to various kinds [of afflictions].
Knowledge and vision: when the defiled and pure minds are exhausted, one dwells neither in bondage nor in liberation.
There is no conceptualization of any conditioned or unconditioned phenomena; with a mind of equanimity, one abides within birth and death, yet the mind remains sovereign.

Ultimately, one does not conjoin with illusory afflictions, the aggregates, elements, birth and death, or the sense bases. Being utterly detached and without dependence, one is unrestrained by anything. Depart.
Abiding in non-obstruction, one comes and goes within birth and death as if passing through an open gate.

When encountering various forms of suffering or pleasure, or matters that do not accord with one's wishes, the mind remains without retreat or dejection. One does not dwell upon fame, reputation, clothing, or food, nor does one crave any merit or benefit.
One is not hindered by worldly dharmas. Although the mind may personally experience suffering and pleasure, these do not disturb the inner breast.
With coarse food to sustain life and mended clothes to ward off cold and heat, one remains steadfast like a fool or a deaf person.

If one has even a slight degree of intimacy with others, yet within the midst of birth and death merely seeks extensive learning and intellectual understanding to pursue fortune and wisdom, this is of no benefit to the principle; instead, one is caught by the winds of the realm of conceptual understanding.
It drifts away and returns once more to the sea of birth and death. The Buddha is one who seeks nothing; to seek him is to deviate from him.

Principle is a principle that requires no seeking; to seek it is to lose it. If one grasps at "seeking nothing," one again becomes identical to those who have something to seek. This Dharma is neither real nor false.
If one can, for the duration of a single lifetime, make the mind like wood or stone, it will not be disturbed by the aggregates, the realms, the five desires, or the eight winds.

Once one is no longer adrift or drowning, the causes of birth and death are severed; one attains freedom in coming and going and is no longer bound by the causes and effects of any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
At another time, one becomes identical to the unconditioned body. One benefits sentient beings with an unconditioned mind, responding to all mental states.
With unbound wisdom, one unties all fetters; one can also prescribe medicine according to the illness. The monk asked:
"If one now receives the precepts, purifies body and speech, and has already perfected all virtues, will one attain liberation? He replied:

"One attains a partial liberation, but has not yet attained liberation of mind, nor has one attained complete liberation. The monk asked: "What is liberation of mind? He replied: "It is not seeking Buddhahood, nor..."

Seeking to know and understand, when the notions of defilement and purity are exhausted, one neither clings to this state of non-seeking as being "right," nor does one dwell in the place of exhaustion.
One does not fear the bonds of hell, nor does one accept the pleasures of heaven. When one is not constrained by any phenomena, this is for the first time called unimpeded liberation.
Thus, both body and mind, as well as all things, are termed liberation. You must not say that there is even a fraction of precept remaining.

Excellent! But do not think that you have already finished. There are gates of the outflow-free precepts, concentration, and wisdom as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and you have not yet touched upon even a hair’s breadth of them.
Exert yourself with vigor and act quickly; do not wait until your ears are deaf and your eyes dim, until your head is white and your face is wrinkled, and old age has overtaken your person.
Tears stream from the eyes; the heart is filled with terror and alarm. Having no place to go, when one reaches such a state, there is no way to steady one's faculties.

Even if one possesses merit, wisdom, and extensive learning, none of these can provide salvation. Because the mind’s eye has not yet opened, one merely pursues external objects and fails to engage in self-reflection;
furthermore, one does not perceive the Buddha-way. All the evil karma accumulated throughout one’s life then manifests in its entirety.

Standing before them, they experience either joy or terror. Within the five aggregates of the six realms, they see nothing but magnificent mansions, boats, ships, carriages, and palanquins, all resplendent with brilliant light.
Because they have indulged their own minds, what they perceive through craving transforms entirely into pleasant objects.

They are reborn wherever their gaze lingers most intensely, having no freedom whatsoever. Whether as dragons or animals, noble or base, their status remains entirely undetermined. [The interlocutor] asks: "How can this be?"

"Freedom. Answer: "If, regarding the five desires and the eight winds, one’s mind neither grasps nor rejects, and both defilement and purity are forgotten—like the sun and moon in the sky, illuminating without being conditioned;
like the mind being as wood or stone, or like a fragrant elephant crossing a torrent, passing through without further obstruction—such a person cannot be encompassed by either heaven or hell."
The Master said: "When reading the sutras and examining the teachings, all words and phrases must be turned back toward one's own self.

All these various verbal instructions serve only to clarify the present awakened nature of one's own self. When one is no longer swayed by the objective realms of existence or non-existence, one is a True Teacher.
Being able to illuminate and shatter all realms of existence and non-existence, one is a Vajra; thus, one possesses true freedom."
This is the section on independence. If you cannot attain it in this way, even if you can recite the twelve *Veda* scriptures, you will merely fall into the arrogance of superiority;

this is actually slandering the Buddha and is not true cultivation. Reading the sutras and examining the teachings may be considered a good and virtuous deed according to worldly standards, but from the perspective of those who have realized the truth, such people are merely obstructed and blocked. Even those at the stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) must shed [these attachments].
Do not go; you will flow into the river of birth and death. Simply do not seek to understand the meaning of words or phrases.
Understanding belongs to craving, and craving turns into illness. Right now, simply remain detached from all dharmas of existence and non-existence, and pass beyond the three propositions.
Naturally, you will be no different from the Buddha. Since you are already the Buddha yourself, why worry that the Buddha does not understand your speech? I only fear that you do not [realize this].
This Buddha was turned by the various dharmas of existence and non-existence and could not attain freedom.

For this reason, before the Principle (Li) was established, he was first carried away by merit and wisdom, like a lowly servant serving a noble. He did not know that once the Principle is first established, there is subsequently merit and wisdom;

at such a time, one becomes the master of oneself, able to take earth and turn it into gold, transform the waters of the sea into ghee and curd, and break Mount Sumeru into fine dust—all within a single [thought].
To make the manifold meaning one; to make the one meaning manifold.
Yunyan asked, "Master, for whom do you labor so busily every day? The Master said, "There is someone who needs it. Yunyan said:
"Why not teach him to do it himself? The Master said, "He has no livelihood.
Zizang asked the Master, "What will you do after this, elder brother? The Master rolled his hands back and forth on both sides and showed them to him.
Zang said, "How else could it be? The Master pointed at the sky three times with his finger.
The Master said to the assembly, "I want one person to go and deliver a message to Xitang. Who can go? Wupeng came forward and said, "I can go.
The Master asked, "How will you deliver the message? Wupeng said, "Once I see Xitang, I shall—"
The Master said, "Speak. Feng said, "I will tell you when I get back.
Later, while the Master was supervising the communal labor of hoeing the ground, a monk heard the drum signal, threw down his hoe, laughed heartily, and went away.
The Master said, "How excellent! How excellent! This is the gateway through which Avalokiteśvara enters into principle. He then summoned that monk.
Question: "What principle did you just perceive? He replied: "Just now my stomach was hungry; hearing the sound of the drum, I went to eat.
The Master then laughed heartily.

I ask the Master to choose an auspicious day for their burial. The Master said, "Tomorrow, I will bury them all at once for you."
A monk asked, "I come to you, Master, bearing my raw jade; I pray you, grant me a definitive resolution. The Master said, "Last night, a tiger on South Mountain bit a great beast.
The monk said, "The true teaching is not in error. Why do you not extend a skillful means? The Master said, "You are a fellow who covers his ears while stealing a bell.

The monk said, "If one does not meet the discernment of Liang Cai (Zhonglang), it is no different from firewood in a wild shed. The Master then struck him. The monk cried out, "Heaven! Heaven! The Master [said], "... (The text here ends abruptly).

One who understands this pays homage. The Master said, "I accept it all as it is.
Fojian said, "The old man Baizhang sat alone on Mount Daxiong; his every cough and spittle stirred the wind.
Throughout the world, who dared to look upon him? Yet, when seized by the attendant at the heels, he was left with no choice but to part his hands."
[The Master] said: "Even so, only a foster child knows the affection of his father. A monk asked:

"To interpret the meaning based on the scriptures is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three periods; to depart from a single word of the scriptures is like the speech of a demon. The Master said:
To cling rigidly to its application is an offense against the Buddhas of the three periods. To seek it elsewhere than this is the teaching of demons.
A monk asked, "What is the extraordinary matter? The Master said, "Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak. The monk bowed, and the Master struck him.
Xuedou’s verse says: In the ancestral realm, celestial colts gallop side by side; The unfolding and rolling of the gate of transformation follow different paths.
Like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint, they exist as shifting mechanisms; How laughable that someone would come to stroke a tiger’s whiskers!
Chan Master Zhichang of Guizong on Mount Lu (11th case) addressed the assembly, saying: "The ancient worthies of old were not without understanding;
they were men of lofty caliber, unlike the common run. These days, people cannot achieve self-reliance and merely waste their time in vain.
My sons, do not apply your minds in error. No one can take your place, nor is there any place for you to apply your minds. Do not—"

One seeks it elsewhere; from the outset, one has merely relied on others to form understanding. Consequently, every word uttered is obstructed, and the light does not penetrate through, simply because there is something before the eyes.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "I now wish to speak of Chan; all you sons, come forward together. The great assembly stepped forward, and the Master said:
"Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara, which skillfully responds to all places. A monk asked: "What is the practice of Avalokiteśvara? The Master snapped his fingers and said:
"Do you hear it? The monk replied: "I hear it. The Master said: "You lot, what are you looking for here? He then struck him with his staff.
He drove him away with his staff. Laughing loudly, he returned to the abbot’s quarters.
While Master [Linji] was taking leave of Nanquan, they were brewing tea; Nanquan asked, "Regarding the words and phrases we have previously discussed together, brother,..."
They had already known each other. Later, when someone asked Mazu, "What is the ultimate reality? the Master said, "This plot of land is good for building a hermitage.
Baizhang Quan said, "Setting aside the building of the hermitage for a moment, what is the ultimate reality? The Master kicked over the tea kettle.
Quan said, "Brother, you have finished your tea; I have not yet drunk mine. The Master said, "Speaking such words as these, you are dripping [with delusion]."
"Water is difficult to digest. Quan retired. Yunyan came to pay his respects.
Upon seeing him, the Master made the gesture of drawing a bow. After a long while, Yunyan made the gesture of drawing a sword. The Master said:
It was very late when the Master was weeding grass. A presiding lecturer (zuozhu) came to visit him. By chance, a snake passed by, and the Master cut it with his hoe.
The lecturer said, "I have long admired Guizong; I never expected you would be such a coarse monk. The Master looked at the lecturer and said, "You..."
"Coarse self, coarse. The Master asked, "What is coarse? The teacher held up his hoe. [The Master] asked, "What is fine? The teacher made the gesture of severing a snake.
[The Master] said, "If it is thus, then I shall rely upon it and act accordingly. The teacher said, "Setting aside for a moment the 'relying upon it and acting accordingly'—"
"Where did you see me kill the snake? The host had no reply.
Xuefeng asked Deshan, "What was the meaning of that ancient's killing of the snake? Deshan struck him; Xuefeng immediately fled.
Deshan called out, "Robe-wearing fellow! Xuefeng turned his head back; Deshan said, "In time, when you attain realization, you will understand."
"The old fellow has exhausted his wife-like compassion. Xuedou said: "Guizong only knew how to be cautious at the beginning, but could not protect the end.
Deshan was quite capable of enforcing his command, yet he did not understand the 'slaying of the snake. He then said: "Everyone, look!"
Today Xuezhao has executed thirty or five people. [He] took up his staff and dispersed the assembly.
While the Master was on a communal work assignment gathering vegetables, he drew a circle and enclosed a single stalk of vegetable within it. The assembly all offered words of response.

This did not accord with the Master’s intention. The Master then pulled out the vegetables, took up his staff, and drove them away, saying, "Not a single one in this group of fellows possesses wisdom."
A monk asked, "What is the profound principle? The Master said, "No one can comprehend it. The monk asked, "How about if one directs oneself toward it?
The Master said, "If there is directing, you have already deviated. The monk asked, "How about if one does not direct oneself toward it? The Master said, "Who would seek the profound principle?

The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Go; there is no place for you to apply your mind. The monk asked, "Is there not some skillful means by which you might enable a student to enter? The Master said, "Observe."
"The power of the wondrous wisdom of Avalokiteśvara can rescue the world from suffering. [The monk asked: "What is this power of the wondrous wisdom of Avalokiteśvara?
The Master struck the lid of the cauldron three times and said, "Did you hear it? The monk replied, "I heard it. The Master said, "Why did I not hear it? The monk was at a loss.
The Master took up his staff and drove him away.
Because the junior monk Dayu was about to take his leave, the Master asked him, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to study the 'five flavors' of Chan in various quarters.
The Master said, "There are the five flavors of Chan in various quarters, but here I have the one flavor of Chan.
Why do you not study it? Dayu asked, "What is the Master’s one flavor of Chan? The Master struck him a blow across the mouth, and Dayu attained great enlightenment on the spot. He then said:
"Hah! I understand! I understand! The Master hurriedly demanded, "Speak! Speak! As the fool was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him again and immediately drove him out.
Xuedou said: "What difficulty is there in using the strong to overpower the weak? Here I have this one flavor of Chan;
why do you not study it? Just say 'Hold! and wait for him to pick it up. There are a certain kind of sightless fellows who simply go on eating.
Ho! Ho! Who would dare under Xuedou’s gate?"
While the Master was plastering a wall, Layman Bai came to visit. The Master asked, "Are you a scholar of the noble way or a scholar of the base way?
Bai replied, "A scholar of the noble way. The Master struck the mud-tray once, and Bai immediately passed the mud over. The Master took the mud and used it right away.
After a long while, the Master asked, "Are you not the quick-witted Layman Bai? Bai replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "You have only the capacity to pass the mud over."
Censor Li Bo asked, "In the scriptures it is said that Mount Sumeru can contain a mustard seed; I have no doubt of this. But as for a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru—is this not mere idle talk?
The Master asked, "It is said that you, Excellency, have read ten thousand scrolls of books; is this true? Li replied, "Indeed.
The Master said, "From the crown of your head to the soles of your feet, you are no larger than a coconut. Where, then, would you place those ten thousand scrolls?"
He simply lowered his head.
Li asked, "What matters does the entire Great Canon of the Buddha’s teachings clarify? The Master raised his fist and showed it to him, saying, "Do you understand?
He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A well-read scholar like you does not even recognize a fist! He said, "I truly do not understand. The Master—
It is said: "When meeting people, it is for use on the path; when not meeting people, it is for circulation within the conventional truth.
Chan Master Daimei Fachang of Mingzhou (the thirteenth): He was a member of the Zheng family of Xiangyang. He asked Great Master Mazu, "What is the Buddha?
Great Master Mazu replied, "The very mind is the Buddha. Upon these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. Later, at Mei...
Zizhen was a former recluse who had chosen this place to dwell.
A monk from Yanguan, while gathering firewood, lost his way and arrived at the Master’s hermitage. He asked, "How long has the Monk lived on this mountain?
The Master replied, "I have seen only the four mountains turn green and then yellow. The monk asked, "When you leave the mountain path, where will you go?"
"Go," the Master said. "Go with the flow. The monk returned and related this to Yanguan. Yanguan said, "When I was in Jiangxi, I once saw this very monk.
I have not heard of him since; could it be he? He then sent a monk to summon him. The Master replied with a verse:
"Withered wood, broken and battered, leaning against the cold forest; Through many springs, its heart remains unchanged. When a woodcutter encounters it..."
Even so, he did not look back. How could the man from Ying have pursued him with such distress?
Master Ma sent a monk to ask the Master, "What did you receive from Master Ma that you have come to dwell on this mountain?
The Master replied, "Master Ma told me, 'The mind itself is Buddha,' and I have dwelt here ever since."
The monk said, "Master Ma, these days the Buddha-dharma has become something else. The Master asked, "In what way has it become different?
The monk said, "It is also said that it is 'neither mind nor Buddha'. The Master said, "This old fellow will continue to delude people without end.
Let him say 'neither mind nor Buddha'; here, I simply maintain 'this very mind is Buddha. The monk returned and reported this to Master Ma.
The Great Master said, "The plum has ripened.
When Layman Pang heard this, wishing to verify the Master’s realization, he went specifically to test him. As soon as he saw him, he asked, "I have long admired the Great Plum;
I wonder, has the plum ripened yet? The Master replied, "Where would you even begin to bite into it? The Layman said:
"Shattered into a hundred pieces! The Master reached out his hand and said, "Give me back my kernel!
The scholar was speechless. He addressed the assembly, saying: "Each of you must turn your minds back to realize the source; do not pursue its branches.
If you attain the source, the branches will arrive of themselves. If you wish to recognize the source, simply understand your own mind. This mind is originally the origin of all worlds."
Regarding worldly dharmas: because they are rooted in the mind, when the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of dharmas cease.
Furthermore, the mind does not arise in dependence upon any good or evil. All phenomena are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*).

There was a monk who came from the presence of Master Ma. As soon as they met, he circumambulated the Master once, held up his sitting mat, and said, "At this very moment, neither guest nor host stands. The Master said, "Who is it that does not stand?
The monk again circumambulated the Master once. The Master said, "I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. The monk [acted].
The Master said, "Hūṃ hūṃ! You still lack the courtesy of a host. The monk said, "Not only I, but all Buddhas are likewise so.
The Master said, "Hūṃ hūṃ! You still lack the courtesy of a guest. The monk covered his ears and departed. The Master called for the *vina* (chant leader) and said:
Very well. Consider this monk: he came from the place of Master Ma.
While traveling together with Jianshan, they were conversing. Dingshan said, "If there is no Buddha within birth and death, then there is no birth and death.
Jianshan said, "If there is a Buddha within birth and death, then one is not deluded by birth and death. Their debate did not cease. II.

A man went up the mountain seeking a definitive judgment on who was closer. As soon as his business was concluded, Jia Shan brought up the previous conversation and asked, "I do not know which of the two is closer.
The Master said, "One is close; one is distant. Jia Shan asked again, "Which one is close?
The Master said, "Go now and come back tomorrow. The next day Jia Shan asked again. The Master said, "He who is close does not ask; he who asks is not close."
Shanzhu later said, "At that time, I was at Damei; I lost one eye.
Xuedou said, "Jiashan ultimately did not realize that at that moment he had gained an eye.
Had the old fellow Damei heard this being cited at the time, he would have driven them both out with his staff all at once—not only would he have severed the path for those two, but...
A tangle indeed! Yet he was nonetheless a patriarchal master of the world.
When a monk from Silla arrived, the Master asked him, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "I wish to inform you of my place of origin, yet I fear it might incur the Master’s reprimand."
The Master said, "It cannot be that he has no place of origin. The monk said, "Silla. The Master said, "And why should we be surprised by you?
The monk bowed. The Master said, "Whether right or wrong, whether known or unknown, you are still just a person from the kingdom of Silla."
There was a monk named Raushe Zhao (Rao-she Zhao) who paid his respects and asked, "What is the Master of Damei? The Master struck his meditation seat to indicate it to him.
Zhao said, "In that case, sound and form are one and the same. The Master said, "'One and the same'—and what else is 'one and the same'?
Zhao said, "Today, for the first time, I have attained a state of vast clarity. The Master said, "For all this time, what [have you been doing]?"
[The monk] stepped back. Zhao said, "Today I have fully received the Master’s majestic light. The Master said, "You may go down [from the seat].
A monk asked, "When you first arrived at the place of Master Mada, through what words or phrases did you gain entry?
The Master gazed for a short while and said, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "You must harmonize with him before you can attain it. The monk asked, "How so?"

"Is it appropriate to go to him? The Master said, "You must go with your tracks completely severed; only then can you be in accord with him. [The student] asked, "Since one's tracks are already severed, why is it necessary to be in accord with him?
The Master said, "It is complete right where you are, without the need for deliberate effort. This is the place where tracks are severed.

Where mind, intellect, and consciousness are without self—this is the place of being in accord with him. [The student] asked, "After being in accord with him, what is it like? The Master said, "Not..."
The monk asked, "If one assumes the original face, then is it the case that consciousness is entirely true and there are no external objects?
The Master said, "If consciousness were truly real, there would naturally be no external objects. Who else would you want to ask? The monk bowed.

The Master then said, "Although there is no arising within or without, the functions of illumination and application do not cease. Therefore it is said: 'There is no self, no agent, and no recipient. This is good."
The karma of evil is likewise never forgotten; this is why the thousand sages share a single mind. Consciousness is also the same:
whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, there is fundamentally no before or after. When one simply lets each object pass away without a mind, this is called Prajñāpāramitā.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "There is no meaning in his coming from the West. Yanguan said, "One coffin, two dead men.
Xuansha said, "Yanguan was a true master. Xuedou said, "There were three of them too."
A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Mulberry blossoms and willow catkins; bamboo needles and hemp thread.
When the Master was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Coming cannot be suppressed; going cannot be pursued.
In this state of ease, I heard the cry of a flying squirrel. This is that very thing, not something else. Guard and maintain it well; I am now departing."
Xuedou said: "This fellow was reckless while alive and negligent after death. It is this very thing, not some other thing—what thing is it?
Is there anyone who can hand it over? There are a certain kind of fellows who cannot cut off their heels;
they simply say, 'He was rushing too fast.'"
National Teacher Zhai An of Hai-men County, Hangzhou Yan-guan (Case 2). He was the son of the Li family. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"With space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the drumstick—what person can strike it? The assembly was silent.
Nanquan said, "Old Master Wang does not strike this broken drum."
Fayan said, "Master Wang does not strike. Xuedou said, "Those who strike are many; those who listen are extremely few.
But tell me, who is it that understands how to strike? Do not slander Yanguan! Nanquan said, 'Master Wang does not strike this broken drum.
Fayan said, 'Master Wang does not strike. Since these two [masters] have both spoken thus..."
"There is nothing to be done. One person is even more *mālava*. He also said: "If Master Wang does not strike, will he be accepted by the various quarters?
He spoke on his own behalf: "A field of a thousand years has eight hundred owners."
One day the Master called to his attendant, "Bring me the rhinoceros fan. The attendant said, "It is broken.
The Master said, "The fan is already broken; give me back the rhinoceros."
Touzi said, "I do not decline to bring it forth, but I fear its horns and head will not be complete.
Xuedou said, "I want the incomplete horns and head. Shishuang spoke on his behalf, saying, "If it were returned to you, Master, then there would be none at all.
Xuedou said, "The rhinoceros calf is still here. Baofu spoke on his behalf, saying, "Master, you are advanced in years; please ask someone else."
"Good. Xuedou said, "A pity that he labored in vain without merit. Zifu drew a circle and wrote the character for "ox" (牛) inside it.

Xuedou said, "Why did you not bring this out earlier? He then picked up the brush and said, "If you wish for the pure breeze to be restored and the horns to grow anew, I ask all you Zen guests to provide a turning word. He then asked:
"The fan is already broken; give me back my rhinoceros! At that time, a monk came forward and said, "The assembly, please proceed to the hall.
The Master shouted, "I cast the hook to catch the great whales, yet I have caught only a frog!"
Yunju Shun said: "At that time, if the attendant had seen it and said, 'The fan has already been broken;
give me back the rhinoceros,' Yunju would have simply told him, 'It has already been cast away atop the pile of firewood.'"
Chan Master Huaiyun of Zhangjing in the Capital Prefecture (sixth in the series). He was a native of the Xie clan of Tong’an, Quanzhou. Addressing the assembly, he said:

“The ultimate principle transcends words, yet people of this age do not understand it. They strenuously practice other matters, taking them to be spiritual achievements, while failing to realize that their own nature is fundamentally not a realm of sensory dust.
This is a subtle and wondrous gate of great liberation; all that is reflected and perceived therein remains unstained.”
It is unobstructed. Such radiance has never ceased or been abandoned; from past kalpas until now, it remains eternally unchanged.
It is like the solar orb, which shines equally upon both the distant and the near; though it reaches all forms, it does not merge with anything. This spiritual torch is wondrously luminous.

It is not that one must undergo artificial refinement; rather, it is because of a lack of understanding that one grasps at objective forms. This is merely like pressing on the eyes and falsely perceiving floating flowers in the sky—exhausting oneself in vain and needlessly passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes.
If one can turn the light inward to reflect, there is no second person; every movement and action is [the manifestation of this].
This does not detract from the true nature (*dharmatā*).
When Magu arrived, he circumambulated the Master three times, struck his monk’s staff once, and stood there motionless. The Master said, "Right, right.
When Magu went to Nanquan, he did the same. Nanquan said, "Not so, not so. Magu said, "Zhangjing said it was right; why does the Master say it is not?"
[The Master] asked, "Why do you say it is not so? Quan said, "Zhangjing is indeed so; it is you who are not so. This is turned by the power of the wind;
in the end, it will fall into ruin."
Daguang Zhe said: "Zhangjing’s ‘It is so’ falls within Magu’s sphere;
Nanquan’s ‘It is not so’ also falls within Magu’s sphere. I, Dawai, am not like this:
suppose someone were to take up their staff, circumambulate the meditation seat three times, snap the staff once, and stand there upright. I would simply say to him: 'Not yet.'"
"Having arrived here, you shall receive thirty blows from me.

Master Baizhang sent a monk to me with these instructions: 'Go there; wait for him to ascend the hall, then come forward, spread your sitting cloth, and after prostrating, take one of his shoes, brush the dust off it with your sleeve, and turn it upside down.'"
The monk followed the instructions exactly as taught. The Master said, "This old monk is at fault.
The Master had a junior disciple who returned from traveling abroad. The Master asked, "How much time has passed since you left my place here?
He replied, "It has been nearly eight years since I left the Master. The Master asked, "What have you realized? The junior disciple [pointed] to the ground.
He drew a perfect circle. The Master said, "It is just this; yet there is more. The junior monk broke the circle and then prostrated. The Master said, "Not it, not it."
A monk asked, "Within this body of the four elements and five aggregates, which one is the original Buddha-nature? The Master called to the monk. The monk responded.
After a long silence, the Master said, "You have no Buddha-nature."
A monk asked, "When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, where does one point back to? The Master said, "The man of Ying has no stains;
it is merely a laborious wielding of the axe. Chan Master Baizhi of Panshan in Youzhou (total of ten cases) was once in the assembly of Mazu Daoshi.
One day, while out on the street carrying his alms bowl, he suddenly saw a guest buying meat. He said to the butcher, "Cut me a pound of the finest [meat]. The butcher...
The man dropped his knife and, with palms joined, said, "Director, which of these is not essential? At this, the Master attained realization.
Later, one day, seeing a funeral procession being carried along, a singer shook his bell and sang: "The crimson sun is certain to sink in the west; I know not to what realm the soul shall go.
Below the curtain, the sons of mourning wailed, "Alas! Alas! At that moment, the Master was greatly enlightened and leaped for joy.
He returned, and Mazu validated his realization. Addressing the assembly, Mazu said:
"If the mind has no affairs, the myriad dharmas do not arise. When the intention is cut off from the subtle and profound, how can even a speck of dust be established?
The Way has no substance; it is because of the Way that names are established. The Way has no name; it is because of the name that its title is obtained. If one says..."
The mind is itself the Buddha. At present, you have not yet entered the profound and subtle. If one says "neither mind nor Buddha," this is still merely pointing toward the ultimate limit.
The path that transcends all is not transmitted by the thousand sages; students exhaust their bodies in vain, like a monkey grasping at a reflection.
Langya Huijue said: "The eulogies and praises offered above constitute boundless roots of goodness.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The Great Way has no center; who, then, can speak of before or after? The vast sky leaves no trace; what use is there for measurement?"
Since emptiness is thus, what more can be said of the Way?
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The moon of the mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the ten thousand phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist."
When both light and object are forgotten, what thing is there? Zen student, it is like casting a sword into the air: do not debate whether one reaches it or not;
this is the wheel of emptiness where all traces are severed, and the blade remains unimpaired. If you can be thus, mind after mind will be without cognition.
The whole mind is Buddha; the whole Buddha is the person. When there is no distinction between person and Buddha, one has finally entered the Way.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "O Zen practitioners, you may study the Way within this. It is like the earth supporting a mountain, unaware of the mountain’s towering loftiness;
or like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade’s flawlessness. If you can be thus, you are truly a renunciant. Thus spoke the Master.

It is said: "Phenomena are fundamentally non-obstructive; the three periods of time are likewise so. Even for one who is unconditioned and without affairs, they remain as difficult to transcend as a golden chain.
Thus, the spiritual source shines alone; the Way is cut off from birth. Great wisdom is beyond names; true emptiness leaves no trace.
True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words. Buddhas and sentient beings are merely figurative designations. You must simply look within yourself. No [external reliance].

[The Master] substituted another person. He addressed the assembly, saying: "In the three realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind? The four great elements are fundamentally empty; upon what does the Buddha rely to dwell?
The revolving pivot is unmoving; in silent stillness, words cease. Face-to-face presentation—there is nothing further."

When the Master was about to pass away, he said to the assembly, "Is there anyone who can capture my true likeness? The assembly all drew portraits and presented them, but none accorded with the Master's intent.
Puhua came forward and said, "I have captured it. The Master said, "Try presenting it to this old monk for a look."
Puhua performed an aerial somersault and departed. The Master said, "This fellow, where will he go to act like a madman in the future?
Baofu Zhan said, "Puhua’s madness was no small matter; Panshan’s ugliness and clumsiness were even more so."
Chan Master Lingmo of Wuxie Mountain in Wuzhou (Case 1). A native of the Xuan clan of Piling, the Master questioned Shitou, saying, "If a single word accords with me, I shall stay;
if it does not accord, I shall depart. Shitou remained seated. The Master brushed his sleeves and departed immediately.
The Head Monk called out, "Acarya! The Master turned his head. The Head Monk said, "From birth until old age, it has been nothing but this.
Why do you turn your head and twist your brain? At these words, the Master suddenly attained awakening and broke his staff in two (he was the tonsure master of Dongshan).
Dongshan said, "At that time, had it not been for my late teacher Wuxie, it would have been very difficult to take up [the responsibility].
Even so, one is still traveling on a path. Cuiyan Zhi said, "Shitou takes his seat; Wuxie turns his head back.
Shitou calls out to him, yet he creates a great deal of trouble. Yunfeng Yue said, "How great indeed is Shitou!"
Unable to sit still, unable to hold on—such a fellow who carries a wooden board across his shoulders. Let him go and leave it at that;
yet you call him back, and he smears something over it, saying, "I have attained enlightenment here. When will you ever see such a thing in your dreams?
Chan Master Mazu Baoche of Puzhou (Seven cases total). While the Master was traveling with Danxia, they saw fish in the water.
Pointing at them with his hand, he indicated them to Danxia. Danxia said, "Natural! Natural! The Master then stopped speaking.
On the following day, he again asked Danxia, "What was your meaning yesterday? Danxia threw himself down and made a reclining gesture. The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven!"
The Master asked Linji, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the True Eye? Linji said, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, what is the True Eye?
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Master pulled Linji down from his meditation seat and sat back down.
Linji rose and said, "How do you do? The Master hesitated, whereupon Linji gave a shout, pulled him down from the seat again, and sat back down. The Master then went out.
Daguan Ying said: "All you venerable practitioners of Chan, these two masters were like this. But tell me, how was it?
People nowadays all say that 'illumination and function are simultaneous,' but what bowl are they illuminating?
Everyone only knows how to mount their own horse to go catch a thief, or take up their own sword to go kill a thief; these two men, however, were able to mount the thief’s horse."
“Catch the thief! Seize the thief! Strike the thief down! Although it is so, although Linji may have gained the advantage, he has actually fallen into a disadvantage.
You, Master, and Nanquan—two or three of you—went to visit Jingshan. On the road, you encountered an old woman, who asked: “Jingshan?”
[The Master] asked, "Where is the road going? The old woman said, "It goes straight ahead. The Master said, "The water ahead is deep;
can you cross it? She said, "Without getting my feet wet. He asked again, "The rice on the upper bank is so fine; why is the rice on the lower bank so poor?
She said, "It has all been eaten by crabs. The Master said, "The grain is fragrant. The old woman said, "It has no scent. Again—
Question: "Where does the old woman reside? [The Master] replied: "She is right here. The three men arrived at the shop;

the old woman brewed a pot of tea and brought out three cups, saying, "If you monks possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), then drink the tea. As the three looked at one another, [the old woman departed].
Baoyun said, "Watch this old fellow display his supernatural powers! He took up a cup, poured tea, and departed.
The Master sat within the tent, covering his head with a handkerchief. When Heshang Piyun came and saw him, he immediately let out a cry of lamentation.
After a long while, he went out. In the Dharma Hall, he circumambulated the meditation seat once, then returned, pushed aside the curtain, and saw the Master remove his handkerchief and sit down.
Piyun said, "To find life within death—there is not one in ten thousand. The Master descended from the seat.
Baizhang made a gesture as if to pull up his sitting mat. Yunmen seized him and said, "Dead before, alive after—do you accept this?
The Master said, "It would be very acceptable, but what could you possibly do, Master? Yunmen pushed the Master aside and said, "I know that your former words do not match your subsequent speech."
While the Master was fanning himself, a monk asked, "The nature of wind is constantly in motion and pervades everywhere; why then, Reverend, do you still use a fan?
The Master said, "You only know that the nature of wind is constantly in motion, but you do not yet know that it pervades everywhere.
The monk asked, "What is the principle of its pervading everywhere? The Master then shook his fan. The monk bowed, and the Master said, "There is none."
Even if a master were to employ ten thousand such monks, what benefit would there be?
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "I do not presume to inquire after your welfare. The Master asked again. The monk said, "Please take care.
The Master descended from his rope-seat, seized him, and said, "This monk, when questioned, immediately answers with the Dharma. He is very much like one who has no eyes."
The Master released his grip and said, "I grant you your life; I allow you your breath. The monk bowed. The Master again seized him by the arm; the monk pulled his elbow and walked away.
The Master said, "Do not take a three-year-old bamboo and attempt to compare it with a ten-thousand-year-old pine."
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Zhangzhou. The Master said, "There is pestilential miasma there.

How have things been lately? He replied, "It has been extremely severe. The Master said, "Why, then, are you unharmed, Reverend? He replied, "I passed through during the winter months. The Master said, "..."
"Where is it most fully realized?
Shigong said, "The words are correct, but the principle is not yet.
