National Teacher Wuye Dada of Fenyang (5), Dharma Heir of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi of Jiangxi.

A native of the Du family from Shangluo in Shangzhou, he first visited Master Mazu and inquired into the doctrines and principles of the Three Vehicles, which he investigated with some degree of depth.
He had previously heard of the Chan school’s teaching that "the mind itself is Buddha," and [this realization] was truly...
“I do not yet understand clearly; I beg the Venerable Master’s compassionate instruction. The Great Master said, “It is simply this very mind of yours that does not understand.
There is nothing else besides it. When deluded, one is a sentient being; when awakened, one is a Buddha. It is like a fist becoming an open palm, or an open palm becoming a fist.”
The Master attained realization upon hearing these words.
He asked Mazu, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Mazu replied, "Virtuous One, you are right in the midst of a bustle;
go now and come back at another time. As soon as the Master stepped out, Mazu called out, "Virtuous One! The Master turned his head, and Mazu said, "What is it?"
The Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment, whereupon he prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "You dull-witted fellow! Why do you prostrate?
After the Master took up residence, when students came to question him, he mostly replied, "Do not engage in false conceptualization.

The temple steward asked, "In your daily responses, Master, you only say, 'Do not engage in false conceptualization. Now, you may rest from that. The Master called out, "Steward! The steward responded, "Yes? The Master—
He said, "This time, it must stop. From then on, whenever anyone questioned him, he would always say, "This time, it must stop.
A monk asked, "The twelve divisions of the teachings have flowed into this land, and those who have attained the fruits of the Way are not merely one or two.

Why did the Patriarch come to the East and separately proclaim the Esoteric Principle, pointing directly at the human mind and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha? Was it not the World-Honored One [who taught this]? He said, "It was indeed the World-Honored One."

He preached the Dharma, yet there remained things he had not fully exhausted. It was simply like the virtuous and eminent monks of former ages, whose learning permeated the nine schools of thought and who were profoundly enlightened in the Tripitaka;
men such as Daosheng, Sengzhao, Daorong, and Sengrui, whose spiritual wonders were manifest throughout their lives—how could they have been unaware of the distance and nearness of the Buddha-dharma?
I, [Name], am dull and ignorant; I pray that the Master will instruct me. The Master said: "The Buddhas have never appeared in the world, nor is there a single..."

The Dharma is given to people; it is merely the application of remedies according to their illnesses, resulting in the twelve divisions of the teachings. It is like exchanging honeyed fruit for bitter gourds:
they serve only to wash away the roots of your karma and possess no substantial reality whatsoever. This includes supernatural transformations and the hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi.
To transform those celestial Māras and heterodox teachers through the twofold adornment of merit and wisdom, one must shatter the views of clinging to existence and stagnating in emptiness.
If you do not grasp the Way and the intent of the Patriarchs, what does it matter who they were—Dao-sheng, Seng-zhao, Daorong, or Huirui?

Today in this world, there are as many as the sands of the Ganges who interpret Chan and the Way, and hundreds of thousands of millions who discourse on the Buddha and the Mind; yet not even a speck of dust has been removed from them.
To escape the cycle of saṃsāra, one must not forget even a single thought; otherwise, one will inevitably sink into the depths.
Those of such a kind cannot even recognize the karmic consequences of their own actions, yet they falsely claim to benefit both themselves and others.

They consider themselves superior to others and equal to the sages of old, merely saying that everything before one's eyes is the Buddha-work and every step one takes is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Yet, when examining what they actually practice, it is not even equal to a single person observing the five precepts.
Ordinary people of the ten wholesome paths observe their speech and find fault with those of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages.
Furthermore, although the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) is prized by the world, when encountered by such individuals, it instead turns into poison.

Even Nanshan did not permit this, calling them a "crowd of Mahāyāna practitioners who merely parrot words," who vie for supremacy amidst the lips and tongues, and who drum up arguments regarding matters that do not manifest in form. All [of these]...
Those former worthies were truly diligent and endured great hardship. Even a reclusive gentleman of the wilds understands to rest his head on a stone and rinse his mouth in a stream;

he renounces profit and honor yet still possesses strategies for pacifying the state and governing the people, refusing to respond when summoned. How much more so for us of the Zen school, whose path is distinct?
Observe those ancient virtuous practitioners: after they had attained their realization, they dwelt in thatched huts or stone chambers, facing broken-legged [stools]...
Cooking rice in a cauldron to eat, for thirty or twenty years, he did not harbor thoughts of fame or profit, nor did he give a thought to wealth or treasure.

Having utterly forgotten the ways of the world, he hid his traces among the mountain crags and thickets. When kings sent messengers for him, he did not come; when feudal lords invited him, he did not attend.
How could he be compared to those like us, who crave fame and love profit, wallowing in the paths of the world like petty peddlers with meager hopes?
They seek [the path] yet forget the Great Fruit. How could the sages of the Ten Stages not understand the Buddha’s principle?

Is it not better than a single ordinary person of the mundane world? Truly, such a thing is impossible. Though their preaching of the Dharma is like clouds and rain, they are still rebuked by the Buddha, who says:

"Your seeing of nature is as if separated by fine gauze. This is solely because their emotions cling to the measure of sainthood and their understanding remains fixed on cause and effect; they have been unable to transcend the sages.

Sentient beings surpass all shadows and traces. The sages of old, the virtuous of antiquity, the great scholars, and the eminent men were profoundly versed in the past and present and thoroughly illuminated the net of the teachings;

yet this was merely because they used their knowledge to interpret texts and discerned the difficulty of distinguishing between water and milk, rather than because they understood the ultimate principle. They sought the Truth through the contemplation of stillness. Alas!
Those who obtain a human body are like the soil upon a fingernail, while those who lose a human body are like the soil of the great earth—this is truly lamentable.

How lamentable! Suppose there is one who awakens to the principle, possessing some measure of knowledge and understanding, yet does not recognize that this is the rule within awakening and the gateway for entering the principle;

they instead treat it as a mere worldly benefit for this life. Wandering the mountains and following the mountain streams, they neglect the source of the current, causing mental outflows to remain unexhausted and the ground of principle to remain obscure.
Reaching old age without achievement, they waste their years in vain. Moreover, their intelligence is not...
This is capable of countering karma. Those of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) cannot yet escape the wheel of suffering.

Even if one’s talent were equal to Aśvaghoṣa and one’s wisdom matched Nāgārjuna, it would only ensure that for one or two lifetimes one does not lose the human body; with faculties and thoughts already stilled from past lives, one understands upon hearing—like that Master Sengzhao.
What is there to envy in such? It is entirely at odds with the Way. With my brothers, we discuss reality, not fiction. It is simply this mouth.

To consume food and clothing while doing nothing but deceiving the worthy and deluding the sages—seeking to acquire these for oneself—is viewed by those with the wisdom-eye of others as being like eating pus and blood;
one must inevitably repay such debts before one can attain it. Who among you possesses the fruit of the Way that naturally attracts the offerings of the faithful?
Those who do not accept them are Bodhisattvas practicing Prajñā; they must not deceive themselves, remaining as firm as icebergs.

To ascend [the path] is like walking upon the edge of a sword. At the moment of death, if even a single hair’s breadth of the mental calculations of ordinary or sage remains unexhausted, or if the slightest speck of thought has not been forgotten, one will be reborn according to that very thought.
With the five aggregates—light or heavy—one takes form within the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse;
or, having finished being boiled once in the cauldrons of the hells, one follows former memories, recollections, views, and wisdom.
Wisdom was lost all at once; relying on his former state, he became an ant again, and from the beginning, he became a mosquito or a gadfly once more.
Although these were virtuous causes, they resulted in such evil fruits. Brothers, what was his aim?

It was simply because greed had become his nature that the twenty-five realms of existence remained tethered beneath his heels, with no hope of liberation. The Patriarch observed the sentient beings of this land and saw that—
The root-nature of the Mahāyāna transmits only the Mind-Seal (citta-mudrā) to point out deluded sentiments.
Those who attain it do not discriminate between the ordinary and the sage, nor between the ignorant and the wise; moreover, much emptiness is not as good as a little reality.

A true man of great capacity should, right now, directly come to rest, suddenly stilling all activities, transcending the stream of birth and death, and soaring far beyond conventional patterns, so that the numinous light shines alone.
Radiant and majestic, unbound by the entanglements of material things, he stands towering and magnificent, walking alone through the three realms.
Why need one be six feet tall, with a purple-golden luster, a halo encircling the neck, and the mark of the broad and long tongue? To see me in form is to walk upon a deviant path.
Even if there were retinues and adornments, they would be attained without seeking; mountains, rivers, and the great earth would not obstruct the eye’s vision. One attains the Great Totality.
He maintained it; upon hearing it once, he attained awakening in a thousand ways. He did not seek even the price of a single meal.

If you all were not like this, the arrival of the Patriarch in this land would have been nothing but detrimental rather than beneficial. As for those who find benefit, among hundreds or thousands of people—
If one or two individuals are fished out who are fit to serve as vessels for the Dharma, those who are damaged have already been explained above.

As for others, it does not hinder them from practicing according to the teachings of the Three Vehicles; they may nonetheless attain the four fruits and the three stages of worthiness, possessing the capacity for further progress.
Therefore, the former masters said: "When realized, karmic obstacles are originally empty; when unrealized, one must repay past debts."
When the Master was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The nature of your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is coeval with the great void;
it is neither born nor extinguished. All realms of experience are by nature empty and still from the beginning; not a single dharma can be grasped.
Those who are deluded do not understand this and are thus bewildered by objects, wandering through saṃsāra without end. You all should know that the nature of mind is inherently..."
It exists. It is not produced through conditioning; it is like a diamond, indestructible.
All phenomena are like shadows and echoes, devoid of substantial reality. Thus, a sutra says: "Only this one thing is real; the other two are not true.
If you understand that all things are empty and there is not a single object to engage the mind, this is precisely where the Buddhas apply their minds. You all—
"Practice it with diligence. Having finished speaking, he became silent.
Chan Master Xitang Zhizang of Qianzhou (the fifth in this series), a native of the Liao family of his own prefecture, was once engaged in communal labor.
"It is said that cause and effect are clearly manifest; what can be done? What can be done? At that time, a monk stepped forward and propped his hand against the ground.
The Master asked, "What are you doing? The monk replied, "To save me! To save me! The Master called out, "Great assembly! This monk is still somewhat capable.
The monk then brushed his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "A worm within the lion's body eats the lion's own flesh."
A monk asked, "Setting aside for a moment the case where there is a question and an answer, what is it like when there is neither question nor answer?
The Master said, "I am afraid you will rot away. Baizhang said, "I have always harbored doubts about you, elder brother. A monk asked Baizhang, "Please, Master, speak.
Baizhang said, "The unified whole (yīhéxiàng) cannot be grasped. Later, a monk asked Changqing, and Changqing said, "When we meet, everyone says 'enough.'"
The official departed. "In the forest below, when have I ever seen a single person?
While the Master was on the road, he encountered an imperial messenger who invited him to a meal. By chance, he heard a donkey braying; the messenger called to the Master, who looked up.
The messenger pointed at the donkey, but the Master pointed back at the messenger. The messenger was speechless.
Baofu Zhan said, "Xitang, upon celebrating the meal, praised the Dharma-eye; otherwise, he would simply bray like a donkey.
A lay official asked, "Are there heavens and hells? The Master replied, "There are. [The official] asked, "Are there the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha? The Master replied, "There are."
The Master said, "Yes. There were many more questions, and he answered each one, saying, "Yes. The official asked, "Have you not made a mistake, Preceptor?
The Master said, "Whom have you ever met before? [The official] replied, "I once attended upon the Preceptor of Mount Jing. The Master said:
Jingshan asked, "Tell me, what do you say? He replied, "Whenever I am asked anything, I always answer that there is 'nothing'.
The Master said, "Do you have a wife and children? He replied, "I do. The Master said, "Does the Abbot of Jingshan have them too?
He replied, "Jingshan is an ancient Buddha; please do not slander him, Master. The Master said, "The Abbot of Jingshan can indeed say that there is 'nothing'."
Li Ao asked a monk, "What sayings did Master Mazu have? The monk replied, "Sometimes he said 'this very mind is Buddha,' and sometimes he said 'neither mind nor Buddha.
Li Ao said, "Both of these fall into the trap of verbal extremes. Li Ao then turned to ask the Master himself. The Master called out, "Li Ao!"
Li Yingnuo replied. The Master said, "The drums and horns are sounding.
Chan Master Dazhu Huikai of Yuezhou (sixth in the lineage). A native of the Zhu family of Jianzhou, he first visited Mazu.
Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from Dayun Temple in Yuezhou. Mazu asked, "What do you seek by coming here? The Master replied, "I seek..."
Regarding the Buddha-dharma, the Patriarch said: "In my place here, there is not a single thing. What Buddha-dharma do you seek?

You have your own precious treasury, yet you disregard it; why do you abandon your home and wander about? The Master asked: "Which one is this precious treasury of mine? The Patriarch said: [The Master’s own body].
"The one who is questioning me right now is your own treasure-trove. It is fully complete; you may enjoy it with mastery, lacking nothing further.
There is no need to seek it externally. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment, recognizing his own original mind without depending on the awakening of another.
He leaped for joy, prostrated himself, and offered his thanks.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you are naturally fine, good people with nothing to do. Why do you toil so hard, seeking to take up the cangue and fall into prison?
Every day until nightfall, you rush about, saying, 'I am practicing Chan and studying the Way; I understand the Buddha-dharma. In doing so, you only move further away from the truth.
You are merely chasing after sounds and forms; when will you ever find rest? The Poor Monk heard that along the Yangtze River...
The Western Monk said: "Your own family treasure is complete in every respect; its use is at your own disposal, requiring no seeking from without.
From this moment on, I shall rest for a time. With the wealth of one's own house, enjoying it according to one's needs—this can truly be called happiness."
There is not a single dharma to be grasped; there is not a single dharma to be abandoned. One does not perceive the signs of arising and ceasing in a single dharma;

one does not perceive the signs of coming and going in a single dharma. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not even a speck as small as a mote of dust that is not one's own precious treasury.
Simply observe minutely for yourself: the Three Jewels of the single essence of your own mind are constantly manifest before you; there is no need for doubt or anxiety. Do not...
Investigate; do not seek or search, for the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"All phenomena are unborn; all phenomena are unceasing. If one can understand them thus, the Buddhas are ever present before one. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:

"Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way. If you do not let your thoughts move following sounds and forms, and do not give rise to understanding by chasing after appearances, you will naturally be free from affairs.
Do not stand for long. Take care. The assembly remained for a long time without dispersing. The Master said, "Why do you all stay here and not leave?
I have already presented [the truth] directly to your faces; are you still willing to rest? What more is there?"
The matter is suspicious; do not misapply your mind, nor waste your energy and strength. If you have a point of doubt, feel free to ask as you please at your earliest convenience.
At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked: "What is the Buddha? What is the Dharma? What is the Sangha?"
"What is the Three Jewels as a single essence? The Master said: "The mind is Buddha; do not seek Buddha by means of Buddha. The mind is Dharma;
do not seek Dharma by means of Dharma. Since Buddha and Dharma are non-dual, their harmonious union constitutes the Sangha—this is the Three Jewels as a single essence.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. When body, speech, and mind are pure, this is called the appearance of a Buddha."
In this world, when the three karmas are not pure, it is called the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. This is analogous to how there is no joy when one is angry, and no anger when one is joyful;

it is but a single mind, truly without two distinct entities. Fundamental wisdom is its natural state, and when the untainted manifests, it is like a snake transforming into a dragon without changing its scales.
When sentient beings turn their minds to become Buddhas, they do not change their faces; their nature is fundamentally pure. It is not...

Awaiting cultivation and realization, there is both realization and practice; this is identical to those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*). In true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) there is no obstruction, and its application is inexhaustible.
Without beginning and without end, those of sharp faculties attain sudden enlightenment, and their application is peerless;

this is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. That the mind has no form or characteristic is itself the subtle and wondrous form-body (*rūpakāya*); that it is without marks is itself the reality-mark Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This is the essence of nature and characteristics.
Emptiness is precisely the boundless body of empty space. Adorned with the myriad practices is precisely the dharma-body of merit.

This dharma-body is the source of all transformations; it receives various names according to its location. Its wisdom and function are inexhaustible, and thus it is named the "Inexhaustible Treasury."
That which can give rise to the myriad dharmas is called the Dharma-treasury (dharmagarbha). That which possesses all-knowledge is called the Wisdom-treasury (jñānagarbha).

That wherein the myriad dharmas return to suchness is called the Tathāgata-treasury (tathāgatagarbha). As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. It further states:
"Among all the arising and ceasing dharmas in the world, there is not a single dharma that does not return to suchness."
The Seat-Master Vimalakīrti asked: "The Sūtra says: 'Those six heterodox teachers and their like are your teachers;
because you have gone forth under them, wherever your teachers fall, you shall likewise fall. Those who give to you do not call you a field of merit;

those who make offerings to you will fall into the three evil realms. You slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma; you are not numbered among the assembly, and in the end, you shall never attain nirvāṇa.'"
"If you are thus, then you may take this food. Now I request that the Meditation Master clearly explain this for me. The Master said:

"To wander deludedly through the six sense organs is called being a 'Six Teachers' (heretic). To seek the Buddha outside of the mind is called being a 'Non-Buddhist' (tīrthika). To have a thing that can be given away is not called a 'Field of Merit.
To give rise to a thought to receive offerings is to fall into the three evil realms. If you are able to slander the Buddha, then you are non-attached."
To seek the Buddha is to not seek by clinging to the Dharma; to not enter the ranks of the assembly is to not seek by clinging to the Saṃgha;

that one ultimately does not attain extinction (nirvāṇa) is the manifestation of the functioning of wisdom. If there is such an understanding, one shall obtain the food of the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna.
A presiding master asked: "The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that one delivers the nine classes of sentient beings, all of whom enter nirvana without remainder;
yet it also states that in reality, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction. How can these two passages of scripture be reconciled from beginning to end?"

People all say that you truly deliver sentient beings while not grasping at the mark of a sentient being; yet I have always harbored doubts and cannot reach a decision. I beg the Master to explain this for me. The Master said:
"The nine classes of sentient beings are fully present within a single body; they are formed as one acts. Therefore, ignorance constitutes birth from an egg;
being enveloped by afflictions constitutes birth from a womb; being moistened by the waters of craving constitutes birth from moisture; and when affliction suddenly arises—"
Delusion constitutes birth through transformation; awakening is itself Buddhahood. To be deluded is called being a sentient being; the Bodhisattva takes every thought-moment as a sentient being.
If one realizes that the substance of every thought-moment is entirely empty, this is called "delivering sentient beings.

The wise person, from the perspective of their own primordial limit, delivers those who have not yet taken form. Since that which has not yet taken form is empty, they know that in reality there are no sentient beings, and thus they attain parinirvāṇa.
A Dharma Master asked: "If I were to pose a question, would you, Master, answer it? The Master said: "The moon’s reflection in a cold pool—take hold of it as you will.
[The Master] was asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "In clear conversation face-to-face—who else could it be but the Buddha? The Master continued: "You have spoken."
"What Dharma do you teach? For what kind of person do you intend to provide a means of deliverance? The Master said, "I have never had a single Dharma by which to deliver people.

Emperor Xianzong remarked, "The Dharma Master has lectured on limitless sutras and treatises, yet regarding this single point, he is utterly helpless."

The Master asked the eminent virtuous ones, "In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, what do you take to be the Way? One replied, "That which knows is it. The Master said, "It cannot be known by wisdom;
it cannot be cognized by consciousness. How can you say that 'that which knows' is it? Another replied, "That which is free from discrimination is it.
The Master said, "One who is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena remains unmoved within the primary truth (*paramārtha*). He then remained in peace.
"One who has attained non-discrimination is [the one]. Someone said, "The four dhyānas and eight samādhis are [it].

The Master said, "The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into any numerical categories. How could the four dhyānas and eight samādhis be it? Thereupon, the entire assembly remained speechless.
Miaoxi said, "If you scold one another, I will spare you by taking up the challenge; if you spit at one another, I will spare you by splashing water.
Emperor Shunzong asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty has asked. The Emperor attained silent realization.
Chan Master Zhijian of Shanshan in Chizhou (fourth in the series), along with Guizong and Nanquan, encountered a tiger while traveling on the road.
Each passed it by its side. Nanquan asked Guizong, "What was that tiger you just saw like? Guizong said, "It was like a cat.
He then asked the Master, who replied, "It was like a dog. The Master then asked Nanquan, who said, "It was like..."
Dachong was serving as the master’s attendant during a communal work session for selecting ferns. Nanquan picked up a stalk of fern and said, "This is excellent for making an offering.
Dachong replied, "He does not care for this alone; he does not even regard the hundred flavors of exquisite delicacies. Nanquan said, "Even so..."
"Each and every one must experience it for themselves before they can truly understand.
During a meal, Nanquan gathered up some raw rice and asked, "What is this 'raw'? The Master said, "Non-arising. Nanquan said, "Even 'non-arising' is still secondary.
After Nanquan had walked a few steps, the Master called out, "Elder! Nanquan asked, "What is it? The Master said, "Do not speak of it."
This is excellent.
A monk asked, "What is the original body? The Master said, "In all the world, there is nothing like it.
Chan Master Mingxi Daohang of Fengzhou (Case 1) addressed the assembly, saying: "I have a great illness; it is not of this world."
Later, a monk asked Caoshan, “I have heard it said of old: ‘I have a great illness, which cannot be cured by worldly physicians.
I wonder, what kind of illness is this? Caoshan replied, “It is an illness that cannot be gathered together. The monk asked, “Do all sentient beings have it as well?
Caoshan said, “Everyone has it. The monk asked, “Does the Master have it too? Caoshan said, “I am currently searching for its arising.”
[The monk] said, "It cannot be found. Why then are all sentient beings not ill? Cao said, "If sentient beings were ill, they would not be sentient beings.
[The monk] asked, "I wonder, do the Buddhas also have this illness? Cao said, "They do. [The monk] said, "Since they do..."
"Why are you not ill? Cao replied, "Because he is wide awake.
Chan Master Huizang of Shigong in Fuzhou (four cases in total).
Originally a hunter pursuing deer, he passed by Mazu’s hermitage and asked, "Do you see my deer? Mazu said, "Who are you? He replied, "A hunter. Mazu—
[The Master] asked, "How many does your single arrow shoot? He replied, "A single arrow shoots one. The Patriarch said, "You are not a skilled archer.
He asked, "Does the Master shoot well? The Patriarch said, "I am a skilled archer. He asked, "How many does a single arrow shoot? The Patriarch said, "A single arrow shoots a whole flock.
He said, "Since both sides possess life, why use it to shoot a whole flock? The Patriarch said, "If you know this to be so, why [do you act otherwise]?"
He did not shoot himself. [The Master] said, "If you tell me to shoot myself, there is simply no place to begin.

The Patriarch said, "This fellow’s ignorance and afflictions from kalpas past have today been suddenly stilled. The Master cast down his bow and arrows and entered the Patriarch’s community to leave the household life.
Fadeng said: "Tell me, what is the principle of 'one arrow piercing a flock'?
Truly, even the life-force of the three thousand great chiliocosms does not require a single arrow."
From that time on, whenever any monk arrived, the Master would set an arrow to his bow and point it at him. One day, Sanping came;
the Master called out, "Look! An arrow! Sanping spread open his chest and said, "This is a 'killing arrow. What about a 'life-giving arrow'?"

The Master struck the bowstring three times. Baizhang immediately prostrated himself. The Master said, "For thirty years, I have set up a single bow and two arrows, yet I could only shoot half a saint.
He then snapped the bow and arrows in two. Later, Baizhang went to visit Dayuan and recounted the previous conversation.
Dayuan said, "Since it is a 'living man's arrow,' why did you identify it by the bowstring? Baizhang was speechless.
Dian said, "Thirty years from now, it will be difficult to find anyone who can bring up this story.
While the Master was performing manual labor in the kitchen, the Patriarch asked him, "What are you doing? He replied, "I am tending the ox. The Patriarch asked, "How do you tend it?"
[The Master] said, "Once you have entered the grass, I will pull you back by the nose. Guishan said, "You truly know how to herd an ox.
The Master asked Xitang, "Do you know how to catch empty space? Tang said, "I know how to catch it. The Master said, "How do you catch it?
Tang reached out his hand and grasped at the air. The Master said, "You do not know how to catch it. Tang asked, "How about you, Elder Brother?"
The Master seized Xitang by the nose and pulled. Tang made a cry of pain and said, "You are pulling my nostrils so hard that they are about to fall right off.
The Master said, "One must grasp it exactly like this before one succeeds."
Chan Master Daoming of Nanyuan in Yuanzhou (in two parts) addressed the assembly, saying: "A swift man needs but one word; a swift horse needs but one lash.
If you have something to say, why do you not put your head out? If you have nothing to say, each of you should take care of yourselves. A monk asked, "What is this one word?
The Master stuck out his tongue and said, "Wait until I possess the mark of a broad and long tongue, and then I shall tell you."
Dongshan came; as soon as he stepped onto the Dharma Hall, the Master said, "We have already met. Dongshan then went down.
The next day he came up again and asked, "Yesterday I was already graced by the Master’s compassion; I do not know where that meeting took place."
The Master said, "Mind after mind, without interruption, flows into the ocean of nature. Dong said, "I should have let this pass," and then took his leave.

Yangshan bowed and said, "I have just now received the Master’s analogy; there is nothing I do not understand."

Chongshou Zhenchou said: "Is there anyone who can definitively grasp this principle?

Lingyan An said: "Lingyan has a monkey whose six sense-faculties are completely sealed and in whom not a single thought arises.
You cannot pull it forward, nor can you push it back. How would you call it? If it responds when called, I grant you that you possess the single eye.
If it does not respond when called, I also grant you that you possess the single eye."
Chan Master Fuguang Ruyuan of Luojing (1) Emperor Shunzong of the Tang dynasty asked: "From what direction does the Buddha come? Toward what direction does he go when he passes away?

Since it is said that he dwells eternally in the world, where is the Buddha now? The Master replied: "The Buddha comes from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and goes toward the unconditioned when he passes away.
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is equal to empty space; it is ever-present in the state of no-mind. When thought arises, it returns to non-existence."
Contemplate this: abiding, one returns to non-abiding; coming, one comes for the sake of sentient beings; going, one goes for the sake of sentient beings.
The ocean of pure *tathatā* is serene, its essence eternally abiding. The wise who contemplate well should no longer give rise to doubt or hesitation. The Emperor asked again:
"The Buddha was born in the royal palace and passed away at the twin śāla trees. He dwelt in the world for forty-nine years, yet it is also said that he taught no Dharma. Mount... [text ends]
The rivers and the great earth, heaven and earth, and the sun and moon—all these, when their time comes, return to extinction. Who would say they are not subject to arising and ceasing?

Such are the lingering doubts. The wise distinguish them well. The Master said: "The essence of the Buddha is fundamentally unconditioned; it is only through deluded feelings that one falsely discriminates.
The Dharmakāya is equal to empty space; it has never undergone arising or ceasing. When conditions exist, a Buddha appears in the world; when conditions are absent, a Buddha enters [nirvāṇa]."
Extinction: Manifesting among sentient beings everywhere like the moon in water, it is neither permanent nor annihilated, neither arising nor ceasing.
It has never arisen, nor has it ever ceased. To clearly perceive this state of no-mind is naturally beyond verbal expression.

Master Zizai of Funiu at Ique (two instances): He was the son of the Li family of Wuxing. He served as a messenger for Mazu.
The Master [Baizhang] paid his respects to National Teacher Huairang. The National Teacher asked, "How did Master Mazu instruct his disciples? Baizhang replied, "He said, 'The very mind is Buddha.
The National Teacher remarked, "What kind of talk is that? He asked again, "Are there any other sayings? Baizhang replied, "'Neither mind nor Buddha.'"
Someone said, "It is neither mind nor Buddha. The National Teacher said, "That is still somewhat off the mark. The Master then asked, "I wonder, how do you instruct your disciples here?
The National Teacher replied, "The three dots are like flowing water; the curve is like a sickle for reaping grain."
At the point where Xuedou says, "He was still slightly off," he gives a shout. Furthermore, at the point where it says, "It is like a sickle cutting grain," he asks, "What kind of talk is this?

He addressed the assembly, saying: "To say 'this very mind is Buddha' is like seeking medicine when one is not ill. To say 'neither this mind nor Buddha' is for the medicine and the illness to treat one another.
A monk asked, "What is the phrase that brings liberation? The Master said, "It has been passed down through ancient and modern times beneath Mount Funiu."
Chan Master Ruhui of Dongsi Temple in Hunan (fourth in the series). He was a native of Qujiang in Shixing. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. The sword has long since departed, yet you are still marking the boat."
The Master asked Yangshan, "Where are you from? Yangshan replied, "I am a man from Guangnan. The Master said, "I have heard that Guangnan possesses the 'Taming the Sea' Bright Pearl.
Is this true? He replied, "It is. The Master asked, "What is this pearl like? He replied, "In the bright moon it is hidden;
in the dark moon it appears. The Master asked, "Can you bring it here? He replied, "I can bring it here. The Master said, "Why do you not present it to me, old monk? He replied—
"Yesterday, I went to Mount Gui and was asked for this pearl. I was left with no words to respond and no reason to proffer.

The Master said, 'A true lion cub, truly capable of roaring. It is like a tiny gnat building a nest upon the eyelashes of a mosquito, yet standing at a crossroads and shouting loudly, 'The land is vast and the people are few; those who encounter me are rare.'"
Yangshan arrived. The Master said, "We have already met; there is no need for you to come up. Yangshan asked, "If we meet in this way, would that not be improper?

"What kind of mental activity is this? Yangshan said, "If it were not so, how could one recognize him?

The Master entered the Buddha hall together with Prime Minister Cui. Seeing a sparrow dropping dung on the Buddha’s head, he asked, "Is it true that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature?

The Master said, "It would never go so far as to drop it on a hawk’s head."

Nanquan merely managed to see through the wall."
Dongshan came forward to pay his respects and stood in attendance. After a short while, he went out, but then entered again.
The Master said, "Just so, just so; that is why it is like this. Dongshan replied, "Many people would not agree with this. The Master said, "How can you take such verbal cleverness?
Dongshan then attended upon him for several months.
A monk asked, "What is the tree of the Twin Śāla groves? The Master said, "The formless body within the body with form.
The monk asked, "What is the formless body? The Master said, "An iron Kunlun man beneath a golden incense burner."
A monk asked, "What is 'speaking without speaking'? The Master said, "Where is your mouth? The monk replied, "I have no mouth.
The Master said, "What do you usually use to eat your meals? The monk was speechless.
Dongshan said, "He is not hungry; what rice would he eat? Xuedou said, "A good back-breaking blow!
This fellow cannot close his mouth once it is open, nor can he open it once it is closed."
Chan Master Mingzhe of Bairyam in Dingzhou (Part Two). When Dongshan and his senior teacher Mi arrived, the Master asked, "Where have you two monks come from?
Dongshan said, "From Hunan. The Master asked, "What is the surname of the Military Governor? Dongshan said, "He has no surname.
The Master asked, "What is his given name? He said, "He has no given name. The Master asked, "Does he still attend to administrative affairs? He said—
"Since there is naturally a vast expanse," the Master said. "Does it still enter and exit? Dong said, "It does not enter or exit.
The Master said, "How can it not enter and exit? Dong shook his sleeves and left. The next morning at dawn, the Master entered the hall and summoned the two head monks;
the two immediately came out. The Master said, "Yesterday, when I spoke a phrase to you, head monks, it did not satisfy me. All night long—"
[The Master] was uneasy. He then requested the Elder to provide a different turn of phrase; if it pleased the old monk’s mind, he would open the gruel and stay together for the summer retreat.

Dongshan said, "Please ask the Master. The Master said, "Neither entering nor exiting. Dongshan said, "How very noble you are! Thereupon, the Master opened the gruel and stayed for the summer together with him.
The Master saw Youshan reading a sutra and said, "Old Monk, do not act like a monkey. Youshan set aside his sutra and asked, "Is it early or late in the day?
The Master replied, "It is midday. Youshan said, "There is still a trace of literary artistry there.
The Master said, "I have nothing at all. Youshan said, "My friend is truly clever. The Master said, "I am simply this way; what would you have me do, Teacher?"
"How is it? The Master said, "Lame and hobbling; a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses. Just pass the time like this.
Chan Master Weikuan of Xingshan Monastery in Jingzhao Prefecture (Case 2). He was the son of the Zhu family of Xin'an in Quzhou.
When a monk asked, "Where does the Way reside? the Master said, "It is right before your eyes. The monk said, "Why do I not see it? The Master said, "Because you have a self."
"Therefore, one does not see. Because one says 'I have an I,' one does not see. I do not yet know, Master: do you still see or not? The Master said:

"When there is you and there is me, we pass each other by and do not see. When there is no you and no me, do you still see or not? The Master said: "When there is no you and no me, who is it that seeks to see?"
A monk asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? The Master said, "It has. The monk asked, "Does the Master have it too, or not? The Master said, "I do not.
The monk asked, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; why then do you, Master, lack it? The Master said, "I am not a sentient being.
The monk asked, "If you are not a sentient being, are you then a Buddha? The Master said, "No."
[The student] asked, "What is this 'ultimate'? The Master said, "It is not even a thing. [The student] asked, "Can it be seen or can it be thought?
The Master said, "It is beyond the reach of thought; it cannot be deliberated upon. Therefore, it is called 'inconceivable' (acintya)."
Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai of Hongzhou (Part II). One day he said to the assembly, "You all shall cultivate the fields for me, and I shall expound the Great Meaning for you.
When the monks had finished cultivating the fields, they said, "We request the Master to expound the Great Meaning.
The Master opened both hands wide.
Baizhang said, "The Great Meaning has been explained here; it ends at this point.
Where did those who were present at that time and had already studied under Mazu go? If one says there is more, it is no different from adding feet to a snake.
But how can one know where the old man Baizhang stood? When a guest arrives and there is no tea or refreshments—how vexing!
Tang prepared the ritual protocols (this is an error; it should read "uttered words of great wisdom" when picking up the whisk).
The Master asked Nanquan, "Among the masters of the past, was there any Dharma that they did not teach to others? Nanquan said, "There was."
The Master asked, "What is this Dharma that is not spoken for the sake of others? Fayan said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
The Master said, "If that is so, then you have already spoken it. Fayan said, "I am only like this; how about you, Master?
The Master said, "I am not even a spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra); how could I know whether there is speaking or no speaking? Fayan... [remained silent].
Baizhang said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "I have explained it to you thoroughly enough.
Daguai Zhe said: "Baizhang only knew how to look forward; he did not know how to look back.

Had he waited until the other said, 'I do not understand,' and simply replied, 'I do not understand either,' he would not only have served as a teacher and a craftsman for Nanquan, but [would have been so himself]."
He was also a teacher and a master for all people under heaven.
Chan Master Ledu Tan of Hongzhou (Case 1): The Master asked Mazu, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Mazu said, “Lower your voice. He then called to the Master, “Come closer. When the Master drew near, Mazu struck him.
The Master said, "One hand clapping makes no sound; six ears do not share a secret. Go now, and come back tomorrow.
The next day, the student asked again. The Master said, "Wait until I ascend the hall; I will come out then to bear witness for you. At these words, the student attained realization.
Chan Master Lètán Chángxīng of Hongzhou (Part Two). Once, while serving food, the Master was with Layman Páng.
As the Layman reached for the food, the Master withdrew his hand and said, “To receive a gift with a conceptual mind was already rebuked by Vimalakīrti.

Apart from this single instance, would you, Layman, still find it acceptable? The Layman replied, “At that time, was Subhūti not a master himself? The Master said, “What business is that of his? The Layman—
[The Master] said, "When food reaches the edge of my mouth, it is snatched away by someone. The Master then set down his food.
The Layman said, "Not even a single phrase will suffice. The Layman asked, "Does the Master transmit the point where Master Mazu truly benefits people?
The Master said, "I do not even see him; how could I know his point of true benefit? The Layman said, "Even with such an understanding, there is nothing to be sought."
The Master said, "Layman, you must not speak with one-sidedness. The Layman said, "If I were to speak with one-sidedness, you, Master, would still lose the essential point.
But if I were to speak from two directions or three directions, would you, Master, still be able to open your mouth?
The Master said, "Truly, one cannot open one's mouth; this may be called reality. The Layman clapped his hands and departed.
Nanquan arrived and saw the Master sitting with his face against the wall. Nanquan patted the Master’s back once. The Master asked, “Who is there?
Nanquan replied, “Puyuan. The Master said, “What is it? Nanquan said, “It is quite ordinary. The Master said, “Why do you trouble yourself so much?”
Miaoxi said, "One must also verify this.
Chan Master Shanjue of Hualin in Tanzhou (three times in total) constantly carried his staff; at night he would go out from the forested foothills and shake his staff once.
Once, upon the mere utterance of Avalokiteśvara’s name, Jia Shan asked, "I have heard from afar that you, Master, recite the name of Avalokiteśvara; is this true? The Master replied, "It is so.

Shan said, "What is it like when one has already mounted the head? The Master said, "If you come out of the head, I will let you mount it; if you do not come out of the head, what is there to mount? Shan was speechless.
A monk arrived and was just unfolding his sitting mat when the Master said, "Slowly, slowly. The monk asked, "What have you seen, Reverend? The Master said, "What a pity!
You've just smashed the bell tower. From this, the monk attained awakening.
Prime Minister Pei Xiu asked the Master, "Do you have any attendants? The Master replied, "I have one or two.
He added, "They simply cannot see guests. Pei asked, "Where are they? The Master called out, "Dàkōng! Xiǎokōng! Immediately, two tigers emerged from behind the hermitage.
Startled and trembling, Pei was seized with fear. The Master said to the two tigers, "There is a guest here; depart for now. The tigers roared and left.
Pei asked, "What kind of practice did you perform to evoke such a response? The Master remained silent for a long while and then said, "Do you understand? Pei replied, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, constantly recite the name of Avalokiteśvara."
Chan Master Zhen Shu of Yangqi in Yuanzhou (Part II). Addressing the assembly, he said: "The myriad spirits share a single source; it is provisionally named 'Buddha.

Though the physical body is exhausted and form dissolves, it does not perish; though the metal melts and the raw ore disperses, it remains ever-present. In the ocean of nature, where there is no wind, the golden ripples surge of themselves.
In the spiritual source, where all signs cease, the ten thousand phenomena are simultaneously illuminated. Those who realize this principle traverse everywhere without speaking."

Like the sands of the Ganges, though they do not exert themselves, their merit increasingly deepens the mysterious transformation. How can you turn your back on awakening and instead return to worldly toil, delusively imprisoning yourself within the aggregates and realms?
Chan Yue asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master held up his rosary. Chan Yue was at a loss for words.
The Master asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. The Master said, "I have studied under Shitou.
Chan Yue asked, "Master, what realization did you obtain from Shitou? The Master pointed to a deer in front of him and asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. The Master said, "He..."
"I have attained freedom.
Once, while Master Tanchang of Xiyuan on Mount Nanyue (Case 1) was burning wood for a bath, a monk asked him, "Master, you do not employ śrāmaṇeras or novices;
why do you burn it yourself? The Master clapped his hands three times. Later, the monk related this to Caoshan.
Shan said, "In one sense, they are equally people clapping their hands and patting their palms; yet among them, Xiyuan was extraordinary.
As for Juzhi’s 'one-finger Zen,' it is because his way of taking up the task was not thorough. The monk asked, "When Xiyuan patted his palms, was that not merely the business of servants and slaves?
Shan said, "Yes. The monk asked, "Is there anything further beyond this? Shan said, "There is."
The monk asked, "What is the matter that transcends [the ordinary]? Mount [Shan] rebuked him, saying, "You wretched servant!

Chan Master Yi of Dayang in Yingzhou (Case 1): Once he arrived at Shilin, Lin said, "Lately there is a certain type of Chan master who instructs people to 'realize the matter before one's eyes' as a means of helping others. Do you understand this when the literary patterns have not yet emerged?"
Linji said, "Is it not so? The Master said, "I intend to pose a question here; I do not know if it is permissible. Linji said, "I have already answered you;
do not speak of permissibility or impermissibility. The Master said, "Do you recognize what is right before your eyes? Linji said, "How would one recognize that which is right before one's eyes?
The Master said, "One cannot avoid being scrutinized by others. Linji said, "By whom? The Master said, "By me. Linji said, "By me."
[Zhaozhou] let out a shout. The Master [Linji] stepped back and stood there. Linji said, "You only know how to look forward; you do not yet know how to look back.
Zhaozhou said, "Adding frost upon snow. Linji said, "Neither of us has gained any advantage."
Chan Master Lanrang of Xibei (1): Once, when the Elder Hu Tangliang asked him, "I have heard that you, Elder Brother, have painted a portrait of our late master;
may I borrow it for a moment to pay my respects? The Master patted his chest and showed it to him. Tangliang immediately prostrated himself.
The Master said, "Do not prostrate! Do not prostrate! Tangliang said, "Elder Brother, do not be mistaken; I am not prostrating to you. The Master said, "You..."
He was about to pay respects to the true image of the former master when [the Master] said, "Why do you instruct me not to pay respects?
The Master replied, "When have I ever been mistaken? Chan Master Datong of Ziyu Mountain in Tangzhou (two cases). He was the son of the He family of Lujiang.

When Prime Minister Yu Di asked about the ultimate principle of the Buddha-dharma, requesting a word from the Master, the Master said, "If you, Prime Minister, would ask, you must first eliminate your own conceptual attachments."
Li Yu invited the Master to his residence. The Master said, "Just ask whatever you wish. Li Yu asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master called out, "Yu Di! Li Yu responded, "Yes? The Master said, "Do not seek anything else. When Yaoshan heard of this, he remarked, "Alas!
What a man from the Yu family, buried alive within Mount Ziyu. Upon hearing this, the Duke went in person to visit Yaoshan. When Yaoshan saw him, he...
The official asked, "I have heard that you, Great Master, are performing great Buddhist rites on Mount Ziyu. Is this true? The Master replied, "I dare not say so.
The official said, "I have heard the Master say that this man from the Yu family is a pity to be buried alive on Mount Ziyu.
Today I have come specifically to request the Master’s instruction. The Master said, "If you have a doubt, ask away. The official asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master called out to him.
Yu Di responded, "Yes. The Mountain (Shan) asked, "What is this? At these words, Yu had an awakening.
Later, while Zhaoqing and Luoshan were discussing the case together, Zhaoqing said, "In one sense it is the Way;
Yaoshan was truly extraordinary. There is a vast difference between clouds and mud. Luoshan said, "One must not be too casual. At that time, it was fortunate that it was Yu Di."
"In the midst of a patch of weeds, he stirs up a scorched-tailed tiger. Where is there a Yaoshan?
Qingsong said, "How so? Luoxi replied, "Do you still recognize that Yu Di is refined pure gold?"
One day, Lord Yu asked, "What is it like when black winds blow their ship and they are cast adrift into the realm of rākṣasa demons?
The Master said, "Yu Di, you hired laborer! Why do you ask such a question? Yu turned pale with fear.
The Master pointed and said, "This very thing is being blown by black winds and cast into the realm of rākṣasa demons. Yu bowed and thanked him.
Chan Master Shenzang of Matou Peak in Cizhou (1) addressed the assembly, saying: "To know while being without knowing—this is not a state of non-knowing that one speaks of as 'knowing nothing.'"
Nanquan said, "To follow the Master's way in such a manner is only to achieve half of it.
Huangbo said, "It was not that Nanquan was stripping away his words; he intended to complete the previous statement."
Chan Master Deng Yinfeng of Mount Wutai (total of eight entries). A native of the Deng clan of Shaowu, he appeared as if lacking intelligence in his youth.
His parents permitted him to leave the household life. He first studied under Mazu and later traveled back and forth to Shitou.

On two occasions, he did not achieve success. Later, he asked Shitou, "How can one become in accord with the Way? Shitou replied, "I, too, am not in accord with the Way. The Master said, "Ultimately, it is like..."
"What? Tou asked. "How long has it been since you were struck by this? The Master had no reply. Later, he had his mind certified by Mazu Daoshi.
While the Master was in Shitou’s assembly, as Shitou was weeding grass, the Master stood to his left. Shitou tossed the hoe [at him].
He went before the Master and cut down a blade of grass. The Master said, "The Master [your teacher] can only cut this;
he does not know how to cut that. Daowu raised the hoe. The Master snatched the hoe away and made a gesture of cutting grass.
Daowu said, "You can only cut that; you do not yet know how to cut this. The Master then desisted.
The Master was in Mazu’s assembly. One day, while he was pushing a cart, Great Master Mazu sat down on the path with his legs extended.

The Master said, "I ask the Master to withdraw his feet. Mazu replied, "Once extended, they are not withdrawn. The Master said, "Once advanced, one does not retreat," and he pushed the cart over, injuring the Great Master's foot.
Mazu returned to the Dharma Hall, grasped an axe, and said, "Just now, you injured the soles of this old monk's feet."
"Come forth! The Master stepped out. The Patriarch extended his neck before him, whereupon the Master set down the axe.
When the Master arrived at Nanquan, Nanquan pointed to a water pitcher and asked him, "The pitcher is an object. There is water inside it;
do not disturb the object. Bring me some water. The Master picked up the pitcher and poured it directly onto Nanquan’s face.
Quánxiū departed.
Guīzōng Chéng said, "Dèng Yǐnfēng was extraordinary, yet he was ultimately a chaotic outpouring.

When the Master arrived at Wúshān, Wúshān heard of his arrival and immediately assumed a formal demeanor; descending from the hall, he went to meet the Master. Upon seeing him approach, the Master simply performed a backward somersault.
Shishan returned to the abbot’s quarters, and the Master departed immediately. After a short while, Shishan asked his attendant, "Is the Senior Uncle still here?
The attendant replied, "He has already left. Shishan said, "Did he say anything? "He did not say anything," the attendant replied.
Shishan said, "Do not say he said nothing; his voice was like thunder."

While the Master was at Xiangzhou, he demolished the Hall of Dignified Manners (Weiyi Tang). Wearing only his undergarments, he stood by the side of the wooden block and mallet, picked up the mallet, and said, "If you can say something, I shall not strike you.
The assembly remained silent. The Master then struck him once.
Fayan said, "Deng Yinfeng was extraordinary; he was truly extraordinary. Yet, for all his efforts, he could not strike the mark.
He further remarked, "At that time, the entire assembly appeared quite by chance."
Cuoyan Zhi said: "These words contain a point of penetration.
But tell me, whom did he penetrate? The Master once burned a monk to death. One day, the monk manifested his form and said, 'Give me back my life!
The Master said, 'Are you dead yet? He replied, 'I am already dead. The Master said, 'Since you are already dead, who is it that demands your life? At that moment, [the monk] vanished."
As the Master was about to pass away, he asked the assembly, "In various places, I have seen those who have passed away while seated. Is there anyone who has passed away while standing?
The assembly replied, "There is. The Master asked, "Is there anyone who has passed away while standing upside down? The assembly replied, "We have never heard of such a thing."
The Master died while standing on his head, remaining perfectly upright; his robes clung to his body, and he could not be moved even when carried away. The Master had a younger sister who was a nun;
seeing this, she exclaimed in reproach, "While my elder brother was alive, he did not follow the laws and regulations; now that he is dead, he continues to delude people."
He pushed it with his hand, and it fell over with a thud. He then proceeded to cremate it, collected the relics, and erected a stupa.
The Monk of Longshan in Tanzhou (Case 2) asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "I have come from the place of the elder. The Master said:
"What words and phrases are there? [The monk asked. "If one speaks, there are thousands and tens of thousands of phrases; if one does not speak, there is not even a single character.
The Master said, "In that case, even a fly has laid its eggs. The monk bowed, and the Master struck him.
Dongshan and his senior teacher Mi arrived. The Master asked, "This mountain has no path; from where have you come, Ācārya?
Dongshan said, "Setting aside for a moment the matter of there being no path, from where did the Master enter? The Master said, "I have never been a wandering monk.
Dongshan said, "How long has the Master resided on this mountain? The Master said, "I do not involve myself with spring or autumn. Dongshan...
[Daowu] said, "The Master has resided here first; this mountain has been inhabited by you first. The Master said, "I do not know. Dongshan asked, "Why do you not know?
The Master said, "I have not come from the realm of humans or devas. Dongshan asked, "What did the Master obtain that you now reside on this mountain?
The Master said, "I saw two clay oxen fighting and entering the sea; until this very day, there has been no news of them. Thus it was.
Dwelling on this mountain, he composed a verse, saying: "I have always lived in a three-bay thatched cottage; A single divine light illuminates ten thousand tranquil realms.
Do not bring matters of right and wrong to judge me; In this floating life, artificial analysis is irrelevant."
When Guishan asked the Monk of Xiuxi in Tanzhou (Case 1): "Sound and form are pure and true; what is the Way?
The Master said, "Why do you disturb the Way? Guishan walked from west to east and stood there. The Master said, "If you had not done so, disaster would have arisen.
Guishan walked from east to west and stood there. The Master descended from his rope seat; as soon as he had taken two or three steps, Guishan seized him and said:
"Voice and form are pure and true. [The Master asked,] "And how about this? The Master gave him a slap.
Shanshan said, "Thirty years from now, there will not even be a single person to serve tea. The Master said, "What would you do with an old fellow like Guoshan? Shanshan laughed heartily.

The Oxhead Monk of Zhènzhōu (in two parts). Whenever the Master ate his meals, he would carry the rice bucket to the front of the hall, perform a dance, and say, "Sons of the Bodhisattvas, come and eat!
Then he would clap his hands and laugh loudly, "Ha ha!"
Changqing Ling said, "It is very much like celebrating and praising because of a vegetarian feast.
Xuedou said, "The Golden Ox did not have good intentions.
Xuedou’s verse says: Laughing heartily within the shadows of white clouds, He takes both hands and hands it over to him.
"If one is a true cub of the golden-maned lion, one will see the point of contradiction even three thousand *li* away.
Later, a monk asked Da Guang, "When Changqing said, 'Celebrating and praising because of the feast,' what was his intended meaning?
Da Guang performed a dance. The monk bowed. Da Guang said, "What did you see that you immediately bowed? The monk performed a dance. Da Guang said, "Wild!"
The Fox Spirit.
Xuedou’s verse says: "The first arrow was still light, but the second arrow went deep. Who would say that yellow leaves resemble gold?
When the waves at Caoxi are like this, countless ordinary people sink beneath them."
The Monk of Ruyuan in Shaoyou (in two parts) addressed the assembly, saying: "The intent of the one who came from the West is not easy to proclaim.
At that time, a monk stepped forward; the Master struck him across the back and said: "What kind of season is this now, to come forth with your head?"
He then returned to his quarters.
Chengtian Zong said, "The Dharma-treasury is not easy to uphold. These two fellows could not uphold it.
I say that had this monk not stepped forward, the staff would have had to be eaten by Yunju himself."
Xichan Xu said: "Although this old fellow does not spare his own life, plunging into the mud and the water, he nonetheless blinds the eyes of all people in the world."
When Yangshan was a śrāmaṇera, he was reciting a sutra. The Master (Dongshan) scolded him, saying, "This śrāmaṇera’s recitation of the sutra is just like weeping.
Yangshan asked, "How about you, Master? The Master looked at him. Yangshan said, "If it is like this, how is it any different from weeping?"
The Monk of Hejian at the Capital (Case 1). A monk asked, "What is the secret chamber? The Master said, "Cutting off one's ears and lying in the street.
The monk asked, "Who is the person within the secret chamber? The Master said, "Changing hands and beating one's breast."
The Monk of Xingping in Jingzhao (Part Three). Dongshan came and paid his respects. The Master said, "Do not bow; I am but an old decrepit man.
Dongshan said, "The one being bowed to is not the old decrepit man. The Master said, "If it is not the old decrepit man, he would not accept your bow. Dongshan said, "He does not stop either."
Dongshan asked, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha? The Master said, "It is your very own mind.
Dongshan said, "This is still a point of doubt for me. The Master said, "If that is so, then go ask the wooden man.
Dongshan said, "I have a phrase that does not borrow from the mouths of the various sages. The Master said, "Try and say it. Dongshan said, "It is not I."
Dongshan was taking his leave. The Master asked, "Where are you going? Dongshan replied, "Following the current, there is no fixed destination.

The Master said, "Is it the Dharma-body following the current, or the Reward-body following the current? Dongshan replied, "I do not offer any such interpretation at all. The Master then clapped his hands.
Baofu Zhan said, "Dongshan has a distinct style of his own. He then called out, "How many people have you found?
[This refers to] the Monk of Fuyi in Wenzhou (Case 2). When the Master saw a monk approach, he struck the ground with his staff and said, "The Buddhas of the past were like this;
the Buddhas of the future will be like this. The monk asked, "At this very moment, what is it? The Master drew a circle.
He showed it to the monk. The monk performed a woman’s bow, whereupon the Master struck him.
The monk asked, “What is meant by ‘different species’? The Master tapped the bowl and said, “Huanu, Huanu, come and eat your rice.”
Master Caizheng (three cases). Layman Pang came. The Master said, "A worldly person enters a monastery so frequently;
what are you looking for? The Layman looked left and right and said, "Who says such a thing? The Master then gave a shout. The Layman said, "Right here.
The Master said, "Are you speaking from the front? The Layman said, "What about the one behind? The Master turned his head and said, "Look!"
"Look! The scholar said. "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. The Master retired.
The layman asked, "How many *li* is it from here to the peak? The Master said, "Where have you come from? The layman said, "It is truly steep and formidable;
I did not dare to ask further. The Master said, "How much is it? The layman said, "One, two, three. The Master said, "Four."
The Layman said, "Why not say 'seven'? The Master said, "As soon as you say 'seven,' there is already 'eight. The Layman said, "It works! It works!
The Master said, "Add as many as you wish. The Layman then gave a shout. The Master also gave a shout.
The Master was walking alongside the layman. The layman took a step forward and said, "I am one step stronger than you, Master.
The Master said, "There is no 'back' or 'front,' old man; you wish to compete for priority. The layman said, "The bitterness within bitterness is not yet this one phrase.
The Master said, "I fear you will not find it satisfying. The layman said, "If I were not satisfied, what would Qifu Peak be good for? The Master said, "If..."
Holding a staff in his hand, he did not grow weary even though he was striking. The Layman then struck the Master with a slap and said, "Not very good.
Only then did the Master pick up his staff; the Layman seized it and said, "This thief has met with a defeat today.
The Master laughed and said, "It is my clumsiness; it is you who are clever. The Layman clapped his hands and said, "An equal match! An equal match!"

One day, Danxia came to visit the Abbot of Gusisi (Episode 1). The next morning at dawn, when the congee was ready, the attendant ladled out a single bowl for the Master and another bowl for himself, paying no heed to Danxia. Danxia then went ahead and ladled out his own bowl of congee to eat.
The practitioner said, "It is already past the fifth watch and nearly dawn; yet there are still those traveling by night.
Yunju asked the Master, "Why do you not instruct this practitioner? He is so impolite. The Master said, "On pure ground, one must not defile the men and women of others.
Yunju said, "I have not even asked about his transgression."

The Monk Wujou (one instance): Two senior monks, Xuan and Shao, came to visit him. The Master asked, "Where did you two Chan masters set out from? They replied, "Jiangxi. Mazu grabbed him by the chest and gave him a kick, knocking him over. At that moment, Shuilao attained great enlightenment; he rose up, clapped his hands, and laughed loudly, saying:

"How truly marvelous! How truly marvelous! All the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and their immeasurable, wondrous meanings can be understood by recognizing their source within a single hair-tip.
Having said this, he prostrated himself.
Jiangshan Quan said, "To suddenly have a flash of realization—this is truly laughable.
Xichan Xu said, "This great Shaodu was kicked and trampled by others, yet he claimed, 'I have attained enlightenment. What enlightenment?
It was nothing but excrement! And when he got up, he lacked even a shred of shame, claiming he had recognized it upon the tip of a single hair."
Go back to the source; for now, do not press your eyes until flowers appear before you. Later, while staying there, he addressed the assembly, saying:

Lishan Wenheshang (Fanyi). A monk asked: "When all forms return to emptiness, where does emptiness return? The Master said: "The tongue does not leave the mouth.

Master Liang of Xishan in Hongzhou (Case 1). He was a native of Shu. Mazu asked the Master, "I have heard that you, Master, lecture extensively on the sutras and śāstras;
is this true? The Master replied, "I dare not say so. Mazu said, "With what do you lecture? The Master replied, [silently].
The Master was lecturing on the Heart Sutra. The Patriarch said, "The mind is like an actor, and the intellect is like the stage manager; how can you possibly explain the sutra?
The Master raised his voice and said, "If the mind cannot explain it, could it be that empty space can explain it? The Patriarch said, "Indeed, empty space can explain it.
The Master shook out his sleeves and departed. The Patriarch called out, "Lecturer! The Master turned his head. The Patriarch said, "It is."
"What is it? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and immediately prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "Dull-witted teacher, why do you prostrate yourself?

The Master asked Nanquan, "What is the Way? Nanquan replied, "Ordinary mind is the Way. The Master said, "Is it still necessary to strive toward it?

Nanquan said, "To intend to strive toward it is already to deviate. The Master said, "If one does not intend, how can one know it is the Way? Nanquan said, "The Way belongs neither to knowing nor to not-knowing.
Knowing is deluded awareness; not-knowing is indeterminate ignorance. If one truly penetrates this, there is no intention."
The Way is like the great void—vast, open, and expansive; how could one forcibly impose right and wrong upon it? Under these words, the Master suddenly realized the profound meaning.
Nanquan gave a teaching, saying: "People of the present day must act among the heterodox before they can attain it.
The Master then asked: "I do not ask about the heterodox; what is the orthodox? Nanquan placed both hands on the ground. The Master stepped forward, kicked him, and knocked him over.
He went back to the Nirvana Hall and cried out, "Regret! Regret! Master Quan sent an attendant to ask him, "What do you regret?
The Master said, "I regret that I did not give him another two kicks."
The Master was on top of the well-house drawing water when he saw Nanquan passing below. The Master clung to a pillar of the house, hanging his two feet down, and cried out, "Save me!
Save me! Nanquan tapped the ladder with his hand and said, "One, two, three, four, five.
The Master then descended from the house, assumed the full ceremonial demeanor, and went to the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects, saying, "I thank the Master for saving me just now."
The Master asked Nanquan, "Please speak on that which is beyond the four propositions and transcends the hundred negations. Nanquan descended from his seat and returned to his quarters.
The Master said, "This old fellow usually talks incessantly, but today, when questioned by me, he was left with no words to answer and no reason to offer.
An attendant remarked, "It would have been better if you had not said the Master was speechless. The Master struck the attendant.
[Zhaozhou] gave a slap and said, "This slap should have been eaten by Master Wang.
He then asked Nanquan, "Does it accord with the bright side, or does it accord with the dark side? Nanquan immediately returned to his quarters.
Zhaozhou returned to the hall and said, "The Old Monk was caught by my single question; he was left with no words to answer and no principle to defend. The Head Seat said, "Do not..."

The Master said nothing; the Head Seat realized then that he did not understand. The Master struck the Head Seat with his palm and said, "This blow should have been taken by the old man at the head of the hall."
The Fifth Patriarch Jie said: "The real thief has fled; the trackers have been beaten.
He also said: "If Nanquan had not acted decisively when it was required, he would have instead invited further chaos."
When Nanquan saw the bath attendant lighting the fire for the bath, he said, "Keep this in mind; we shall invite the Water Ox for a bath. The bath attendant responded with an assent.

The Master was serving as the head of the furnace at Nanquan. One day, he closed the door of the monks' hall, filled the room with smoke, and cried out, "Help!

Xuedou said: "It is truly laughable; one could laugh for thirty years. Suppose a monk were to ask Xuedou, 'What are you laughing at?
He would laugh and say, 'Drawing the bow after the thief has fled.'"
When the Master arrived at Yunju, Yunju said, "You are so old and advanced in years; why do you not seek a place to stay?

The Master asked, "Where would be a place for me to stay? Yunju replied, "In front of the mountain there is the site of an old temple. The Master said, "It would be better if you, Reverend, stayed there yourself."
Later, he arrived at Zhuyou. Zhuyou said, "Old as you are, why do you not seek a place to stay?
The Master said, "Where is my place to stay? Zhuyou said, "Old as you are, you do not even know where your place to stay is.
The Master said, "Thirty years of riding horses; today I have been thrown by a donkey."
Daguizhe said: "Yunju and Zhuyou treated others as they treated themselves; yet how could they avoid Zhaozhou’s failure to enter their patterns?

When the Master arrived at Zhuyou, he took up his staff and walked from west to east and from east to west across the Dharma Hall.
Zhuyou asked, "What are you doing? The Master said, "Probing the water. Zhuyou said, "I have not even a single drop here;
what is there to probe? The Master leaned his staff against the wall and departed.
Langya Huijue said: "In times of chaos, slaves deceive their masters; in times of decline, ghosts toy with men.
One day, the Master went to Zhunyu again. As soon as he stepped onto the Dharma Hall, Zhunyu said, "Look at the arrow! The Master also said, "Look at the arrow!"
Nanyue said, "It has passed. The Master said, "The middle.
Xuedou said, "Both are masters; yet both Nanyue and Zhaozhou are actually not masters."
"Arrow tips do not meet. Even if they were fired and struck simultaneously, he would still be nothing more than a man shooting at a target.
The Master went to visit Daowu. Seeing him coming, Daowu put on a leopard-skin tunic and took up his "tickling stick" (a staff) to wait outside the main gate.
As soon as he saw the Master approaching, he stood there and greeted him with a loud shout. The Master said, "Be careful to attend to your duties. Daowu—
Again, he gave a single shout of acknowledgment and departed.
When the Master arrived at Baoshou, Baoshou saw him coming and sat with his back turned. The Master spread out his sitting mat; Baoshou immediately rose and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
The Master folded up his sitting mat and went downstairs.
Baofu Zhan said, "Baoshou lost his head and his tail; Zhaozhou took a tumble on level ground.
The Master visited a hermitage keeper and asked, "Is there anything? Is there anything? The keeper held up his fist. The Master said, "The water is too shallow; it is not a place for mooring a boat.
He then visited another hermitage keeper and asked, "Is there anything? Is there anything? The keeper also held up his fist. The Master—
Yun said, "He can let go and he can seize; he can kill and he can bring to life.
He then paid his respects. Yunju Shun said, "At that time, Zhaozhou was full of spirit and vigor.
Nevertheless, even so, his nostrils were still in the hands of the two hermits. Jiaozhong Guang said, "Zhaozhou’s bearing was like..."
The King turned toward the two huts; they were forever dissolved like a crumbling wall.
An old master asked the Teacher, "Where have you recently come from? The Teacher said, "From Huazhou. The old master said, "How many stages did it take to get here?
The Teacher said, "I arrived with a single leap. The old master said, "What a swift ghost! The Teacher said, "Ten thousand blessings to Your Majesty. The old master said, "Enter [the hall]."
The Master was about to depart. The teacher said, "Yes, yes.
The Master wished to travel to Mount Wutai. An elder composed a verse to detain him, saying: "Where are the green mountains that are not sites of enlightenment?"
"Why need one lean on a staff to pay homage at Qingliang? Even if a golden-haired lion were to appear amidst the clouds, viewed with the right eye, it would not be auspicious.
The Master asked, "What is the right eye? Xu remained silent and did not respond.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; the wooden Buddha does not pass through fire; the clay Buddha does not pass through water. The true Buddha sits within.
Bodhi, nirvana, suchness, and buddha-nature—all these are but garments upon the body, which are also called afflictions (*kleśa*).
If one does not conceptualize them, there are no afflictions. Furthermore, within the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), where would they be placed? When the single mind does not arise..."
The myriad dharmas are without fault. You need only investigate the principle and sit. If you do not realize it within twenty or thirty years, cut off this old monk’s head and take it!
They are like dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky; to grasp at them is merely to toil in vain. If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are one suchness.
Since they are not obtained from without, what more is there to cling to? It is like a sheep that indiscriminately picks up things and puts them in its mouth.
When I, this old monk, saw Master Yaoshan say, "If someone asks you something, just tell them to shut their mouth," I too told them to shut their mouth.
To grasp at "I" is defilement; not grasping at "I" is purity. It is just like a hunting dog, intent only on devouring things.
Where is the meaning of Buddha-nature? Here, among thousands and tens of thousands of people, all are merely men seeking the Buddha.
"Son, have you not sought out a man of the Way? If you would be a disciple of the Empty King, do not let the sickness of the mind remain, for it is the most difficult to cure.
Before the world existed, this nature already existed; when the world perishes, this nature does not perish.
Since the moment you first saw this old monk, you have been none other than this very person—the true host. This is what you must apply yourself to."
"What is there to seek externally? At this very moment, do not turn your head or change your mind. If you turn your head or change your mind, you have already lost it.
At that time, a monk asked, "I have heard the Master say that when the world is destroyed, this nature is not destroyed.
What is this nature? The Master said, "The four elements and the five aggregates. The monk said, "But these are still subject to destruction. What then [is the nature]?"
"This is this nature. The Master said, "The four great elements and the five aggregates.
Fayuan said, "'Is it one? Is it two? Is it perishable? Is it imperishable? How do you understand this?
