Huayan said, "A skilled Chan guest is indeed quite different [from others]. The Master said, "Attendant, bring some tea for the Master to drink.
Huayan called for the Rector and said, "Arrange for the third seat."
When the Master arrived at Fenglin, Fenglin said, "I have a question to ask you; may I do so? The Master replied, "Why dig into one's own flesh to create a wound?
Fenglin said, "The ocean moon is clear and without shadow; the swimming fish follow the waves in confusion. The Master said, "If the ocean moon has no shadow," [Fenglin continued], "..."
Lin asked, "How could a swimming fish be deluded? The Master said, "Observing the wind, one knows the waves arise; gazing at the water, the wild sail drifts.

Lin said, "The solitary moon shines alone as the mountains and rivers are still; with one long啸 (shout), heaven and earth turn autumnal. The Master said, "Let the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Man) illuminate heaven and earth; try to speak a single phrase on the spot.
Lin said, "When meeting a swordsman on the road, you must present your sword; otherwise—" The Master said, "Not so."
The poet did not present his poem and withdrew into the woods. The Master then offered this verse: "The Great Way is beyond sameness; each goes its own way, east or west.
Like sparks from a flint, nothing can catch up; like a flash of lightning, nothing can penetrate."

Miaoshan asked Yangshan, "Linji said, 'Stone sparks cannot be overtaken; flashes of lightning cannot be penetrated. By what means do the sages of the past define a person? Yangshan asked, "How about you, Master?
Miaoshan replied, "As soon as there is speech, it is entirely devoid of real meaning. Yangshan said, "Not so. Miaoshan asked, "And how about you, my son?

Yangshan replied: *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with Yangshan's response. In the full dialogue, Yangshan would typically offer a verse or a non-verbal response to demonstrate his realization.*
"The official will not allow even a needle; yet in private, he lets pass carriages and horses.
Guishan said, "So it is, so it is. The Master went to Nanyue (Niu). When Niu saw him coming, he leaned his staff across [his shoulders] and sat blocking the gate.

The Master struck the staff three times with his hand and then returned to the hall, taking the seat at the head of the first row. When Niu came down and saw him, he asked, "Now, regarding the relationship between host and guest—"
[The Master] saw [him] and said, "Each has its own etiquette. From where have you, Elder, come? You are far too impolite.
The Teacher asked, "What did the Old Monk say? As Ni was about to open his mouth, the Teacher struck him. Ni assumed a posture as if falling over; the Teacher struck him again.
Ni said, "Today I am not in the right position."
Guishan asked Yangshan, "Do these two venerable masters have victory or defeat between them? Yangshan replied, "If there is victory, they both win;
if there is defeat, they both lose."
At that time, Master [Linji] had a community of five hundred followers at Mount Jing, yet few came to seek instruction.

Every day he would circumambulate the great tree in front of the Buddha hall, practicing the Way and reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara to receive visitors. Mount Huangbo was a fellow student of his, and having sent a letter detailing these circumstances, he instructed the Master to go there.
Upon arriving, Huangbo asked him, "Once you have reached that place, what will you do? The Master replied, "I have my own method."
When the Master arrived at Jingshan, he girded his waist and went straight up to the Dharma Hall. As soon as Jingshan raised his head, the Master let out a shout.
Before Jingshan could open his mouth, the Master shook his sleeves and departed. Shortly thereafter, a monk asked Jingshan, "What words did that monk just use to shout at you, Master?
Jingshan said, "This monk has come from Huangbo. If you wish to know, go ask him yourself."
He took [the challenge] from the other. At that time, more than half of the assembly of five hundred dispersed.
When the Master arrived at Longguang, he asked: "Without deploying the 'tip of the spear' (ji-feng), how can one achieve victory? Longguang sat firmly in his seat. The Master said:

"Great Good Knowledge (Kalyāṇamitra), do you have no skillful means (upāya)? Longguang stared at him with wide eyes and said: "Ha! The Master clapped his hands and said: "The great assembly, look! This..."
"Old man, today you have failed," he said, and then he departed.
The Master went to Fenglin; on the road, he encountered an old woman who asked him, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "I am going to Fenglin."
The old woman said, "It happens that Fenglin is not here. The Master asked, "Where has he gone? The old woman then departed. The Master called out to her;
she turned her head back, and the Master immediately walked away. (Some versions add the subsequent remark: "Who says he is not here? This misses the essential point profoundly.")
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who seek the Dharma do not shrink from the loss of body or life. For twenty years I was with my late teacher Huangbo;
three times I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times he bestowed the staff upon me, as if brushing against me with a bundle of mugwort.
Now, if I were to wish for another blow, who would be willing to strike? At that time, a monk came forward and said:
A certain monk stepped forward. The Master took up his staff and passed it to the monk; as the monk reached out to receive it, the Master struck him.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Upon this lump of raw flesh, there is a true person of no station who is constantly present before the faces of you all."
Coming and going. For those who have not yet attained realization, look and see! At that time, a monk asked, "What is the true person of no station?
The Master descended from his rope seat, grabbed him, and said, "Speak! Speak! As the monk hesitated, the Master pushed him away and said, "The true person of no station—what a dried-up shit-stick!
He then returned to the abbot’s quarters.
Xuefeng said, "Linji is much like a thief who steals in broad daylight.
Langya Jue said, "Linji may truly be said to have crossed over nine layers of ice and frost, and to have picked up his whole body upon the edge of a sword."
Xuedou said, "Now, one who is skilled at stealing is not known even by ghosts and spirits. Since he has been seen through by Xuefeng, Linji was no good hand.
He then called to the assembly, saying, 'Today, Xuedou has changed your eyes for you all.
If you do not believe me, each of you return to your quarters and search for yourselves.'"
A verse by Miaoxi says: "Seeing the temple monk behind one's head, one opens one's eyes wide and yet dreams.
Though one manages to catch the rat, a single blow breaks the oil jar."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "To all who come, I owe nothing; I recognize the place from which each comes. Those who come in such a way seem as if they have lost something;
those who do not come in such a way bind themselves without a rope. At all times, do not engage in random deliberation.
Whether you understand or do not understand, it is all in error. I speak clearly in this manner; let the people of the world judge for themselves."
Pei-bo. Addressing the assembly, he said: "One person stands atop a solitary peak with no way out;
another person stands at a crossroads with no front or back. Tell me, which one is ahead and which one is behind? Not acting as Vimalakīrti."
Fotuo Daoshi did not act as such;
he addressed the assembly, saying: "There is one person who, for kalpas, remains on the road yet never leaves home. There is another person who leaves home yet is not on the road.
Which of these two is worthy of receiving offerings from devas and humans?"
Miaoxi said, "The thief’s own body has already been exposed.
When the Master ascended the hall, a monk came forward and prostrated; the Master immediately shouted. The monk said, "Old Monk, do not poke your head out!"
The Master said, "Tell me, where did it fall? The monk then gave a shout. Another monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master then gave a shout. The monk bowed. The Master said, "Tell me, was that a good shout or not?
The monk said, "A grass-robber has been utterly defeated. The Master said, "Where does the fault lie? The monk said, "A second offense will not be tolerated. The Master said, "The assembly!"
"To truly understand Linji’s phrase regarding host and guest, go and ask the two head seat monks in the hall," he said, and then descended from his seat.
When the Master saw Puhua, he remarked, "When I was in the south and dispatched a letter to Mount Miao, I knew you were already staying here, waiting for me.
Now that I have arrived, I have gained your assistance. I now wish to establish the lineage of Huangbo."
"Understood. You must by all means complete this for me. Puhua said, "Take care," and went down. Ke Fu arrived later and the Master spoke to him in the same way;
he too said, "Take care," and went down. Three days later, Puhua came back up to inquire after him, saying, "What did you say the day before yesterday, Master?
The Master raised his staff and struck him down. Again, three days later, Ke Fu also came up to inquire.
Xun asked, "Master, why did you strike Puhua the other day? The Master also raised his staff and struck him down.
Later that evening, he ascended the hall and said, "Sometimes one seizes the person but not the environment; sometimes one seizes the environment but not the person;
sometimes both person and environment are seized; and sometimes neither person nor environment is seized. At that time, a monk asked, "What is seizing the person?"
"Not robbing the object. The Master said: "The warm sun brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade; the infant’s hair hangs down like white silken threads. He asked:
"What is 'robbing the object but not robbing the person'? The Master said: "The Imperial Edict has already been promulgated throughout the world;
the General is beyond the frontier, where smoke and dust have ceased. He asked: "What is 'robbing both person and object'? The Master said: "News is cut off from Bing and Fen; [only]..."
[The Master] was staying in one place. [A monk] asked, "How is it that for this person, both the environment and the sensory objects are not taken away?
The Master said, "The King ascends the jeweled throne; the village elder sings songs of joy. Puhua and Ke Fu both came out and paid their respects. The Master then returned to his quarters.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who study the Buddha-dharma today must first seek genuine insight.

If one attains genuine insight, one will be unstained by birth and death, and will possess freedom in going and staying. There is no need to seek something extraordinary; the extraordinary will arrive of its own accord.
My friends on the Way, consider that the virtuous predecessors of old all possessed a path for transcending the ordinary, just as I, this mountain monk, point it out to people."
It simply requires that you do not allow yourself to be deluded by others. When you need to act, act; do not hesitate further.
As for those who study now and fail to attain realization, where does their sickness lie? Their sickness lies in their lack of self-confidence.

If you cannot have confidence in yourself, you will immediately become frantic, revolving along with all external circumstances. You will be turned around by myriad objects and conditions, losing your freedom. If you can...

When you can rest and bring to a halt this mind that incessantly runs after objects of pursuit, you will not differ from the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Do you wish to recognize the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
They are simply those who are listening to the Dharma right before you. If practitioners do not believe this, they run outward in search;

even if they manage to find something, it will all be merely the superior marks of words and letters, and they will never attain the living intent of the Patriarchs. Do not err, O virtuous practitioners of Zen! This...

At such times, one does not encounter [the Way]. For ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, one transmigrates through the three realms, carried away by following favorable and unfavorable conditions, being born within the bellies of donkeys and oxen.
O practitioners of the Way! According to this mountain monk’s perspective, it is no different from that of Śākyamuni. In our daily manifold activities, [it is ever-present].
What is lacking? The divine light of the six realms has never ceased. If you can see it in this way, you will simply be a person who has nothing to worry about for the rest of your life.
Venerable Sir, there is no peace within the three realms; they are like a house on fire. This is not a place where you may stay for long.
The demon of impermanence, in a single kṣaṇa, makes no distinction between noble and base, old and young. You must—
The Patriarchs and Buddhas are not distinct; simply do not seek them externally. Within your own single thought-moment, the light of purity is the Dharma-body Buddha within your house.
Within your own single thought-moment, the light of non-discrimination is the Sambhogakaya Buddha within your house.
Within your own single thought-moment, the light of non-differentiation is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha within your house. These three bodies are...
The person listening to the Dharma right before you now possesses this very capacity precisely because they do not run outward in pursuit.
According to the masters of the sutras and śāstras, these three kinds of bodies are taken as the ultimate standard. However, from the perspective of this mountain monk, it is not so;
these three kinds of bodies are merely names and words, and they are also three kinds of robes. As the ancients said: "The body is established based on meaning; the land is grounded in..."
Regarding the *Tilun* (Discourse on the Essence): the Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land are clearly known to be but light and shadow.

Venerable sir, you should first recognize the person who plays with this light and shadow; he is the fundamental source of all Buddhas, the place where the lineage of the Way returns home in all places.

As for your physical body of the four elements, it cannot understand preaching or hearing the Dharma; your spleen, stomach, liver, and gallbladder likewise cannot understand preaching or hearing the Dharma.
The Dharma. Empty space does not understand preaching the Dharma or hearing the Dharma. What, then, understands preaching the Dharma and hearing the Dharma?
It is this very thing, vividly present before your eyes, which has no form or substance; it is this that understands preaching the Dharma and hearing the Dharma.
If you see it thus, you are no different from the patriarchs and Buddhas. Only, at all times, do not let it be interrupted; it is everywhere before your eyes.

It is simply because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptualizations shift that the essence becomes distinct. For this reason, one transmigrates through the three realms and undergoes all manner of suffering.
From the perspective of this mountain monk, there is nothing that is not profoundly deep, and nothing that is not liberation. O practitioners of the Way, the Dharma of the mind is formless.
It penetrates throughout the ten directions: in the eyes it is called seeing; in the ears it is called hearing; in the nose it smells fragrances; in the tongue it engages in discourse;
in the hands it grasps and holds; in the feet it moves and runs. Originally it is a single luminous intelligence, which divides into six harmonious combinations.
Once the one mind is absent, there is liberation wherever one is. Where does the intention lie in this teaching of mine, O monks? It is simply for the sake of you practitioners.

All those who run and seek with their minds cannot find rest. They surpass the ancients by remaining indifferent to the realm of sensory objects. You followers of the Way, take my own perspective: sit and cut off the heads of both the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas.

Even those at the stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) with their minds fully realized are like hired laborers; as for the two levels of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*vairocana-bodhi*), they are likewise so.
"A man bearing a yoke and shackles; even Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are like filth in a latrine. Bodhi and Nirvana are like stakes for tethering a donkey. Why is this so?
It is simply because you, O practitioners of the Way, have not realized that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are empty; therefore, such obstacles exist.
If one is a truly authentic person of the Way, it will never be thus. One should merely follow conditions to exhaust past karma, letting things proceed spontaneously."
Put on your clothes; when you wish to walk, walk; when you wish to sit, sit. Do not harbor a single thought of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood. Why is this so? An ancient said:
"If you wish to perform actions to seek Buddhahood, that Buddha is but a great omen of birth and death. Great Virtue, time is precious;
do not merely intend to wander about from house to house, learning of the Buddha and the Dharma, recognizing names and clinging to phrases. To seek [in such a way]—[is it not futile?]
The Buddha sought the Patriarchs; he sought a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Do not let your intentions go astray. O practitioner of the Way (*dàoliú*), you already have but one set of parents;
what more do you seek? You must reflect upon this yourself. An ancient said: "Yajñadatta lost his head.
When the seeking mind comes to rest, there is nothing more to do. Venerable Sir, you must simply remain ordinary; do not put on a pretense. There is a certain class of people who—

Those who recognize good and evil only as "shaven-headed slaves," who immediately claim to see gods and ghosts, point east and scratch west, and predict fair weather or rain—such types as these must all settle their debts before Old Yama on the day they must swallow glowing iron balls.
When the sons and daughters of good families are possessed by this sort of wild fox spirit-demon, they immediately begin to feign the supernatural; such blind, wretched creatures!
"The day will come when you must pay for your rice.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Followers of the Way, you must earnestly seek the authentic insight that allows you to travel freely throughout the world, so as not to be deluded by these common demons.
To have no affairs is to be a person of noble status; simply do not engage in artificial fabrication. It is nothing other than the ordinary."
The moment you conceive a thought, you have already erred. Do not seek the Buddha; "Buddha" is merely a name and phrase. Do you recognize that which is seeking?
The Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods and ten directions appeared solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma. Even the practitioners of the Way today seek only the Dharma.
Only upon attaining the Dharma is there completion; as long as it is not attained, one continues to transmigrate through the five realms of existence as before.
What is this Dharma? This Dharma is the mind-Dharma. The mind-Dharma is formless and penetrates throughout the ten directions;
it is manifest and functioning right before one’s eyes, yet people fail to believe this. Consequently, they cling to names and phrases, seeking its meaning and measure within words and letters.
This is worlds apart from the Buddha-Dharma. O practitioners of the Way, when I, this mountain monk, preach the Dharma, what Dharma do I preach? I preach the Dharma of the mind-ground.
One is then able to enter the profane and the holy, the pure and the defiled, the real and the conventional. Yet, fundamentally, this is not your reality, conventionality, profanity, or holiness;
rather, it is that which can bestow names upon all realities, conventions, profanities, and holiness. However, reality, conventionality, profanity, and holiness cannot bestow names upon this person.
O followers of the Way! Seize it and use it immediately; do not arrange it further, and only then will you be in accord with it.
The Profound Principle: When this mountain monk preaches the Dharma, it is different from that of others in the world.

Suppose Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were to appear before me, each manifesting their own form to inquire about the Dharma; as soon as they say, "I consult the Master," I have already discerned them. The old monk sits steadily.
Furthermore, when other seekers of the Way come to visit me, I have discerned them all. Why is this so?

It is simply because my perspective is different. Outwardly, I do not grasp at ordinary or holy beings; inwardly, I do not dwell in the fundamental source. Having seen through to the original Dharma, I no longer harbor doubts or errors.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "In the Buddha-dharma, there is no place for the application of effort; it is merely the ordinary state of non-action. It is just wearing clothes, eating food, and relieving oneself."
Carry away the excrement and deliver the urine. When weariness comes, lie down. Fools laugh at me; the wise alone understand. An ancient said:

"To exert effort directed outward is entirely the way of a madman. You should, wherever you are, act as the master; in every place where you stand, there is truth. No circumstances or conditions can alter this.
Even if you possess habitual tendencies from the past or the karma of the five immediate retributions, they shall all become liberation."
Great Ocean! Those who study now do not recognize the Dharma at all; they are like sheep that touch grass—whatever they encounter, they place in their mouths.
They cannot distinguish between master and servant, nor differentiate between guest and host. Such as these enter the Way with a deviant mind;
they enter where it is noisy and cannot be called true renunciants—they are truly just worldly householders. As for those who have left the home life:
One must discern and attain the ordinary, authentic insight that distinguishes Buddha from Mara, truth from falsehood, and the mundane from the sagely.
If one can discern in this manner, it is called true renunciation. If one cannot distinguish between Mara and Buddha, this is precisely "leaving one house only to enter another";
such a person is called a sentient being who creates karma and cannot yet be termed a truly renounced one. As for those who exist now...
Buddha and Mara are one; they are of the same substance and indivisible, like water and milk mixed together. If you are a practitioner with clear eyes, you strike both Mara and Buddha.
If you love the holy and hate the ordinary, you will continue to float and sink within the sea of birth and death with no end in sight.
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha-demon? The Master said, "The place where your single thought of mind harbors doubt—that is the Buddha-demon.

If you can penetrate the fact that the myriad dharmas are unborn and that the mind is like an illusion or a transformation, such that not a single speck of dust or a single dharma remains, then every place is pure."
Thus, there is neither Buddha nor Māra. "Buddha" and "Māra" are but the two realms of defilement and purity. From the perspective of this mountain monk, there is no Buddha and no sentient beings;
there is no past and no present. One who attains it simply attains it, without passing through temporal stages. There is no cultivation and no realization; there is no gain and no loss.
At all times, there is no other dharma whatsoever. Should there be even a single dharma that exceeds this, I would say it is like a dream.
"It is like a transformation. What the mountain monk speaks is this: O seeker of the Way, look now before you at this solitary, vivid clarity. The one who hears the Dharma is not obstructed anywhere;
they penetrate throughout the ten directions and are sovereign within the three realms. They enter all differentiated states without being turned back or exchanged.
In a single kṣaṇa, they pass through into the Dharma-realm; meeting a Buddha, they speak of the Buddha; meeting a Patriarch, they speak of the Patriarch."
The Patriarch encountered an arhat and spoke of the arhat; he encountered a hungry ghost and spoke of the hungry ghost.

Traveling to all places and traversing all lands to teach and transform sentient beings, he never for a single moment departed from this [realization]. Everywhere he was pure; his radiance permeated the ten directions.
All phenomena are of one suchness. O followers of the Way, you great men: today you finally know that there has originally been nothing to do. It is only because of your faith...
They do not attain it; from moment to moment they rush about in pursuit, casting away their heads only to seek new ones, unable to find rest for themselves.

Such as these—like the practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching who, having entered the Dharma-realm and manifested their bodies, yet still look toward the Pure Land, loathing the mundane and delighting in the sacred—are those who have not yet forgotten grasping and rejecting.
The defiled and pure mind remains present, just as it is in the insights of the Chan school. Yet even this is not so; it is simply the present moment, with no further temporal divisions.
Wherever this mountain monk speaks, it is all a matter of medicine and illness treating one another for a single occasion; there is no real dharma at all.
If you can see it in this way, that is true renunciation—one who could digest ten thousand taels of gold daily. O practitioners of the Way, do not be haphazardly influenced by various quarters.

"Teacher, those who 'break through the face' with their seals and claim, 'I understand Chan, I understand the Way,' and whose eloquence flows like a rushing river—all of them are creating karma for hell.
If one is a true student of the Way, they do not see the faults of the world. One must urgently seek genuine insight;
only when one reaches the True Mind and awakens to the perfect clarity of one's nature will one finally reach completion."

A monk asked, "What is true and correct insight? The Master said, "Simply enter everywhere—into the mundane and the sacred, into defilement and purity, into the lands of all Buddhas, into Maitreya’s tower, and into the Dharma-realm of Vairocana."
In every place, lands appear; their formation, subsistence, and dissolution are empty. Buddhas appear in the world, turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, and enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Yet one does not perceive any marks of coming or going; seeking their birth and death, they are utterly unfindable.

Thus one enters the realm of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmadhātu*) and wanders through lands everywhere, entering the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha-lokadhātu*), seeing that all phenomena are empty.
All characteristics are devoid of substantial reality; there is only the person who hears the Dharma without dependence, for this is the mother of all Buddhas.
Thus, the Buddha is born from non-dependence. If one awakens to non-dependence, even the Buddha cannot be attained. To perceive and attain [reality] in this way is true and correct understanding.
Students fail to realize this because they cling to names and phrases, thereby being obstructed by the designations of "ordinary" and "sage. This is why they are hindered.
Their Dharma-eye does not attain clarity. Regarding the twelve divisions of the teachings, all are expressions of manifestation.
When students do not understand, they produce interpretations based solely upon the manifest names and phrases; these are all dependencies that fall within the realm of cause and effect.

One cannot avoid the cycle of birth and death within the three realms. If you wish to attain freedom in the coming and going of birth and death—being able to cast it off or don it at will—you must right now recognize the person who hears the Dharma.
This person has no form and no marks; no root and no foundation; no place of abiding.

It is lively and agile, responding to all manner of arrangements and applications, yet its very functioning is precisely a state of nowhere. Therefore, the more you seek it, the further away it becomes. To seek it...
This turning away from the truth is what is called the "Secret Path," O practitioner. Do not mistake this for a companion in dreams and illusions;
in the midst of time’s passing, you will soon return to impermanence. What thing can you find within this world to call liberation?
Seek only enough food to eat and enough coarse woolen rags to pass the time; meanwhile, you must seek out a true teacher. Do not be negligent.
Chasing after pleasures, you live in vain and die in confusion; time is to be cherished, for every moment is impermanent. On a gross level, you are oppressed by earth, water, fire, and wind;

on a subtle level, you are pressed by the four marks of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. O followers of the Way, at this time you must first recognize the four kinds of signless realms, so as to avoid being tossed about and struck down by those objects.
A monk asked, "What are the four kinds of signless realms? The Master said, "If for a single thought-moment your mind harbors doubt, you are obstructed by this;
if for a single thought-moment your mind harbors attachment, you are drowned by water; if for a single thought-moment your mind harbors anger, you are burned by fire;

if for a single thought-moment your mind harbors joy, you are blown away by wind. If you can discern them in this way, you will not be turned by external conditions, but will employ those conditions everywhere, surging forth from the east."
The west subsides; the south surges while the north subsides; the center surges while the periphery subsides; the periphery surges while the center subsides. Treading upon water as if it were earth;
treading upon earth as if it were water. Why is this so? It is because one has realized that the four great elements are like dreams and like illusions.

O practitioner of the Way, those who listen to the Dharma right now are not your four great elements; rather, they are able to employ your four great elements. If you can see in this way, then you will immediately—
Coming and going are free. According to this mountain monk’s perspective, do not disparage these teachings. If you cherish the "sacred," the sacred is but an empty name.
There are a certain class of students who seek Mañjuśrī at Mount Wutai; they have already made a mistake. There is no Mañjuśrī at Mount Wutai. Do you wish to recognize Mañjuśrī?
He is simply the functioning before your eyes, which remains unchanged from beginning to end, present everywhere.
Doubt! This very thing is the living Mañjuśrī. Your single thought-moment is the light of non-differentiation;
everywhere it is Samantabhadra. Your single thought-moment is free and at ease; wherever you are, there is liberation. This is the samādhi-dharma of Avalokiteśvara.

They are mutually principal and attendant. When they emerge, they emerge simultaneously; one is three, and three is one. You must certainly understand this before you can truly appreciate the teachings.
Addressing the assembly, he said:
"Nowadays, those who study the Way must first have self-confidence; do not seek it outwardly, for that only leads you into the idle diversions of others."

Regarding the realm of sensory dust, one cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox at all. It is simply that the existence of Buddhas and Patriarchs are matters within the traces of the teachings.
When someone brings up a single phrase—whether emerging from the hidden or the manifest—doubt immediately arises.

One seeks answers by questioning others, searching far and wide, yet remains utterly bewildered. Great man! Do not remain merely like this. Discourse upon the master; discourse upon the thief. Discourse...
This discourse is not about debating form or debating wealth, nor is it about passing the days in idle chatter. Here in this mountain monastery, I make no distinction between monk and layperson;
whoever comes here, I recognize them all, regardless of where they emerge from. As long as there is sound, name, or phrase, I know them.
All are like dreams and illusions. To see the person who mounts the realm is the profound purport of all Buddhas.
The Buddha-realm cannot say of itself, "I am the Buddha-realm"; rather, it is this person of no dependence who emerges mounted upon the realm.
If someone were to come forth and ask me for the Buddha, I would respond by manifesting the pure realm. If someone were to ask me for Bodhi...
“Sā. When someone asks me about compassion, I should appear as the realm of compassion. When someone asks me about bodhi, I should appear as the realm of purity and wondrousness.
When someone asks me about nirvāṇa, I should appear as the realm of tranquility. These realms are thus manifold and differentiated.
People are not inherently different; it is for this reason that they manifest forms in response to conditions, like the moon reflected in water.
O practitioners of the Way, if you wish to attain that which accords with the Dharma, you must be a true man of great capacity; if you are weak and compliant, you shall not succeed.
Indeed, a vessel that is cracked and leaking cannot hold clarified butter (ghṛta); only a vessel of great capacity need not be filled.
People are deluded; wherever they act as masters, that very place is true. Yet, should anyone come before you, you must not accept them.
If for even a single thought-moment your mind harbors doubt, then the Māra enters your heart-palace. When a Bodhisattva doubts, the Māra of birth and death seizes the opportunity.

You need only let your thoughts rest and seek nothing more externally. When things arise, simply reflect upon them; you must simply have faith in this one thing that is currently functioning within you.
In reality, there is nothing at all. A single thought of yours gives rise to the three realms; following conditions and being divided by objects, it becomes the six sense-fields.

In your present state of active engagement, what is lacking? In a single kṣaṇa, you may enter the pure or the defiled, enter Maitreya’s pavilion, or enter the land of the Three Eyes. Traveling everywhere, you see only empty names.
A monk asked, "What is the realm of the three eyes? The Master said, "I shall enter with you into the Pure and Wondrous Realm;
donning the garment of purity, I shall preach the Dharma-body Buddha. Again, I shall enter the Realm of Non-differentiation;

donning the garment of non-differentiation, I shall preach the Reward-body Buddha. Again, I shall enter the Realm of Liberation; donning the garment of radiance, I shall preach the Transformation-body Buddha."

These three eyes and the lands are all transformations based [upon something else]. According to the masters of the sutras and śāstras, they take the *dharmakāya* as the fundamental essence and the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* as its functions.
As for my own view, the *dharmakāya* does not understand how to preach the Dharma; therefore, the ancients said:

"The body is established according to its meaning, and the land is discussed according to its substance. It is clearly understood that the *dharmatākāya* and the *dharmatābhūmi* are merely provisional constructions.
This Dharma relies upon the various lands; it is like an empty fist or yellow leaves used to deceive small children.
Upon thorny weeds, briars, and dry bones, what essence can you seek? Outside the mind there are no dharmas, and within, nothing can be found.
What thing do you seek? You all speak of cultivation and realization; do not err. Even if there were such things as cultivation and realization, they would all be the karma of birth and death. You—!
He said: "To practice the six perfections and the myriad deeds in equal measure is all the creation of karma. To seek the Buddha or seek the Dharma is itself the creation of hellish karma;
to seek the Bodhisattvas is likewise the creation of karma; to study the sutras and examine the teachings is also the creation of karma.
The Buddhas and the Patriarchs are people of non-action; therefore, both the contaminated and conditioned, as well as the uncontaminated and unconditioned, constitute pure karma."
There is a class of blind shavelings who, having eaten their fill, practice seated meditation and contemplative cultivation;
they grasp at thoughts and leaks, not allowing them to arise. They loathe clamor and seek stillness—this is the dharma of external paths. The Patriarch said:

"If you dwell the mind to observe stillness, lift the mind to reflect outwardly, gather the mind to clarify inwardly, or concentrate the mind to enter samādhi—all such types are merely artificial fabrications."
"You, who are now listening to the Dharma in this manner—how do you intend to cultivate it, realize it, or adorn it?
It is not something to be cultivated, nor is it something to be adorned. If one were to attempt to adorn it, then all things could be so adorned;
do not make such a mistake, O seeker of the Way! You must take these words from the mouths of such masters as they are."
"Speech. This is the true Way; this is a good spiritual friend. It is inconceivable. I am a mere ordinary person, and my mind does not dare to fathom these venerable elders.
You blind fellow, throughout your many lives you have done nothing but harbor such a view; you have brought shame upon these two eyes of yours.
You are shivering with cold, like a foal on a frozen icefield. I do not dare to disparage the good spiritual friend."

"Śāriputra, fearing the arising of verbal karma, you say, 'O Dharma-stream, a true Great Good Friend would only dare to revile the Buddhas and Patriarchs, judge right and wrong throughout the world, reject the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, and insult all the novices. You seek someone among those who follow or oppose you;
therefore, for twelve years I have sought even a speck of karmic nature the size of a mustard seed, yet it cannot be found. It is exactly as if..."
When Chan Master Xinfuzi was immediately driven out of the monastery in fear and denied food, he was neither at peace nor happy.

Since ancient times, when the predecessors of old went everywhere and people did not believe them, being driven away only then revealed their worth. If one were everywhere accepted by all, what would they be worth?
Therefore, when the lion lets out a single roar, the wild jackal’s brain splits. O practitioners of the Way, the various quarters speak thus.
"There is a Way that can be cultivated; there is a Dharma that can be realized. Tell me: what Dharma do you realize? What Way do you cultivate?
At your current station, what is lacking? Where must it be repaired? You young monks of later generations, failing to understand, immediately place your trust in such wild fox spirits and demons.
You allow them to speak of matters and bind others, claiming their words are the correspondence between principle and practice. Protect [the true teaching].
Regretting the three karmas, one only then attains Buddhahood. To speak in such a manner is like a fine spring rain. As the ancients said:

"When you encounter a person who has attained the Way, first of all, do not point toward the Way. Therefore it is said: "If a person cultivates the Way but the Way does not proceed, ten thousand kinds of heterodox states will vie to arise.
When the sword of wisdom is drawn forth, there is not a single thing; before the bright side is revealed, the dark side is already clear. So it is.
As the ancients said: "The ordinary mind is the Way. Great Virtue, what thing are you seeking?
Right now, before your very eyes, this person who listens to the Dharma without dependence is vividly and clearly manifest; there has never been any lack.

If you wish to be no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, simply see thus and do not allow yourself to be misled. When your mind does not differ from moment to moment, it is called the "Living Patriarch."
If the mind were different, then essence and appearance would be distinct. Because the mind is not different, essence and appearance are not distinct.
Question: What is this place where the mind is not different from itself? The Master said: "The moment you intend to ask, it has already become different;

essence and appearance are each divided. O followers of the Way, do not err! All phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, possess no self-nature, nor do they possess a nature of arising. They are merely..."
There is the name "existence," yet names themselves are also empty. To simply take these idle names as real is a great mistake.

Even if they were to exist, they would all be objects of transformation: there is the support for bodhi, the support for nirvāṇa, the support for liberation, the support for the three bodies, the support for object and wisdom, the support for bodhisattvas, and the support for buddhas. Within this realm of transformed lands, what are you seeking?
All things—even the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings—are merely used paper for wiping away impurities.
The Buddha is a phantom body; the Patriarchs are old bhikṣus. Have you not yet been born of your mother? If you seek the Buddha, you will be seized by the demon of the Buddha;
if you seek the Patriarchs, you will be bound by the demon of the Patriarchs. If you have any seeking, there is only suffering; it is better to have none at all.
There is a certain class of shaven-headed bhikṣus who say to students of the Way: "The Buddha is ultimate;
it was only after three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas of cultivation and the fulfillment of his fruit that he finally attained the Way.
Dàoliú, if you say the Buddha is ultimate, for what reason did he die eighty years later, lying on his side between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara?
"Where is the Buddha now? It is clearly known that he is no different from me in birth and death. You say that the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics constitute a Buddha;
then a Wheel-Turning Sage King should also be a Tathāgata. It is clearly known that these are but illusory transformations. As an ancient said:

The Tathāgata manifests the marks of his entire body merely to accord with the sentiments of worldly beings; fearing that people might give rise to the view of nihilism, he provisionally establishes empty names.
These thirty-two [marks] and eighty [minor characteristics] are but false sounds. To possess a body is not the essence of awakening; formlessness is the true form.
"You say that the Buddha possesses the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) and is inconceivable.
Yet all the devas, ṛṣis, asuras, and powerful spirits also possess supernormal powers; should they therefore be considered Buddhas? Practitioner, do not err. Take for instance the asuras."
He fought with Śakra, Lord of Devas, and was defeated. Leading eighty-four thousand followers, he entered the pores of a lotus fiber to hide. Is this not sacred?

According to what this mountain monk has cited, these are all instances of *karmarddhi* (supernatural power through karma) and *āśrayarddhi* (supernatural power based on a physical support). As for the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) of a Buddha, it is not so.
Entering the realm of form, one is not deluded by form; entering the realm of sound, one is not deluded by sound; entering the realm of fragrance...
They are not deluded by fragrances; they enter the realm of flavors without being deluded by flavors; they enter the realm of tangibles without being deluded by tangibles;

they enter the realm of phenomena without being deluded by phenomena. Thus, they penetrate the six categories—form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and phenomena—all of which are characterized by emptiness.
One cannot bind this person of no-abode. Although they possess the defiled substance of the five aggregates, they are a terrestrial immortal (*bhūcarī-ṛṣi*).
O practitioner of the Way: the true Buddha has no form; the true Dharma has no marks. You merely fashion patterns and models upon these illusory transformations.
Even if you were to seek and obtain something, it would all be nothing but wild fox spirits and demons—it is certainly not the true Buddha; it is a heterodox path.
Regarding this view: Truly, one who studies the Way as it really is does not grasp for Buddhas, nor grasp for Bodhisattvas or Arhats, nor grasp for the sublime excellence of the triple world.
They are utterly and independently liberated, unconfined by external things. Even if heaven and earth were overturned, they would harbor no further doubt.
The Buddhas of the ten directions appear before me, yet not a single thought of joy arises. The three miserable realms and the hells manifest all at once, yet not a single thought of fear occurs.
Why is this so? Because I perceive that all phenomena possess the mark of emptiness: they exist when transformed, and do not exist when untransformed.
The triple world is but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Therefore, as for dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky, what need is there to grasp them? There is only the Way.
It flows before one’s eyes. Those who listen to the Dharma today would not be burned by fire or drowned by water;
they enter the three miserable realms and the hells as if strolling through a garden, and enter the realms of hungry ghosts and animals without receiving retribution.

Why is this so? Because it is a Dharma free from aversion. If you cherish the holy and loathe the ordinary, you will float and sink within the ocean of birth and death; for afflictions arise from the mind.
There is no mind; what can afflictions constrain? Without the trouble of discriminating or grasping at signs, you will naturally attain the Way in an instant.
If you intend to dabble in peripheral matters and strive in agitation, even if you were to learn it over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, you would ultimately return to birth and death.

It is better to remain without affairs, sitting with legs crossed at the corner of a bed in a forest thicket. O practitioners of the Way! If there are students coming from all quarters, [treat them thus].
When master and guest meet, there is immediately a single phrase that distinguishes the preceding *kalyāṇamitra*.
When the student brings forth this path of expedient words and maneuvers it past the master’s lips, we see whether you recognize it or not.
If you recognize it as an objective state (*viṣaya*), seize it and cast it straight into the pit. Then the student shall immediately seek [the truth].
After [the master] had spoken thus, he then sought out the words of a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) and, as before, seized them away. The student said, "What superior wisdom!
This is a great good spiritual friend. [The master] immediately said, "You truly do not recognize good from evil. A good spiritual friend brings forth a 'situation' (viṣaya)."
A clod of earth. He brandishes it before the student. If the student can discern it, he maintains mastery at every turn and is not deluded by external objects.
The Good Knowledge (Kalyāṇamitra) then manifests half his body. The student immediately shouts. The Good Knowledge then enters into all paths of differentiated speech and provokes him.
The student says, "I do not recognize you, you old shaven-headed slave! The Good Knowledge sighs and says:

As for those who truly belong to the lineage of the Way, such as the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in various quarters, when students come to them and ask about bodhi, nirvāṇa, the three bodies, or the realm and wisdom, these blind teachers proceed to explain them to them. Consequently, they are rebuked by those very students.
He then took up his staff and struck him, saying, "You lack propriety! It is because your own spiritual friend lacks eyes that you have come to this; you must not harbor anger toward him.

There is a certain class of ignorant, shaveling brutes who point east and mark west, prattling on about fine weather, fine rain, fine lanterns, and fine pillars, while asking, "Look, how many hairs are there on your eyebrows? This man possesses the karmic conditions, yet the student does not understand.
Their minds immediately become deranged. Such people as these are all nothing but wild fox spirits, enchantments, and demons.
When they encounter those who truly seek the Way, they merely snicker and say, "Blind old bald slaves! You are deluding the people of the world.
O followers of the Way, those who have left the household life must first seek to study the Way. Just as I, this mountain monk, once applied my mind to the Vinaya in the past, and likewise...
Through investigating the sutras and śāstras, one later realizes that these are merely manifest teachings—prescriptions for saving the world—and thus casts them aside all at once.
One then seeks the Way and studies Chan. Only after meeting a great spiritual friend (mahākalyāṇamitra) does one’s Dharma-eye become clear;
only then does one recognize the ancient patriarchs of the world, discerning what is heterodox and what is orthodox. This is not something one knows from birth; it must still be attained.

This is the process of thorough investigation and refinement. One day, through self-reflection, you will realize it, O practitioner of the Way. If you wish to attain a realization that accords with the Dharma, simply do not allow yourself to be deluded by others.
Whether facing inward or outward, kill whatever you encounter. Kill the Buddhas when you meet them; kill the Patriarchs when you meet them;
kill the Arhats when you meet them; kill your parents when you meet them; kill your kinsmen when you meet them. Only then will you attain liberation.

Liberation means not being constrained by things; it is total transcendence and mastery. Among the seekers of the Way from all quarters, there has never been one who emerged without relying on some object.
Here in this mountain monastery, I strike from the very ground up: when you emerge from the hand, I strike with the hand; when you emerge from the mouth, I strike with the mouth;
when you emerge from the eyes, I strike with the eyes. There has yet been anyone who has emerged in solitary liberation.
All of these are merely the ancients’ idle play within the realm of their own experience. I, this mountain monk, have not a single dharma to give to others;
I do nothing but treat illnesses and untie bonds. You practitioners from all quarters, try to come forth without relying on external things, and I will engage in discussion with you.
For ten years and five autumns, not a single person has appeared; they are all merely spirits clinging to grass and leaves, or the numinous essences of bamboo and wood, or wild foxes and demons.
They gnaw recklessly upon heaps of dung. You blind fellows, you waste in vain the offerings of the faithful from the ten directions!
You claim to be renunciants, yet you hold such views as these, telling others that there is no Buddha and no Dharma, and nothing to be cultivated.
Realization is simply this. What else would you seek from others? You blind fellow! To add a head atop your own—what is it that you lack?
O follower of the Way, that which you employ before your very eyes is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; yet you simply do not believe it.
Do not go seeking outwardly; do not err. There is no dharma outside, nor can it be found within.

Rather than taking the words from this mountain monk’s mouth, it would be better for you to rest and remain in non-action. Do not continue what has already arisen; do not allow what has not yet arisen to arise.
This would surpass ten years of your traveling on pilgrimage. According to my own view, there are not so many varieties; it is simply this:
Ordinary people wear clothes and eat their meals, passing their time with nothing to do.

You who have come from all quarters are all possessed of a mind seeking the Buddha, seeking the Dharma, seeking liberation, and seeking to escape the three realms. You fools! If you wish to escape the three realms, where would you go?
Buddhas and patriarchs are merely names and phrases used for praise and binding. Do you wish to recognize the three realms? They are not separate from you.
Now, regarding the ground of the mind that hears the Dharma: if for a single thought-moment your mind is greedy, this is the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*);
if for a single thought-moment your mind is angry, this is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); if for a single thought-moment your mind is deluded, this is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

These are the furnishings within your own house. The three realms do not themselves say, "I am the three realms. Rather, it is the person on the Path, vividly present before one's eyes, who illuminates all manner of things.

One who gauges the depths of the world bestows names upon the three realms. O Virtuous One, this physical body composed of the four great elements is impermanent—down to the spleen, stomach, liver, and gallbladder, as well as the hair, fur, nails, and teeth.
One perceives only the empty characteristics of all phenomena within a single thought-moment of mind.
The place where the mind comes to rest is called the Bodhi tree. The place where your single thought-moment cannot come to rest is called the tree of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ignorance has no dwelling place; ignorance has no beginning or end. If you cannot bring each and every thought-moment of your mind to rest, [you remain in this state].
You have thus climbed the tree of ignorance and entered the six realms and four modes of birth, donning fur and wearing horns. If you can bring this to rest, it is the realm of the pure body.
When not a single thought arises, you have ascended the Bodhi tree. Within the three realms, you manifest supernatural powers and transformations;
through the mind-born body, you find the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna. Your bodily radiance illuminates itself, and you think of garments of fine silk by the thousands.
It is weighty. Contemplate that food of a hundred flavors is fully provided, and there are no further incidental ailments. Awakening has no dwelling place; therefore, there is no one who attains it.
O practitioner of the Way, great man, what more is there to doubt? As for the functioning before your eyes, who else could it be?
Seize it and employ it; do not cling to names. This is termed the "Mysterious Principle" (*xuánzhǐ*).

If you see it in this way, do not disparage this teaching. An ancient said: "The mind turns with the myriad objects; in that turning, there is truly a profound depth. Following the flow, one recognizes one's nature;
then there is neither joy nor sorrow. O practitioners of the Way! According to the insight of the Chan school, life and death are but natural occurrences. Those who study must be most diligent.

In detail: it is like the meeting of host and guest, where there is immediately an exchange of words. Sometimes he manifests a form in response to circumstances; sometimes he functions with his entire being;
sometimes he employs skillful means through joy or anger; sometimes he reveals only half his body; sometimes he rides a lion, or sometimes he rides an elephant king.
When a true student encounters him, he simply shouts, first bringing forth a lumpy ball of glue. The good teacher fails to discern this.
This is their own territory, yet they step onto another’s territory to make imitations and set patterns. When the student shouts, the person before him refuses to let go;
this is a terminal illness that cannot be cured. This is called "the guest looking for the host. Or, if it is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they do not bring forth any object;
rather, as soon as the student asks a question, they snatch it away. When the student is snatched away from their grasp, they cling to it to death and will not let go. This is...
The host observes the guest. There may be a student who presents a single pure object before a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
If the spiritual friend can discern that object and seize it to cast it into a pit, the student will say, "Excellent, O spiritual friend! To which [the friend] replies, "Alas!
You do not recognize good from evil. The student then prostrates; this is called the host observing the host. Or there may be...
The student, wearing his shackles and chains, comes before the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). The spiritual friend further places upon him another layer of shackles and chains.
The student rejoices; neither can distinguish between them, yet they call this "the guest looking at the guest.

O Virtuous One, what I have thus raised is entirely for the purpose of discerning demons from the extraordinary, so that one may know the false from the true. O follower of the Way, the true reality is extremely difficult; it is the Buddha-dharma.
Profound and mysterious! If one could understand it even slightly, this mountain monk would spend the entire day explaining it for them.
Yet, the students pay no attention; though they have trodden over it ten thousand times, it remains pitch black and void, without a single form or trace.

Though it is vividly clear, the students do not believe it, and instead give rise to intellectual interpretations based on names and phrases. Reaching fifty years of age, they continue thus—only to be caught in their own traps.

"Carrying a corpse from house to house, with the burden of the coffin on his back, he wanders all over the world seeking money for straw sandals; the day will surely come when he does so, O Great Virtue!
When I, this mountain monk, say that 'there is no dharma outside,' the student fails to understand and immediately constructs an interpretation within.

He then sits leaning against a wall, pressing his tongue against the upper palate, remaining in a state of profound stillness and motionlessness, taking this to be the Buddha-dharma of the Patriarchal Gate."
A great error! If you take this unmoving, pure state as being real, you are identifying ignorance as your master.
As the ancients said: "A deep pit of profound darkness is truly terrifying"—this is precisely what that refers to.
Thus, that which moves is the element of wind; that which does not move is the element of earth. Both movement and non-movement are devoid of self-nature.
If you move toward him and seize him, he stands in a place where there is no movement; if you stand in a place where there is no movement and seize him, he moves toward you.
It is like a fish in a hidden spring that stirs the waves and leaps up by itself. Venerable Sir, as for movement and non-movement—
These two kinds of objects are used by those who walk the path without reliance: to move them or to keep them still.

For instance, when students from various quarters come here to this mountain monastery, I employ three methods of severance. If those of middling or inferior capacities come, I immediately seize their objects.
Yet I do not remove that dharma. If one of middling or superior capacity comes, I simultaneously seize both the person and the object;
if one of the highest superior capacity comes, I do not seize either the person, the object, or the dharma.

For instance, when a man of extraordinary realization comes, I, this mountain monk, manifest my total being right here, without passing through the stages of capacities. Venerable Sir, when you reach this point, the student must exert their effort.
The place is not through with air; it is like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning—once it has passed, it is gone. If a student’s eyes waver, there is no connection.
To conceive a thought is already an error; to stir a single念 (nien) is already to go astray. If there is one who understands, it is not apart from what is before one's eyes.
Venerable sir, you carry your alms-bag like a burden of excrement, running about from house to house seeking the Buddha and seeking the Dharma; right now, you are just like this, rushing about.

Seek its bottom! Do you recognize it? It is a state of lively, throbbing activity; it simply has no root or stem. You cannot gather it together, nor can you scatter it apart. If you seek it, it recedes further and further;
if you do not seek it, it is already before your eyes. Its spiritual resonance reaches the ear.

If people do not believe this, their hundred years of toil will be in vain. O practitioners of the Way! In a single kṣaṇa, one enters the Flower Treasury World (Avataṃsaka-lokadhātu) and enters Vairocana.
Entering the realm of Vairocana; entering the realm of liberation; entering the realm of supernormal powers; entering the pure realm; entering the dharma-realm;
entering the defiled and entering the pure; entering the mundane and entering the sagely; entering the realms of hungry ghosts and animals—searching and seeking everywhere.
In all cases, there is neither birth nor death; there is only the empty name. It is like an illusion or a flower in the sky—do not trouble yourself to grasp it.
Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once. You followers of the Way: my Dharma is transmitted directly from the Venerable Magu.
Master Danxia, Master Daoyi, Master Yuezhou of Mount Lu, and Master Shitou traveled along a single path that spanned the world;
yet no one believed it, and all raised slander against them. As for Master Daoyi, his application was pure and singular, without any admixture.
Among the practitioners, three hundred or five hundred may all fail to perceive the Master’s intent.

For instance, when Master Lushan acts with sovereign authenticity, whether in accord with or contrary to circumstances, the practitioners cannot fathom his limits and are left utterly bewildered. It is like the case of Master Danxia.
Playing with the pearl, appearing and disappearing; whenever students came, they were all reviled. Ma Gu’s way of employing [the Dharma] was as bitter as Huang Po’s.
Recently, none could approach it, for Shi Gong’s way of employing [the Dharma] was to seek the person upon the tip of the arrow; those who came were filled with dread.

As for the mountain monk’s application today: it is the true formation and destruction, the playful manipulation of spiritual transformations, entering all realms while remaining free from affairs wherever one is;
the realm cannot change him. Yet whenever there is someone who comes seeking, I go out to look at them.

They do not recognize me, so I put on several kinds of robes and follow the ways of ordinary people, leading them toward intellectual understanding. They head straight into my words and phrases—what a pity! You blind ones!
"Bald-headed one! Blind man! You recognize blue, yellow, red, and white in the clothes I am wearing. I take them off and enter the realm of purity;

as soon as the student sees this, he gives rise to longing and desire. I take them off again, and the student loses his wits and becomes bewildered, running about frantically and saying, 'I have no clothes! I then say to him, 'Do you recognize the person who was wearing the clothes?'"
Suddenly turning your head, you have recognized me. Great Virtue, do not mistake the robe; the robe cannot move. It is the person who wears the robe.
There is the robe of purity, the robe of non-arising, the robe of bodhi, and the robe of nirvāṇa. There is the robe of the patriarchs and the robe of the Buddhas.
Great Virtue, all names, sounds, and phrases are merely transformations of the robe. [It originates] from the navel wheel.
Within the ocean of vital energy, it surges and stirs; teeth clatter together to form the meaning of phrases. Clearly know that these are illusory transformations.
Venerable Sir, external vocal karma and internal mental factors—wherever there is volition or thought, all are but clothing.

To merely recognize the clothes worn by others as a true understanding, even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, is nothing more than being permeated by clothing; one will simply continue to cycle through the three realms.

To transmigrate through birth and death is not as good as having nothing to do. Meeting yet not recognizing one another, speaking together yet not knowing each other’s names—this is what students of the present day fail to attain. It is because they take names and words to be understanding;

they copy the words of dead old men onto large tablets, wrapping them in three or five layers of paper and binding them up so as not to let others see them, claiming these are the "mysterious essence" and treating them as something precious to preserve.
A great error! You blind fellow! What kind of juice are you seeking upon a withered bone? There is a certain class of people who do not recognize good from evil;
they seek within the scriptures, using their own mental conjectures and deliberations to construct phrases and meanings.

It is like taking a lump of excrement into one's mouth, spitting it out, and giving it to another person—just like worldly people playing the game of "whispering words. This is how they spend their entire lives.
To pass one's time in vain. You say you have left the household life, yet when questioned about the Buddha-dharma, you immediately close your mouth and have no words;
your eyes are like pitch-black pits, and your mouth is like a flat carrying pole.

Those of such a kind, when Maitreya appears in the world, shall be moved to other worlds to dwell in the hells and undergo suffering. Venerable sir, why do you wander from place to place seeking what thing?
Treading upon your own footprints, you are broad; there is no Buddha to be sought, no Way to be accomplished, and no Dharma to be transmitted.
To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not like you. If you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate. O followers of the Way:
the true Buddha has no form, the true Way has no substance, and the true Dharma has no characteristics. These three dharmas are interpenetrating and unified in a single place. Since...
[The Master] could not distinguish them. He called them "sentient beings of the frantic, deluded consciousness.
A monk asked: "What are the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Way? We beg for your instruction. The Master said:
"The Buddha is the purity of the mind; the Dharma is the luminosity of the mind; the Way is the pure light that is unobstructed everywhere. These three are—"

First: All are empty names and lack substantial reality. Just as a true practitioner of the Way maintains an uninterrupted state of mind from moment to moment—since the Great Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Land, he sought only a person who would not be deluded by others;
later, upon meeting the Second Patriarch, he attained realization in a single word and finally knew that all his previous efforts had been in vain. Today, I, this mountain monk, see...
This state is no different from that of the patriarchs and Buddhas. If you realize it within the first phrase, you shall become a teacher to the patriarchs and Buddhas.
If you realize it within the second phrase, you shall become a teacher to humans and devas. If you realize it within the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of [the Patriarch’s] coming from the West? The Master said, "If there were a meaning, you would not even be able to save yourself.

The monk asked, "Since there is no meaning, how did the Second Patriarch obtain the Dharma? The Master said, "He who obtains it is one who does not obtain it. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'not obtaining'?
The Master said, "It is because you, in every situation, pursue with a restless mind that cannot be stilled; therefore, the Patriarch..."
The Master said: "Alas, O man! You are seeking your head with your head. If, at my words, you immediately turn the light back upon yourself and reflect within, you will have nothing else to seek.
To know that body and mind are no different from the patriarchs and Buddhas, and to be free from all concerns in this very moment—this alone is called attaining the Dharma, O Virtuous One."
Today, this mountain monk has no choice but to speak out at length, though my words may seem unrefined. Do not misunderstand me;
according to my own realization, there are truly not so many varieties of principles. When it is needed, it is used; when it is not needed, it is simply left alone.

As for the various quarters, they speak of the six perfections and ten thousand practices as being the Buddha-dharma; in my way, these are merely gates of adornment and gates of Buddhist activity, not the Buddha-dharma itself.
This extends even to observing the fasts and precepts, or carrying oil without spilling it—if the eye of the Way is not clear, such things are of no avail.

"You must pay it all back; the day will come when you must repay the cost of the meal. Why do you act like this? You have entered the Way but do not understand its principle, and you are returning the offerings of the faithful to your own person.
When the elder was eighty-one, the tree would not grow. ... Even to the point of sleeping alone on a solitary peak."
Eating only one meal a day, observing the fast; sitting upright for long periods without lying down; practicing the Way during the six periods of the day—all these are people who create karma.
They go so far as to give away their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains, as well as their kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures. Such are their views.
Because these all involve suffering of body and mind, they in turn invite bitter fruits. It is not as good as being free from affairs, pure and unadulterated.
Even Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi) who have reached the fulfillment of their minds all seek the traces of this path, yet find them utterly non-existent.
For this reason, the devas rejoice, the earth deities support his feet, and there are no Buddhas of the ten directions who do not praise him. Why is this so? Because—
Now, those who hear the Dharma leave no trace of their whereabouts.
A monk asked: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
I do not understand the meaning of this; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said: "Mahābhijñā (Great Penetration) is oneself."
To penetrate, in every place, that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature and without marks is called "Great Penetration.
To have no doubt regarding anything and to find not even a single dharma is called "Supreme Wisdom. A Buddha is one whose mind is pure and luminous.
To thoroughly penetrate the Dharma-realm is what is called becoming a Buddha. As for "sitting at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas," this refers to the ten pāramitās.
Regarding "the Buddha-dharma not manifesting before one": since the Buddha is fundamentally unborn and the Dharma is fundamentally unextinguished, how could there be anything further to manifest?
As for "not being able to attain the Way of Buddhahood," the Buddha should not need to become a Buddha again. An ancient said: "The Buddha is always in the world, yet..."
Do not be defiled by worldly dharmas, O follower of the Way. If you wish to attain Buddhahood, do not follow after the myriad things.

When the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease. If the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault, whether in the mundane or supramundane realms.
There is no Buddha and no Dharma; they do not manifest before us, nor have they ever been lost.

Should anything appear to exist, it is all merely names and phrases used to guide the immature, established as a correspondence between medicine and illness, and expressed through words and sentences. Furthermore, names and sentences do not, of themselves, constitute names and sentences.
Or rather, it is your own present state—vivid and lucid, the faculty that perceives, hears, and knows, that which illuminates.
Great Virtuous One, only by committing the five deeds of immediate retribution can you attain liberation.

A monk asked, "What are the five deeds of immediate retribution? The Master said, "Killing one's father, killing one's mother, shedding the blood of a Buddha, causing a schism in the Sangha, and burning scriptures and images—these are the five deeds of immediate retribution. The monk asked, "What is the father?
The Master said, "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the father. When you seek the place where your single thought-moment arises and ceases, it cannot be found; it is like an echo in the void."
To be without affairs anywhere is called "killing one's father. [The student asked: "What is the mother? The Master said: "Craving is the mother.
When your single thought-moment enters the realm of desire, you seek that craving and see only the empty nature of all phenomena;
to be unattached everywhere is called 'harming the mother. [The student asked: "What is shedding the Buddha’s blood? The Master said: "When you face the pure Dharma..."
Within the realms, if not even a single thought arises that seeks understanding, one is then in darkness everywhere; this is shedding the blood of the Buddha. [The student asked:

"What is breaking the harmony of the Sangha? The Master said: "When your single thought directly penetrates the afflictions and fetters so that they are like space, having no basis to rely upon—this is breaking the harmony of the Sangha.
[The student asked: "What is burning the scriptures and images? The Master said: "Seeing the cause..."
"Relying on the emptiness of conditions, the emptiness of mind, and the emptiness of dharmas, one decisively cuts through them in a single thought.
To be thus utterly free from affairs is itself to burn the scriptures and images. Great Virtue, if you can penetrate in this way, you will avoid being obstructed by the names 'ordinary' or 'sage.

Your single thought-moment merely gives rise to a false understanding based on an empty fist; you falsely concoct strange notions within the roots, objects, and dharmas, thereby disparaging yourself and falling into despondency."
He says: "I am an ordinary person; he is a sage. Bald and worn-out from birth, what such haste is there for death!
Having donned another's lion skin, he instead lets out the howl of a wild jackal. A man of great character does not produce the breath of a man.
He refuses to believe in the things within his own house, but merely seeks them outwardly, clinging to the idle names and phrases of the ancients, leaning on the dark while seeking the light.
They cannot penetrate directly; they encounter objects and immediately condition them, meet with sense-data and immediately grasp them, and delusion arises wherever they touch.
They have no standard of their own. Followers of the Way, do not take what this mountain monk says as authoritative. Why? Because these words have no basis in reality.
For a time, one merely sketches upon empty space, like the metaphor of a painted image. Followers of the Way, do not take the Buddha as the ultimate goal; even my own views are like a latrine.
The "Hole" (the void). Bodhisattvas and Arhats are all shackles and fetters—things that bind people.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī wielded his sword to slay Gautama, and Aṅgulimāla took up his blade to harm the Śākyas. O practitioners of the Way, there is no Buddha to be attained;

even the three vehicles and five natures, as well as the traces of the Perfect and Sudden teachings, are all merely expedient remedies applied according to specific ailments. None of them possess any real dharma. Even if...
There are. These are all similar expressions, arranged as written characters; for the time being, they are explained in this manner. O practitioners of the Way!
There is a certain class of shavelings who apply their efforts toward the inner realm, intending to seek the Dharma that transcends the world—they are mistaken.
If a person seeks the Buddha, that person loses the Buddha. If a person seeks the Way, that person loses the Way. If a person seeks the Patriarch, that person...
People have lost their ancestral source. Great assembly, do not err! I do not accept your mastery of the sutras and śāstras;
I do not accept you as kings or great ministers; I do not accept your eloquence that flows like a rushing torrent;
nor do I accept your cleverness and wisdom. I require only your genuine insight. O practitioners of the Way, even if you could master a hundred volumes of sutras and śāstras, it would not equal—
There is a master who is simply one who has nothing to do. If you understand this, you will disparage and destroy others;
with your notions of victory and defeat, asuras, and the ignorance of self and other, you will long cultivate the karma for hell.

Like the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, though he understood the twelve divisions of the teachings, he fell into hell in his very body, where the great earth could not contain him. It would be better to rest in nothingness: when hungry, eat; when weary, sleep.

"The eyes! The foolish laugh at me, but the wise alone know. O practitioners of the Way, do not seek within words and letters; the mind will become weary and exhausted, and drawing in cool air will be of no benefit.
It is better to realize in a single thought that dependent origination is birthless, thereby transcending the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles and surpassing the Bodhisattvas.
Great Virtue, do not let the days pass in negligence. In the past, when this mountain monk had not yet attained insight, it was a pitch-black void."
Vainly! Time has passed in emptiness; with a burning belly and a frantic mind, you have rushed about seeking the Way. Only now, having finally gained strength, have you arrived at this day.
Fellow practitioners of the Way, let us speak thus together: I exhort all practitioners not to pursue food and clothing. Behold how easily the world passes away;
a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower, which appears but once in an age. You have heard this from various quarters.
There was an old fellow Linji who, as soon as he came out, intended to pose difficult questions and challenge me with words;
yet I, the mountain monk, employed my entire being in action, leaving the student with eyes and mouth wide open, unable to move at all. Utterly bewildered, he did not know how to answer me.
I said to him: "The treading of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure. You all merely point to your chests everywhere.
Pointing at the ribs and saying, "I understand Zen, I understand the Way," three or two of you—when you arrive here, there is nothing you can do about it!
*Du!* Alas! You take this body and mind and wander everywhere, flapping those two pieces of skin to deceive the common folk;
the day will come when you eat iron rods. These are not true renunciants; they are all categorized within the realm of the asuras. As for the Way of ultimate truth, it is not...
One may seek to stimulate and uplift through debate, and with a resonant, ringing voice, one may crush the heterodox paths.
