The Master said, "Is there anyone else who wishes to ask a question? Whether one asks or does not ask, there is no mechanism of gain or loss. Why is this?

Furthermore, this matter does not reside beneath the reach of verbal expression. Even when the Buddhas of the three periods appear in the world, they employ the myriad phenomena of the forest and the heavens, the sun, moon, and stars, and all things animate and inanimate throughout these lands and others, through the *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi* (Ocean-Seal Samādhi), as a single...
Sealed and fixed by the seal, it pervades heaven and encompasses earth, without the slightest leakage. Even so, it is worlds apart from the staff of a monk.
What is meant by "the staff of a monk"? It possesses the capacity for both killing and giving life, and has its own distinct path.
If I were to raise and strike with this staff toward the ultimate, the stars and constellations would shift their positions, and the sun and moon...

No light. Birds and beasts wail; fish and dragons lock their doors. If one were to pick up and bring it forth by looking downward, it would truly be like a thousand flowers vying for beauty and ten thousand trees welcoming spring:
the wind would not rustle the branches, the rain would not break the clods of earth, fine grain would grow with ears joined together, and people would drum their bellies while singing songs of joy.
Yet, if it is neither above nor below, how then shall we deliberate? After a long silence, he said: "I urge you..."
It is used to carve away the stubborn stone; for those traveling on the road, their mouths are the monument.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they establish gates of transformation that do not depart from the wisdom-eye of the three bodies.

It is like Maheśvara’s three dots forming the character *i*: why is this? One eye is so impenetrable that not even a drop of water can pass through, making it difficult for the ordained and the laity to distinguish."
A single eye. The entire great earth is encompassed; the ten directions are unobstructed. A single eye. With one glance, high and low are seen; all myriad species look up together.
Although it is thus, if you are a monk of true standing who encounters this on the road, you must possess a distinct, authentic eye before you can succeed.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know its existence; the cat and the white ox, however, do know its existence. And so it is.

The Way. What is there to know? After a long silence, he said: "In the deep autumn, rain falls across a thousand homes behind the curtains; at sunset, the wind carries the sound of a single flute from the towers.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "If you wish to attain the soaring brilliance [of the Way], you must first ensure that four conditions are fully met; only then will the path of the Master be revealed."
What does this mean? First, one must possess the nostrils of the patriarchs. Second, one must be endowed with the adamantine eye. Third, one must have the claws and fangs of a lion.

Fourth, one must obtain the monk’s staff that governs both killing and giving life. Having attained these four things, one may manifest transformations at will, rolling up or unfolding as one pleases;
towering above gods and humans, standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. If one is not thus, then those who merely "preserve the good path until death" will fail.
This is the omen of an army. Why? Because striking a stone man with a staff values the reality of things.

Thus, reaching this point, one cannot help but see the Yangtze River shining brightly, vast clouds gathering over the great plains, mist coalescing upon the bamboo, and the green peaks locked in emerald hue; wind and cloud are of one accord.
Viewing the moon in the water as one; a single phrase encompasses all. This has already been revealed by Chanxiu.
Caotang Qing said, having finished his recitation: "Today Huanglong enters the world. The times are those of the final age, when the Buddha-dharma is diluted and decayed.
There is no need for the patriarchs' core essence, no need for the diamond eye, and no need for the lion’s roar."
Fangs and claws; not using a staff for killing or enlivening, there is only this single whisk to serve as the path.

It can also manifest in all manner of transformations, unfolding and contracting according to the natural flow. It can also tower high above gods and humans, standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms tall.
At times, it yields strength when meeting the powerful; at times, it assumes lowliness when encountering the noble. When lifted up, the entire multitude...
The Māras have vanished; the Buddhas and Patriarchs have hidden their traces. To let go is to blend with the water and the mud; holy and ordinary beings travel the same path.
But tell me: is it better to pick up or to let go? "The line on the tip of the pole is for you to handle as you wish; without disturbing the clear waves, the meaning is naturally distinct."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "O worthy ones! If you wish to carry your staff across your shoulders and gaze at the clouds and sky, you will find no door for rest and no ground for dwelling.
On solitary peaks and precipitous cliffs, one cannot linger; in market towns and open plains, how can one endure staying long?
To take a step forward, one cannot avoid treading upon the grassy grounds of kings and lords; to retreat a step, it is likewise to fall short of one's father."
"Qiu Yuan! Furthermore, tell me: as for 'neither advancing nor retreating,' how do you deliberate upon it? He lifts up his staff and says, "Do you wish to understand?
Idly holding a scripture, leaning against a pine tree, he smiles and asks: 'Where have you come from, traveler?'"

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Study must be genuine study; insight must be genuine insight. If you rely upon your own authentic eye, then whether encountering the defiled or the pure, there will be a place of return.

The ancestral teachers' 'sickness-gate' will forever be cast aside as you wield the blade with ease. This means that in every word you utter and every breath you draw, your clarity shall never be in vain."

Dark blades naturally meet; relying on words leads easily to downfall, while valuing speech makes it difficult to encompass the whole. When the Way exists before one's eyes, one has already missed its tracks;

how much more so for those who "wait by the stump for a rabbit" or "kill melons and nest in reeds," wasting away the swift light of reality and ultimately failing to distinguish the black from the white.
Therefore, Master Jia Shan said: "You must brandish the sword; if you do not brandish the sword, the fisherman will take up residence in his nest."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Brothers, if we speak of the matter of our fundamental nature, what could possibly be said?
To speak of Buddhas and Patriarchs is like picking at scabs and gouging out thorns; to speak of Chan or the Way is like scattering sand into one's eyes.

Even if you were as eloquent as the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven or as the old monks throughout the land who appeared in the world, and even if your speech and understanding were as fluent as a hanging curtain—"
River, you have not yet attained even a single word on the true path. Take, for instance, the Old Śākyamuni:
throughout his forty-nine years in the world, he established gates of transformation through all manner of causes and conditions, parables, and skillful means;
yet he never spoke a single word. If you say he spoke a single word, you slander him and will lose your eyebrows and whiskers.
[This] falls [into error]. Nevertheless, although it is thus, do not, upon hearing me speak in this way, dismissively negate [reality] and settle into a void, forming a "liberated" interpretation.
This principle is such that since the appearance in the world of the Buddhas of the three periods, who have established fields of transformation, there has been none who has not received benefit.
Not a single needle or blade of grass deviates from the successive lineages of the Patriarchs and the old masters throughout the land who spread the teaching.
This is not established in vain; it opens up things and accomplishes tasks. Thus, the Sutra says: "Open the gate of expedient means and reveal the mark of reality.
Therefore, reaching this point, gain and loss, right and wrong, inversion and selection—all return to the One Way.
As the ancients said: "If you understand it, it is extraordinary; even if you do not understand, it is still accepted."

Question: "The various sages of antiquity have transmitted that which has never reached anyone. Please, Master, speak of it. The Master said: "The barbarians love to wear hats of eagle-feather and rat-skin;
they say, 'A world all its own, new suns and moons. The Master said: "With an iron whip, he points afar at Mount Helan."
He asked the Great Good Spiritual Friend (Mahā-kalyāṇamitra), "To say there is nothing to talk about is to fall into a trap. What is it that transcends the human eye?
The Master said, "The Yellow River has nine bends. He said, "In that case, you are a true Good Spiritual Friend. The Master said, "The Iron Ox of Shanfu."
Question: "How was it before Niutou had seen the Fourth Patriarch? The Master said: "When it rains, the steps become wet. Question: "How was it after he saw him? The Master said:
"When it is sunny and dry, there is no mud."
Question: "How is it when the lotus has not yet emerged from the water? The Master said: "A scorched brick strikes one, freezing to the very marrow.
Question: "How is it after it has emerged from the water? The Master said: "The vast expanse is tranquil; no wind stirs the waves."

The monk asked, "Your golden-tipped arrows have been well-honed through a hundred battles; your iron whip possesses great strength, yet you lament having no enemy. The student stepped forward and requested, "I ask the Master for the definitive point.
Thereupon, he brushed his sleeve once. The Master said, "A sword for slaying dragons—how could it be wielded against a snake? The monk then sighed repeatedly.
The Master said, "Nowadays there are many like you, who would not yield until they reached the banks of the Wu River."
Xiu asked, "What is the place where all Buddhas do not sever their lives? The Master said, "Tender bamboo shoots forth new sprouts; withered pines grow long branches.
Xiu asked, "What is the pure Dharma-body? The Master said, "Not a single thread hangs upon it."

Chan Master Fashao of Baoying in Ruizhou (Total of Two): Addressing the assembly, he said, "If one discusses this matter, from antiquity to the present, there has never been a single person who has been able to proclaim it.
If there were a single person who could proclaim it, then all the people throughout the entire world [would be saved]."
To lose one's life is like being an iron hammer without a hole; one’s sharp edge vanishes all at once and the tongue is tied.

Even so, it is still slightly better than this. If I were to falsely establish host and guest, move my lips, point a finger, or raise a whisk, I would merely follow your delusions and teach you to have a place for questioning. But before a person of clear eyes, it is truly impossible to bring anything forth.
Look at Zen Master Luzu: as soon as he saw a monk approach, he would simply turn his back to the wall.
Changqing remarked of him, "If you receive people in such a manner, it will be like donkey-year before you reach the goal. Looking at Luzu now, he was truly a man who knew no shame.
Those of you who travel on pilgrimage should take this as a lesson and strive to attain realization for yourselves.
A monk asked, "What is the Dharma of the Dharma King? The Master said, "Three feet long. The monk asked, "How does one employ it?
The Master said, "Looking at the blue sky in a bustling marketplace. The monk asked, "What is the original mind? The Master said, "Large head, small tail. The monk asked, "How can this be seen?
The Master said, "The ground is more than three feet deep. The monk said, "I do not ask about Mañjuśrī’s praise of the good; [what about] Vimalakīrti..."

[The monk] remained silent. [The Master asked,] "How is the matter? The Master struck his chest three times. [The monk asked,] "How is the matter beyond [this]? The Master said, "Stop your ghostly talk.
This was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Cizhao Cong of Shimen in Xiangzhou.
Dacheng Zun Chan Master (1 total). The Master asked Shimen, "What was the meaning when the ancients asked for fire?
Shimen said, "Let it go out. The Master said, "What is it like after it has gone out? Shimen said, "The third of the month, the first of the month.
The Master said, "Just the right season. Shimen said, "What principle have you seen? The Master said, "I am very tired today. He then offered this verse: [Verse omitted]
How truly joyful is the mechanism for seeking fire! Few can fathom the subtle application of concealing the blade’s point. To understand my Master’s essential intent:
when the furnace is red-hot and the fire spent, no more wood is added.

Chan Master Daguang Tanying of Mount Jinshan in Runzhou (the ninth): Initially, he visited Chan Master Dayang Yan and asked, "Dongshan specifically established the categories of 'partial and correct' and 'ruler and minister.
What matter does his intent clarify? Yan said, "The state of affairs before one's parents were born.
The Master asked, "How does one realize this? Yan said, "Midnight is perfectly bright; at dawn, it is not revealed. The Master was left bewildered.
He then visited Shimen and recounted the previous conversation. Shimen Cong said, "Daiyang did not say it was wrong; it is simply that his mouth is too narrow.
Even with his whole mouth full, he could not finish speaking. I, the old monk, am not like this. The Master asked, "What is the state of affairs before one's parents were born?
Cong said, "A brick from the latrine. The Master asked, "What is 'midnight is perfectly bright, yet at dawn it is not revealed'? Cong—

"Clouds beneath the peony flowers; a sleeping cat. The Master became increasingly perplexed and alarmed. One day, during a communal work assignment (*yǒngqǐng*), Cóng asked, "Are you carrying firewood today?
The Master replied, "Yes. Cóng said, "Yunmen once asked a monk, 'When a person carries firewood, does the firewood carry the person?

How do you understand this? The Master had no reply. Cóng said, "This matter is like a person learning to write: one who can accurately replicate the strokes and characters is skilled; otherwise, they are not."
“Crude! It is simply because you have not yet forgotten the Dharma. You must reach the point where the pen forgets the hand, and the hand forgets the mind;
only then will it be possible. The Master then attained silent realization. After a long while, he said, “As Shitou said: ‘To grasp at phenomena is fundamentally delusion;

to accord with principle is likewise not awakening. Cong asked, “Do you consider this to be medicine or a disease? The Master said, “It is medicine. Cong rebuked him, saying, “You take this disease...”
"To serve as medicine—how could it be otherwise? The Master said: "The fact is like a box finding its lid; the principle is like an arrow with a straight shaft and point.

How could there be anything more wondrous than this? Yet you still regard it as a sickness; truly, you have not yet grasped the essential meaning. Cong said: "Even when the wondrous reaches such a state, it is still merely called 'principle and fact.
Yet the intent of the Patriarchs is that which the intellect cannot reach; how much less can facts and principles exhaust it? Therefore, the world..."
The Master said, "In principle, it obstructs the knowledge of right view; in phenomena, it continues the succession of birth and death.
Master Huangruo asked, "How does one make use of this? Cong replied, "If speech does not leave the nest of the Way, how could one escape the entanglements?
The Master sighed and said, "As soon as it touches the lips, it falls into the realm of conceptual thought; all of this is the gate of death and is ultimately no living path."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The moment one involves the lips and tongue, one immediately falls into conceptual thought;

all such paths are dead ends, none are living ways. Even if one manages to break through, one still remains mired in delusion. Do not let your lifelong practice come to naught, nor let this life be spent in vain.
If you wish not to let your lifelong practice come to naught—" He took up his staff, struck once, and said: "You must not be deceived by this staff."
"Attain it! Look, look! This staff pierces through the skulls of you all and leaps right into your nostrils!
He struck the ground once with the staff.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The gate of this mountain monk is unique; I have already altered the tracks of all of you.

To extract the wedge from Mañjuśrī’s eye, I instruct Samantabhadra to cease chewing the iron in his mouth. I urge you to loosen the hand that grips the slithering snake and cut away the hitching stake for the donkey.
If you pause to contemplate with a fixed mind—*shouts once*—*Squeezed! Squeezed!*"
One day, the Master ascended the hall. The Head Seat came forward and paid his respects. The Master said, "Ask well.
As the Head Seat bowed his head and was about to speak, the Master immediately said, "Today I will not answer questions," and then descended from the seat and returned to the Abbot’s quarters.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The five thousand scriptures are the constant discourse of all Buddhas; the eighty thousand afflictions are the wondrous function of sentient beings.
Yet even these are not yet the adamantine eye. But what, then, is the adamantine eye? After a long silence, he said: "Blind!"
Addressing the assembly, he said, "This mountain monk has always been fond of sumo wrestling, yet I have had no opponent. Today, I shall wrestle with the Head Seat.

He then rolled up his *kāṣāya* and descended from the seat, challenging the Head Seat to a match. As soon as the Head Seat stepped out, the Master said, "A fall on level ground," and immediately returned to the Abbot’s quarters.
A monk asked, "Does the Master still practice mindfulness of the Buddha? The Master said, "I do not. The monk asked, "Why do you not practice it?
The Master said, "It defiles people's mouths."
The Commandant Li Gongduanyuan asked, "When a person dies, where does their consciousness go? The Master said, "If you do not know life, how can you know death?
Li said, "I already know life. The Master said, "From where does life come? As Li hesitated, the Master thrust his hand toward Li’s chest and said, "It is right here.
What are you thinking about? Li said, "I only knew the destination; I did not realize I had missed the road."
The Master leaned on his staff and said, "A hundred years are but a single dream.
The Commandant asked, "Ultimately, do hell and its realms exist or not? The Master replied, "The Buddhas speak of existence within non-existence."

The eyes see flowers in the sky; the Grand Marshal seeks them within that very state and finds nothing. He supports his hand against the moon reflected in water. It is laughable: he sees a prison before his eyes yet does not avoid it;
he sees a heavenly realm outside his mind and desires to be born there. Little does he realize that joy and fear reside in the mind, while good and evil constitute the external environment.
Grand Marshal, simply understand your own mind, and naturally you will be free from delusion. Li said, "How does one understand the mind? The Master said:
"Do not deliberate at all upon good or evil. Li asked, "After one does not deliberate, where does the mind go? The Master said, "Please, General, return to your residence.
Observing that Lord Li was upright and refined, he asked about the Western Pure Land: "How can one reach it? The Master said, "Right now, you are sitting."
"You have carved your rafters and painted your beams, yet you still seek to be born in the Western Pure Land—is this not preferring the false over the true?
Li said, "How could the Buddha be a falsehood? The Master said, "The Buddha is not false; it is you, the Grand Marshal, who are false. Li said, "How could I be false?
The Master said, "If you were not false, why would you seek the Western Pure Land? Generally speaking, that which is called 'Pure Land' is purity."
The nature of purity. As for the "Western Quarter," it is the place where the sun sets; it serves merely to provide a place for people to seek refuge.
To know this place of refuge is precisely the Western Pure Land, the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī). Li bowed in thanks and withdrew.
Scholar Diaojingchun asked about Buddhism: "Of what use is it in the world? The Master said, "It is indispensable for daily life. Diaojingchun asked, "How is it used?
The Master said, "In the eye, it is called seeing; in the ear, it is called hearing. Diaojingchun asked, "What does this have to do with the Buddha?
The Master said, "If it did not concern the affairs of the Buddha, what would constitute seeing and hearing? Diaojingchun said, "One naturally possesses eyes and ears."
The Master said: "All people and Buddhas are carved and painted with eyes and ears; yet, because they lack Buddhahood, they are utterly unable to see or hear.
'Buddha' has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*); because there is right awakening, one is called a Buddha. If there is no right view, all is but false understanding.
Furthermore, do not take the burning flame as your headgear or the lotus flower as your footstool, nor regard the yellow scrolls and red volumes as the Buddha's teaching."
[Recorded by] Chan Master Liaotong of Shimen in Xiangzhou (Total: One). Addressing the assembly, he said: "Venerable seniors, when the bell has not yet rung, you should already know the time.
Why do you come forward here, clutching your staff against your chest? This is truly a state of profound frustration for all of you. However—"
Even so, I scatter sand into the eyes of all people. The Buddhas of the three periods dwell upon the nostrils of all people, turning the Great Dharma Wheel.
Look, look! Spring is proceeding with the ordinances of winter.
Chan Master Shizhen of Renshou in Chuzhou (Part II) addressed the assembly, saying: "Clearly there is no awakening; to have a dharma is to be deluded.
When the sun rises without clouds, it shines radiantly upon the heavens; when the eyes are free of cataracts, space is fundamentally without flowers.
Before those who lack wisdom, do not speak erroneously."
A monk asked, "What is the master’s family style? The Master said, "Clay roosters and earthenware dogs.
Duke Li Wenhe Zunxu (sixth in rank) went to visit Chan Master Shimen Cong and asked about the matter of leaving the household life.
Cong said, "In the past, Duke Cui [Yuancong] visited Chan Master Guoyi and asked, 'I, your disciple, wish to leave the household life.'"
"No," he replied. One day [Baizhang] said, "Leaving home to become a monk is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can perform.
At these words, the official attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "To study the Way, one must be an iron man; As soon as the hand touches the heart, judgment is made.
Directly pursue supreme Bodhi; Pay no heed to any right or wrong."
Ciming came to pay his respects. The Master asked, "I have heard there is a golden-maned lion in Western River;
is this true? Ciming replied, "Where did you, Excellency, get such news? The Master then gave a shout. Ciming said, "A jackal howling.
The Master shouted again. Ciming said, "Precisely so. The Master clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
Ciming took his leave. The Duke asked, "What is the one phrase for the moment of departure? Ciming said, "Take good care of yourself.
The Duke said, "In that case, you are no different from those of other quarters. Ciming asked, "And what of your own realization, Excellency?
The Duke said, "I shall give you thirty blows! Ciming said, "If so, then I shall go specifically to propagate this. The Duke then gave a shout.

The Master said, "Brother Shan has a poisonous heart; he always obstructs others. That is why he has come to see the Abbot.
Ciming suddenly asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The monk replied, "Cloudless skies arise over the peaks; the moon descends into the heart of the waves. Ciming became angry.
Muhé said, "With hair as white as snow and teeth fallen out, you still maintain such a view. How can you ever escape birth and death?
The Master did not dare look up; tears flowed down his cheeks. After a long while, he finally asked, "I do not yet know: what is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?"
Mingyun said, "Cloudless skies arise above the peaks; the moon appears within the waves. Upon these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.
His spirit was refined and transcendent, and his wit and discernment were swift and sharp; the monastic communities stood in awe of him. Later, he emerged into the world at Cuiyan.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Sentient beings are hindered by their understanding; Bodhisattvas have not yet transcended their awakening. He held up his staff and said:
"This staff—this is the hindrance. Which one is awakening? If you understand this, then being hindered by your understanding becomes a hindrance, and you will lack freedom.
If you do not understand this, the source from which all returns is non-dual, though the skillful means are manifold."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "To not perceive a single dharma is a great calamity. Mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars, form and emptiness, light and darkness—these are not a single dharma.
Raising his staff, he said: "Ordinary people see the staff and call it a staff.
Śrāvakas see the staff and recognize it as a mere void, thereby negating the staff. Bodhisattvas see [it]..."
As for the staff, has it ever been hung upon one’s teeth? When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep; when cold, approach the fire;
when hot, seek coolness. Have you not heard it said that the wisdom of all wisdoms is pure? To speak in such a manner would make even the local deity laugh his head off.
Addressing the assembly, the Master raised an anecdote: A monk asked Baling, "What is the Way? Baling said, "A person with clear eyes falls into a well.
Again, he asked Baoying; Baoying said, "Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion. Again, he asked Shoushan; Shoushan said, "Three feet deep beneath one's feet.
The Master said, "These three responses: one response stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high; one response is a boat traveling on dry land; [the third is]..."
A turning phrase: guest and host intermingle. Is there anyone among the assembly who can discern and extract [the truth]? Come forward and speak!
If there is none, then practice the compassion of an Arhat to destroy the thieves of the fetters; practice the compassion of a Bodhisattva to bring peace to sentient beings;
practice the compassion of a Tathāgata to realize the mark of suchness.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "To resist the enemy on the battlefield without fear of life or death is the courage of a general.
To enter the mountains without fear of tigers or wild oxen is the courage of a hunter. To enter the waters without avoiding dragons or sea-monsters is the courage of a fisherman.
But what is the courage of a patch-robed monk? He raised his staff and said, "This here is the staff."
If you can pick it up, grasp it, and move it, the three thousandfold world system will all at once tremble.
If you cannot pick it up, cannot grasp it, and cannot move it, then Mañjuśrī remains Mañjuśrī and liberation remains liberation.
When the Master was residing at Shanglan, there was a state scholar who asked Baizhang Huaheshang, "Since you are Baizhang, why are you so short and small?
Huaheshang replied, "Today is a fine, clear day. The scholar did not accept this and requested the Master to provide a response on his behalf.

The scholar repeated his previous question, and the Master said, "On the southern side of Mount Sumeru, we walk hand-in-hand together. The scholar stood in thought for a moment, then said, "I do not yet understand."
"What is the meaning of this? the Master said, "A mosquito on an iron ox. Xuefeng Bo asked, "I beg the Master to explain this for me. The Master said, "Go away;
leave your wife and children behind, and then I will explain it to you. Bo asked, "As for the Elder himself, can he walk or not?
The Master said, "Every day, at Shanglan Temple, I see off guests; I have walked there over a hundred times."

Chan Master Kuān of Dàníng in Hóngzhōu (sixth in the series) addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddha-dharma is a matter of no concern; it is people themselves who are deluded regarding its source.
Thus, the Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared to set everything right. Consequently, the teachings spread throughout the realms of sand, and the Way was disseminated in all four directions.

Everyone abandoned their shortcomings to follow what was superior, exhaustively investigating their original nature. If one penetrates this original nature, all things are empty. One simply picks them up with the hand of faith."
"A thousand ways of enjoyment. Now tell me: speaking in such a manner, does it accord with the affairs of the ancestral masters' school?
After a long silence, he said: "To cry until the blood flows is of no use; it is better to keep one's mouth shut and pass through the remainder of spring."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The wondrous secret of Shaolin and the ancestral style of the Buddhas and patriarchs are applied according to circumstances;

they unfold and retract with sovereign ease. Like a fist becoming an open palm, their opening and closing occur at the proper time; like water forming bubbles, their arising and ceasing have no fixed point.

Movement and stillness are both revealed; speech and silence are fully manifest. All functions are spontaneous, requiring no exertion of mind or effort. Reaching this point, it is called 'letting a boat drift downstream.'"
"This person can go; they pull against the wind. "Who is the one who knows? After a long silence, he said: "To play with the tide, one must be a player of the tide.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "High yet not precarious; full yet not overflowing. Amidst the mundane, one does not abandon the mundane; dwelling in the sacred, even the sacred is difficult to attain."
He flees. The ten directions are all illuminated as one; the great earth is devoid of even a hair’s breadth. But tell me, what is this? He lets out a shout.
Addressing the assembly, he takes up his staff and says: "The life-force of the Buddhas of the past and the governing principles of the Buddhas of the future are both contained right here.
Now they are put to use: becoming clouds and rain, becoming auspicious omens and blessings; benefiting humans and gods, entering birth and exiting death. He continues: "He..."
Throughout the worlds, appearing and disappearing, rolling up and unfolding—if one’s entire being were a mouth, one could not exhaustively speak of it;
if one’s entire being were an eye, one could not fully illumine it. When there is resonance in a single thought-moment, a single instant is ten thousand kalpas.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Non-thought is the school; non-abiding is the root; true emptiness is the essence; wondrous existence is the function. Therefore it is said:
'The entire earth is true emptiness; throughout the dharma-realm is wondrous existence. Now tell me, who is it that can employ this? The four seasons revolve, the sun and moon shine ever bright;
the Dharma is fundamentally immutable, and the Way has no fixed location, following conditions as they arise."
He is sovereign, rising or sinking according to things; he enters this land or other lands, and enters the state of ordinary beings or the state of sages. Although it is so, tell me:
how would you express the phrase "entering a village, following its customs"? After a long silence, he said: "The Sanskrit of the Western Heaven; the Chinese of this land."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The matter that has been handed down from of old is not obtained from the Buddha, nor sought from the Patriarchs.
The nature of a man of integrity is inherently and spontaneously true. His movements accord with propriety; his coming and going are free from attachment.

Like a fish in water, he floats and sinks according to his own nature; like a bird flying through the sky, he is entirely without hindrance. Who among you can recognize this talk as such? (After a long pause) A single breath."
Without speaking, it contains all forms; where could the myriad spirits go to express their gratitude for His impartiality?
A monk asked, "The scriptures say that one only then knows that sentient beings have been fundamentally enlightened from the beginning. Why, then, are there afflictions and bodhi?
The Master said, "Licorice is sweet; yellow bitter gourd is bitter. The monk said, "In that case, they become two separate things. The Master said, "You..."
"It is not an obstacle to attaining excellence.
[A student] asked, "Since it is the single true Dharma-realm, why are there nevertheless a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions?
The Master said, "The roots are deep and the leaves are lush. [The student] asked, "I wonder, can one ever transcend this? The Master said, "Seeking cleverness results in clumsiness."
Question: "What is the white ox in the open field? The Master took a pair of fire tongs, stuck them into the brazier, and said, "Do you understand?
He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The head is not lacking; the tail is not in excess."
Question: Regarding the four maladies taught in the scriptures—exertion, cessation, indulgence, and extinction—how should those of later generations proceed? The Master said:
"When a skilled craftsman wields his axe, he chops the wood without using a measuring line."
Question: When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why did the temple steward’s eyebrows and beard fall off?
The Master said: "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor. While the Master was at Tong’an, a monk asked: "Since it is Tong’an (Peaceful Together), why did the sick monk instead pass away?
The Master said: "Giving alms is not as good as repaying one's debts. Question: "The Dharma has nothing to be grasped or rejected; why then do they [people] treat one another... [The text ends here.]

Regarding "Transmitting and Bestowing," the Master said: "In transmitting and bestowing, there is nothing to be taken up or rejected. Question: "Why did Kāśyapa’s correct vision consist in seeing the flower and then smiling?
The Master said: "He could not restrain his impatience. Question: "Why is it that the Chan practitioners of the world cannot produce this [circle]?
The Master said: "It is often like this."
Chan Master Wuzhen of Daowu in Tanzhou (the tenth of ten) addressed the assembly, saying: "The sun and moon are as they were of old;
the mountains and rivers remain as before. If you can understand this, then the Bhagavats of the ten directions all share the single path to Nirvāṇa.
If you cannot understand it, you slander this sutra, and thus you shall incur such retribution."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "An ancient said, 'If you recognize it, as before, it is not. This is truly difficult to understand. The Earth-Dweller has a profusion of beard and whiskers beneath his chin;
the Persian has deep-set eyes and large nostrils—how extraordinary! Suddenly he breaks through to the borders of Silla."
Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised a case: A monk asked Shoushan, “What is the Buddha? Shoushan said, “The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while the mother-in-law leads it.
The Master said: “Hand in the nose-ring, foot on the tail; looking up at the sky, listening to the flowing water;
at daybreak sent out by the roadside, at night’s quiet returning to the thatched hut.”
Addressing the assembly, he raised the case of Dongshan, who said: "On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the steps of the Buddha Hall, it is a 'dog-urine day';
atop the bannerpole, a *zhuanzi* is being fried; three monkeys toss coins at night. The Master said:
"The old fellow was not like this: A three-faced *lilu* cat treads upon the moon; A two-headed white ox grasps smoke in its hands; A crowned blue hare stands—"
The cypress in the courtyard; the shell-shedding turtle flies up into the sky. This old monk’s entanglements have been completely seen through by everyone.
The old man Dongshan is truly extraordinary; nevertheless, he could only manage three or four steps.
"Let us not go beyond seven or eight leaps. Now tell me, where does the error lie? Today, this old monk, without sparing his eyebrows, bestows it all at once.
After a long silence, he said: "Excessive caution harms one's virtue; silence truly possesses merit."
"Let the blue seas change as they may; I shall never act as your messenger.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The lion cub roars; the dragon-horse colt leaps. Within the mirror of the ancient Buddhas, the solitary moon over the three mountains shines bright.
Thereupon he performed a dance and descended from his seat.
The Master asked a monk, "I have a matter to inquire about you; it is simply that you must not strike this old monk. The monk said, "What grounds are there for such a request?
The Master held up his sitting cloth and said, "What can be done about this? [The monk] said, "Do not act recklessly. The Master then struck him.
The monk said, "Do not act recklessly. The Master struck him again and said, "Sit and drink tea for now.
The monk said, "Just now you asked, 'On what grounds? Why did the Master strike me? The Master said, "Where have you been just now?"
The monk remained silent. The Master struck his chest once.
The Master asked the monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From the Hall. The Master said, "What did the Holy Monk say? The monk stepped forward and said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "At one neighbor's house he is a donkey; at another neighbor's house he is a horse. The monk asked, "Where does the fault lie? The Master said:
At Cliff State (Yazhou), ten thousand *li* away, the Master was unwell. A monk asked, "How is your venerable health these days, Master? The Master said, "The head cook cannot manage his duties.
The monk was speechless. The Master snapped his fingers once.
A monk asked, "What is the first mystery? The Master said, "The light of Śākyamuni Buddha shoots across Ānanda’s shoulder. The monk asked, "What is the second mystery?
The Master said, "The solitary wheel [of the moon] amidst a throng of elephants. The monk asked, "What is the third mystery? The Master said:
Weeping toward the withered mulberry tree, his tears flowed in unceasing streams. He asked, "What is the first essential? The Master said, "The finest thing is the illumination of the coarse.
He asked, "What is the second essential? The Master said, "A flash of lightning; the light of heaven and earth blazes forth. He asked, "What is the third essential?
The Master said, "Ancient pines grow old, flanking the path."
A monk asked, "What is it like when one understands immediately upon encountering stillness? The Master said, "A mouse carries a grinding stone on its tail.

This was Chan Master Wenyue of Yunfeng in Tanzhou, a successor of Chan Master Shouzhi of Dayu in Junzhou (in all, nine [generations]). He was the son of the Xu family of Nanchang. Initially, he went to visit Dayu and heard...
Addressing the assembly, [Zhaozhou] said: "Everyone has gathered here to eat some vegetable broth. If you call it 'a ladle of vegetable broth,' you will enter hell as fast as a shot arrow.
He then descended from his seat and offered no further words. The Master (Xuedou) was greatly startled. That night he went to the abbot’s quarters;

Zhi asked him, "What do you seek in coming here? The Master replied, "I seek the Dharma of the mind. Zhi said, "The Wheel of Dharma has not yet turned; first, the Wheel of Food must turn. Young man, go away!"
"Your physical strength is robust. Why do you not go out for alms for the sake of the assembly? I am occupied with enduring hunger; how have I the leisure to explain Zen to you?
The Master did not dare disobey. Before long, Dazhu Zhizhe moved to Cuiyan. After the Master had submitted his formal letter of resignation, he went back to Cuiyan to seek further instruction.
Zhizhe said, "The Buddha-dharma has not yet reached the point of being 'rotten. The snow is cold; you should go out for the sake of the assembly to beg for charcoal. The Master again complied.
When his duties were completed, he was appointed to oversee the construction of the Abbot’s quarters. Zhi said, "The Hall Office is lacking personnel; I now entrust this task to you.

The Master accepted it with reluctance, harboring resentment toward Zhi that would not leave his mind. One day, while he was repairing a wooden bucket on the upper shelf, the rim of the bucket suddenly gave way, and it fell from the shelf.
At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment and clearly perceived Zhi’s underlying intent. He hurried to the Abbot’s quarters; when Zhi saw him coming, he smiled.

The Master said, "I am glad that the great matter is now concluded. The teacher bowed twice more, unable to utter a single word. He served him diligently for eight years. Later, he emerged into the world at Cuoyan.
At that time, the head seat led the assembly out to welcome him and asked, "I do not ask about the Dharma-lineage of Deshan; [what about...]"
"What is the Great Function of Linji? The Master said, "Where have you come from? As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
As the monk attempted to respond, the Master shouted, "Lead the assembly back! From then on, the entire assembly was awed and submissive.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Is there not a masterly Chan guest, a monk of the fundamental lineage? What prevents you from coming forth to provide mutual verification? Is there anyone?
A needle held within a cloth bag—if it does not poke its head out, that is a true adept. Generally speaking, to uphold and establish the Dharma-lineage, one must indeed be such a person.
If you have not yet attained the state where the sword-blade passes through a rushing torrent, or the flash of lightning and sparks,"
The hand-eye of the depths need not be brought forth. Have you not seen how when Linji and Deshan were sitting together, Deshan said, "I am tired today"?
Linji said, "Old man, why do you speak in your sleep? Deshan raised his staff; Linji then overturned the rope bed. The Master said:
"How strange, O virtuous practitioners of meditation! Behold these two masters: one pressing, one nudging, briefly revealing their style.
It is much like leading someone by the hand up a high mountain. Even so, they cannot avoid being laughed at by the bystanders.
But tell me, who is the bystander? He let out a shout and struck the meditation seat once.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The ultimate principle of the Buddha-dharma is not sought through competitive debate. To strike out with resonant clamor in order to crush heterodox schools—could this be the Way of the Patriarchs?
Therefore, the entire Canon of the Great Teaching cannot explain it for itself; the Buddhas of the ten directions cannot proclaim it.
Its brilliance transcends past and present, utterly severing all seeing and knowing. It fills the entirety of the ten voids; how could there be..."

Regarding spatial location: it is simply because the arising of emotion creates a barrier to knowledge, and the shifting of conceptions causes the essence to become distinct. Thus, though one walks all day long, one does not realize it oneself.
For this reason, the former sages labored to turn their heads back toward the realm of dust and toil, skillfully opening up expedient means (*upāya*).

Within these expedient means, is there anyone who can provide proof and realization? If you can indeed provide such proof and realization, you will be able to benefit others according to their capacities, manifesting transformations without fixed direction.
Appearing and disappearing, unfolding and rolling up, whether among humans or in the heavens—though it may be so, one must not pass through the gate of the patch-robed monk.
Why? Because it would break his mouth with laughter.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddhas of the past have already passed away; the Buddhas of the future are not yet born.
Right now, at this very moment, the Buddha-Dharma rests entirely with Cuiyan. To let go is to benefit beings according to their capacities; to hold fast is for things to dissolve like ice melting.
Now tell me: is it better to hold fast, or is it better to let go? After a long silence, he said: "Tsk! You wild fox spirit! He then struck his meditation seat once.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you who have come up here in this manner are much like thrusting your heads into a vat of glue.
To go away in this manner is also like tripping on level ground. Even if you neither come nor go, I shall strike you three thousand times in the morning and eight hundred times in the evening."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Is the Way distant? It is true in every encounter. Is the Sage distant? He is manifest when one realizes his essence.
Thus, in the Sahā world, the Buddha-work is performed through sound; in the Gandhavatī world, the Buddha-work is performed through fragrant food.
Here at Cuoyan, within the very movement of inhalation and exhalation, we offer sustenance and serve the Buddhas of the past, present, and future."
"Among the sand-like Buddhas of the past, present, and future, there is not one who has passed by. There is not one among these sand-like Buddhas who did not have a servant in Cuiyan;
if even one had not been so, you would have received thirty blows of the staff. Do you all understand, venerable elders?
To offer this profound mind to the dust-motes of the lands—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The root of sentient beings relies upon the ocean of wisdom as its source; the stream of conscious beings takes the Dharma-body as their substance.

It is only because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptualizations shift that the substance becomes distinct. When one realizes the root, emotions vanish; when one knows the mind, the substance merges.
Do you all understand, venerable practitioners of Chan? The ancient Buddhas intersect with the pillar; the Buddha hall vies with the lantern for the top of the forehead."
If you do not understand, I shall simply provide a brief, layered analysis. Small Talk (Xiaocan):
Master Baizhang addressed the assembly on the eve of the New Year, saying: "You lot, this group of young monks—you certainly know nothing of the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Abhidharma;
yet when it comes to joining the assembly to practice Chan, you do not understand Chan either. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month, what will you do?"
[The Master] said, "To sum it up: O venerable practitioners of Zen, the time since the Sage has passed far away and the hearts of men have grown indifferent.

Looking at the monastic communities of today, they are even worse than that. Wherever they may be, they gather three hundred or five hundred disciples in great numbers, yet they consider their prosperity to consist only in abundant food and drink and comfortable quarters. In the midst of this, they are diligently intent on..."
As for the Way, there is not a single person who possesses it. Even if there were ten or five, they would run up and down, half-green and half-yellow;
when meeting [a teacher], they all claim, "I understand! I understand! Each one considers themselves to be grasping the jewel of the divine serpent, yet who is willing to recognize their error?
When pressed and prodded by the master’s staff, there is truly not one in ten thousand. How bitter, how bitter! This is what is called *prajñā*.
The monastic groves wither year after year; the weeds of ignorance grow longer with each passing season.
Among them, the younger generation of the present day, as soon as they enter the assembly, immediately sit upright with hands folded in a gesture of formality, coveting the offerings of others.

Everywhere they go, they do not pluck a single stalk of vegetable nor carry a single bundle of firewood; their ten fingers never touch water, and they have no concern for any of the hundred affairs of the monastery. Although this may be so for a time—
How pleasant! But alas, how can you avoid the three miserable realms (trāya) weighing upon your person? Have you not seen it said in the teachings:

"It would be better to have glowing iron wrapped around one's body than to accept the robes of a person of faith; it would be better to have molten copper poured into one's mouth than to accept the food of a person of faith"?
Elder, if you are truly so, then even if you were to transform the great earth into gold and churn the long rivers into ghee and milk, to offer such as these—

"Venerable Elder, this is not beyond your capacity. If it were not so, then for even a drop of water or a thread of silk, you would have to wear fur and horns, pull the plow and drag the harrow, before you could repay him.
Have you not seen the Patriarch say: 'If one enters the Way but does not penetrate its principle...'"
Furthermore, returning the body to those who offered it in faith is a matter of ultimate certainty; it shall never be in vain. Venerable Elders, time is precious and the moment does not wait for man.

Do not wait until the light of your eyes falls to the ground, only to find that your "field of black robes" lacks even a single basketful of earth, while you suffer the agony of a hundred punishments as you sink into the Iron Ring Mountains. Do not say that I have not warned you.

A monk asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? The Master said, "The Yellow River has nine bends. The monk said, "If that is so, then there is no interruption between the present and antiquity.
The Master said, "Pitifully, the wild geese fill the sands, their cries echoing as they await the spring."
Question: "What is the first phrase? The Master said: "His hands hang down past his knees. Question: "What is the second phrase?
The Master said: "Ten-thousand-li away at Yezhou. Question: "What is the third phrase? The Master said: "A dung basket and a broom."
Question: "Are there many instances of the Buddha-dharma upon steep mountains and rocky precipices? The Master said: "There are. Question:
"What is the Buddha-dharma on steep mountains and rocky precipices? The Master said: "A monkey climbing a tree upside down."
Question: "How was it before Bodhidharma had yet come? The Master said: "The waves are vast across the shifting sands. Question: "And how was it after he had come?
The Master said: "Mount Xionger is high."
A layman asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Dress, eat, and measure your household's means.

The man said, "If that is so, I shall step back three paces and place my palms together at my chest. The Master said, "Adding another cup after one is already drunk is better than having none at all."

Chan Master Fang of Jiangshan in Yuezhou, Dharma heir of Chan Master Huijue of Langya in Chuzhou (the seventh of seven): Addressing the assembly, he said, "It is not that one can speak of it or cannot speak of it;
everywhere people take this to be something extraordinary. Hanshan, his head covered in ashes from burning fire, laughed at Fenggan, calling him an old thief."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Passing through clouds but not crossing waters; crossing waters but not passing through clouds. Holding fast to heaven and earth, yet not holding them fast;
letting go into empty space, yet not letting it go. Transverse and vertical, three and four; parting and joining, long and short—these are indeed not absent.
You people, as for the phrase 'rice is made from grain,' it is truly difficult to speak of. After a long silence, he said: "Privately..."
Matters cannot be compensated by official titles.
A monk asked, "The rushing torrent passes the blade; the swift flame exceeds the wind. I wonder, under the gate of Jiangshan, is it permitted to borrow [the Way] or not?

The Master said, "The sky is cold, the days are short, and the nights are longer. [The monk] said, "An embroidered phoenix and mandarin duck on a brocade curtain—passersby find it difficult [to discern]."
[The monk] said, “I have seen it. The Master said, “The breath within the skull gushes toward heaven. The monk said, “Master! The Master said, “The head of a rooster and the tail of a phoenix.
[The monk] said, “Everywhere else they wash in the mud; Jiangshan has brought it here painted. The Master said, “Today Jiangshan is acting as a guest.”
Furthermore, I hope that you, Ācārya, will transmit this well. Nevertheless, even so, one must not let it pass. [The Master] struck the meditation bench once.
A monk asked, "What is 'one mote of dust entering right concentration'? The Master said, "A snake holding the tail of a rat.
The monk asked, "What is 'arising from the samādhi of all motes of dust'? The Master said, "A turtle biting a fishing rod. The monk said, "If that is so, then east and west..."
[The monk] said, "North and south are no longer distinguishable. The Master said, "Before the hall is a bowl of night-bright lamp; outside the curtain are several stalks of slender bamboo.
A monk asked, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? The Master said, "I do not know the wine-pitcher. [The monk] asked, "After he appeared in the world..."
"How is it? The Master said, "Giving three hammers on a fishing boat. Question:
"How is it when the lotus has not yet emerged from the water? The Master said, "One frowns at the eye being too small for threading a needle. Question: "How is it after it has emerged?
The Master said, "Throughout the day, one spreads a brow of sorrow. Question: "What is the Immovable Honored One? The Master said, "Wearing only a single garment."
He spread his robe and passed through the marketplace. [The student] said, "I, a student, do not yet understand. The Master said, "Riding a donkey, one tramples through the waves of Lake Dongting.
[The student] asked, "Having penetrated the three-tiered waves, one waits intently for a single clap of thunder. The Master said, "Stretching out one's hand, one cannot see one's own palm.

[The student] said, "Do you permit this student to advance further? The Master said, "Treading upon the ground, one addresses the void. [The student] said, "Beneath the Gate of Thunder... [The Master continued: "...spread your robe."
The drum was difficult to sound. The Master said, "Upon the eight-flowered ball, there is no need to embroider a red banner.
He added, "Thirty years from now, these words will spread widely," and then he struck him.
Chan Master Dinghui Haiyin Xin of Suzhou (Sixth in the series) addressed the assembly, saying: "In Mahādeva’s room, the calculations were not yet complete;
in Vimalakīrti’s silence, all skillful means were exhausted. A single blow or a shout does not yet suffice for a patch-robed monk;

raising a whisk or lifting an eyebrow is but leftover gruel and stale rice. You worthy ones, when I, this mountain monk, speak in such a manner, it is because of these idle matters that [the mind] grows long."
Ignorance. Now tell me: how do you express the single phrase that does not harm the meaning of things? After a long silence, he said:
"I have always loved it, deep within the winter months of Lingnan, when the first branch of plum blossoms unfolds amidst the snow."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If you recognize prajñā, you are bound by prajñā; if you do not recognize prajñā, you are likewise bound by prajñā.
Setting aside both recognition and non-recognition, what is the essence of prajñā? After a long silence, he said:
"Go to the hall for meditation."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Sometimes a single shout stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high; sometimes a single shout plants its four corners firmly upon the ground.
He gave a shout and said: "Tell me, where does it land? If you can discern this, I shall give you another shout as well."
The Master asked a monk, "Regarding National Teacher Zhong’s 'insentient things preaching the Dharma,' how do the venerable elders of the South discuss this?

Chan Master Zu Xin of Huanglong in Hongzhou (total of twelve [generations]). He was the son of the Wu family from Shixing in Nanxiong. Initially, he visited Chan Master Yunfeng Yue;

because Yunfeng was solitary and rigid, it was difficult for him to enter, and in the end, he did not attain realization. When he informed Yunfeng that he intended to depart, Yunfeng said, "You must go and rely upon Chan Master Nanyuan of Huangbo.

why did you, O Preceptor, teach people to 'investigate the phrase' and search for it with every possible means?

Nan said, "If I had not taught you to investigate and seek in this manner until you reach the state of no-mind, where you see for yourself and accept it for yourself, then I would have buried you alive."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "To know illusion is to leave it; no expedient means are required. To leave illusion is to awaken; there is likewise no gradual process.
The Old Śākyamuni has, at once, flung open a thousand gates and ten thousand doors. A man of keen faculties, upon hearing this mentioned, seizes his staff and goes forth immediately.
If you hesitate any longer, you will find yourself heading for Xiqin while I am off to Donglu."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The phrase with meaning and the phrase without meaning are like a vine leaning against a tree; let the various quarters nod their heads as they will.
But when the tree falls and the vine withers, there is no scheme to pierce the heavens above, nor any plot to enter the earth below.
You men of keen intelligence—if you can apply a single eye here, you will see it moving freely in all directions. He then raised his whisk and said: "The great sun floods the eyes; ten thousand..."

The ears of all of you are within a single sound; that single sound pervades the ears of all of you. If you are a soaring falcon reaching the clouds, you should immediately mount it."
At that time, he was like one trying to stop fish in a shallow pond, laboring in vain to stir up the waves.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "To not be a companion to the myriad dharmas is the Samādhi of Non-contention. Even if you proceed in this manner, what can be done?
If the strings are too tight, the sound is short. If you could scatter genuine pearls within a purple silk curtain, it would not necessarily be a good cause.
This brings about evil consequences. He addressed the assembly, saying: "Where there is obstruction, it is not the wall; where there is penetration, it is not empty space.
If you can understand it thus, mind and form are fundamentally the same. Raising his whisk, he said: "The whisk is form; which one is the mind? O clever ones! As soon as...

Upon hearing the mention of it, one sees its horns over the wall and immediately knows it is an ox. If you were to deliberate or reflect further, white clouds would stretch a thousand miles and ten thousand leagues.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If you clarify only yourself and do not awaken to what is before your eyes, this person has eyes but no feet. If...
To realize what is before one's eyes yet not understand oneself—such a person has feet but no eyes.

Based on these two types of people, throughout the twelve hours of the day, there is always something harbored within their chests. Since this thing is in the chest, the signs of unease are constantly before one's eyes.
Because they are before one's eyes, every path encountered becomes an obstruction. But how can one attain peace and stability? The Patriarch did not say:
If one clings to it, one loses the proper measure and will inevitably enter a deviant path; if one lets go into the natural state, the body has neither going nor staying.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The foolish person eliminates external objects but does not forget the mind; the wise person forgets the mind but does not eliminate external objects.

Not knowing that the nature of mind and objects is fundamentally suchness (tathatā), they encounter obstacles at every turn when meeting conditions. Raising his whisk, he said: "Look! Look! The whisk is running away!"
Having traveled to the Western Heavens, he has now returned to the land of Silla. Those who understand me say that I am dragging mud and water along;
those who do not understand me say that I have won a field of strange and absurdity.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "When a master craftsman has not yet appeared, jade and stone cannot be distinguished; when a skilled smith is absent, gold dust and sand are mixed together.
Is there anyone here who has attained self-awakening without a teacher? Come forth and discern this! He then raised his whisk and said: "Tell me now—"
"This is gold; this is sand. After a long silence, he said: "If you see it but do not take it, it will be of use a thousand miles away.

To the assembly, he said: "Striking the void produces sound—who is the one who understands? Striking wood produces no sound—it is but a vain labor to strain the ears. This is not a dharma of the present moment;
do not give rise to various thoughts. Arising and ceasing are mutually unknown; within this, there is neither front nor back. (The *xiang* [elephant]...)
Where the King travels, foxes and rabbits leave no tracks; when the moon appears in the water, the wind and clouds naturally differ.
Arriving here, heaven and earth cannot contain it; the universe does not know its name. A thousand sages stand downwind; who dares speak against its head?
O virtuous ones, whatever your former livelihoods and activities may have been—whether you understand them or not—sweep them all away at once. Do not...
Like one with a staff returning to the mountains, a long cry resounds as the mist deepens.

the ultimate truth cannot be realized through the persistence of 'I'; the supreme achievement cannot be produced through the cultivation of affairs. Ancient...

If you were to manifest yourself in wine shops and brothels, I would dwell alone upon a solitary peak. Now tell me, what [is the point]?
At this time, Huanglong was serving as the "Eye of Men.

Xia Yi Gong engaged in an animated discussion with the Master on the *Zhao Lun* (Treatise on Emptiness), arguing that all phenomena are one's own self and that sentient and insentient beings share a single essence.
At that moment, a dog was lying beneath the incense table; the Master picked up his ruler and struck the dog, then struck the incense table as well.
Zhuo said, "The dog has sentience and thus departs; the incense table lacks sentience and remains in its place.
How can sentience and insentience become one body? Gong was unable to provide an answer. The Master said, "As soon as you enter into deliberation, it becomes a superfluous dharma.
When have you ever realized that the myriad things are oneself?"
Chan Master Zhenjing Kewen of Baofeng in Hongzhou (18th in the lineage), a native of the Zheng family of Shanfu, spent the summer retreat at Dayue.
There, he heard a monk cite a saying of Yunmen: "The Buddha-dharma is like the moon in the water—is it so? Yunmen replied, "In the clear waves, there is no path through.
The Master attained sudden enlightenment and subsequently went to Jicui to see Chan Master Nan. Nan asked, "Where have you come from?"
Nanquan approached. The Master said, "Daoyi has come. Nanquan said, "It happens that the old monk is not here. The Master asked, "Where have you been?
Nanquan said, "I went to Tiantai for communal labor and to Nanyue to sightsee. The Master said, "If that is so, then the student has attained mastery.
Nanquan said, "As for the shoes on your feet, where did you get them? The Master said, "For seven hundred and fifty wen from Mount Lu."
Nanquan called out, “Master! Yunmen replied, “When have you ever attained mastery? Nanquan pointed to his sandals and said, “When have you ever not been masterful? Nanquan was struck with awe.

On the day the Master ascended the hall, the head monk struck the gavel and said, “O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast, you should contemplate the primary truth. The Master [then spoke].
He summoned the great assembly and said: "You must observe for yourselves. To observe in this way is called right observation; to observe otherwise is called wrong observation.

Before the distinction between the wrong and the right has been made, if you have doubts, please ask. A monk asked: "The successive patriarchs ascended the hall and worthy lords earnestly invited [the masters to speak].
Regarding the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage, we wish to hear you proclaim it. The Master said: "Six times six is thirty-six. The monk pressed further: "Constantly..."
"Recalling Jiangnan in the third month, where the partridges cry and the hundred flowers are fragrant. The Master said, "What a fine message!
The student stepped forward and said, "Today, Layman, having received this question, I withdraw three paces and prostrate to thank the Master for his grace. The Master said, "Profound."
The Master then said: "Let us cease this questioning for a moment. You know only to ask about the Buddha and the Dharma, yet you do not know the source from which the Buddha and Dharma come.
Tell me, from where do they come? He then lowered one foot and said: "In the past, Huanglong personally issued this command;
the Buddhas of the ten directions have dared not disobey it, and the ancestral masters of all generations, as well as all the sages and worthies, have dared not transgress it."
Regarding these immeasurable Dharma gates and all their wondrous meanings, the tongue of the World-Honored Elder (Lao Heshang) has been a single seal from beginning to end;
none dare to differ. Let us set aside for now the matter of there being no difference. Where does this seal reside? Do you see it?
If you see it, you are neither monk nor layman; without faction or partiality, it is bestowed in its entirety. If you do not see it, I shall take it back myself. Thus he spoke.
He withdrew his feet and gave a shout, saying: "The army follows the seal; the general pursues the talisman.
As for the old man with the Buddha-hand and donkey-feet—his karmic conditions are ripe—and yet you would give him thirty blows! Is there anyone here in this assembly who does not find this bitter?
If there is, it is truly extraordinary. If there is not, then I, the new elder, have deceived you all. Therefore, our Great Awakened World-Honored One..."

In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, on the eighth day of the twelfth month, when the morning star appeared, he suddenly awakened to the Way, and all sentient beings of the great earth attained Buddhahood at once.

Now, there is a śramaṇa named Ke-wen, a son of the Śākyas, who, in the city of Jinyang in the eastern land of Zhendan, on the thirteenth day of the sixth month, when the blazing sun appears—what else has he awakened to? By means of this...
[The Master] takes up the whisk. He makes a single stroke with it and says, "I do not dare to slight you;
you shall all become Buddhas. He ascends the hall. A monk asks, "What is the Buddha? The Master laughs loudly. The monk steps forward and says, "Why do you laugh?
The Master says, "I laugh because you produce interpretations based on words. [The monk] says, "I have merely happened to lose my advantage. The Master shouts and says, "Do not prostrate!"
The monks then returned to the assembly. The Master spoke again, saying, "To produce understanding based on words.
He then asked, "Is there anyone else who wishes to ask a question? After a long silence, he said, "For thirty years I have been riding a horse, yet I was thrown by a donkey.
He struck his knee and said, "It is enough to make Mount Sumeru tremble and the waters of the sea surge in waves, reaching as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
At one time he abdicated his throne; when the eighteen hells were exhausted, their bitterness ceased. Do you see this?
If you can see it here, Śākyamuni folds his hands in submission and Maitreya furrows his brow; Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra serve as his attendants. If you do not see it, however—
Behold me, leaping and bounding in every direction! For now, seek realization within the tangled vines.
A-he-he! All you venerable ones, tell me: what am I laughing at? Alas! I laugh at the "firefly light" and "mosquito-like understanding" of the ancients Yunmen, Linji, Deshan, and Yantou.
One said, "I revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs"; another said, "I have attained..."
Regarding the "Final Word": one person said, "Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma consists of nothing more than this.
Another said, "When the Great Awakened World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, saying, 'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
Had I seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow of my staff and fed him to a dog—this lot is merely empty boasting."
Han: In general, he alone was honored as supreme in an era where there was no Buddha.

If it were like the present day, we would summon them all at once and subject them to a thorough examination. As for the rest, they simply cannot be let off. Have you not heard? A monk asked Qianfeng:
