[The Master] takes up his staff, makes a single stroke, and says: "Right here! But as for Qianfeng’s saying this—have you ever even dreamed of it? If it were I, it would not be so.
'The Buddhas of the ten directions all enter the gate of Nirvana by one path. I wonder where the beginning of that path is?
[He] strikes him across the back with the staff and then asks him: "Where is the beginning of the path? He waits...

Just as he was about to open his mouth, [Yunmen] gave a hot shout and sent him out. Furthermore, there was that old, lame monk Yunmen, who could not distinguish between the black and the white, nor discern the heterodox from the orthodox.
He held up a fan and said: "The fan leaps and bounds; it ascends to the Thirty-three Heavens and strikes the nostrils of Śakra.
A carp of the Eastern Sea—give it a single blow and the rain pours down like an overturned basin. To act in such a manner is merely to mix mud.
Mixing water with excrement, pushing the head of a discarded rag—burying ten or five of these, what fault is there? Aha ha! Is it joyful or not? Is it sufficient or not?
Now, fortunately, we face green mountains and blue waters. In recent years, all matters have been set aside at once;
I let my body and mind be as they are, free from constraint. O assembly, do not nod off to sleep!
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things are one body with me.
From head to toe, they are arranged horizontally and vertically. When a fire breaks out in the continent of Uttarakuru, it burns the eyebrows of Śakra.
The Dragon King of the Eastern Sea cannot endure the pain and lets loose a thunderclap, shaking the mountains and overturning the seas, darkening the vast sky with clouds. [He drew] a cross.
The Street-Currier Huzi was startled awake from his drunken stupor; he rose, clapped his hands, and laughed heartily, saying, "In the city of Junyang, there have been few thieves lately.
Suddenly, he seized his staff and cried, "Thieves! Thieves!"
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddha-dharma requires no human sentiment. Elders from all quarters open their mouths wide and say, 'I understand Zen;
I understand the Way. But tell me, do they actually understand it? Without cause, they sit in a pit of excrement, deceiving the gods and terrifying the ghosts."
It is like someone who would rather kill hundreds of thousands of beings and give them to dogs to eat—what fault would there be in that?
Furthermore, there are certain practitioners of Zen who keep their eyes wide open, yet they are seduced by such fox-like deceptions without realizing it at all;
they are suddenly doused with excrement, yet they feel no revulsion. O Great Assembly, we are all men of spirit; how can we endure such things? We must act for ourselves!
"How is it? He addressed the assembly, saying: "A lion does not eat the remains left by a vulture; a swift falcon does not strike a dead hare.
Let loose the Great Dragon of Linji; withdraw Yunmen’s single glance. He then raised his staff and said: "Clouds move and rain falls; the three types of grass and two kinds of..."
Muzhou addressed the assembly, saying: "Under the gate of Dongshan, when one wishes to walk, one walks; when one wishes to sit, one sits.
To defecate in the alms bowl or spit into the water pitcher—such people who cling to the Dharma and practice it are like oxen pulling a millstone."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Under the gate of Dongshan, sometimes we blend mud and water; sometimes we stand like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.
If you people of all quarters intend to see Dongshan in the place where he blends mud and water, Dongshan is not to be found there.
If you intend to see Dongshan in the place where he stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, Dongshan is likewise not to be found there."
"Intent on reaching everywhere, you see Dongshan; yet Dongshan does not reside in any place at all.
If you intend not to see Dongshan, the nose-rope is still in Dongshan’s hand.

Even if you intend to nod off, he will pull the nose-rope once more, and you will see your own eye-sockets twitching, yet you will still not recognize him. I do not require you to recognize Dongshan; simply—"
It is also possible to recognize one’s own nature. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"Fenyang, do not engage in deluded thoughts! Jueyi, point your finger upright! The matters of the Buddhadharma throughout past and present—when they reach this point, they all come to rest at once.
Rest, rest! Yet I recall Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman; even in that which is not intentionally graceful, there is grace. (He then held up his whisk.)
Holding up his staff, he said, "Exerting one's utmost effort for the sake of the assembly.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "The two words 'Buddha-dharma' are truly difficult to encounter. There are those who do not believe in their own Buddha-work."
Relying solely on a small amount of the echoes and influences of the ancients, one encounters a semblance of prajñā, objects of knowledge, and dharma-gates of fixed characteristics.
As soon as there is movement, one turns one's back on awakening and joins with the dust; being stuck, one cannot escape. Or, when students come, it is like a seal impressing its mark upon clay.
Handing this down to one another in succession, they not only deceive themselves but also deceive others. Under the gate of Dongshan, there is no Buddha-dharma to give to people;
there is only a single sword. To anyone who comes before it, he cuts them off one by one, so that their very life-force has no place to remain.
When both seeing and hearing have vanished, turn back toward the time before your parents were born and meet him there. As soon as you see him coming forward, cut him off at once.
Now, although a steel blade may be sharp, it does not slay one who is innocent. Is there anyone who is innocent?
Even so, they deserve thirty blows of the staff.
Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised the following case: Three Sages asked Xuefeng, "The golden fish that has passed through the net—what do you take for food?

Xuefeng replied, "Wait until you have emerged from the net, and then I will tell you. The Sages said, "A teacher of fifteen hundred people, and yet you do not even recognize the point of the question!
The Master said, "How brilliant! How brilliant! How joyful! How joyful! It is just like a hawk."
"Do not be startled. Baoning said, "That is not so. As for the golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net—what do you take as its food?

Wait until it emerges from the net, and then I will tell you. [The Master] waited for him to say, "A man of knowledge who has guided fifteen hundred people," but he did not even recognize the pivot of the phrase.
[Baoning] simply pulled his staff and drove him out through the triple gate. He then said, "This is truly a source of joy; it is just like..."
"A tiger! Do not move! All you practitioners of Chan, tell me: which is more joyful, Baoning’s joy or Sansheng’s joy?
Is there anyone here who is truly joyful? Come forth and let us settle this! After a long silence, he gave a shout and said, "I take him by the hand, yet he cannot be pulled back."
Addressing the assembly, [Zhaozhou] raised the case: Xuefeng said, "On the South Mountain there is a crooked-nosed snake;
you all, when entering or leaving, must look well at it. The Master said, "Xuefeng lacks the bearing of a great man. Furthermore, a snake does not move without a head.
Changqing was just like a young bride who is afraid of her mother-in-law; thus he said, 'In the hall today, there is a great deal...'"
A person loses their body and forfeits their life. Yunmen picked up his staff, thrust it toward the man’s face, and made a gesture of fear;
this was like adding legs to a snake. Xuansha said, "What use is Mount Nanshan? To claim that one's realization is intimate and direct is still to remain within a nest;
there is not a single person who possesses even a trace of natural magnanimity. Under Baoning, is there anyone with such natural spirit?
As for your spirit and resolve: I dare not hope that you will separately suspend the sun of wisdom or alone shake the profound breeze.
For now, it is already difficult enough to gain even a whiff of the vital energy within the "hawk-stink" robe of the ancients.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Head-Dhuta Rock is enveloped in moss; the Peak of Thrown-Pens is entangled by brambles.
In the Arhat Hall, three novices are ordained each year; at Guizong Monastery, one drinks tea after the formal meditation session."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "This day has passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly. Like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be?

Only those of the Two Vehicles find joy in the stillness and extinction of meditative concentration; this is their true joy. For Bodhisattvas who study Prajñā, the joy of Dharma and the bliss of meditation are their joy;
this is their true joy. The Buddhas of the three periods of time take the four immeasurable minds—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—as [their joy]."
Bliss—this is true bliss. Shishuang Puhui said: "Rest! Cease! Go into a state of cold stillness!
This is called the bliss of the nirvana of the Two Vehicles. Yunmen said: "All-knowing and all-pervading without obstruction.
He raised his fan and said, "The Old Man Śākyamuni has arrived! This is called the bliss of Dharma-joy and Chan-delight. Deshan’s staff, Linji’s...
"Jie-he! This is the bliss of the compassion, joy, and equanimity of the Buddhas of the three periods.
Apart from these three kinds of bliss, there is no other bliss. Now tell me: does the assembly at Guizong reside within these three kinds, or outside them? After a long silence, he said:

"Today the master of the manor has prepared rice with sesame seeds and distributed money for funeral shrouds. When the formal session ends, everyone is invited to the Sangha Hall for tea. He gave a shout. One.
"Ho! The Master asked a monk, "Have you finished yet? The monk replied, "Not yet. The Master said, "Have you finished eating your congee yet? The monk replied, "Finished.
The Master said, "Then you say again that you have not finished. He then asked, "What sound is that outside the gate? The monk replied, "The sound of rain. The Master said, "Then you say again..."
[The Master] said, "It is finished. He then asked, "What is this right before you? [The monk] replied, "A screen. The Master said, "You say again that it is not finished.
He then asked, "Do you understand? [The monk] replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Listen to this verse: 'In accordance with conditions, every matter is finished;
In daily life, what is lacking? Everything is simply ordinary; Naturally, there is no inversion.'"
A monk asked, "This student has a lute that is not made of ordinary wood. Today I bring it forth; I beg the Master to play a single melody.
The Master said, "The assembly, lend your ears! You shall hear what you have never heard before. The monk asked, "What kind of fingering technique is this?
He raised his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The Master said, "Alas, alas! How very short your life will be! The monk said, "For now..."
Xihui withdrew from the discussion. The Master said, "You are not a connoisseur. Xihui said, "It would be better to go back; someone in the Onion Range (Congling) remembers me.
The Master said, "How can you forget the *jiaotong* lute? Xihui said, "It is right here. The Master said, "Put it down."
The Master has three verses on the Three Contemplations of the Dharma-realm and six verses [in total]. The first says: Form and emptiness are unimpeded; as one wishes, there is sovereign mastery.

The myriad phenomena are arrayed, their reflections appearing within and without. They emerge and subside, depart and arrive, across other realms and this world. The seal of the mind is vast and open, penetrating and expansive.
The second says: Principle and phenomena are unimpeded; as one wishes, there is sovereign mastery. One holds Mount Sumeru upside down, planting it firmly within a tiny mustard seed.
The pure *dharmakāya* is a perfectly round clod of earth; a single point is the mirror-lamp. Throughout the ocean-like assemblies of the ten directions—this is called the third:

the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*), sovereign as one wishes. Within the immovable site of enlightenment, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is rising in the east and sinking in the west;
amidst a thousand differences and myriad wonders, the cricket in the fire swallows the crab. This is called the fourth: the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena, sovereign as one wishes.
Holding a pig's head in his hands while reciting the pure precepts in his mouth, he drives it out of the brothel before even repaying his wine debt.
At the crossroads, he unties the sack; the fifth point is: all things are unimpeded, as one acts with sovereign ease. Picking up a single hair, the entire dharma-realm unfolds;
in a single thought, one enters infinite oceans of lands—all of which reside right before one’s eyes, appearing and disappearing at will. The sixth point is:
Ignorant of every single thing, who can comprehend emptiness and form? When both principle and phenomena have ceased, the iron boat descends into the sea.
Like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning—how distressing! Grasping the Mohe sword crosswise, the demons' hearts shatter.
Chan Master Shouzhi of Yungai in Tanzhou (fourth of four): A native of the Chen family of Longjin in Jianzhou. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"Tightly laced water-proof boots tread upon the moon over Lake Xiang; hand grasping iron caltrops, one breaks through the lair of dragons and tigers."
Turning over, he climbs up the tree; only then does he see that there is neither arising nor ceasing. He laughs at old Gautama, who snaps his fingers and claims to surpass Maitreya.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "Without leaving this very place, it is eternally serene; seek it and you will find it cannot be seen.
Although the ancient sages spoke thus, for now, fashion a mold and cast it away. If you cannot emerge from it, you will merely be clutching the past.
This is the level of ordinary people. Only if one can transcend this will there be even a slight degree of resonance with the truth. Yun-gai, however, was not like this:
"Riding a fine steed around Mount Sumeru, passing over mountains to seek the tracks of ants—how many people could possibly know this?"
Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised the following case: Zhaozhou asked a monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to pick tea. Zhaozhou said, "Idle. The Master said:
"To speak of it or not to speak of it—where can one search? A dragon’s scales behind; a donkey’s hoof before. A somersaulting tumbler;
a solitary cloud and a wild crane. A-he-he!"
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The single, firm, and dense body manifests within every atom of dust. Today, Yun’gai, the thousand mountains are lush and verdant;
birds and beasts cry out; the hundred flowers compete to bloom; and the myriad plants send forth their branches—all these are the Buddhas, each and every one True Suchness (Tathatā).
You people here, as you roam the mountains and play by the waters, must truly exert your eyes; do not be deceived by them."
Chan Master Baoben Yuan of Huzhou (sixth in the lineage). A native of the Ni clan of Chaozhou, he first visited Huanglong, who showed him the "Three Barriers" (Sanguan) kōans.

One day, while sitting on his meditation mat, he suddenly reached out his hand and turned it over repeatedly, saying, "I would rather speak according to principle than say that the Buddha’s hand knows my home.
Later, at Jieyang, he asked again, "Where is your place of origin? After a long time—
He immediately resolved their doubts, addressing the assembly by saying:
"The Great Dharma Drum is struck to expound the Great Dharma Meaning. Before the drum has even been struck, there is the Great Being Mañjuśrī."
Upon the eyebrows and eyelashes of all people, he appears and disappears, rolls up and unfolds, performing great Buddha-work.
When the Dharma drum is struck, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, moreover, turns the Great Wheel of Dharma upon the ears of all people. Do you hear it yet?
Even if you were able to see it and hear it, that would already be a failure to find the opportunity; if you truly do not know, that is simply as it is.
There are no branches or leaves; do not resent the spring sun. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"The white clouds disperse, and the red sun rises in the east. Look up at the heavens; look down at the earth.
East, west, south, and north—let one go freely to behold the sights. The eyes of Bodhidharma cannot be measured even by bushels. Yanluo, when did you ever recognize them?"
Ying. "Good Wealth does not go south. The nostrils of the patch-robed monk reach up to the heavens; when it comes to this, they are all pierced through at once. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"Prajñā is without knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know. How can one explain the principle of 'without knowing'?

If you say it means blocking off sight and hearing, how is this different from the nihilistic heretics? Or if you say it means forgetting knowledge and discarding illumination, then it is precisely..."
These are ordinary people who turn their backs on the objective realm. Do you all still understand? Old Śākyamuni spends his days by the lanterns and the pillars;

following "existence," there is existence; following "non-existence," there is non-existence. Although he does not immediately identify with existence or non-existence, he likewise does not depart from them.
Such talk as this leaves the Patriarchs at a loss; even clear-eyed monks must yield to his cold laughter. Now tell me: what is it that they laugh at?
"What is this? [The Master] gave a shout.
A monk asked, "Before leaving Tuṣita Heaven, he had already descended into the royal palace; before emerging from his mother’s womb, he had already finished saving sentient beings.
What is your intention today? The Master said, "Waiting by a stump for a rabbit is a waste of energy. [The monk] said, "If it were not for entering the water, how..."
He saw a tall man. The Master said, "Before you have even asked, there is still a slight margin.

A monk asked, "What is it like when black and white are not yet distinguished? The Master said, "The heavens are high and the earth is deep. [The monk] asked, "What is it like after they are distinguished?"
The Master said, "The sun is warm and the moon is cool. [The monk] asked, "If one goes forth in this very way, what then? The Master said, "Mount Sumeru stands upside down.
Chan Master Hongying of Baofeng in Hongzhou (the eighth of eight) was the son of the Chen family of Shaowu. Because he read the works of Li Zhangzhe...

Upon reading the *Daśaprajñā-śāstra*, he attained a sudden and profound awakening. While walking in meditation at night, he heard two monks discussing the karmic cause and condition regarding Huanglong’s "Buddha's hand and donkey's feet.
The Master was struck by this and went to question them: "Where does Master Nan currently reside? The monks replied, "At Huangbo in Junzhou.
At dawn, the Master went straight to Huangbo. Upon seeing him and engaging in conversation, Nan realized for himself that he was no match for him.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If one discusses this matter, it is truly difficult to deliberate upon. Why is this?
Furthermore, the heart-seal of the ancient Buddhas resembles the mechanism of an iron ox. Should you wish to advance toward it, you will lose your body and life;

should you retreat, it will crumble like a collapsing wall and vanish forever. Even if you neither advance nor retreat, it is still but a robe of red brocade—a stinking meat shirt clinging to the skin."

It clings to the body; it is difficult to break free from. O practitioners of Zen, even if you were to attain clarity here—remaining without revealing a single trace of sharp edge or sign—it would still be like a numinous tortoise dragging its tail or a rat gnawing at a dry skull. If you turn toward the gate of Kāśyapa, heaven and earth are as far apart.
But tell me, how do you speak that one phrase under Kāśyapa’s gate? After a long silence, he said: "The sea moon at night."
Coming to the Stone Grotto, the mountain clouds occasionally moisten his meditation robes.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The stone gate is treacherous and the iron barrier is firm; looking up, layer upon layer, it rises ten thousand fathoms high.
Only the hornless iron ox can break through it; within the ocean of Vairocana, waves and tides surge. "Tell me, Great Assembly: what is that which does not involve the waves and tides?"
[The Master] said, "How do you say it? After a long silence, he said, "A single phrase was not sufficient for Wuzhuo’s question; even now, he remains a monk of the wild fields.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "The ancient sages said: 'The river moon shines, the pine wind blows; throughout the eternal night and clear sky, what is there to do? Buddha..."
The nature-precepts are the pearl; the mind-ground is the seal. Mist, dew, clouds, and rosy mists are the garments upon one’s body.

O virtuous practitioners of Zen, although the Way is indeed as you have described, it might be called "spoiling the salt" or "spoiling the vinegar. If I, this mountain monk, were to speak of it, it would not be so: the river moon shines, the pine wind blows.
"What is there to do on this eternally clear night? A cowherd atop a ridge blows a single note on his flute; it startles a flock of crows, which fly up to circle the tree.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Patriarch said: 'The nature of all sentient beings is pure and clear; from the very beginning, it is unborn and cannot be extinguished.'"
"This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit. Great assembly, when the ancient sages spoke thus, it was indeed extraordinary.
Nevertheless, when examined from the standpoint of the monastic community, it is like the saying: "Eating too much harms the heart;
sitting too long aches the back."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "A-he-he! What is this? Last night, the moonlight shone as I sat alone.
Counting on my fingers from the beginning, I recall my old friend Pao-tso T’uo of yore. Pao-tso T’uo! What is he?
Before you can even raise your eyebrows, you have already missed him. He struck the meditation seat once.
Ascending the hall, a monk stepped forward. As he rose from his prostrations, he let down a corner of his *kāṣāya* and asked, "What is it like when one strips off the robes and discards the armor?

The Master said, "Fortunately, the smoke of war has subsided; the bow hangs suspended on the wall. The monk pulled up his *kāṣāya* and asked, "What is it like when one readies the robes and arms oneself for battle again?
The Master said, "Had you not reached the banks of the Wu River, I would have known you were unwilling to rest. The monk then [departed].
"Hai! The Master said, "This has startled me to death. The monk gave a clap. The Master said, "This too is finding life within death. The monk bowed.
The Master said, "I thought you were a talent capable of subduing Yan and defeating Zhao; it turns out you are merely a smuggler of salt."
A monk asked, "What is it like when one plays the game upon meeting the occasion? The Master said, "A cast-iron tortoise tossed out from a red furnace.
Chan Master Cigan of Nanyue Foyan (the second of two entries), a native of the Du family from Zizhou, addressed the assembly, saying:

"Before the Peak of Throwing the Alms Bowl, the spring breeze sweeps vast and wide; within the waters of the Xiang River, white waves roll on and on. This Dharma is impartial, manifesting itself clearly."
It moves and acts, yet it is so even though it is not so. Having encountered the pointing south, one does not meet [the truth].
One simply keeps the nostrils reaching to the heavens. Nanquan’s every head and limb provides instruction; Dadian remains silent and speechless. Vimalakīrti long kept his room open;
who would dare to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with him? *Pah!* (With the whisk, he strikes the meditation seat.)
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The mind of the ancient Buddhas is just as it is now. If you do not understand this, you will suffer in deep reflection.

The autumn rain falls lightly; the autumn wind whistles. Moving here and there, how can one respond? On the sandy banks, the reeds and flowers are intermingled in green and yellow. Upon what can the Chan practitioner rely?
After a long silence, he said: "Zha! (A sharp, decisive word).
Chan Master Hesheng of Huangbo in Junzhou (in two parts). A native of the Luo family in Zhongjiang, Zizhou. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"Luohan writes characters; Yangshan strikes the mallet; Heshan beats the drum; Qingping tramples the mud.

These four have consistently acted as their mother-in-law, unaware that they were leaking the true mechanism. Although they leaked the true mechanism, for the time being, later people did not know it. [Selected]
The Buddha must be such a heroic spirit; to overcome his adversaries, he returns as a lion’s cub. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"Silent and desolate—like the bright moon descending into the empty valley. Vast and expansive—like the blazing radiance of the sun flowing through the four seas.
On the road of Caoxi, the passage of men is utterly cut off; before the Many-Son Stupa, the crowds are as dense as throngs.
Marketplace! Even if you can recognize this point here—being bold and clear—it is still not the livelihood of a patch-robed monk.
A true great man must strike the shackles and break the chains within the dark prison; he must set fire to the ranks of hungry ghosts and seize their gruel.
Overthrowing the Tower of Maitreya, tearing down the Palace of the Empty King, uprooting the auspicious sprouts and rare grasses by their very roots—
let thorns and briars grow everywhere as they please.
Chan Master Yuanyou of Yunju in Hongzhou (the fifth of his lineage), a native of the Wang family from Shangrao in Xinzhou, addressed the assembly, saying:
A student of the Way must attain awakening and bring forth realization of the mind-ground.

If you awaken to the Lord of the Dharmakāya, then all the grasses and trees of the entire earth take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. If you awaken to the Teacher Vairocana, then the world of empty space takes refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
But tell me, what do you call the Lord of the Dharmakāya? What do you call the Teacher Vairocana? Do you wish to understand this directly? It is the eye.
Light radiates from within his eyes, manifesting auspicious signs; from within his ear-cavities, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel.

Addressing the assembly at the commencement of the summer retreat, he said: "Within the light of formlessness, there is a True Person of No Rank who appears and disappears throughout the three realms, revolves through the five paths, does not abandon the ten evil deeds, does not fall into the body of the five aggregates, does not relinquish the hindrance of afflictions, and does not realize [nirvana]."

The mind of nirvāṇa does not increase through the violation of prohibitions, nor does it show disrespect for those who uphold the precepts; it does not linger through winter, nor does it pass beyond summer.
Do you all know where it has gone? After a long silence, he said: "Within the ninety-day mirage, the fivefold Dharma-body is perfected."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Tathāgatas of the past have no further examination to conduct; the Bodhisattvas of the present cannot afford to let anything pass;
and those who study in the future must not deceive others by even a single point. Therefore, it is said in the scriptures:
'If one wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: everything is created solely by the mind. Nevertheless..."
It is so. For those beneath the gate of an Arhat, these very words are like gold dust falling into the eyes.
[The Master] addressed the assembly, citing a monk who asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.
The monk said, "Master, do not point to external objects to show people. Zhaozhou said, "I am not pointing to external objects to show you. The monk said, "If..."
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Governor said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. The Master remarked, "How extraordinary!
The ancient sage has bestowed a single word or half-sentence; it may truly be called cutting off the gates for both sages and ordinary folk, directly revealing the eye of Maitreya.

It has never faltered from past to present. Yet among the assembly, there are many divergent interpretations and numerous ways of deliberating upon it, which bury the fundamental principle and misjudge its name."
It is said: "The verdant green bamboo—all is True Suchness (tathatā); the lush yellow flowers—none are not Prajñā. Or it is said:
"Mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees—every single thing is the manifestation of the true mind; why should it be limited solely to the cypress tree in front of the courtyard?"
Dust, hair, tiles, and rubble are all but the single Dharma-realm, wherein phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused in infinite layers.
Some say that when the "cypress tree in the courtyard" is raised, one must directly realize it at once; for in the interval of deliberation, one has already fallen into the realm of Māra.
It requires the functioning of the person themselves to meet the situation as it arises—whether by staff, shout, or raising [the whisk].
A fist. A single sweep of the sleeve. This eye is like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning.
Some say, "The cypress tree in the courtyard—what else is there? Zhaozhou speaks directly for people, speaking with utter sincerity:
when hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps. Every movement and every action is entirely one's own enjoyment. Such is the vision.
[The Master] said: "They are like millet or hemp seeds; they all belong to the lineage of celestial Māras and the heterodox teachings of external paths.

They merely grasp at the discriminations of conscious thought, employing their minds to accept and reject, forcibly fabricating views and insights, and transmitting them through oral tradition to deceive and delude others.

Their sole aim is to seek fame and profit—what kind of karmic seed is this? It defiles the ancestral style. Why do you not travel far and wide to seek out a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and resolve [your doubts]?"
"Discerning that body and mind are roughly like those of a patch-robed monk—since ancient times, there have been masters of our school.

Our Buddha-mind lineage is such that Brahmā, Śakra, and the various devas join their hands in respectful faith, while the Three Sages and Ten Saints cannot fathom its source. He then raised his whisk and said:
"If you awaken here, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth will all participate in your realization. He then looked around to his left and right.
[The Master] said, "How would I dare degrade the worthy to the lowly?
A monk asked, "What is it like when a tortoise hides its six limbs? The Master said, "The patterns are already manifest. The monk said, "But how can one avoid leaving traces everywhere?
The Master said, "I leave you to it—dragging through mud and water as you please. The monk asked, "What is it like when one proceeds in this very way? The Master...

To follow [the Way] is to realize Bodhi; to oppose it is to produce affliction. The lantern always dozes off; the pillar is also vexed.
The Great Way is right before one's eyes—where else would you go to seek it? With his whisk, he struck the meditation seat.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "On all four sides there are no gates; throughout the ten directions there is no azure void. Hair disheveled, ears prominent—every one of you is a manly great being.
How can you be without ropes yet bind yourselves? Now tell me: what is the phrase that transcends and escapes?
After a long silence, he said: 'Treading through straw sandals, walking barefoot.'"
A monk asked, "I do not ask about Mount Sumeru containing a mustard seed; but as for the turning of the Great Dharma Wheel within a mote of dust—what is it like?
The Master said, "One step forward, another step forward. The monk said, "If that is so, then one arrives in India in the morning and returns to the land of Tang in the evening.

The Master said, "Being a guest is not as good as returning home. The monk said, "I have long admired your reputation for the Way's wind; I pray that you will grant me an audience. The Master said, "Clouds and moon."
They are the same, yet the valleys and mountains differ.

On the fishing boat, he reveals his family style. People of the time look only at the fishing line, Failing to see the reeds."
Regarding Liaohong, there was also someone who asked Fahua, "What is the pure Dharma-body? He replied to him simply, "The stench of excrement perfumes the heavens.
He also said, "A child born by transformation upon a lotus leaf. Tell me, is this the same as the ancients, or is it different? Fahua also had a verse which says:
"The stench of excrement perfuming the heavens is also merely coincidental; how would Fahua dare [to claim otherwise]?"
For Your Majesty’s Proclamation: If there were a celestial aperture within the nose, one could travel crosswise at will without being pierced.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "Sometimes the tip of the pestle blooms with flowers; sometimes the Buddha's face is covered in a hundred uglinesses.
When Master Li falls drunk on the street, it is simply because Master Zhang is drinking wine. The lantern has its brows knit in frowns; the pillar claps its hands with a hearty laugh."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "For those who have not yet penetrated [the truth], you must cause them to recognize it; for those who have already penetrated it, you must walk together with them.
The entire earth is the single eye of a śramaṇa—whom would you have recognize it? On the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is admitted—where would one walk?
Therefore it is said: 'Where others dwell, I do not dwell; where others walk, I do not walk.'"
It is not that it is difficult to dwell together with others; rather, it is that the distinction between the ordained and the laity must be clearly defined.

One should subtract a little from where there is too little, and add a little to where there is too much. Why? Because one would further subtract from what is already scarce and further add to what is already abundant. This is a secret talisman of the immortals, not transmitted even between father and son.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If you can truly manage to break into a sweat once, then upon a single blade of grass you will manifest a palace of jade and crystal.

If you cannot truly manage to break into a sweat once, then even if there were palaces of jade and crystal, they would be covered over by a single blade of grass. How do you get yourself to sweat? Here is a pair of poor hands."
"I have never easily performed the Three-Platform Dance.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "When the ancients left behind a single word or half a phrase, those who have not yet penetrated it are as if they have run into an iron wall."
One day, suddenly seeing through it, one finally realizes that one's own self is an iron wall. Now, how will you penetrate it?
After a long silence, he said: "An iron wall, an iron wall."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "It is clearly known that it is simply this very thing. Why, then, can one not penetrate it?
It is merely because when one sees a person open their mouth, one immediately calls it 'words and phrases'; and when one sees a person close their mouth, one immediately calls it 'a long silence.
Furthermore, it is said that in every movement, every action, every opening of speech, and every breath, throughout the entirety of the ten directions of the world, there is nothing that is not it."
This is precisely why one falls into the middle way. Secretly harboring old resentments, one still has not yet seen Yunmen’s teaching:

“Upon hearing the sound, one awakens to the Way; upon seeing form, one clarifies the mind. He raised his hand and said, “Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,” then with his hand lowered, added, “Buying sesame cakes with money;
when the hand is lowered, it turns out they are actually steamed buns. Have you not seen? When this mountain monk resided at Fahua, he said: “There is none.”
Chan Master Jie said: "If even a single hair-tip of ordinary or holy thoughts has not been exhausted, one cannot avoid entering the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse.
Even if every last hair-tip of ordinary or holy thoughts were suddenly exhausted, one still could not avoid entering the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse.
You blind fellows! Just investigate in this way."
A monk asked, "At the place where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly avoid speaking. What is it like when one speaks? The Master said, "Blown by the wind and scorched by the sun.
The monk said, "In that case, there is nowhere left to take a stand. The Master said, "Pounded by the pestle and ground by the millstone.

The monk said, "The official allows no needle, yet the private man passes carts and horses. The Master said, "Worthy of high price, worthy of low price. The monk snapped his fingers once. The Master said, "Just so."
The monk stuck out his tongue. The Master said, "Poverty at home is still tolerable; poverty on the road is what kills one with grief.
The monk laughed heartily. The Master said, "I let you off by one move."
A monk asked, "How is it when one has not yet passed through the Dragon Gate? The Master said, "This is not the right tune. The monk asked, "And how is it after passing through?
The Master said, "This is not the right tune. As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "Buying and selling at an improper price."
Chan Master Renyong of Baoning in Jiankang Prefecture (14th in the series). A native of the Zhu family of Mingzhou, he studied the Tiantai teachings in his youth.
Later, changing his robes [to those of a monk], he went to visit Chan Master Xuedou Xian. Xuedou gazed at him intently and rebuked him, saying: "Disaster-bringing Preceptor!"
The Master felt a sense of indignation and, driven by his resolve, descended the mountain. Gazing toward Mount Xuedou, he spread out his meditation mat and performed three prostrations, vowing:
"If in this life my practice of traveling to study Chan does not equal that of Xuedou, I shall never return home. He then went to visit Yangqi, where he realized the nature of his own mind.
After Yangqi passed away, he followed the fellow practitioner Chan Master Shouduan, delving into and mastering the most profound and subtle mysteries.
Later, he appeared in the world and dwelt at both Baoning and Zhonglao.

Addressing the assembly, he said: "The true mandate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs causes both ordinary beings and sages to be forgotten. Where wit and intelligence are difficult to discern, mind and object are both severed.
Therefore, when the Buddhas and Patriarchs arrive here, they all lose their sharpness and remain tongue-tied. Even if there were a single word or half a phrase, it would all be..."
To draw legs on a snake is a talk that falls into the weeds, an explanation that goes beyond the mark. Within the reality of the ultimate truth (*bhūtakoṭi*), such things do not exist at all.
Why is this so? It is because you must cause people to turn their heads and take a sidelong glance; not to pursue words, but to return to the root and restore the source;
not to enter byway of divergent paths, but to trample through the illusory city (*parikalpita-nagara*) and sever both extremes, thereby returning home.
Sit steadily. Why do you not realize it when the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world? Realize it when the Patriarchs had not yet arrived.
Realize it before your parents were born. Now, at the very moment before your parents were born, tell me:
what is the appearance of your own original life-spirit (*mūla-prāṇa*)? Do you understand? After a long silence, he said: "The ancient round mirror."
There is not even a trace of obscuration. Please try turning your head and looking once. He addressed the assembly, saying:

"Night after night one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning one rises together with him. Rising and sitting, we are always in each other's company; speaking and remaining silent, we dwell together.
Not separated by so much as a hair’s breadth, they are like a body and its shadow. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this."
[The questioner] said, "It is the sound of speech. The Master said, "Regarding this one verse by the Great Master Fu (Fotuo Dashi), it has not fallen into decline throughout the ages.
Many people have had a sudden flash of realization upon encountering it, yet few have avoided misunderstanding it.
Xuansha said, 'Big or small, Fotuo Dashi recognized only that which is bright and alert. Master Cong of Dongshan said, 'Tell me, what about the monk? "
"Did you ever sleep during the day? These two venerable masters each offered a turning phrase: "Who says there are no immortals in this world?
One must believe there is another heaven within the alchemical elixir jar. Baoning also has a verse: "When one wishes to sleep, one sleeps;
when one wishes to rise, one rises. Washing the face, the skin glows; sipping tea, the beak is moistened. The great ocean gives birth to red dust; the plains..."
The waves of the earth arise. He-he, a-he-he. Ra-li-li ra-li. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"That which belonged to the ancients is used by those of today; that which belongs to those of today was practiced by the ancients. Between ancient and modern, there is no front or back."
How many people, ancient or modern, know this? *Yemuyi*. Nine and twenty-nine; when they meet, they do not take a hand.
To the assembly: I cite Zhande, who said: "Those who enter through the gate of Mañjuśrī, for them walls, bricks, and rubble shall trigger their awakening.
Those who enter through the gate of Avalokiteśvara, for them frogs and earthworms shall trigger their awakening. Those who enter through the gate of Samantabhadra, they need not move a step."
"Pervading the ten directions—O Great Assembly! East, west, south, north, the four quarters, and above and below—it strikes and bumps against everything, yet one is neither aware nor cognizant of it.
Where does the fault lie? After a long silence, he said: "A beautiful woman is easy to adorn with rouge and powder; but without money, it is difficult to make a fine gentleman."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The wind whistles through the branches; the rain breaks up the clods of earth. At dawn, upon the pillow, the oriole’s song shatters the stillness.
Frogs and earthworms all cry out at once. Miaode and Śāriputra neither understand.
Neither understanding, three form a cluster and four make a troupe—lovely and graceful, light and airy—they head north, south, east, and west, gathering blossoms from the pear and plum trees."
"One pendant, two pendants.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Old Śākyamuni preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, yet never uttered a single word.
Upagupta filled his chamber with tally-sticks, yet never ordained a single person. Bodhidharma did not dwell in Shaoshi [Cave], yet..."
If the Patriarch had not dwelt at Caoxi, who would have been the descendant, and who would have been the one first awakened? Since it is thus, he himself has no wound;
do not inflict injury upon him. Striking his knee and looking at the assembly, he said: "How joyful it is that all under heaven is at peace!"
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Great Square has no exterior; the Great Circle has no interior. With neither interior nor exterior, saints and ordinary beings meet universally.
Even tiles and pebbles emit light, and Mount Sumeru is pulverized. The immeasurable Dharma gates and hundreds of thousands of samādhis—" He raised his staff and said:
All is gathered here. Do you understand? *Suru suru, siri siri, svāhā*. He addressed the assembly, saying: "The true form is formless;
yet by manifesting forms, it reveals its characteristics. A thousand wonders and ten thousand transformations are made manifest from this.
When joyful, light radiates across the face; when angry, the two eyebrows suddenly bristle. It is neither ordinary nor holy; it may be right or wrong. Man—"
It is immeasurable; even the heavens cannot fathom it. To grasp it directly is not yet to be called a true man. If you do not turn your head when called, do not mistakenly resent me.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Xu You washing his ears was merely a display of refined aloofness; Chao Fu feeding his oxen was but a vain boast."
Regarding matters of spirit and intent: when Grand Duke Tai lowered his hook, he still harbored a purpose; when Fan Li sailed upon the lake, how could he have truly left no trace?

Even if one were to achieve such perfect harmony between sovereign and minister that the seas are calm and the rivers clear, the wind does not rustle the branches, and the rain does not break the clods of earth—how can these compare to the wildflowers blooming everywhere in the third month, or the yellow leaves filling the void as they fly in the ninth autumn? It is better to sing wildly before the azure caverns.
He was deeply intoxicated within the jade pitcher. Clapping his hands and laughing loudly, he said: "Do you know?
Yesterday was late autumn, cold with frost; this morning is early winter, gradually growing colder."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Śākyamuni shut his room in Magadha, yet he already leaked the celestial mechanism. Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī, yet he spoke at great length.
Bodhidharma faced the wall for nine years at Shaolin; in his old age, he did not let his mind rest. Yongjia stayed only one night at Caoxi, yet he vainly boasts of his own brilliance and talent.
He then called to the assembly, saying: "Now, as Baoning speaks thus, is there any fault in it?"
[The Master] said, "There is none. He added, "When meeting a swordsman on the road, one must present a sword; if one is not a poet, one does not offer a poem. The Master ascended the seat.
A monk prostrated and, rising, made a gesture with his hand toward his breast as if taking an object to present it. The Master looked to the left. The monk stood up and made a gesture of offering.
The Master looked to the right. The monk extended his hand, made a gesture of receiving an object, and placed it back in his breast.
Regarding "Internal Power": The Master pointed straight down with his hand. The monk hesitated. The Master said, "There is only this;
there is no 'that'. The monk made a sweeping gesture with his hand. The Master said, "As expected. The monk returned to the assembly, and the Master laughed heartily.
Another monk stepped forward, prostrated, and rose. He drew a circle in the air. The Master tossed it backward with his left hand.
The monk drew another circle. The Master tossed it backward with his right hand. The monk returned to the assembly, and the Master said, "What else is there?"
The monk remained silent. The Master struck his knee and said, "A dragon’s head with a snake’s tail. The monk said, "Drawing the bow after the thief has fled.
The Master then sighed repeatedly. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Baoning? The Master said, "The main peak stands upside down. [The monk] asked, "What is the realm?"

[The monk] was an ordinary person. The Master said, "Your nostrils are missing half. [The monk] asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "In the boiling cauldron, there is no place that is cold."

Chan Master Daopei Muze of Tanzhou, Dharma heir of Chan Master Zhenke of Cuiyan in Hongzhou (the ninth [in this lineage]), was the son of the Wen family of Wenchuan in Fuzhou. He addressed the assembly, saying:
The moon arises as one: the vast expanse of the great earth—who would suffer humiliation? The moon arises as two: east, west, south, and north—there is no trace to be found.
The moon arises as three: Sudhana specifically heads south to seek instruction. Therefore it is said: "When letting go, the Tathāgata radiates light."
"Seizing it, the silt and sand hide the radiance. Now tell me: is this letting go, or is this seizing? After a long silence, he said:
"The three dots of the character *yī* are complete; all things are naturally fresh and new."
Addressing the assembly, he said: "Alala! What is this? Reflecting back on when Puo-zao-duo was struck by my staff, I only then realized that I had betrayed him.
With his staff, he struck the incense altar once and said: "Duō! Duō! (Fallen! Fallen!)
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Way of the Ancient Buddhas: In the past at Vārāṇasī, they turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths—falling into pits and over precipices.
Now, once again, they turn the most wondrous, unsurpassed Great Dharma-Wheel—adding mud upon the earth.
Is there anyone present now who, without traversing the steps, transcends alone beyond the mundane world? After a long silence, he said: "Look out beyond the heavens; who is this one?"
Zhongren addressed the assembly, saying: "To feel for echoes in empty space is merely to weary your spirit. Once the dream is awakened and its unreality realized, what further matter remains?
The old man Deshan dwells upon the eyebrows and eyelashes of you all; do you perceive him yet? If you do perceive him..."
Go! To dream and then awaken is to realize it was not real. If you have not yet awakened, you are merely clutching at empty space and chasing echoes; there will never be an end to this.

Even if you were to attain a state of bold clarity here, it would still be like climbing a mountain to present tribute to the court. Is there anyone who transcends alone beyond the boundaries of the mundane world?
After a long silence, he said: "For now, do not pretend to be clever.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The white clouds are limpid; the waters flow into the vast ocean. All dharmas are fundamentally at rest—what further matter is there?
Therefore it is said: there is the provisional and there is the real; there is illumination and there is function. When people reach this point..."
"What is it that one treads upon? After a long silence, he said: "Wherever there is a path to ascend, even those higher than men shall walk it.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "At the hour of the rising sun (the卯 hour), when putting it into use, there is no need to employ clever artifice. Raising his staff, he said:
"The staff leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, startling Śakra Devānām Indra, who then recites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* for all."
The purity of wisdom and wisdom itself are non-dual and indivisible; they are without distinction and without interruption.

Now tell me: what is the true meaning? After a long silence, he said: "Where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly refrain from speaking. He struck the meditation staff and descended from his seat.
Addressing the assembly, he raised his staff and said, "When a single speck of dust arises, the entire earth is fully contained within it.
He struck the ground once and said, "The World of Wondrous Joy shatters into a hundred fragments. Now tell me, where is the Tathāgata Immovable One right now?
If anyone can recognize this, they may be said to have ascended to wondrous enlightenment without moving a step. If you do not yet recognize it, look toward the eyebrows of all of you.
"Within the eyelashes, one goes to Nirvana. He struck once more and addressed the assembly.

Holding up his staff, he said, "This staff of Zhizhai sometimes acts as the Vajra King’s precious sword, sometimes as a crouching lion, sometimes as a probing pole or a blade of grass, and sometimes it does not function as a staff at all. Do you all still recognize it?"

Do you understand thoroughly? If you do understand thoroughly, you will be like a dragon obtaining water or a tiger relying on a mountain—appearing and disappearing, rolling up and unfolding, applying yourself with mastery in every direction.
If you have not yet understood thoroughly, it is very much like trying to escape one's shadow at midday.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of Zhaozhou’s 'Courtyard Cypress'? The Master said, "Last night the wind grew fierce; the solitary traveler was already cold.
The monk said, "The former master did not say those words. What then? The Master said, "Only when one travels does one know suffering.
The monk said, "Ten years wandering through the red dust; today, alone, he reveals his true body. The Master said, "Adding frost to snow."
Question: “What is the Buddha within the city? The Master said: “In a crowd of ten thousand people, one does not set up a signpost.
Question: “What is the Buddha in the village? The Master said: “A pig in mud and a dog with scabies. Question: “What is the Buddha in the mountains? The Master said:
“Cut off from the coming and going of men. Question: “What is the single phrase of the separate transmission outside the teachings? The Master said: “It cannot be translated.”
Question: "The Great All-Knowing One, the Victorious Buddha, sat at the site of enlightenment for ten eons; why was he unable to attain the Way of Buddhahood?
The Master said, "It would kill me with grief."
Question: "How was it before Niutou had seen the Fourth Patriarch? The Master said: "The hairs on his body stood on end. Question: "How was it after he saw him?
The Master said: "Sweat broke out on his forehead."

Chan Master Qixiao of Chongshou Monastery in Guizhou, Dharma Heir of Chan Master Wenyue of Yunfeng in Tanzhou (Third Series), addressed the assembly, saying: "If you do not realize the Way upon seeing it with your own eyes, you are still somewhat off the mark.
To move your feet while asking about the path is to utter false words and phrases. O virtuous ones, today this mountain monk shall take what is wrong..."
"You have made a mistake. You all see that there are eyes, hear that there are ears, smell that there are noses, and taste that there are tongues;

for what reason, then, do you fail to understand? After a long silence, he said: "Emperor Wu sought immortals but could not find them; Wang Qiao sat upright and ascended to heaven. *Du!* (A shout of rebuke.)
A monk asked, "The great assembly has gathered like clouds; what should we discuss? The Master said, "A Persian enters a bustling marketplace.
The monk said, "In that case, it is as when grass bows and wind blows. The Master said, "From ten thousand li away, one gazes toward the home country."
Question: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "Dressing and eating. [The student] said: "Stepping back three paces and placing my hands together at my chest [to depart].
The Master said: "Adding a cup after one is already drunk."
Chan Master Huanglong Wuxin of Hongzhou, the fourteenth-generation successor in the lineage descending from Mount Heng and heir to Chan Master Huanglong Zuixin of Hongzhou (eleven cases total).
He was a native of the Wang family in Qujiang, Shaoyang Prefecture. Initially, he visited Zuixin.
The Chan Master’s eloquence was unimpeded. Xitang said, "If this is all your skill, it is like describing food;
how can it satisfy one's hunger? The Master was cornered and had no further response. He spoke with composure, saying, "I have already broken my bow and exhausted my arrows.
I pray that the Master will, out of compassion, point out a place of peace and happiness. Xitang said, "A single speck of dust flies up and obscures the sky; a single mustard seed falls..."
It covers the ground; it is a place of peace and bliss. One must truly fear the many antiquities of the senior monks (*upādhyāya*).

Only when one has died away the entire mind accumulated over immeasurable eons can one succeed. The Master stepped out. One day, while sitting in silence after descending from his seat, he heard the sound of a staff as the administrative official (*karmadāna*) was beating a novice.
Upon hearing the sound of the staff, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He sprang up, forgetting to put on his sandals, and rushed to the Abbot’s quarters to see Huixin. Thereupon—
He said to himself: "All people under heaven are those who have merely learned; Wuxin is one who has awakened. He thought:
"To be ranked as a top graduate in the selection for Buddhahood—how could such a thing be possible?"
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddhas of the past, manifesting kindness and exercising compassion—this is adding a head atop one's own head.
The Buddhas of the present, arrayed in their ranks and positions—this is like cutting off one's head and seeking to stay alive.

The Buddhas of the future, distinguishing the provisional to reveal the real—these too deserve thirty blows of the staff. But tell me, where does the fault lie? After a long silence, he said: "If you wish not to invite [retribution]..."
Regarding intermediate karma: do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
He said to the assembly: "To drill into solid rock is difficult to accomplish; to crush withered wood is easy to exert force upon. That which is easy to exert force upon yields no firm retribution;
that which is difficult to accomplish results in a certainty of fruition. This 'not firm' and 'certainty' are still within the realm of arising and ceasing. Furthermore—"
The Way does not fall into arising and ceasing—how do you express this? "Since childhood I have observed the fast until now I am old;
seeing others, I lack the strength to descend from my meditation seat."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "When a pure pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot but become clear.

When mindfulness of the Buddha is directed toward a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot but become the Buddha. Since the Buddha is not distracted, the turbid water naturally clears. Now that the turbid water has cleared, to whom does the merit belong?
After a long silence, he said: "How many times have black winds overturned the great ocean? Yet never have we heard of a fishing boat capsizing."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Outside the mind there is no dharma, yet dharmas can be clarified. Outside dharmas there is no mind, yet the mind can be penetrated.

When it can be penetrated and can be clarified, mind and dharma constitute the complete school. When the school is complete, every dharma is the school. When the mind is complete, every mind is no-mind.
Since the mind is no-mind, one directly reaches the source; thus, manifesting a great body, one fills the void of space."
He manifests a small body, yet not even a speck of dust can be established. What is this "not even a speck of dust can be established"? After a long silence, he said:
"A single drop of ink forms two dragons."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Mind-Doctrine of Bodhidharma has been transmitted to this day without a single drop leaking away and without shifting by so much as a hair’s breadth.
Since it has not shifted by a hair’s breadth, how was it transmitted? The Precious Seal is wondrous when facing the wind; layer upon layer, the seams of brocade open."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Ordinary people are not sages; sages are not ordinary people. Ordinary people are themselves sages; sages are themselves ordinary people.
When one reaches the point where the conceptualizations of sagehood and ordinariness are exhausted, one must know that there is a path for turning back."

If you can transform and attain it, you will not drown when entering water, nor be burned when entering fire. If you cannot transform and attain it, there shall be cold and heat that shorten your lifespan, and there shall be ghosts and spirits that envy your blessings.
Rising from illness, he addressed the assembly. Holding up his whisk, he said: "Look, look! When the whisk is ill, the mind of death is ill;
when the whisk is at ease, the mind of death is at ease. The whisk passes through the mind of death; the mind of death passes through the whisk.
At such a time, if you call it the whisk, it is again the mind of death; if you call it the mind of death, it is again the whisk. In the end, what would you call it?"
After a long silence, he said: "Do not bring right and wrong to judge me; the fabrications of this floating life do not concern me.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Where it cannot be spoken, how can it be raised? Where it cannot be raised, how can it be understood?
Where it cannot be understood, how can it be clarified? If you can clarify it, then the three barriers are a single arrow, and the single arrow is the three barriers."
"Not yet clear. For now, how would you resolve this? After a long silence, he said: "In the summer months, bare-chested; in the winter months, covered by a quilt while sleeping."
A monk asked, "The vast and mysterious Great Way, the true teaching of non-attachment—since it does not involve verbal explanation, I pray that the Master will speak quickly.

The Master said, "The grass is deep, and wild deer abound. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The cliffs are high, and the *xièzhài* (unicorn-like creatures) are rare. The monk bowed.
The Master said, "Do not touch it; if you touch it, I will break your back.
A monk asked, "What are the four great poisonous snakes? The Master said, "Earth, water, fire, and wind. The monk asked, "What are earth, fire, water, and wind?
The Master said, "The four great poisonous snakes. The monk said, "I do not yet understand; I beg the Master for a skillful means. The Master said:
If one great element is thus, the four great elements are the same.
Zhengyan asked: "I have heard that birth occurs through the conjunction of three conditions, and I have also heard that one dies and is immediately reborn.

For what reason is there such a thing as being 'snatched from a womb' to be born? I am greatly perplexed by this. The Master said: "It is like when you, Zhengyan, served as the Commissioner of Transport (Zaoshi)."

Wherever he stayed, he would immediately take up that position. [The King] asked again, "Are you not suspicious? The King said, "I am not suspicious. The Master said, "Then why do you still have doubts?
This was precisely to lead him to understanding beneath the words.
Chan Master Huanglong Weiqing of Hongzhou (fourth in the lineage), a native of the Chen family from Wuning in his home prefecture, attained the seal of mind under Huaitang.

He often said to people: "Among those who study the Way today, none have yet escaped birth and death. Where does their sickness lie? It lies in the fact that their 'stealing mind' has not yet died out.
Yet this is not their fault; it is the fault of the teachers. It is like the Han Emperor Gaozu, who deceived [his subordinates]..."
Han Xin killed him. Although it is said that Xin died, was his mind truly dead? As for the students of antiquity who claimed to transcend birth and death beneath a word, where was the proof?
It lay in the fact that their "thieving mind" had already perished; yet this was not something the students could achieve on their own.
A true teacher is one whose hammer and tongs are subtle and precise. It was like Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty:

when he beheld Hou Jing from the great hall, he did not move a muscle or change his expression, yet the heart of Jing was already withered and drained of all vitality. What is taught by various schools is not without its beauty;
however, it is like the flowers painted by Zhao Chang—the flowers are so lifelike they seem real, yet they are not actual flowers.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know that there is [this reality]; thus, their kindness remains unrequited. The cat and the white ox, however, do know that there is;
thus, their merit is not bestowed in vain. When the great function is revealed and the total mechanism is understood, one's traces are inconceivable.
It is best to go back when no one knows. One breaks through the azure void where pines rise a thousand feet; one cuts off the red dust of the world with a single stream of water."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to all under heaven. The total capacity can both release and gather. The golden ripples' shadows fall within a thousand rivers;
the jade dew hangs like beads upon the tips of a hundred grasses. Without a trace, yet there is a source. The Dharma-body is truly a bustling hubbub.
Since it is the Dharma-body, tell me, what is it that bustles? After a long silence, he said: "From the beginning, it has never fallen."
The profound purport within the mystery: why speak today of its turning being obscure? Addressing the assembly, he said:
"As soon as the drum sounds, the great multitude gathers like clouds; infinite celestial mechanisms are all at once revealed.

Chan Master Shanqing of Baofeng in Hongzhou (in all, eight [cases]). He was the son of the He family of Baochang in Nanxiong. Initially, he visited Chan Master Daopei Zhe of Daguangming Temple at Dayun Monastery on Mount Mian;

all its faculties are directed toward the prey; from head to tail it is straight as an arrow; there is nothing it does not hit when it intends to strike. If you can truly be like this..."
With no other objects in the mind, the six sense-faculties naturally became still. In silent contemplation, he investigated until not one thing was lost among the myriad phenomena.
From that time on, the Master withdrew from all distracting conditions. After more than a year, he attained sudden and clear enlightenment. He expressed this to his own mind in verse:

"Following, following, following; From of old, from of old, from of old. Following, following, following—no one recognizes what follows. Last night the bright moon ascended the high peak; It has always been just this."
“This is a thief. Xuefeng nodded his head in understanding. He further told him: “To attain the Way is not difficult; to propagate the Way is difficult.

Generally speaking, when a master preaches the Dharma, a single phrase contains the three mysteries, and each mystery contains the three essentials. Your entry into this path is authentic; you have attained the seat.”
He donned his robes and looked back at himself; naturally, he went forth with unimpeded mastery in every direction.

He remained in attendance upon his teacher for another seven years, after which he took leave to travel extensively through the monastic communities. Later, he emerged as the abbot of Huanglong and passed away at Letan.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddhas appear in the world with many skillful means; the Patriarchs came from the West to establish no reliance on words and letters.
There is nothing to be attained, yet they transmit that which cannot be transmitted. It is solely this One Mind, with no other dharma.

Even if there were the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, these are all merely administering remedies according to the illness. Illnesses vary in a thousand ways, so medicines arise in ten thousand kinds. Nevertheless, though there are many..."

Various skillful means, various expressions, and various parables were employed to accommodate those of middling and inferior capacities—like using yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying—and possess no ultimate reality.

If one possesses superior faculties and superior wisdom, hearing this once brings a thousand awakenings; one attains the Great Dharani without relying on verbal explanations, for how could there be room for intellectual understanding?
One simply realizes the Way directly. If one can have such faith and understanding, and practice in such a manner...
To realize such an awakening and enter [this state] may be called being a great man; one thereby accomplishes the deeds of a great man.
Being able to accomplish the deeds of a great man, one is then able to clearly comprehend the birth and death before one’s eyes—whether they exist or do not exist, whether they are real or illusory.

Once one can thoroughly discern the reality and delusion of birth and death, and turn back to observe all phenomena within both the mundane and supramundane realms, they are seen to be entirely like dreams and illusions.
As the ancients said: "An illusory person preaches the Dharma; an illusory person listens. From the beginning, these two have been entirely without sentience.

When preaching, there is no preaching—let it be preached as you will. When listening, there is no listening—leave it to be heard as it may. Since there is no listening when one listens, [there is likewise no preaching when one preaches].
Furthermore, there is no speaking; where there is no speaking, there is no hearing. This is called "one principle and two meanings.

If one attains clarity regarding this, then whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is nothing that is not the manifestation of the Great Matter. Whether looking up, looking down, bending, or turning, there is nothing further to be added.
If one has not yet attained clarity regarding this, then even if the winds and waves of the Five Lakes are stilled, it is all in vain while the sun shines beyond the heavens.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Form and mind are not two; self and other are without distinction. Raising up his whisk, he said:
"If you call this a whisk, you enter hell as fast as an arrow. If you do not call it a whisk, you have eyes but are like the blind.
Even if you manage to transcend both extremes, it is still like a black ox lying in stagnant water."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The mind has no self-nature; it manifests entirely through phenomena. Phenomena have no self-substance;
they appear entirely through the mind. Raising his whisk, he said: "The whisk manifests its entire body and transforms into a Celestial Great General.
He patrols the four continents, reporting at once to Śakra, Lord of Devas, all those who possess the Way and those who do not, those who maintain their integrity and those who do not."
Now he has returned to Huanglong’s hands. You all must not call this "is," nor must you call it "is not.
But tell me: what would you call it? Three heads and six arms, supporting heaven and earth; the wrathful Nātha smashes the celestial bell.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Śākyamuni has already passed away; Maitreya has not yet been born. It is precisely this very day:
to whom is the Buddha-dharma entrusted? Raising his whisk, he said: "Look! Look! To those who are good, the whisk responds with goodness; to those who are evil—"

How does the whisk respond? Good and evil are both forgotten. How does the whisk respond? Though a calendar from a thousand years ago may be of no use, if one offends, it must cause the entire clan to be extinguished.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The profound waters are without waves; bubbles are stirred up by the wind. When the wind ceases, the bubbles vanish; when the water is still, it reflects the void.

At this very moment, even if there were gold from Yan to fill the seas and mountain crickets to shake the peaks, and crimson-tailed golden-scaled fish swimming at ease—now, is there anyone who can distinguish between floating and sinking, or recognize the depth of the water, to cast their line and let down their hook? If there is such a person,"
"Come out and meet me. When [the monk] did not come, the Master said, "If there is no one, then return to the crag for now;
let us look at the full moon together later. A monk asked, "How was it before Niu-tou saw the Fourth Patriarch? The Master said, "Three in the capital, four in Bianzhou.
The monk asked, "How was it after he saw him? The Master said, "Ash on the head, dust on the face. The monk asked, "What is it ultimately? The Master said, "A single scene of *māra*."
A monk asked, "What is the living word? The Master said, "Attained within death. The monk asked, "What is the dead word? The Master said, "Attained within life.
The monk asked, "What is the word that is neither dead nor alive? The Master said, "Jing three, Bian four."
Chan Master Huanglong Zhiming of Ezhou (the fifth in the series) addressed the assembly, saying: "The single secret of the North and South cuts through nails and severs iron.

One day, as the Master ascended the hall, just as the assembly had gathered, he said, "We must not continue to open our eyes and speak of dreams. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"The one path that points upward is beyond the reach of even the most diligent monk. To seek the subtle or the profound is like the man from Handan who tried to learn to walk."
A monk asked, "When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, the realm of Māra collapsed. When the Master opens the hall, what auspicious signs are there?
The Master replied, "A night of falling blossoms and rain; the entire city filled with the fragrance of flowing water."
The Master was with Inspector Hu when they arrived at Ersheng Temple in Gong’an. Hu asked, “Darmakṣema told Emperor Wu of Liang that ‘it is vast and empty, there is no sage.
Why then are there two sages here in Gong’an? The Master said, “A single drop of ink forms two dragons.”
Chan Master Hongzhou Baofeng Wenzhun (5 in total), a native of Shu, was a successor of Chan Master Hongzhou Baofeng Kewen. Initially, he visited Chan Master Zhenjing Wen.
Wen asked, "Where did you recently leave? The Master said, "Dayang. Wen asked, "Where were you during the summer retreat?

The Master said, "I do not understand. Wumen said, "Everything is already accomplished; who else is there to be made to understand? At that moment, the Master was suddenly relieved.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Great Way extends horizontally and vertically; it is manifest and complete in every encounter. The clouds part and the sun emerges; the waters are clear and the mountains are green.

Profitable! One does not see the square head of the chisel. Baofeng was not like this; he threw down his staff and said:

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The pivot of the Patriarchs' seal is hidden in mystery; few know it. Unless one is a person who has awakened to the mind, how could they possibly express it to others?

Sweeping away all traces until nothing remains. Today, Yunyan cannot help but emulate the ancients. (He strikes the whisk. Just so!

[The Master] says, "Flow. "There is nothing superior to realizing this Dharma first. He lifts his staff, strikes once, and says, "This Dharma cannot be understood through conceptualization or discrimination.

Addressing the assembly, he said: "Stop! After long rains that do not cease, it has come to pass that at the peak of Mount Wulao, black clouds gather thickly;

Joining his palms at the three gates, he offered this prayer and aspiration: "May the Stone Woman of Huangmei give birth to a son; may mother and child be reunited.
May the hornless iron ox of Shaoshi graze upon sweet water and grass. He gave a shout and said, "What connection is there?"
Chan Master Foyun Fozhao Gaofeng of Dongjing (fourth in the series). Having traveled extensively throughout various regions, he later visited Zhenjing.
There, upon reading a verse by an ancestral master, he said: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; it manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When one realizes empty space,"
"There is no 'is' and no 'non-dharma. At this, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment.

A Dharma Master of the Hundred Dharmas remarked, "The followers of the Chan school mostly love empty talk. The Master went before him and asked, "I have heard that you, Dharma Master, can lecture on the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*;
is this true? The Master replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "Yesterday it rained; today it is sunny."
"In what Dharma is this included? The host had no reply. The Master struck him and said, "Do not say that those of the Chan school are fond of empty talk.
The host said indignantly, "Wait, Master; tell me then: 'Yesterday it rained, today it is sunny'—in what Dharma is this included?
The Master said, "It is included in the forty-second category: the category of phenomena that do not correspond to time. The host was humbled and prostrated himself.
[The Master] took his leave.
A monk asked, "When Yunmen was questioned, 'What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharmakāya?', he replied, 'Hide one's body within the Northern Dipper.
What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A sincere heart, slice by slice. [The monk] said, "If it were I, a student, it would not be so. The Master said, "..."
"What do you say to this? he asked. [The monk] replied, "Last night I raised my head and looked at the Big Dipper; it was somewhat like a sugar-cake with dots on it.
The Master said, "Just think of water and grass; know nothing else."
A monk asked, "What did Bodhidharma transmit when he came from the West? The Master said, "The Zhou, Qin, Han, and Wei dynasties.
Chan Master Congyue of Doushuai in Hongzhou (the seventh of seven): a native of the Xiong clan of Qianzhou.
While serving as the head seat under Daowu, he led several monks to visit Master Zhizhe of Yungai. Before he had spoken even a few sentences, [Zhizhe] fully understood what was in his mind.
Yunmen laughed and said, "Observing the Senior Seat’s refined character and bearing, how is it that his speech and breath are like those of a drunkard?
The Master’s face flushed and he broke into a sweat, saying, "I pray that the Abbot will not withhold his compassion and further instruct me with piercing words."
He was at a loss for words and then requested to enter the room. Zhi asked, "Have you ever met Master Fanchang Yu? The Master replied, "I have read his records;
they are sufficient for my own understanding, so I have no wish to meet him. Zhi asked, "Have you ever met Master Dongshan Wen?"
The Master said, "A man from Guansi has no sense. Dragging a hempen skirt about, he reeks of urine. What excellence does he have?
Zhi said, "You should simply investigate where that smell of urine arises. The Master followed these instructions and went to see Dongshan, where he deeply grasped the profound essence.
He then returned to see Zhi. Zhi asked, "Since you met the man from Guansi, how is the Great Matter? The Master said, "If..."
Having failed to receive the Master’s instruction, he eventually wasted his entire life;
thus, he paid his respects and departed. The Master subsequently visited Zhenjing. Later, the Master appeared in the world at Lüyuan. There was one named Qing Su who had long studied under Ciming;
