"Explaining Chan on a continent. Furthermore, how is it so? "Clouds steaming rice atop Mount Wutai; dog-urine sky before the Buddha hall steps;
a hammer frying on the top of the banner-pole; three monkeys winnowing coins at night."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Whenever there is anything displayed or entrusted, it all falls into the realm of the present moment. To neither display nor entrust is to fall into pits and ditches.
Even if one were such that the wind cannot enter and water cannot touch, if one examines this closely, one still fails to save oneself.
Have you not heard it said: 'It is like the moon’s reflection in a cold pond, or the sound of a bell in a silent night; it is never diminished by being struck, yet it touches upon every wave.'"
Yet it does not disperse; it remains merely a matter of the shore of birth and death. [The Master] picks up his staff, draws a line, and says:
"With this stroke, I cut through the ancient tangle of many years. The Nodding Stone, without realizing it, claps its hands and laughs aloud. But tell me, what is it that it laughs at?
If you see his cheek behind his ear, do not associate with him.
Chan Master Huguo Jingyuan of Taizhou (the fifth of five): He was the son of the Zhang family of Leqing, Wenzhou.
The Master went to visit Yuanwu at Jiangshan. There, two monks were reading the records of Siji (Sishin), which stated: "When one is deluded, one must attain awakening."

Once he had attained awakening, he realized that within awakening there is still delusion; thus, with both delusion and awakening forgotten, he established all dharmas from the standpoint of wordlessness.
Master Xinxin criticized him, whereupon he shook out his sleeves and departed. After walking several paces, he suddenly reached a profound accord and ran back to inform Yuanwu.
Wu recognized the depth of his understanding. Later, when [Zhaozhou] took his leave of Wu, Wu asked, "When someone asks you in the future, what will you say?
The Master patted the back of a nearby monk and said, "The Master asked you; why do you not answer him? Wu laughed heartily.
Later, he established the Dharma at Nanyue (South Bright) in Chuzhou and passed away at that same mountain.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Śākyamuni did not understand the Way; Bodhidharma did not understand Chan. The Patriarchs had no contrivances;

the patch-robed monks have no handle to grasp. This is so, yet how do you take it up? If you can take it up right here, the Dharma of the Buddhas and the worldly dharmas will be forged into a single piece.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, there will not be the slightest shift or change. But if you have not yet..."
Nevertheless, do not remain in a cold cave where the wild grasses turn green; sitting amidst white clouds, the essence of the school will not be realized.

Addressing the assembly, he raised his whisk and said, "Great assembly, do you see it? With this, he shattered the silver mountains and iron walls, overturned the tiger’s lair and the demon’s palace, cut off the mechanisms of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and swept away all the paths laid out by others everywhere, until even Deshan was left with no recourse.
A step! Linji swallowed his voice; not a single monk under heaven dared to draw a breath.
Even if Muzhou himself had entered the gate, he would still have been struck with a blow to the crown of his head. But tell me, where is the corner of the cloud-joined banner? Do you know?
If you travel to various regions, take care not to misquote me.
Addressing the assembly, I say: The wild jackal howls; the lion roars. Eyes opened, mouth agape; the Southern Star moves, the Northern Dipper slips.
O Great Assembly, do you know where this falls? A Vajra-knife crouches beneath the steps; a divine tortoise runs through the flames.
A monk asked, "What is the Linji school? The Master said, "Killing people and bringing them back to life without blinking an eye. The monk asked, "What is the Yunmen school?
The Master said, "Three eyes in the crown of the head illuminate heaven and earth. The monk asked, "What is the Guiyang school?"
The Master said: "Pushed forward, it does not go ahead; pulled back, it does not retreat. [The student] asked: "What is the Fayan school? The Master said:
"Arrowheads meet point-to-point, neither yielding to the other. [The student] asked: "What is the Caodong school? The Master said: "Holding a night-illuminating talisman in one's hand."
How few know the dawn of Heaven!

Chan Master Zhibing of Nanhua in Shaoyou, successor to Chan Master Fojian Huiqin of Jiangshan in Jiankang (eight in total), was a native of Shu. Having followed Fojian for a long time, he mastered [his teachings] completely.
Profound and subtle. He began his career at Shu-zhi Tianping and concluded it at his own mountain monastery.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Śākyamuni never appeared in this world, nor did he show a single dharma to anyone.

Bodhidharma was not at Shaolin; how could the Second Patriarch have ever obtained the marrow? As for the elder masters of all quarters and the teachers of the realm, whether they used the staff or the shout—"
Whether expansive or concise, some employ dense and meticulous language to open up various paths of meaning and establish their own sectarian styles.
This is much like painting a cake to satisfy hunger or steaming sand to make rice; even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will only lead to weariness in vain.

You all are fortunately people with nothing to do, so you must not hastily take this upon yourselves or easily grasp its meaning. Though gold dust is precious, if it falls into the eye, it becomes a thorn.
Yi! Today at Nanhua, you have already been wounded by the blade and injured your hand. Is there any other expedient means for one who recognizes good and ill fortune?
Even if you were to understand it immediately, you would still be a mediocre fellow. Ultimately, how is it so?
If one possesses the Śākarākṣa eye, one can see the errors from three thousand li away.
Ascending the hall, he said: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both together, nor without a cause.
Therefore, it is said that they are unarisen. This dharma of non-arising is by nature originally empty. Sentient beings recklessly conceptualize and thus wander through birth and death.
For this reason, the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past appeared in the world to beat the great Dharma drum and expound the great Dharma meaning, desiring to cause all beings..."

Birth. To be liberated from those deluded emotions, turn one's back on the dust of sensory objects and unite with awakening. If one suddenly eliminates the deluded sovereign, the void will not produce flowers;
if one gradually exhausts the source of craving, gold will be free of its ore. Now that the Dharma drum has been struck—[the Master] strikes the staff once and says:
"The Great Meaning has already been expounded. Is there anyone who fully understands it? Originally there was no wound; do not inflict injury upon it."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The matters prior to the fifteenth day cannot be reached by the teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods.
The matters subsequent to the fifteenth day cannot be fully expressed by the entire Great Canon. On the very fifteenth day itself, it is like a long sword leaning against the heavens."
Who dares to face this? Steep cliffs and precipitous crags—how can one find a foothold?

Only when the mind has nothing to dwell upon, the eyes see nothing, the ears hear nothing, and the mouth says nothing, will even a single fragment not yet have been attained. Arriving here, what is it like?
When meeting people, speak but three parts of your words; do not yet cast away your whole heart.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To say 'this very mind is Buddha' is to mistake a servant for a lord. To say 'neither this mind nor Buddha' is to cut off one's head while seeking life.

When neither of these applies, it is like a weary fish resting in a pond or a sick bird perching on a reed. Yet there is another mechanism that avoids the wind and thunder, only to be struck by a bolt of lightning once again.
Tell me, where does 'Peaceful Prosperity' benefit people? If you can understand this, then when salt is called, you will hear it."
Salty. To eat vinegar and not perceive its sourness—if one does not even know this, one is an old crow in a cloth bag; though alive, one is as good as dead.
Entering the hall, he said: "I speak of it day after day; I raise it up moment after moment. It is like the earth supporting a mountain—how much difference does that make?
The parrot from Longxi is beloved by people, mostly because it can speak. Cease your deliberations; bring along your companions. Let the wise hear this briefly."
"Seize it fiercely! There is another thing that is also most extraordinary: the cat is uniquely adept at catching mice.
He ascended the hall and said: "Foam and illusion are equally unimpeded; why do you not awaken to this? To penetrate the Dharma within this is neither of the present nor of the past.
You people, the four elements and five aggregates are foam and illusion; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are foam and illusion."

The twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twenty-five states of existence, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world—none of these are not like bubbles or illusions.
Which among them is unimpeded? If you can see this, only then will you know that all day long you are busily rushing about.
That matter is of no concern. Should it be otherwise, the path up the mountain stream is easy to find, but the sky within the cave is difficult to seek.
Entering the hall, he said: "The five eyes cannot behold its form; the two ears are cut off from hearing its sound. Thus spoke the ancients.

Little do they realize that the words are incomplete and the meaning is deficient. The five eyes cannot behold his countenance. [The Master] raises his whisk and says: "Those with eyes see him all at once;
how could they fail to behold his countenance? The two ears are cut off from hearing his resonance. He then strikes the meditation seat and says:
"Those with ears hear him all at once; how could they fail to hear his resonance? If there is neither hearing nor seeing, what is it?

Unlike those who are blind or deaf, you have both heard and seen. By what ultimate principle do you not touch the waves yet summon the moon of auspiciousness, and move the clouds and rain yet drum the thunder of Mount Sumeru? Descend from your seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Delusion does not delude itself; it is established in opposition to awakening. Awakening does not awaken itself; it is spoken of because of delusion.

Therefore, awakening is the substance of delusion, and delusion is the function of awakening. Both delusion and awakening are without source; within this, there is neither distinction nor commonality.
Without distinction or commonality, it cannot be moved by a shove. The Patriarch could not bring it here; its nostrils weigh a thousand catties."
Chan Master Shigui of Gushan in Fuzhou, Dharma heir of Chan Master Qingyuan of Longmen in Shu Prefecture (the fifth): a native of Western Sichuan. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"Those who have been going straight ahead like this all along—if they do not turn their heads when called, they have already received thirty blows beneath their heels. Those who have been..."
For one who comes in such a manner, it cannot be grasped; right at the crown of the head, I strike once more with the awl.
At Tianning, we treat illness by recognizing illness; thus, we use a wedge to extract a wedge. Only such a person as this can achieve it. Do you understand?
A sword leaves its precious sheath because of imbalance; medicine comes from its golden jar because of the need to save the sick.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Clearly there is no awakening; to have a dharma is to be deluded. You people cannot stand here;
you people cannot dwell here. To stand here is to err; to dwell here is to be blind. You must let the mind not rest."
"Profound! Sentences do not halt the meaning; their application does not halt the mechanism. Once these three are clarified, there is no need for supervision in any situation;
[the truth] manifests naturally before one. There is no need for vigilance in any situation; it is naturally understood.
Nevertheless, you must know that there is a matter beyond this before you have attained it. He then called to the assembly, "What is the matter beyond this? And he said:
The rain has not stopped for a long time.

[The Master] lets out a shout and addresses the assembly, saying: "To employ sharp mental flashes is to guard against dull stupidity; to rely on intellectual understanding is to dwell in profound silence. Thus one remains sitting within a nest."
"Even if you do not employ sharp wit, do not maintain a dull, wooden stillness, do not rely on intellect or principle, and do not dwell in profound silence—you have still not escaped the nest.
How will you all escape the nest? After a long pause, he said: "The asura lifts the sun to cover the face of heaven;
the wrathful Nanda and Upananda strike down the celestial bell. He let out a shout.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his servants; Linji and Deshan—what weeds and brushwood are they? The single path that points upward is a forest of thorns.
If you wish to turn yourself around, you will fall over a cliff or into a pit. If you remain entirely unmoved, you will be buried alive where you stand.
When the vital mechanism is applied at the moment, it instead becomes a chaotic mess. For all of you, I have now settled this all at once."
"It is not so," he said. "It is not not so. "Both 'so' and 'not so' are not acceptable.
"How then? After a long silence, he said: "The pierced-eared barbarian monk on the Onion Range; this morning his horse's hooves tread lightly through the snow."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The reality that is inherently present cannot be sought through delusion; the established doctrine that is difficult to believe ultimately yields nothing.

From the entrustment at the Snowy Mountains to the transmission of the robe at Cock’s Foot Mountain, crossing the vast ocean by day and navigating upon a single reed by night—all these were due to the failure of the patriarchs above, whose errors have reached us, their descendants. You all, each and every one, must return to your original mind."
Having left the household life, you must act with self-respect from the very first step of your journey; do not allow yourself to be deceived by others.
Otherwise, when smoke rises from beneath your feet in the future, you will have no grounds for blaming Tianning.
Chan Master Daoheng of Jianfu Temple in Raoyou (Seven in total), a native of the Ye family of Guocang, addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Buddha preached the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings—sudden and gradual, partial and complete. One must not speak of dreams before a fool.

When the Patriarch came from the West, he pointed directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha. As for Linji’s Three Mysteries and Dongshan’s Five Ranks, they are [all for] fools..."
"You must not speak of dreams in my presence. When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, will you be exempt from the censure of the various quarters?
Therefore, the ancients said: 'If the stone man’s wit were like yours, he too would know how to sing the Ba song.
If you were like the stone man, you would surely also harmonize with the Snow Song. Is there anyone here who can harmonize it? If there is, call him here; let him wash the old monk’s feet."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If one's entire being were a mouth, one could speak only half of it. If one's entire being were an eye, one could employ only a single portion of it.
Where employment reaches its limit, speech remains in excess; where speech reaches its limit, employment is inexhaustible. As it is said: 'When there is employment, there is no speaking.'"

When it is said that there is no function, the function is spoken of as being simultaneous; the function is spoken of as being non-simultaneous. If any person should hesitate or deliberate, this old monk is already beneath your feet.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If you understand, then you understand; jade is inherently without flaw. If you say you do not understand, then flowers bloom upon the tip of a pestle.
Let me ask: how does nine years of facing a wall compare to the Great Assembly’s picking of a flower? For Nanyue Ming to deliberate in such a manner is merely to scatter sand with the wind."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The first thing for a student of the Way must not be to follow the path of principle; if you follow the path of principle, it will exhaust you to death.

The first thing for a student of the Way must not be to follow the path of thought; if you follow the path of thought, it will bind you to death. To be exhausted to death means wandering between heaven and humanity;
to be bound to death means being caught in the three vows and six arms. One who neither runs nor is bound is a teacher of the 'stump' (dògēn) who follows along."
This constitutes a fault of falling into error. Tell me, where exactly does the transgression lie? If you can discern this, I grant that you possess the eye that penetrates all quarters.
Addressing the assembly, he raised the case of Master Ji opening the hall for the monks: "What is the meaning of Chan? The assembly offered various responses, but none accorded with the principle.
The assembly requested further instruction from Ji. Ji spoke on their behalf: "To slander is its meaning. O Great Assembly, the Buddhas of the three periods are slanders;
the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven are slanders; the Sixth Patriarch of the land of Tang is a slander; and the old monks of the world are all slanders."

"All these people are slandering; this mountain monk is also slandering. Among them, is there anyone who does not slander? Though those who discourse on the profound and speak of the wondrous are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, how can they compare to the intimacy with which Shuangfeng slanders?"
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Śākyamuni shut his room in Magadha; the true mandate was not followed, for he twisted the crooked to make it straight.
Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī; the servant of the eastern house was actually in the western house.

Subhūti was made to chant 'non-explanation' to manifest the Way—this is one person passing on a rumor. Śakra and Brahmā ceased listening while the flowers rained down—this is ten thousand people passing on a reality. This...
All things are governed by the divine principle of *li*; therefore, the mouth remains silent because of it. To emerge from within the grass—how could this be called a lack of eloquence?
It is that which eloquence cannot express. "I am amazed," says the clumsy fellow, "that he has gone off in such a manner."
A monk asked, "What is the one phrase for the Master’s way of benefiting others? The Master said, "The stone pagoda in front of the gate.
Chan Master Fashun of Xianlin Chan Monastery in Baiyang, Fuzhou (the seventh in this lineage), was the son of the Wen family from Weicheng in Mianzhou.
He attended upon Foyan for several years. Once, during a general discourse (*pǔshuō*), Foyan cited the *Heart-King Inscription* by the Great Being Fu Dashi, saying:
"The flavor of salt in water; the indigo in lacquer. It is certainly present, yet its form is not seen. Upon these words, the Master attained realization.
The following day, he entered the room for instruction, and Xuansha asked, "Where does the True Buddha dwell? The Master replied, "He dwells in no fixed place.
Xuansha asked, "Since it is the True Buddha, why is he not fixed? The Master said, "If he were fixed, he would not be the True Buddha."
The Buddha nodded his head in approval. From that time on, [the Master’s] reputation reached the inner sanctum, and his fame shook the monastic community.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "O worthy ones, from the beginning, this mountain monk has not recognized good from evil.
To tell you all to investigate this one great matter of cause and condition is already to pour foul water upon your heads."

I see that you do not understand. Having no other recourse, I once again raise my whisk and clench my fist. There may be a monk who cannot distinguish between good and evil, who steps forward and chants with phrases, raising his head toward the whisk; yet he does not realize— [The text continues: ...that he is merely grasping at shadows. This is why it is said: "If you wish to see the Buddha, look at the ten thousand phenomena. If you can see the Buddha within the ten thousand phenomena, then you will know that the ten thousand phenomena are themselves the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the Buddha, then the Buddha is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-Buddha, then the non-Buddha is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the Buddha and the non-Buddha, then neither the Buddha nor the non-Buddha is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the Buddha nor the non-Buddha, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the seeing, then the seeing is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-seeing, then the non-seeing is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both seeing and non-seeing, then neither seeing nor non-seeing is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither seeing nor non-seeing, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, then these are not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-hearing, non-smelling, non-tasting, non-touching, and non-cognizing, then these are the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, as well as non-hearing, non-smelling, non-tasting, non-touching, and non-cognizing, then neither hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, nor non-hearing, non-smelling, non-tasting, non-touching, and non-cognizing, is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, nor non-hearing, non-smelling, non-tasting, non-touching, and non-cognizing, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the mind, then the mind is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-mind, then the non-mind is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the mind and the non-mind, then neither the mind nor the non-mind is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the mind nor the non-mind, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the arising of thoughts, then the arising of thoughts is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the ceasing of thoughts, then the ceasing of thoughts is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the arising and ceasing of thoughts, then neither the arising nor the ceasing of thoughts is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the arising nor the ceasing of thoughts, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the past, then the past is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the future, then the future is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the past and the future, then neither the past nor the future is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the past nor the future, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the present, then the present is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-present, then the non-present is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the present and the non-present, then neither the present nor the non-present is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the present nor the non-present, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the body, then the body is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-body, then the non-body is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the body and the non-body, then neither the body nor the non-body is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the body nor the non-body, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within speech, then speech is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within silence, then silence is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both speech and silence, then neither speech nor silence is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither speech nor silence, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within movement, then movement is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within stillness, then stillness is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both movement and stillness, then neither movement nor stillness is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither movement nor stillness, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the ordinary, then the ordinary is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the sacred, then the sacred is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the ordinary and the sacred, then neither the ordinary nor the sacred is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the ordinary nor the sacred, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the self, then the self is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-self, then the non-self is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the self and the non-self, then neither the self nor the non-self is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the self nor the non-self, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the dharma, then the dharma is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-dharma, then the non-dharma is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the dharma and the non-dharma, then neither the dharma nor the non-dharma is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the dharma nor the non-dharma, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the eye, then the eye is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, then these are not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-eye, non-ear, non-nose, non-tongue, non-body, and non-mind, then these are the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the non-eye, non-ear, non-nose, non-tongue, non-body, and non-mind, then neither the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, nor the non-eye, non-ear, non-nose, non-tongue, non-body, and non-mind, is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, nor the non-eye, non-ear, non-nose, non-tongue, non-body, and non-mind, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the realm of form, then the realm of form is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the realms of sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena, then these are not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-realm of form, non-realm of sound, non-realm of smell, non-realm of taste, non-realm of touch, and non-realm of phenomena, then these are the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the realm of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena, as well as the non-realm of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena, then neither the realm of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena, nor the non-realm of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena, is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the realm of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena, nor the non-realm of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the world, then the world is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within the non-world, then the non-world is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both the world and the non-world, then neither the world nor the non-world is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither the world nor the non-world, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within birth, then birth is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within death, then death is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both birth and death, then neither birth nor death is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within neither birth nor death, then the Buddha is truly the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within life, then life is not the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within extinction, then extinction is the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha within both life and extinction, then neither life nor
To give it to you yourself—it has absolutely no connection [to your current state].
Why do you not speak a single phrase, securely and profoundly, from before principles were established and the paths of thought had yet traveled? Do you lack the guts of Xianlin?
Not only would he consume ten thousand taels of gold daily; Elder Xianlin used his own body as a seat to teach the Master to speak.
To bring sentient beings into the Dharma is not beyond one's capacity.

Addressing the assembly, he said: "The rooster crows at the dawn moon; the dog barks at the withered stump. These can only be understood in silence; they are difficult to enter through discursive thought.
Where there is nothing to be seen, the earth trembles and light is emitted. Where words cannot reach, heaven and earth are dark and yellow. He then presented a six-foot-tall statue of a city guard.
Paper. Originally produced in Qingjiang. O assembly, it is clearly spoken of, yet people find it difficult to see. Last night at the third watch, the moon shone through the window.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "This firm and dense body of mine is seen within all dust motes. It possesses the thirty-two marks; how could it [be otherwise]?"
Accommodating skillful means: A rat enters the grain barn; a black dog ascends the Buddha hall. The night moon bears a double halo;
the morning clouds drag white silk. These forms fill the world, yet few people see them. If one sees both the mundane and the sacred, awakening and delusion become a single piece.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and the conditions of light, darkness, form, and emptiness—these are the fundamental radiance of sentient beings and the realm of the Buddhas' freedom from thought.
To be deluded regarding this is called being an ordinary person; to realize this is called primordial awakening. O Great Assembly, I have no vision;
the green mountains before my eyes have become a single expanse. The golden crow flies upon the azure sky..."
Xiaolai: At the edge of the meadow, the shadows of flowers shift. Right at such a time, how can one speak of the principle of "no-seeing"?
To maintain a view here is not to be among my followers. After all, how does one speak of the principle of "no-seeing"?
Those who possess the eye of discernment—please try to examine this.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "After the morning gruel, one nap; at the midday meal, a bowl of rice. Beyond this, there is no seeking.
The work of the Way is spontaneously accomplished. But as for this very act of sleeping and eating—how can one speak of the principle by which the work of the Way is accomplished?
This is the circumstance by which Xianlin brings about for you all the very conditions of sleeping and eating. If, in this regard..."
You should understand this: when you fall asleep, light radiates throughout the four continents; when you eat your meal, light radiates throughout the four continents;
even in every movement and stillness, every word and silence, it is all light that radiates throughout the four continents.
Whether you have attained liberation or not, do not misunderstand Xianlin’s words. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"The water washes the stones by the brook; the wind blows the banners in the ancient hall. If you know where the point of rest lies here, why must it be on Vulture Peak?"
Chan Master Daopei Shanguo of Tanzhou, a successor of Chan Master Daoning of Kaifu in Tanzhou (the third in this lineage), was a native of Xinzhou. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"In general, those who study the Way must investigate the 'live word,' not the 'dead word. If one can attain clarity beneath the live word, one may then serve as a standard for weighing all things."
The Buddhas and Patriarchs manifest the orthodox and crush the heterodox; they cover and nourish all living beings and provide relief to the orphaned and destitute.

If you can understand this under the "dead word" (*sijù*), you will merely be clinging to grass and wood, burying the ancestral style so that you cannot even save yourself. But what, then, is the "live word" (*huójù*)? Is it not:
"When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it; carry it home in a bottomless basket"? Or is it not: "In Shanfu..."?
Does the Iron Ox swallow the Great Image of Jiazhou? Is it not the case that the ox of Huaizhou eats the grain, while the horse of Yizhou suffers from a bloated belly?
Is it not the time for the general assembly at Tiantai, or the lecture hall session at Nanyue? Is it not a phrase that reveals neither its edge nor its bone?
"Before you have even raised it, have you already handed it over? If it is like this, it is all dead words. But what is a live word? He struck the meditation staff and said:
"Sentient beings and principles both consist of three sections; a single ray of divine light shoots toward the Dipper and Ox."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "When the mind arises, phenomena also arise; when the mind ceases, phenomena also cease. When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, one calls a tortoise a turtle.
All you practitioners of Zen, have you said it yet? If you have said it, Daolin will give you this staff."
If this were not yet so, go back to the hall and drink tea.
A monk asked, "I have long heard of Moon Hermitage; yet now that I have arrived, neither the hermitage is seen nor the moon appears. The Master said:
"The old monk has committed a transgression. The monk prostrated. The Master said, "An adept, an adept!
This is the seventeenth generation descendant under Mount Heng, the Dharma heir of the former Chan Master Fatai of Daopei in Tanzhou.

Chan Master Zhong’an of Lingyan in Dingzhou (five fascicles), a native of Shu, addressed the assembly, saying: "If one studies Chan without investigating its profound source, every encounter will become an obstacle.
Thus, by merely maintaining silence and stillness, or abiding in a state of tranquil voidness, one falls into a sea of poison.

To overcome the strong with weakness, to assert oneself while disparaging others, to establish the view of self and other, and to measure things with partiality—suddenly, [one realizes this is not so]."
If one can kill but cannot bring to life, or can bring to life but cannot kill, then one is subject to the wandering of phenomena.

If killing and bringing to life were suddenly brought to equal effect, such that superiority and inferiority could not be distinguished, then illumination would fail to engage in function, and function would not depart from its nest. This is because the locus of study is not profound;

it is entirely mundane. At this point, one must know that there is penetration and liberation within killing, and the concealment of the mechanism within bringing to life. Even a Buddha cannot [reach this].
[The Master] said, "I know. Your ancestors could not fathom it. Therefore, the ancients said: "Sometimes illumination comes first and function follows;
I must consult with you on this. Sometimes function comes first and illumination follows; you must be a true man before you can understand this.
Sometimes illumination and function are simultaneous; how will you respond to that? Sometimes illumination and function are not simultaneous; then where do you turn?"
"Converging and mooring—do you still know? This startling phrase within the arrow that pierces the willow was not learned on the spot.
The Master, acting as the attendant for Chan Master Fohsing, went to Chan Master Yuanwu at Jiangshan to deliver the letter of succession.

Yuanwu received the letter in the Dharma Hall and asked, "You have traveled a thousand miles to bring this; you have not disgraced our ancestral tradition. When it comes to a ready-made public case, how do you proceed?"
Regarding "communication," the Master said, "Presented face-to-face, there is no further evasion. Yuanwu said, "This is Deshan’s; what about Shanzhao’s?
The Master said, "How could there be a second person? Yuanwu said, "What about the one behind?
The Master then delivered the letter. Yuanwu said, "A master of Chan. The Master said, "Deliver it to Jiangshan."
The Master went before the Sangha Hall, held up the letter, and paid his respects to the Head Seat (Venerable Penglaiqing). The Head Seat asked, "Xuan Sha’s white paper?"
"From where does this come? The Master held up the letter and said, "Do you see it? The Seat-holder reached out his hand to take the letter;

the Master withdrew it and said, "I have long kept silent on this essential point and did not strive to speak of it hastily. Today I present it to you; I hope you will deign to look upon it. The Seat-holder then gave a shout.

The Master said, "An adept. The Seat-holder also shouted. The Master then struck him with his whisk. As the Seat-holder reached out to catch it, the Master said, "You have not yet understood three, eight, and nine;
you cannot help but brood over it yourself. The Seat-holder was speechless. The Master struck him again with the whisk and said, "Catch!"
At that time, Yuanwu and Foyan were together in front of the Dharma Hall when they saw [the incident]. Yuanwu said, "I have beaten my Head Seat to death.
Foyan said, "It is like two official horses kicking each other; what evidence is there for it? When the Master heard this, he replied immediately, "What 'official horses kicking each other'?
This is precisely the treading of dragons and elephants. Yuanwu called the Master over and said, "Among my five hundred followers, you are the Head Seat."
"Why did you hit him so hard? The Master said, "The Abbot should have had a beating as well before it would be right.
Wuzu looked at Fuyan and stuck out his tongue. Fuyan said, "Not yet. Fuyan then asked the Master, "Empty-handed, holding a hoe;
walking, riding a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not flow. How do you understand this? The Master bowed and said, "As above."
All that was offered was entirely in accordance with the facts. Xianshou said, "So you are truly one of our own household.
The Master went to the place of the Fifth Patriarch, Zen Master Zizang, and presented his letter. Zizang asked, "What does the letter say? The Master replied:
The patterns [of his realization] were already manifest. He himself asked, "Ultimately, what have I said? The Master said, "Brandishing a precious sword in broad daylight.
He himself said, "Come closer; here one does not even recognize a single character. The Master said, "Do not feign defeat. He then looked at his attendant and said:
"This is a monk from such-and-such a place. The other said, "This is the Head Seat; he once sat at the feet of the Master.
He added, "I wonder why his bones are so sturdy. The Master said, "He was indeed once neglected by the Master.
Then, taking a letter, he held it over the incense burner and offered incense, saying, "Namo Samantabhadra. The Master approached and merely snapped his fingers.
Chan Master Qingdan of Furuang in Tanzhou (sixth in the series), a native of the Yan clan from Pengzhou, visited Chan Master Deshan Xuanzhao.
Upon hearing him ascend the hall, [Desan] cited Zhaozhou’s words: “The old woman of Mount Tai has already been thoroughly scrutinized for you;
where does the meaning lie? After a long silence, [Desan] said: “Pluck the yellow leaves from the tree and go. [Qingdan] entered the mountain and was expelled.
"Baiyun comes. At these words, the Master was suddenly enlightened. The following day, he entered the room for private instruction.

Baizhang Tai asked, "Regarding the former Baizhang’s 'not falling into cause and effect,' why did he fall as a wild fox? Regarding the latter Baizhang’s 'not obscuring cause and effect,' why did he escape from being a wild fox?

The Master replied, "It would be best to bury them both in a single pit. Baizhang continued to interrogate him with further questions, and the Master’s responses were consistently sharp and penetrating; his words were all extraordinary. Later...

Furthermore, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he encountered a passage that said, "Breaking through the dust, one brings forth the sūtra scrolls. At that moment, the Master’s mind and environment dissolved;

all sentiments regarding the holy and the mundane were exhausted. Unconsciously, he danced with his hands and feet for the entire day. Daoyi then established the system of appointing monks, and his reputation moved the world at that time.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Ultimate truth transcends all forms, yet there are no forms by which truth can be revealed. Ultimate principle is beyond words, yet there are no words by which the Way can be clarified.
Therefore, principle accords with changing phenomena and takes on its essence according to conditions; phenomena attain harmony with principle and respond to things according to their capacity.
It is like clouds emerging from mountain caves, or like a valley echoing sound. One must necessarily forget both self and others; then, the perfect mechanism will naturally manifest everywhere."
It should be so. Only then can one leave names behind and sever appearances; sounds and forms become purely true. It is simply the exhaustion of ordinary sentiments;

there is no separate "sage's understanding. He addressed the assembly, saying: "To see form and clarify the mind is to fall into a pit or a ditch. To hear sound and awaken to the Way is to辜负 (gu fù—betray) one’s entire life.
Even if sounds and forms are purely true and every dust mote enters the subtle, if you remain sitting within the light and shadow, it is not yet the ultimate. You must..."
Ten thousand affairs are brought to rest; not even a single sage can carry it away. Letting go there, one leaps out of the nest. Arriving here, there is neither person nor Buddha.
The great chiliocosm is but a bubble in the sea; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning.
Now tell me, where does the Old Śākyamuni show his head? After a long silence, he said: "I let this one point pass."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Night after night one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning one rises together with him. Rising and sitting, we are always in his company; speaking and remaining silent, we dwell together.
Not a hair’s breadth separates us; they are like a shadow following its form. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of my voice.
Among the assembly, those who do not understand the meaning of the ancients will mistake their own karmic consciousness for the true nature of mind, like someone riding...
To attempt to cross the great ocean with a broken boat, or to try to satisfy a hungry stomach with a painted cake—such things are impossible.

You must know that this gate of mine is deep, firm, remote, and far-reaching; no one can reach it. Yet if there were one who did reach it, though they entered and exited the same gate all day long, each would remain unaware of the other.
Though they share the same tongue all day, each remains unacquainted with the other. Within the sameness, there is difference.
In difference there is sameness; sameness and difference do not know one another. At every step there is neither before nor after. If you can be thus, then form is mind, and the person is the Buddha.
Mountain flowers bloom like brocade, yet they have never been hidden throughout the realm. Valley waters are as deep blue as indigo, yet there is no reflection of a body within them.
Even if you attain such a state, you still fall into the stagnant water of death. Now, what is the phrase for turning back?
"How would you say it? "The dragon emerges from the cave bearing rain; the phoenix returns from amidst the flowers carrying fragrance.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to all under heaven. When a single speck of dust is raised, the entire earth is gathered up.

Those with wisdom, upon merely hearing this, should grasp it vigorously; do not wait until in an instant you lose your head. But tell me, what is that 'single speck of dust'? "A man of clear eyes has none."
The old nest and trap. As soon as one hears it mentioned, they take it up and use it immediately.
Without stirring a single speck of dust, the sixteen-foot golden body manifests from a heap of refuse. Without stirring a single scene, they open out a world within the eye of a gnat.

Hidden within a single speck of dust, they cause all people under heaven to see no trace of them. Within that single speck of dust, they shift their bodies and change their steps, overturning heaven itself.
To open the eyes of those below, it is said: "The numinous blade of the precious sword is constantly revealed before one.
Sometimes it emerges, and even Buddhas and Patriarchs do not exist; even Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra must be banished beneath the Iron Ring Mountains.

Sometimes it enters, and when the wind is clear and the moon is bright, the cat and the white ox enter directly into the midst of the lotus throne. As for the time when there is neither emerging nor entering, it is like this:"
"What designation? After a long silence, he said, "Hūṃ. Later, upon the capture of Caizhou, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"To speak of Buddhas and Patriarchs is like gouging a sore on healthy flesh; to cite the ancients and the present is merely leftover soup and rancid rice.
To awaken upon hearing once already falls into the second head; to act upon being prompted once is already 'not quite there.'"
It is so. You must understand this matter: it is like the sky covering all universally, like the earth supporting all universally;

like a lion roaming, seeking no companion; like a strongman extending his arm, borrowing no external force. Buddhas and patriarchs cannot pick it up or move it; even a patch-robed monk has no door through which to wish to see it.
Delusion and enlightenment are both forgotten; the paths of sage and ordinary are cut off. Now tell me: by what dharma have the sages of antiquity shown people?
"Ha! Do not engage in false conceptualization.
A monk asked, "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes discrimination. What is it like at such a time? The Master said, "The river water is turbid from its source."

Chan Master Dingxu of Xichan Monastery in Fuzhou, Dharma heir of Chan Master Zonggao of Mount Jing in Lin’an Prefecture (Seven in total). He was the son of the Lin family in Changle County of that same province.

Originally a student of Confucianism, on a day of rest he entered a Buddhist monastery and saw the *Śāriputra-prakaraṇa* (The Bequeathed Teachings Sutra). After casually glancing through it several times, he suddenly attained realization. Thereupon...
Taking leave of his parents, he shaved his head and traveled alone with a single staff through Lake and Xiang. Wherever there were renowned monasteries, he visited them all to seek instruction.

Finding no difference in the flavor of the Dharma, as it was like water and milk blending together, his vision became empty of all quarters; finding nothing to satisfy his mind, he returned to his native place.
He built a thatched hut on the summit of Qiang Peak, where he kept no servants or attendants, possessing only a single rope bed. When guests arrived, they simply sat upon the ground. He did not...

It had been three years since Chan Master Caicai of the Mahayana Buddha-heart lineage descended from the mountain. Although he was repeatedly invited [to leave], he did not go forth. Later, [the Master] wrote a letter reprimanding him, saying:
"Now, as for those who have left the household life, once they have attained a state of peace and happiness, they ought to propagate the Great Dharma to repay the Buddha's kindness."

One who detests clamor and seeks stillness, seeking only to perfect themselves alone—how could such a person be considered a wise man or an enlightened scholar? He strove to draw them out and lead them to emerge as a leader among the Mahayana.
Once, while he was at Miaoxi Hermitage on Yangyu, he asked his students about the causal conditions for "the mind itself is Buddha.
At that time, the hermitage’s abbot, Mi Guang—a friend of the Master—wrote to him, saying: "The methods of this abbot are different from those of other quarters; you should come."
After a brief exchange, [Dahui] asked, "How is it? The Master smiled but did not answer. Dahui, employing a stratagem, invited the Master for a meal.
When the Master went to accept the invitation, he had just reached the gate when he encountered Miaoxi, who was conducting a *shumi* (entering the room) session with his disciples.

The Master joined them to observe the ceremony. Miaoxi asked, "When a monk asked Zhaozhou, 'What is Buddha? Zhaozhou said, 'This very mind is Buddha. What about that? The Master offered a response, and Miaoxi struck him.
He said to him, "With such understanding as yours, how dare you presume to act as a teacher to others?

I shall beat the drum for a public sermon and expose all those places where you have cherished and found strength throughout your life, categorizing them as erroneous interpretations. The Master’s tears flowed down his cheeks; he did not dare look up.
He thought silently to himself, "Since that which I have attained has been thus rejected, could the essential meaning transmitted from the West have stopped at this?"

He subsequently turned his heart toward the Dharma and joined the ranks of the disciples. One day, Miaoxi asked the Master, "When you do not let anything go out from within, nor let anything enter from without—what is it like at such a time?
As the Master was about to open his mouth, Miaoxi took up his bamboo staff and struck him three times across the spine.
At this, the Master attained great enlightenment. He cried out, "The Master has already given too much! Miaoxi struck him again.
[The monk] bowed once. Master Miaoxi smiled and said, "Only today do you finally know that I have not deceived you.
He then sealed [the realization] with a verse: "The eye of Mahesvara stands upright at the crown of the head; A life-snatching talisman hangs askew behind the elbow.
Blind the eyes and cast off the talisman— Zhaozhou hangs his gourd on the eastern wall. Thereupon, his reputation spread throughout the monastic community.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The meaning within the phrase; the phrase within the meaning—Mount Sumeru towers over the vast river. When the phrase eradicates the meaning and the meaning eradicates the phrase, the hero manifests his wild abandon.
Even if one’s teeth were like a forest of swords and one’s mouth like a blood-basin, it would be in vain to flaunt the sharpness of one's rhetoric or falsely display one's spirit.
Thus, when Vimalakīrti remained silent, he had already fallen into prolixity; when Mahākāśyapa closed the gate, he had already..."

To expose the family’s disgrace: as for that old fellow from Waguan and Master Yantou, who at the summit of Qiang Peak whipped up the wind and stirred the waves, playing with divine transformations—his heels should be given thirty blows. But tell me, where does the fault lie?
After a long silence, he said: "The mechanism was not made by Han Guang; do not treat your own inner depths as something trivial. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"To cross the flowing current with a blade is not yet to be a master; for a swift flame to pass through the wind still leaves one a dull-witted fellow.

Therefore, to awaken to the Way by pressing one's fingers is merely to add more sores to a wound; to forget consciousness upon striking a bamboo is but a scene of blinding confusion. Even if one possesses such skill..."
Both are exhausted; there is no breath at all. Even upon close inspection, it is truly not yet there.

The path beyond—where the thousand sages did not transmit—is such that students weary their bodies like a monkey grasping at a reflection. Since it is not transmitted, why has the school of Bodhidharma reached the present day?
[He lets out a shout and says: "Do not, for heaven’s sake, mistake the bridge of a donkey’s saddle for your father’s chin."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "A sword hangs in the great void to manifest our school. With a majestic presence that presses down upon one as one sits, how can anyone draw near?
Even if you possess the skillful means to turn heaven and earth and to move like lightning or a shooting star, you will still be no match for this formidable opponent.
Is there anyone here now who can discern fortune or misfortune? If so, please come forward and meet me. If you hesitate even slightly, [you will be struck]."
"Hammer it right to pieces! [He lets out a shout.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "To rely on words is easy to fall into; to be stuck in phrases leads further into delusion. To sit upon one's own tongue requires that one must have eyes elsewhere.
Even if you claim to know this, you are not yet among the elite. To knit one’s brows and turn back is not yet to be called 'temperamental' (xingcao). To suddenly cast it aside—*teng*!"

Transcending the great void—this very majesty, who would dare look upon it? As soon as you cast a glance toward his station or set foot in his gate, everything becomes a mere shadow and echo, lacking true reality;
like a fox lingering in its den, it is all smashed to pieces by a single blow, yet this does not yet match one’s lifelong endeavor.
Have you not heard it said: "If you wish to know this matter, you must brandish the sword; if you do not brandish the sword, the fisherman will settle in his nest"? It is precisely thus.
"At what time? How is it so? After a long silence, he said: "To offer this profound mind to the lands of the dust motes—this is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
On the festival day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Before the twenty-fifth day, the masses of yin have subsided; the mud-dragons close their doors. II.
After the fifteenth day, the first yang returns; the iron trees bloom.
It is precisely on the twenty-fifth day that the intoxicated guests amidst the dust ride their donkeys and horses through the streets before and behind, welcoming one another with celebration.

But the idle man beyond the mundane world, his head shrouded in a patched robe, sits cross-legged around the hearth. The wind whistles and the rain falls; it is cold and desolate—who cares for you, Zhang?
The Master, Li the Daoist, and Hu the Dharma-teacher addressed the assembly, saying:
"To hold the Mohe sword crosswise and display empty arrogance, or to pierce through an iron wall, is merely to waste one's spirit.

Even if you were to refrain from brandishing the blade of the spirit and achieve a state of Great Peace by sitting idly, even the reigns of Kings Yao and Shun still left something remaining to be transformed."
Chan Master Miguang of Guishan in Fuzhou (seven in total) was a native of that same province. He traveled extensively through various monastic communities before visiting Miaoxi.
Throughout his life, he exhausted his efforts in the five arts [of Chan practice], yet for half a year he found no way to open his mouth. One day, upon entering the inner quarters, Miaoxi asked him:
"The rice gruel has been eaten; the bowl has been washed; the incense has been burned and the path of practice completed—depart."
Miaoxi said, "Set aside your prohibitions regarding medicine; bring me a phrase. The Master replied, "Torn asunder! Miaoxi, his expression solemn, said, "You have come here again to talk of Chan.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment; sweat poured from his entire body, and he prostrated himself.
Miaoxi confirmed this with a verse, saying: "Grasping the hair of a tortoise, one laughs heartily; A single blow opens ten thousand layers of locks. What joy and liberation!"
"Throughout my life, today is the day. Who says that a thousand li have deceived me in coming? The Master also composed a verse on seizing the opportune moment, saying:
"A light nudge, and the angry thunder roars; It startles the Dharmakāya hidden within the Northern Dipper. The vast waves surge, flooding the heavens."
He grasped the nostrils but lost the mouth. Later, he opened the teaching of Fashui Jiaozhong and spent his final years at the mountain monastery.

Addressing the assembly, he said: "The rain has cleared and the clouds have vanished; the peaks and ridges stand out in emerald green. The wind is gentle and the sun is warm; the halls and pavilions are filled with spring.
Between the rafters, the young swallows chirp *guan-guan*; upon the plains, the young peach blossoms bloom a brilliant red. Most excellent is Lingyun’s single glimpse."
He claimed that throughout his life he had never doubted [the teachings]. When Xuansha heard of this, he said:

"Deeply discussing the true mark—those two old fellows possess the eye on the crown of their heads and carry the talisman behind their elbows. Yet, when examined closely, they cannot avoid chasing after sounds and pursuing forms.
Now tell me: what about that one phrase of transcendence? Do you understand? It is a day of shifting rain and sun during the Cold Food Festival; half-light...
On a half-dark, smokeless day, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"When the moon arises as one, a single word exposes Vimalakīrti. When the moon arises as two, one plays at will upon the tips of the hundred grasses.
When the moon arises as three, the white ox and the stray cat let loose their natural spontaneity. To let go is to add flowers to brocade."
If you hold fast, even true gold loses its luster. I dare ask the assembly: is it better to hold fast, or is it better to let go? After a long silence, he said:
"In the deep autumn, rain falls from a thousand screens; at sunset, a single flute sound stirs the wind among the towers."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The phrase exists; the phrase does not exist—like a vine leaning against a tree. The Master said, "Why do you act so foolishly?
Then, when the tree falls and the vine withers, where does the phrase return? I knew well that you all would ultimately fail to find its head or nose. Why is this so?
It is simply because it is so extremely clear that it, in turn, causes what is attained to be delayed.
Addressing the assembly, he raised his staff, struck it once, and let out a shout, saying: "It is not that I frequently urge you to drink while seated;
since we parted, I have rarely seen you."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky—what need is there to grasp them? Gain and loss, right and wrong—let them all go at once.
He then cast down his whisk and said: "I, this mountain monk, have already let go today. As for you all, what will you do?
He then called to his attendant and said: "Gather up the whisk."

A monk asked, "It is said that 'if one's insight is equal to the teacher's, it reduces the teacher's merit by half; only when one's insight surpasses the teacher's is one fit to receive the transmission.
Now, if one's insight is equal to the teacher's, why does it reduce the teacher's merit by half? The Master said, "I cannot claim not to have studied Yunmen Chan.

The monk said, "Regarding the statement that 'only when one's insight surpasses the teacher's is one fit to receive the transmission,' I wonder what it is that is transmitted. The Master said: [He] transmitted nothing.
Do not slander others; this is good.
Chan Master Siyue of Dongchan Monastery in Fuzhou (three instances total), a native of that very province, addressed the assembly, saying:
"I shall shut my mouth, yet I must speak; I shall block your ears, yet you must not miss it. Yesterday, someone came from Tiantai..."
He came and then said: "The Great Sage of Sizhou is sitting in meditation in Hongzhou, selling his wares at the crossroads. What are these?
A straw sandal with broken heels and a bamboo hat with a pointed brim."
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Huangbo. The Master said, "What words or phrases did Huangbo say?
He replied, "When I arrived here, I forgot them all at once. The Master said, "Have you not come from Huangbo, Seat-Holder? He replied, "I have."
The Master said, "It is also said that you have forgotten. As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout and sent him out.
The Master asked another monk, "When practitioners meet, what is it like? The monk replied, "There is nothing else.
The Master said, "Zhaozhou spoke of presenting a lacquerware vessel; what about that? The monk then shouted. The Master said, "You say there is nothing else, yet you also shout."
"Ma! The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him, saying, "Do not say there is nothing else to it.
Chan Master Shoujing of Xichan in Fuzhou (total of four records) addressed the assembly, saying: "Before reaching Yunmen, one cannot avoid stumbling at crossroads;
before reaching the village ahead and before reaching the shop behind, once you have arrived, you must still penetrate through to the other side."
It can be attained. If you do not break through and emerge, but remain sitting within, there are venomous snakes swarming before you and countless fierce tigers behind you;
fire erupts from atop your head, and swords and halberds stand in dense array beneath your feet.
Now, this entire assembly is entirely within this state—your eyebrows are alike, your eye-sockets are the same. Who among you has broken through? Who has failed to break through?
"O man of clear vision and high caliber, please point this out for Yunmen. This way, our entire summer retreat here will not have been spent in vain.
If it is otherwise, then return to me the cost of my ninety days' worth of meals."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Those skilled in combat do not look back for their heads; those skilled in war surely achieve merit. Once that merit is achieved, peace prevails through effortless means.
When peace is established, one rests with head upon pillow, free from anxiety. One may set aside the three-foot sword and cease handling the bow.
Horses are returned to the southern slopes of Mount Hua, and oxen are released into the wilds of Taolin. The winds blow according to the seasons."
Yet the rains fall in their proper season; the fisherman sings and the woodcutter dances. Even so, the reigns of Emperors Yao and Shun still left behind a legacy of transformation.
How can they compare to the Heavens and Earth, which cannot be contained? To Yao and Shun, even their names are unknown; the entire household pays no heed to matters of rise and fall.
They simply prefer to occupy the Lake Dongting together with the clouds.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Close your mouths, yet speak at all times; cut out your tongues, yet never cease.
Never ceasing—how most extraordinary! How most extraordinary! Yet why does that which is so extraordinary become mere dust in the eye?
When one has thoroughly understood, there is nothing to be understood; even the realm of the profoundest mystery must be cast aside."
Addressing the assembly, he cited the teaching: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who act as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are all seen as the Buddha himself.
Later, Master Nanzheng Guizong said, "Those who act as spiritual friends must not be taken lightly;
nor should one treat those whom one perceives as spiritual friends with disrespect. The Master remarked, "Guizong speaking in this way is just like a new bride."
I fear my mother-in-law; I cannot help but follow the turnings of her tongue. Little do they realize that those who act as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are merely blind men.
To see such spiritual friends is like encountering an enemy from a previous life; one should simply gouge out their eyes and tear off their skull-caps.
Even so, this would not suffice to repay their kindness.
Chan Master Daokuan of Kaishan in Jianning Prefecture (eightth in the series) was a native of this very prefecture.
Initially, he went to the capital to visit Chan Master Yuanwu, but he did not achieve any realization. Later, he followed Miaoxi while Miaoxi resided in a hermitage in Quannan;
when Miaoxi took charge of Mount Jing, the Master also attended him there. Not long after, Miaoxi sent the Master to Changsha to communicate with the layman Ziyang, Chancellor Zhang.
The Master wrote: "I have practiced Chan for twenty years and have found no point of entry. If I continue this journey, I will surely fall into neglect;
I intend to abandon traveling. A friend named Zongyuan rebuked him, saying, "It is not that you cannot practice Chan while on the road.
Come, I shall go with you. The Master had no choice but to set out. On the way, he wept and said to Yuan:
He said, "I have spent my life practicing Chan, yet I have gained no real strength from it. Now, as I am traveling along this road in such haste, how can I attain resonance with the Way?
Yuan told him, "Simply do not concern yourself with anything you have studied in various quarters, anything you have realized, or anything that Yuanwu and Miaoxi have explained for you.
Regarding matters that can be set aside while on the road, I shall [explain them all]..."
“On your behalf, there are only five matters. You cannot act on their behalf; you must know them for yourself.
The Master asked, “What are these five matters? I wish to hear their essentials. Yuan said, “Wearing clothes, eating food, defecating, urinating, and carrying a corpse along the road.
At these words, the Master realized the essential meaning and, without realizing it, began to dance with his hands and feet. Yuan spoke again:
He said to him, "Now you may deliver this letter to Ziyuan. You may proceed; I shall return. Yuan immediately returned to Mount Jing.
When the Master arrived at Changsha, he stayed for half a year. The Lady of the State of Qin was a regular reader of the scriptures.
He asked the Master, "How does the Abbot of Jingshan usually instruct people to practice Chan?
The Master replied, "The Abbot instructs people to set aside all miscellaneous affairs and look only at this: A monk asked Zhaozhou, 'Does even a dog have Buddha-nature?'"
Zhaozhou said, "No. Again, a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha? Yunmen said, "A dried-up shit-stick.

At all times and in all places, you must repeatedly call this to mind and look into it, taking awakening as your standard. National Lady, if you wish to discern this matter, you should cease reading the sutras and focus exclusively on internal investigation;
only then will you succeed. Following these instructions, before more than a month had passed, National Lady suddenly attained realization.
Fafa composed a verse, saying: "Reading the sūtras day after day is like meeting an old acquaintance; do not say that frequent repetition causes hindrance—for every recitation, it is renewed.
When he returned to Mount Jing, Miaoxi was waiting at the gate leaning on his staff. Upon seeing him, Miaoxi said with joy, "Son of Jianzhou, this time you are truly different.

He moved to Kairan Temple in Jianning and spent the remainder of his life there.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "In the school of the Patriarchs, this is the fundamental framework. Even for a monk with clear eyes, upon reaching this point, one knows not what to do.

With supernormal powers and radiant light, he gives rise to inexhaustible eloquence and wisdom, yet employs not a single point of them. Directly, the workings of the mind are extinguished;
ordinary and holy beings leave no trace. It is like a precipice ten thousand fathoms high, standing sheer—there is no place for any person to find a foothold.
Proceeding thus, the Dharma is exhausted and there are no subjects left. Reaching this point, having no other recourse, he opens a single thread of the Way.

Therefore, the former sages spoke of casting off precious and noble robes to don tattered and soiled garments; turning their backs on the dust of worldly toil, they skillfully opened up expedient means.

This is why Master Bodhidharma came from the Western lands and suppressed his boundless majestic radiance, facing a wall for nine years at Shaolin—like one guarding a stump while waiting for a rabbit.

The snow reached his waist. He then severed his own left arm. Bodhidharma asked, "For what purpose have you been standing in the snow and severing your arm?
Huikang replied, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to pacify my mind. Bodhidharma said, "Bring me your mind, and I shall pacify it for you."
Guang sat for a long while and said, "I have sought the mind, but it is utterly unattainable. Bodhidharma replied, "I have finished settling your mind for you.
*Silence.* How frustrating! Why did he not, at that moment, turn his face around and cause this old fellow to be utterly humiliated?
It is a pity he was let go. Even until now, it causes people to wring their hands in frustration. Later, [Dongshan] asked again, "Since you first saw me, what have you attained?

It becomes increasingly unbearable to witness. From this point on, one person transmits what is false, and ten thousand people transmit it as true;
they call this "transmitting the Dharma to save deluded sentiments. In this way, everyone falls into the den of wild foxes.
Not a single person remains loftily independent, immune to deception—a truly liberated Great Man. Is there anyone like this right now? If there is, come forth and face me!

Before this assembly of devas and humans, I speak clearly and openly. Whether you fly like a flash of lightning, seize the drum and snatch the banner, I must still act as a boat and a bridge, as a tortoise and a mirror.
Only thus shall I not fail the benefactor who has invited this mountain monk to appear in the world today.
And yet, this mountain monk has not come forth in vain to provide these arrangements. That we may both benefit one another—how joyful this is!
Is there anyone here? Is there anyone? If not, then look at this staff as it displays its spiritual powers. [Suddenly] he picks up the staff, strikes once, and says:
"Do not resent my former haughtiness; he has already trodden upon the highest pass."
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The mind of the Great Immortal of the land of Chu was secretly transmitted from east to west. What is this mind that was secretly transmitted?
After a long silence, he said: "In the autumn of the eighth month, where is there any heat?"
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Deshan’s act of striking as soon as one enters the gate is much like being oblivious to those around.
Linji’s shouting as soon as one enters the gate is likewise merely a swelling of empty breath. Jueyi spent his entire life merely holding up a finger;
how could a shrimp ever leap out of a measuring bucket? Xuefeng rolling the ball, Heshan beating the drum, Bimozhi holding up a fork, and Daowu performing a dance—all of these are nothing but..."
The antics of children; as for the rest of such folk, they are truly a matter of great heat and no small urgency. But in the end, what of it?
The flowers must bloom through the night; do not wait for the morning breeze to blow.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "To conceive of it is to lose it; to move toward it is to deviate from it. To neither conceive nor move is like a holeless iron hammer—what means is there to lift it up?
Reaching this point, you must possess the skillful hands and feet used for catching pigs and dogs. Have you not seen?"
Linji was attending on Deshan. Deshan said, "I am exhausted today. Linji said, "Old fellow, why are you talking in your sleep?
As Deshan was about to raise his staff, Linji overturned the rope seat. Look at those two veteran masters: they are carefree and unassuming, with no sharp edge showing;
yet when suddenly provoked, they are like tigers leaping from within a thicket of grass. Sudden!
The ground—dare anyone approach it? To approach it is to lose one’s body and forfeit one’s life. Therefore it is said: "Seizing the tiger's head and gathering its tail;
under the first phrase, clarify the fundamental principle. I dare ask the assembly: tell me, how does one seize the tiger's head?
"How does Huigui gather it in? What does he take as the first phrase? What constitutes his fundamental principle?
Master, do not hide it away; try to reveal it before this assembly. If you cannot, I, this mountain monk, shall speak for myself.
Suddenly he took up his staff, struck once, and said: "The eye atop the peak is as clear as the sun; if you wish to recognize true gold, look within the fire."

"Look! He addressed the assembly, saying: "Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high—where the Buddhas of the three periods have no place to set foot—is it so? It is so, yet it is far too devoid of human sentiment.
To let down a single thread of the Way, where the oceans of lands in the ten directions emit light and shake the earth—is it so? It is so, yet how [can one...]"
When pears are mixed with mud and water, one must know the place where a single thread-way passes. Where there is a wall standing ten thousand fathoms high, there a single thread-way passes;

where a single thread-way passes, there is a wall standing ten thousand fathoms high. Held crosswise and used upside down, pressed straight on and lifted from the side, like a flash of lightning or the crash of thunder, like a collapsing cliff or splitting rocks—it is so, it is so, yet it still falls into the gate of transformation.
Reaching this point, even a wall standing ten thousand fathoms high has no connection; the single thread-way passes through.
A single track. There is no engagement. It does not conform to human sentiment. Muddying the water and mixing the mud—there is simply no engagement.
This very lack of engagement is itself a lack of engagement. It is so, yet it lacks the principles of the Buddha-dharma.
If you can emerge from these four paths, you will surely stride alone through heaven and earth. But as for this phrase, "striding alone"—how is it?
The Way. Do not be surprised that I have been so full of spirit in the past; my predecessors have already trodden upon the highest pass. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"To speak of Buddhas and preach the Dharma is to delude the blind and the deaf. To discuss nature and discuss the mind is to throw oneself into a pitfall.
To wield the staff or shout 'Ho! is to rely on one's power to deceive others. To blink an eye or raise an eyebrow is the work of wild fox spirits. It is none of these things. Great!
It is like raising one's voice to silence an echo; there is something extraordinary about it, yet it is merely calling out into the empty air. Ultimately, how is it?
Where the white clouds end, there are green mountains; the traveler lies even beyond those green mountains.

What kind of clamor is this from a hot bowl? Behold the great capacity and great function of the masters of the land: like lightning rolling and whirlwinds spinning, they move with the flow of clouds."

The pouring rain is like a dream; what is there to say about the summer retreat (*an-guo*), the confinement of the feet (*jin-zu*), the establishment of the rules (*jie-zhi*), or the protection of life?

To strictly guard the "wax man" (the body) is to bind oneself with no rope—this is merely a matter of floundering and has nothing to do with the essential point. Even if one reaches such a state, one may then be called a patch-robed monk (*na-seng*).
Yet, this ordinary way of walking and acting is not yet the supreme matter of the Zen school (*zong-men*). So, what is this supreme matter of the Zen school?
Regarding the matter of transcending [the mundane]: wishing to speak, words fail; beneath the forest trees, one may deliberate well.

Chan Master Daoyan of Donglin in Jiangzhou (twelfth in the lineage) was a native of Shu. Having studied under Yuanwu for a long time, one day they were discussing the teachings of the past and present.
When it was his turn to speak, the Master did not yield to the sense of propriety. Yuanwu shouted, "When you practice Chan, you do not seek authentic awakening;
why do you merely go on talking nonsense at will? Startled, the Master broke into a cold sweat. He returned to the hall and sat in meditation, remaining awake throughout the entire night.
Suddenly, he had a powerful realization and could not help but laugh. The next day, he again met Yuanwu, and their discussion was sharp and incisive, with no lingering doubts or obstructions.
Yuanwu nodded his head. The Master said, "Yesterday I answered you in this same way, yet why did you not approve?
Today it is just the same, and you nod your head. Yuanwu rebuked him, saying, "You fool! Yesterday you were mixed up..."
"It is a mind of deluded conceptualization. The Master prostrated and said, "So it turns out that Śākyamuni Buddha had no supernatural powers after all.
Later, while waiting for Yuanwu to go on a mountain excursion, the Master saw Yuantou burning manure; as smoke rose, Yuanwu asked, "From where does this smoke arise?"

"It all rests in the hands of each person.

If it is so, gold and brass cannot be concealed; if it is not, jade and stone are both struck. Should you hesitate or fail to respond, the silver mountains will shatter into dust. All...
It is not so. Furthermore, how is it? Right and wrong do not hang upon one’s natural mouth; there are naturally bystanders who speak of their merits and demerits.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The myriad things begin with birth-and-birth; that which is born is unborn. Transformation does not occur at the beginning of a beginning. Beginning—

This has no beginning. Thus, being without birth and without beginning is the nature of things. All phenomena possess both nature and emotion; throughout antiquity and the present, there is death and birth.
Because there is death, it depends upon birth; because there is birth, it depends upon emotion. When emotions accumulate without ceasing, the cycle of birth and death flows on.
For this reason, the Tathāgata appeared in the world to expound the causal blossoms of the myriad practices, and the Patriarch came from the West to shout the One Vehicle.

Regarding this wondrous Dharma: there are those whose faculties and natures are sharp and keen, whose spiritual awakening remains solitary, who sit and cut off the heads of both the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* Buddhas, and who take a shrimp for their eyes or borrow another’s nostrils to breathe.
