The practitioner Ding (once in total) visited Xingkong. Xingkong struck him once with his staff and said, "I have blinded your original eyes.
Ding said, "Not only today; the ancients also carried out this command. Xingkong said, "Who told you there is 'ancient' and 'modern'?"
Ding shook his sleeves and went out. Kōng said, "Under the clear blue sky and bright sun, there is a lost traveler.
Ding asked, "Do you not wish to point the way? Kōng struck him. Ding said, "Please do not blind people's eyes. Kōng replied, "I am merely blinding the eyes of the worldly."
What fault is there?
[He was] a Dharma successor of Zen Master Tianhuang Daowu of Jingzhou, the fourth generation under Qingyuan.
Chan Master Chongxin of Longtan in Lǐzhōu (in three parts): He was originally the son of a sesame-cake seller from Zhūgōng; his family name and clan are unknown.

His master would daily order him to deliver ten cakes to the Emperor of Heaven. Once the Emperor had finished receiving them, he would invariably set aside one cake and give it back to him, saying, "I bestow this upon you to provide for your descendants.
The Master suddenly thought to himself, "I brought these cakes away; why have they returned?"
“You have left me behind; is there perhaps some other meaning to this? He asked the Emperor. The Emperor replied, “This was brought by you yourself. What fault is there in returning it to you?

Under these words, the Master attained realization of the ultimate meaning and consequently entered the monastic life. The Emperor said, “In the past you honored and cultivated merit and goodness; now you believe my words.”
He may be named Chōshin.
The Master asked the Emperor, “Since I first arrived, I have not received the instructions on the essentials of the mind from you, O Monk.
The Emperor said, “From the moment you arrived, there has never been a time when I have not instructed you on the essentials of the mind. The Master asked, “Where, then, was my instruction?”
"The essential point of the mind," Huang said, "is this: when you bring me tea, I receive it from you;
when you bring me food, I accept it from you; when you bow to me, I simply lower my head. Where have I not pointed out the essential point of your mind to you?

The Master pondered this for a moment. Huang said, "If you see, you see directly at once; if you hesitate to think about it, you are already mistaken. At that moment, the Master attained awakening and asked:
[The monk] asked, "How does one maintain this? Huang said, "Roam freely according to your nature; be expansive and relaxed in accordance with conditions. Simply exhaust the ordinary mind;
there is no separate 'sage's understanding'."
The Master asked the Emperor, "How is it that you have inherited the matter transmitted from of old? The Emperor replied, "It is not that I cannot clarify where you have come from.
The Master said, "How many people possess such an eye? The Emperor replied, "In shallow grass, even a reed grows easily."

Chan Master Daowu Zongzhi of Tanzhou, Dharma Heir of Chan Master Yueshan Weiyen of Former Lizhou (12th in the lineage). A native of Haihun in Yuzhang, son of the Zhang family. Initially, he went to see Yueshan.
Yueshan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from wandering the mountains. Yueshan said, "Without leaving this room, quickly speak!"
[The monk] approached. The Master said, "The crows on the mountain are white as snow; the fish swimming in the water have no moment of leisure.
Because Yaoshan had addressed the assembly, saying, "I have a single phrase that I have never spoken to anyone," the Master said, "It has come along with you.
A monk asked Yaoshan, "How can this one phrase be explained? Yaoshan said, "It is not something expressed through speech. The Master [repeated this].
[The Master] said, "I have already explained this.

When the Master visited Nanquan, Nanquan asked, "What is your name, *ācārya*? The Master replied, "Zongzhi. Nanquan said, "At the place where wisdom does not reach, how can there be a 'principle' (*zong*)?
The Master said, "Above all, do not speak of it. Nanquan said, "That is so. But if you speak of it, you will immediately manifest your head and horns."
Three days later, while the Master and Yunyan were mending clothes on the back rack, Nanquan saw them and asked, "The other day you said, 'Where wisdom does not reach, do not try to speak;
if you speak, horns will grow. How, then, should one conduct oneself?"
The Master then withdrew his body and entered the Sangha hall. Quan departed. The Master returned and sat down.
Yank asked, "Disciple, why did you not respond to the Master just now? The Master said, "You are so exceptionally sharp-witted. Yank was at a loss for words;
he went instead to ask Nanquan, "Regarding the matter that just occurred, why did Dharma Master Zhi not respond to the Master? Nanquan said, "He, however—"
"This is walking among those of a different species. Yankun asked, "What is it like to walk among those of a different species? Quan said, "Have you not heard it said:
'Where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly avoid speaking of it'? If you speak of it, horns will grow; you must simply walk among those of a different species."
He finally attained it. Master [Dongshan] knew that Yanguan had not yet realized it, so he thought to himself, "This person's karmic conditions do not lie here.
He then returned with him to Yaoshan. When Yaoshan saw the two men returning, he asked Yanguan, "Where have you been? Yanguan replied:
He arrived at Nanquan. Nanquan asked, "What words or phrases did you hear? Yan recounted the previous conversation. Nanquan asked, "How do you understand this?
Yan had no reply. Nanquan laughed heartily. Yan asked, "What is it like to walk among those of different species?
Nanquan said, "I am tired today; come back another time. Yan said, "I have returned specifically for this matter. Nanquan said, "Go for now," and Yan departed.
The Master was outside the abbot’s quarters when he heard that Yunyan had failed to realize the meaning; unconsciously, he bit his finger until it bled.
The Master then went down and asked Yunyan, "Brother, go ask the Abbot about that karmic cause—what did he say?
Yunyan replied, "The Abbot did not explain it for me. Thereupon, the Master bowed his head.

thus you say, "I am a practitioner," and you strike out with artificiality and affectation, making a face exactly like that of one who has attained the Way.
Do not apply your mind in such a casual manner! Ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes of transmigration within the three realms are all due to having a [discriminating] mind.

Why is this? When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise. If one can remain for even a single thought-moment without arising, then one will forever be liberated from birth and death, no longer bound by them.
When you wish to walk, you walk; when you wish to sit, you sit. What else is there to do?
O worthy ones, I see that you all have resolved to practice wherever you go, seeking the Buddha-dharma under the tutelage of old bald slaves. How noble!
Disregarding his own body and life, he had the eyes of all his sons nailed shut and severed their life-roots.
Resembling two or three hundred courtesans, he claimed, "I am establishing the Dharma-banner through the King’s transformation, opening the eyes for future generations."
"Can you save yourself? You, O worthy one, speak of practicing in such a manner. Have you not heard it said that the Old Barbarian practiced for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
where is he now? After eighty years, he will die; how does this differ from you?"
"Sons, do not be reckless! I urge you: it is better to rest; it is better to go where there is no business. The moment you give rise to a single thought, you belong to the family of Māra;

you are but a layperson who has broken the precepts. You have seen Deshan appear in the world, and when ten or five of you tried to gather together to pose difficult questions, he left them with their tongues tied and speechless. You are all mere beggars—why do you not come out now?"
A needle kept inside a torn cloth bag does not show its head; such is a skilled hand. I wish to ask you for the ultimate reality—do not err, O worthy one!
You run from house to house in a frantic rush, saying, "I understand Chan, I understand the Way," patting your chest and ribs, praising the Yangs and the Zhengs.
When you arrive here, you must vomit it all up completely before you can attain peace. Simply do not let external sounds attach to you.
As for form: internally there is nothing that can be known or understood; its essence is neither ordinary nor sage-like. What more is there to learn?

Even if you were to master hundreds of thousands of subtle meanings, you would still be nothing but a "sore-eating ghost," a mere malevolent spirit. To me, this space here—though one might say it exists—is [empty].
It is neither existent; one cannot say it is non-existent. It is neither ordinary; one cannot say it is sagely.
In every respect, there is no place to fix it. This old fellow serves as the teacher of the ten thousand dharmas for you; I do not dare to slander him.
Therefore, the Old Barbarian spat out so many expedient teachings and saliva-like words to instruct you to go where there is no business and not seek outside;

yet you still refuse to comply, wishing instead to collect superior phrases and store them within your breast, using clever rhetoric to settle matters with your tongue, wearing your cloth skirt high to ensure others know that you are a Chan Master. You desire this—what for?
This is the point of emergence. If you hold such a view, I shall strike that ghost’s rump and cast you into the Hell of the Plucked Tongue;
the day will surely come. You go everywhere seeking people, saying, "I am a guest under the Gate of the Patriarchs.

Yet when questioned about the fundamental matter, your mouth is like a wooden mortar. You then proceed to preach to them of *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, *tathatā*, and *vimokṣa*, citing extensively from the scriptures.
"The teachings of the Tripiṭaka—claiming they are Chan and the Way—are merely deceiving the common folk. What connection do they have [to true realization]?
You slander my ancestors! Old Hanshan De (Deshan) did not see it this way: 'Here there is no Buddha, there is no Patriarch; Bodhidharma was an old hirsute barbarian;
the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages are dung-carriers; the Two Enlightened Ones, Equal and Wondrous, are precept-breaking commoners.'"
Now, Bodhi and Nirvana are but hitching posts for donkeys; the twelve divisions of the teachings are registers of ghosts and spirits, or paper for wiping sores and warts.

The four fruits and the three stages of worthiness, as well as the initial mind and the ten stages of the bodhisattva, are merely ghosts guarding ancient tombs—what use are they? Even to save oneself, there is nothing to be gained.
The Buddha is an old barbarian’s dung post. Do not make a mistake, O worthy one! You are already wearing clothes made of sores and warts; what matter are you studying? Eat your fill!
Having finished eating your rice, you speak of True Suchness and Nirvana. Is there still blood beneath your skin? You must be a true man before you can succeed.

Do not crave the "sacred"; "sacred" is but an empty name. If, within the three realms and the ten directions of the world, there were even a single speck of dust or a single dharma to be grasped, such that you would seize upon it to give rise to understanding, or preserve and value it as something precious, you would fall entirely into the ranks of celestial Māras and external paths.
This is something attained by those still in training; it is merely like spirits clinging to grass and wood, or wild foxes possessed by demons.
My sons, in this place, I have not a single dharma to offer you for your understanding. I myself do not understand Zen;
I am no spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). I understand nothing at all; I am simply one who defecates and urinates, begs for food and begs for clothing.
What more is there to say? Old Hans Deshan advises you: it would be better to go where there is nothing; rest early. Do not act like a madman.

Each person carries a corpse and wanders about in great clamor, everywhere seeking to swallow the spittle from the mouth of this old bald slave, claiming, "I have entered samādhi" or "I am cultivating and accumulating practices," thus nurturing [delusion].

"Sacred embryo! May you vow to attain the fruit of Buddhahood! When the old man Deshan saw such people as these, it was like a poisoned arrow piercing his heart and flower-needles disorienting his eyes;
he felt they were betraying the former sages and bringing disgrace upon his own school, fearing that others would claim he was merely a monastic.
In this way, you squander the offerings of the donors throughout the ten directions; even water cannot wash away such deeds.
Do not boast that you dare to walk upon the land of kings. If you do not provide your parents with fine delicacies, how can you claim to be without fault?
Do not misapply your mind. The King Yama will one day demand the price for your straw sandals; he will pierce your nostrils and bind you to a stake to repay your past debts.
Debt. Do not say I have not told you. You all are truly fortunate to have encountered Deshan appearing in this world;
he shall untie your ropes for you, remove your headstalls, and take down your yokes, so that you may become true men.
Within the three realms and six paths, they shall be unable to capture you. There is no other method: it is this blazing void, unimpeded and self-existent.
It exists. It is not something you can adorn or embellish. From the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, all have transmitted this Dharma and thereby attained liberation.
The entire Great Canon of teachings is merely intended to rectify you people of the present day. My sons, do not seek it elsewhere.
Even when the little blue-eyed barbarian monk Bodhidharma came here, he did nothing but teach you to be without affairs.

Go! I teach you not to engage in contrived activity. Put on your clothes, eat your food, defecate, urinate, and there will be no more birth-and-death to fear, nor any nirvana to be attained, nor any bodhi to be realized; it is simply the ordinary state of an unburdened person.

First, do not stand with hands folded like a Chan master, seeking a place to emerge from [delusion], skillfully crafting words to bewitch the younger generation, and wishing for others to call you an "Elder. Within your own nature, there is no connection whatsoever;
it is merely that your consciousness is vast and turbulent, ceaselessly fabricating strange wonders day and night, claiming "Yang" or "Zheng," and asserting, "I am Mazu of Jiangxi."
Disciples, the old man Deshan was not one of you followers. When I saw the Old Man Shitou, I saw an old fellow who did not recognize good from evil;
that is why he reviled his own sons. Do not become attached to sounds and forms, nor to names, phrases, and meanings.

Regarding the mechanisms of sensory objects, the principles of good and evil, the acceptance and rejection of ordinary and sagehood, the clinging to defilement and purity, and all thoughts of light and dark, existence and non-existence—if you can attain suchness within these very states, only then are you a person of no affairs. Even the Buddhas are not like you;
even the Patriarchs are not like you. O worthy one, do not tread upon your own feet with such broad strides! There is no other Chan or Way to be learned. If...
Those who have attained [realization] as learners are those with two heads and three faces; they possess the views of external paths and likewise cannot attain supernatural powers or transformations.
You claim that supernatural powers belong to the sages, yet such powers are also found among devas, nāgas, spirits, the five-attainment immortals, externalists, and asuras.

He also possesses supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), so he ought to be a Buddha. He dwells alone on a solitary peak, eats but one meal at dawn, sits constantly without lying down, and performs prostrations and recitations during the six periods of the day.
Yet he doubts the cycle of birth and death. The Old Barbarian [the Buddha] had this saying: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing.

If you say that [enlightenment] is attained by entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and concentrating the spirit through tranquil contemplation (*dhyāna*), then the Nirgranthas and other teachers of the non-Buddhist paths would also [be Buddhas].
"You have entered the great samādhi of eighty thousand kalpas; could you not be a Buddha? [The Master replied: "I clearly know you are a demon of false views.
You, O Benevolent One, are not a sage; the Buddha is but an old barbarian's dung-stick.

I merely wish for you to discern right from wrong and not cling to self and others, so that you may avoid being pinned by the 'sage-stakes,' the 'bodhi-stake,' or the 'liberation-superiority'—all of which are drowning you in mere names, words, and subtle meanings."
I bind you! Why? Because as long as even a single moment of deluded mind is not exhausted, this is the continuity of birth and death.
O worthy one, time does not wait for man; do not let the days pass by in negligence. Time is to be cherished. This old man does not expect you, a mere field-slave, to carry my burden.
If you are willing, then believe and take it up; if you are not willing, every person has their own bowl of excrement—take that away with you! Old man!
Han does not seek you out either. There are many old, shaven-headed slaves in all directions who occupy a particular place to speak of Chan and speak of the Way;
you must go quickly to learn from them and copy their words. In this place of mine, I ultimately have not a single dharma to give to you people.
You gentlemen, go ask them and learn from them to form your own intellectual understanding. This old man cannot enter the Hell of Plucking Out Tongues. If there were...
"A single speck of dust is a single dharma. To show this to all people, he says there is a Buddha and there is a Dharma, and that there are the three realms from which one may emerge;
these are all merely wild fox spirits and enchantments. Do you wish to recognize what "all people" are? They are simply empty space, wherein not even a trace of dust can be found.
Everywhere is pure; light penetrates through and through, transparent from the inside out. There is no desire and no reliance. No...
Regarding this place of rest: what business is there? From birth until death, I have been nothing but an old bhikṣu.
Although I am born within the triple world, I am free from defilement. If you wish to attain liberation, where could you go?
Even if there were a place to go, it would still be a cage, giving Māra an opportunity. You, virtuous one, need not employ body or mind; there is nothing to be attained. It simply requires all—

At that time, do not employ the sounds or forms of others. You should at once cast aside everything from your previous conduct, suddenly shedding all fetters and forever leaving behind the entanglements of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
When not a single thought arises, the past and future limits are severed; there is no thinking and no recollecting, and not a single dharma can be grasped by the mind.
O worthy one, how could you even attempt to open your mouth? You possess much knowledge and understanding, but have you ever...
Do you recognize his face? Even for an ordained one, up to a Bodhisattva who has reached the fulfillment of the tenth stage, his traces cannot be found.
For this reason, the devas rejoice, the earth deities support his feet, the Buddhas of the ten directions offer praise, and the Mara King weeps.
Why is this? Because this void is lively and agile; it has no root and no place of abiding. If...
Upon arriving here, if your eyes flicker and move, you have already missed the point. You, virtuous ones, must not seek the Buddha;
the Buddha is a great murderous thief who deceives many people, causing them to fall into the pit of the demon of lust. Do not seek Mañjuśrī or Samantabhadra; they are merely stewards of the fields.

Why begrudge such a thing? A single, dignified great man, having consumed that toxic medicine, immediately sets out to assume the countenance of a Chan master, seeing spirits and ghosts, becoming deranged in the future, wandering among others, seeking female shamans, and going to have divinations with clay figurines.
Then, some ignorant old bald slave immediately performs a divination for him, instructing him to prostrate before the ghost of the Patriarchs and the ghost of the Buddha.
The "ghost of Bodhi and Nirvana" is something this little harlot does not understand; she immediately asks, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
This old bald slave [Baizhang] then strikes his rope bed, creating a dramatic scene, and holding up his whisk, says, "Fine weather, fine rain;
fine lanterns. He artfully crafts his words and forcibly creates complications, claiming there is a mysterious path—a bird-track unfolding.
[He] takes [it] in his hand. If one were to speak thus: it is like taking a precious vessel and filling it with impurities;
it is like taking human excrement and treating it as sandalwood incense. O worthy one, since he is a man, so am I. Before whom would I feel timid?
Having spent the entire day at the mouths of various old, bald slaves from all quarters, receiving their spittle and saliva and eating it, I am without shame or remorse. Alas! Alas! How mad!
Go away, you fellow! Cause and effect are distinct. That water-buffalo, pulling the plow and grasping the handle, has its eyes bulging out, yet it lacks the strength to pull its weight.
A great club strikes its back; it robs the Buddhas of their food and clothing, yet claims, "I have attained cultivation and realization.
If you do not understand the Great Principle, even if you could pass through the Buddha’s belly, you would still be nothing more than a walking piece of dung. You have never—
If you encounter a good person, you will immediately recognize the light and shadow at the gates of the six sense organs;
you can then speak it from your mouth as a proclamation—words that are hidden yet wondrous, brilliant and fresh. But alas, what can you do? It is not your own portion, O benevolent one;
it is the spittle of another. Furthermore, there is another class of people, gathering in groups of three or two, who deliberate together, asking: "Where is there no [Buddha-nature]?"
Things are well. Having passed through winter and summer, you have spoken freely of Chan and the Way.

You who possess intellectual understanding and grasp at principles, O benevolent ones, all hold such views as these, seeking only convenience. How could there be such a principle? There will come a day when you enter hell;
do not say that I have not told you, my sons. Everywhere I go, I do not pick even a single stalk of vegetables, nor carry away even a bundle of firewood. One day—

When one's merit is exhausted, one will simply go to graze on grass. Having consumed the offerings of the faithful in vain and falsely claiming to be a seeker of the Way, you further affect the manner of a Zen master;
this is of no benefit to others. As for your own state, throughout the twelve hours of the day, in every place where you walk and act, your mind is constantly attached to external objects.
When seeing people, they desire only to appear seductive and coquettish; they wag their tails and point east while speaking of the west.
Though it is right before their eyes and at their very lips, they truly do not see it; they merely wish to use similar-sounding words to test for understanding.

Old man, how are you any different from all these people? Gentlemen, do not seek momentary satisfaction of the eyes or the tongue; having consumed his "poisonous medicine," you will become like lustful women.
Those who do not observe the precepts are blind, shaven-headed slaves and sheep-like monks; they overturn others and enter hell.

O worthy one, do not recklessly examine the *cèzǐ* (commentaries), seeking out phrases and meanings or hunting for victory and defeat. Passing them from hand to hand and mouth to mouth—when will this ever cease?
This old man’s exhortation is no evil thing; you must surely bring your own eyes with you to distinguish the pure from the turbid. These are the words of the Buddha.
These are the words of Māra. Do not allow yourself to be deluded by others. All those superior names and titles are merely the temporary, skillful devices of the old barbarian [the Buddha].
You must utterly cease from them; do not rely on a single thing, nor take up the words of others to form intellectual interpretations.

Discerning between kin and stranger, being frivolous, hollow, and deceitful, or memorizing the idle talk and long-winded speech of others—all these are merely *anumāna* (inferential cognition). O Benevolent One, the old...
I, Han, only fear that you sons will fall into pits and ditches, perform deeds of meager merit, and rely on mere lip-service.

Thinking they have gained enough by achieving little, they stand still in quiet places and refuse to advance. They delude themselves with various objects and wander aimlessly elsewhere, constantly circling through the myriad dharmas.
This is because they do not believe that empty space is fundamentally without affairs—that it cannot be increased or diminished. You people, take heed!
He resembles an old owl: his body is in the void, yet his mind is on a pile of dung, seeking only to eat dead things.
Disciples, do not say that this old man of Daoshan has never entered a monastic community; he debates with a loud voice, scolding those who lack human feeling, and he fears no karma.
It is simply because you disciples do not maintain your proper station, but instead gallop about in all directions, hanging at the doors of others—just like a woman.
A ghost of a senior monk. He transmits words and conveys messages; he interprets things according to their literal meaning and does not forget his mental traces. Even his own self is not established;
he constantly carries a corpse, bearing a cangue and wearing shackles for five hundred and one thousand li, until he arrives before Deshan.

Standing there with his eight characters [his name] fixed upon the ground, he appears as if he were in debt to this man regarding the Way of Chan. "Master, you must speak for me; point it out to me! This old fellow is completely...

"Body and function! This great staff and armor—this field-slave! You who revile the thief’s excrement-hole face and do not distinguish between good and evil, coming here to me is just like meeting a man from Liuzhou who eats a meal of fish stew and rotten broth.
It is simply to allow you to lay down your heavy burden and cast off your shackles, so that you may become a true person. Will you agree? If you agree, then stay; otherwise, depart."
"Agreed. Leave it as it is. Take care.
Xuefeng asked, "What was the meaning behind the ancients' slaying of the snake? The Master struck him. Xuefeng immediately ran off. The Master called out, "Wait!"
Punna was sweeping. Feng turned his head back. The Master said, "Only after he later attains enlightenment will he know that this old fellow’s heart is entirely that of a grandmother.
When the Master saw a monk approaching, he closed the door. The monk knocked on the door. The Master asked, "Who is it? The monk replied, "A lion cub. The Master opened the door; the monk prostrated.
The Master suddenly mounted him on the neck and said, "You beast! Where have you been coming from?"
A monk came to visit him and made a gesture like that of sumo wrestlers. The Master said, "To act so impolitely deserves a blow from this mountain monk’s staff.
The monk brushed his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "Even if you were such as this, you would only have received half [the teaching].
The monk turned around and shouted. The Master struck him, saying, "It must be I who strike you before it is right. The monk said, "In other quarters there are those who are enlightened..."
The monk said, "A person with eyes is here. The Master said, "Naturally possessed of eyes. The monk opened his eyes wide and said, "A cat! and then departed.
The Master said, "The Yellow River clears itself only once every three thousand years."

A monk asked, "When one encounters a person who has attained the Way on the road, one does not respond with speech or silence. I wonder, what will you use to respond? The Master said, "Just like this.
The monk remained silent for a long while. The Master said, "Ask me again. As the monk was about to ask once more, the Master gave a shout and sent him out.
Miaoxi said, "That was indeed a fine shout; it was simply delivered too late.
A monk asked, "What is bodhi? The Master said, "Get out! Do not defecate here. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "The Buddha is an old bhikṣu from the Western Heaven."
The Master was ill. A monk asked, "Is there anyone who does not fall ill? The Master said, "There is.
The monk asked, "Who is this one who does not fall ill? The Master said, "Ayaya! Ayaya!"

When the Master was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying: "To feel for echoes in the void exhausts your spirit; when the dream is over and you realize it was not real, what further matter remains?
Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed into stillness. This was on the third day of the twelfth month in the sixth year of the Xian-tong era (the year of Yiyou).
He was eighty-six years of age and had sixty-five years of ordination. His stupa was erected at his home mountain.
The Master of Baofeng in Hongzhou (the fifth instance): The Master asked Yantou, "In this way, in this way—how do you understand it?
Yantou said, "Not in this way, not in this way. The Master asked again, "How do you understand it?
Yantou said, "These are words of plain reality. The Master said, "Your belt has no hook. Yantou said, "It cannot be fastened around the waist. The Master said, "This is plain reality."
This is a true story.
A monk came from Yantou; the Master held up his whisk and said, "Those who fall under this device have not yet attained the eye.
As the monk was about to step forward, the Master said, "You have just fallen under this very device. The monk returned and related this to Yantou. Yantou—
[Zhaozhou] said, "If I were to see you, I would snatch away your whisk; let me see what you will do.
Upon hearing this, the Master [Touzi] held up his whisk and said, "I raise my whisk and let him snatch it away. But if he brings no object at all, what then?
Touzi heard this and said, "A scale without weights—what way is there to distinguish anything?"
The Master saw a monk reciting a sutra as he passed before the abbot’s quarters. The Master said, "Your mouth speaks to its full capacity, yet you simply lack the eye.
The monk pointed his finger at the Master and said, "Speak! Speak! The novice attendant standing by the Master's side asked, "Where is the eye?
The monk lifted one foot and said, "Just so, just so. The Master remarked, "Lowering the hook into the long river, they swallow it even without bait."
The monk then shouted, "This old monk, you have groundlessly smeared me with falsehood! The Master said, "A man-eating lion does not show its teeth.
The monk made a gesture as if biting. The Master said, "A large-trimmed hat is worn on another part of the head."
The Master asked a monk, "As for that matter within, it is easy to speak of; as for not falling into that matter within, it is difficult to speak of from beginning to end.
The monk said, "When I was on the road, I already knew there would be this question. The Master said, "Even if you had traveled for twenty more years, it would not have been much different.
The monk asked, "Is it that I did not accord with the Master's intent? The Master said, "A bitter gourd is hardly fit to entertain guests."
The Master asked a monk, "The ancients had a single path to receive beginners and those of later standing; do you know it? The monk said, "Please, Master, point it out.
The Master said, "If that were so, you would already have known it. The monk said, "That would be adding a head atop a head.
The Master said, "It was not fitting for this old monk to ask. The monk said, "What harm is there in asking? The Master said, "In my place, I have never allowed people to pass."
Disorderly! Get out! Chan Master Qingzhu of Shishuang in Tanzhou, Dharma Heir of Chan Master Zongzhi of Daowu in Tanzhou (twelfth generation).
A native of the Chen family of Luling. When the Master arrived at Mount Gui, he composed [this verse]:
The Head of the Rice Storehouse was winnowing rice. Mount Yun said, "This is the property of a donor; do not scatter it. The Master said, "I shall not scatter it.
On the ground, Mount Yun picked up a single grain of rice and showed it to the Master, saying, "You say you do not scatter it, yet from where did this come?
The Master remained silent. Mount Yun said, "Do not underestimate this one grain; hundreds of thousands of grains all come from this one."
"A grain grows. The Master said, "I wonder from where this single grain grows? Guishan laughed heartily and returned to his quarters.
That evening, he ascended the hall and said to the assembly, "There are worms in the rice!"
The Master asked Dao Wu, "What is bodhi as it meets the eye? Dao Wu called out, "Novice! The novice responded, "Yes?
Dao Wu said, "Add water to the pure jar. Dao Wu then asked, "What were you asking just now? As the Master was about to speak, Dao Wu rose and departed.
At this, the Master attained a secret realization.
Daowu said to the Master, "I am afflicted with illness and am about to depart this world. There is something within my heart that has long been a source of distress;
who can remove it for me? The Master replied, "Both the mind and its objects are non-existent. To attempt to remove them only increases the affliction. Daowu praised him.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The temporal teachings of a single lifetime are for the purpose of adjusting the hands and feet of people of this age. Whatever has a causal origin falls into the realm of 'this present time.
Even reaching the ultimate principle of the teaching—that the Dharma-body is no body—is still merely the pinnacle of the doctrinal school.
For us śramaṇas, there is no path of acquiescence. To differentiate is to err; not to differentiate is to sit mired in the mud and water."
A monk asked, "Within a mere span of a few feet, why do I not behold the Master’s countenance? The Master said, "I say that the entire world has never been hidden.
Later, the monk asked Xuefeng, "What is the meaning of 'the entire world has never been hidden'? Xuefeng said, "Where is it not Shishuang?
The monk returned and related this to the Master. The Master said, "What kind of desperate urgency does this old fellow have?"
Xuansha said, "The old fellow on the mountainhead has missed it. Dongshan said, "He makes the local deity laugh to death.
Langya Huijue said, "Although Xuefeng had the intention to benefit others, he lacked the eye to transcend them."
Although Shishuang possessed eyes that surpassed others, he did not yet know the uppermost aperture.
A monk asked, "The spiritual bone of the former master was golden in color; when struck, it produced the sound of a bell.
I wonder, where has it gone? The Master called to the monk. The monk responded. The Master said, "You do not understand my words. Begone!"
A monk took his leave of his teacher, who asked him, "By boat or by land? The monk replied, "If I meet a boat, I take the boat; if I meet land, I take the land.
The teacher said, "I say that the halfway point will be somewhat difficult. The monk was speechless.

Yunmen, acting as his representative, said: "Thirty years from now, this story will spread far and wide. He also said: "The words spoken at the moment of departure shall not be forgotten for eternal kalpas. A monk asked: "From three thousand li away, we have heard that Shishuang has a 'non-regard. When the brilliant faculty does not rely on the business of sharp edges, what matter is there here? O Ācārya, let the thread upon the fishing pole be played with by you as you will.
"Not transgressing the clear ripples, one’s intent is naturally distinct.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If someone were to suddenly ask me, I would tell them: 'Upon the tips of the hundred grasses, bring all the affairs of your life to rest.'"
Even the roots and stumps leave no trace. The old monk sits in his own place; where he sits, no captive remains.
Ācārya, to recognize the Son of Heaven within the palace hall, or to recognize the true Master within the house—what use is that? You must go out to the gate of the bustling marketplace.
Recognize the celestial son; to discern the old monk at the tips of the hundred grasses is to be a man of true effort.
The golden crow leaves no trace of wind or clouds; how could the waterfowl cross the Nine Heavens? Under the bright moon at night, the hook is hidden; one knows not into whose hands it has fallen.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "I, the old monk, have established a selection hall at the head of the ancient path. If there is one who advances alone, I shall let them pass.
If there is one who belongs to the inner circle, there is yet another path for them. There is no dharma before the eyes; the intent lies within the eyes.
It is not a dharma of the present moment; it is beyond the reach of ears and eyes. Heaven has no cause; earth has no effect. The sun and moon merely circulate."
Turning within the void: even if a blue pool is as clear as a mirror, it will ultimately make it difficult for the bright moon to descend.
You may sing the Hu melodies as you wish; the Qin zither is plucked in the night. Beyond the sound of clarity lies the meaning, which has no concern with others. Ācārya!
The dragon has no phrase of being a dragon; it does not follow its original form. A swift horse does not display its wind-bone. An old monk once said: "Heaven has no merit of moving illumination;

Seeking it mistakenly within the water; the Nine Yangs follow another, for even the Son of Heaven is noble. When the golden crow declines in the west, one must surely grieve.
The empty gate has no intention of being bound by locks; wind and clouds do not concern those who stand between two worlds.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "For twenty years I have lived on this mountain, and I have never once raised a single matter concerning the School of the Patriarchs.

One day, a monk asked, "I have heard it said that you, Master, have remarked that for twenty years you have lived on this mountain and have never once raised a matter concerning the School of the Patriarchs—is this true?

"Please, dig a pit. Have the attendant summon the monk who engaged in dialogue yesterday. The monk then came forth.

If you do not beat me to death, then you shall beat yourself to death and bury yourself in this pit."
Just as he was about to attain it, that monk returned to the hall, packed his belongings, and departed in secret.
Under the Master’s guidance, there was a monk who went to Shishuang; as soon as he entered the gate, he said, "How do you do? Shishuang replied, "Not necessary."
The monk said, "In that case, take care. He then went to Yantou and said, "I hope you are well? Yantou sighed twice. The monk said, "In that case, take care.

When the monk returned and related this to the Master (Linji), the Master ascended the hall the following day and called out, "Yesterday’s one who returned from Shishuang and Yantou!"
"Teacher, come forth! Raise this according to the Dharma. When the monk had stepped forward and finished recounting the previous conversation, the Master said, "Does the assembly understand?
If no one speaks, I shall not spare my two eyebrows; let me speak! He then said, "Although Shishuang possesses the sword that kills, he lacks the sword that gives life.
Yantou also possesses the sword that kills, and likewise the sword that gives life."
"Human Sword.
Miaoxi said, "One must not speak of dreams in the presence of a fool.
There was once a patriarch in Western Shu who lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and asked Baima: "At one time, a single mote of dust contained the infinite Dharma-realm..."

"How is it? Mazu replied, "It is like the two wheels of a cart, or the two wings of a bird. The Master said, "I thought there was something extraordinary and unique in the Chan school, but it turns out it does not go beyond the teachings of the scriptures.
He then returned to his original station. Later, hearing that the Master was flourishing in his propagation of the Dharma, he dispatched a junior monk.
He took up the previous conversation and questioned the Master. The Master said, "Carving sand yields no talk of engraved jade; binding grasses contradicts the thoughts of a man of the Way.
The junior monk returned and reported this to his own teacher, who praised him, saying, "I thought the meaning of the Chan school was no different from that of the Teachings;
it turns out there is something truly extraordinary here."

The Master had a junior disciple who was traveling on pilgrimage. Hearing that the Master’s reputation for the Way resounded far and wide, he returned to visit him and said, "Master, you possess such extraordinary and marvelous qualities;
why did you not tell them to me? The Master replied, "When you were steaming rice, I lit the fire;
when you were walking, I spread out my bowl. Where was I failing you? From this, the junior disciple attained enlightenment.
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Dongshan. The Master said, "What sayings or phrases did he have?
He replied, "Ordinarily, he permits people to study the three paths: the Path of Mystery, the Bird’s Path, and the Outstretched Hand. The Master said, "Is it true that he spoke these words?
He replied, "Yes. The Master said, "A guidebook for a thousand miles; a lament for the practitioners beneath the forest trees."
The Master asked the Senior Monk Houtou, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Hunan. The Master said, "Have you been to Shishuang?
He replied, "I had to pass through that main road; how could I not have reached it? I have heard that Shishuang has the 'ball' koan—is this true?
He replied, "Even you, Master, must keep your eyes open before you can succeed. The Master said, "What is this ball? He replied, "It cannot leap out."
The Master said, "What is a ball-stick? [The monk] said, "Do not use hands or feet.
The Master said, "I have never known you, Reverend; get out!"
Xuedou said, "He personally saw this monk coming from Shishuang; why did he say, 'I do not know you'?
The next day, the Master ascended the hall and called out, "Is that newly arrived one still here? Houtou responded, "Yes. The Master said:
"It cannot be grasped at present. It is intended for the present moment, yet it is not a dharma of the present moment. It is not something reached by the ears or eyes.
Deshan said, "Though we are together today, it is nonetheless not so. Linji said, "Though the crescent moon is bright, it has nothing to do with heaven and earth.
Deshan said, "Do not stir up a boiling cauldron," and he made a gesture as if to overturn the meditation seat. Linji said, "Wait, wait! How could you possibly wrong the Venerable One?"
[Daowu] raised his head, stood up, and with his fist clenched, said: "Can you endure this before your very eyes? The Master said: "An adept, an adept.
Daowu then made a gesture of overturning the meditation seat. The Master said: "The assembly, look at this warrior!
As for establishing the gate of the school, I am not his equal; but as for entering deeply into the principle and discussing it, he still falls short of me by one step."
[The Master] was at Jidi Monastery. A monk asked, "What is the 'dharma-less state' of the present moment? The Master said, "The night moon flows with radiance; the clear pool has no reflection.
The monk made a gesture as if to overturn the meditation seat. The Master said, "How about you, Elder? The monk said, "There is no dharma before the eyes; it is finished."
"It cannot be grasped. The Master said, "The assembly, look! This is a warrior.
A monk asked, "When one sweeps away the dust to see the Buddha, what then? The Master said, "If you wish to know this matter, you must brandish the sword.
If you do not brandish the sword, the fisherman will nest in his hut. Later, the monk asked Shishuang. Shishuang said, "He has no land; where [could he be]?"
When the monk returned, he related this to the Master. The Master said, "As for establishing the gate and providing expedient means, Jiangshan is certainly not lacking;
yet, when it comes to a profound discourse on entering into principle, he is still a hundred paces behind Shishuang."
A monk asked, "What is a 'similar phrase'? The Master said, "The lotus leaf is round and round, as round as a mirror;

the water chestnut is pointed and pointed, as pointed as an awl. He spoke again, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The wind blows the willow catkins like a ball;
the rain beats the pear blossoms as butterflies fly."
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "The great sun with eyes closed; ten thousand miles without a single speck of cloud.
The monk asked, "How does one realize this? The Master said, "In the clear, pure water, the swimming fish are naturally lost."
A monk asked, "How can one recognize the supreme treasure within the home? The Master said, "In the midst of busyness, how can one become a person at leisure?
The monk asked, "If I intend to pose a question, will you grant me permission? The Master said, "When the four seas are devoid of fish, it is in vain to cast down the hook.
The monk asked, "What is 'one who is old and one who is not old'? The Master said, "The green mountains never move; the mountain stream flows forever."
Holding a *yeming* (night-illuminating) talisman in hand, how many know when day breaks? [A monk] asked, "What is the practice of a śramaṇa?
The Master said, "Movement brings forth its shadow; awakening gives rise to ice."
Chan Master Dàtóng of Tóuzǐ in Shūzhōu, Successor of Chan Master Wúxué of Cuīwēi in Jìngzhào Prefecture (Fifteenth): He was a native of the Liú family in Huáiníng County of this province.
Initially, he visited Cuīwēi and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Cuīwēi looked at him. As the Master was about to offer a reply, Cuīwēi said:
"Furthermore, you need a second ladle of foul water! From this, the Master realized that [the student's] understanding had penetrated samādhi.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you come here seeking fresh phrases and sentences, weaving patterns like brocade and clustering flowers, hoping to have something worth saying in your mouths.
I, an old man, am somewhat lacking in strength and my speech is dull; I have neither idle talk nor long-winded discourse."
It has reached you. If you question me, I shall answer you accordingly; there is nothing profound or mysterious that surpasses you.
Nor do I teach you to rely on rote memorization; I will never speak of "above" or "below," nor of "Buddha" or "Dharma," nor of "ordinary beings" or "sages."
Nor do I maintain that sitting [in meditation] binds you people. The thousandfold manifestations are all your own productions of understanding;
you have brought them along with you yourself, and thus you receive what you yourself have made. Here, there is nothing to give to you, nor do I dare to deceive you.
Without exterior or interior, it can be explained to you—do you understand? At that time, a monk asked: "When neither exterior nor interior is grasped..."
"How so? The Master said, "What do you intend to do here? You are trying to turn your heels backward.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "All of you, your mouths are like knives or tweezers; what place for them to land? Even so, do not flaunt your cleverness.
If you say there is something that is not confused, I will strike you down. Do not say I did not warn you."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Everyone says that Touzi is straightforward. Suppose, however, that after you have gone down three steps from the mountain, someone asks you about the matter of Touzi’s straightforwardness—how will you respond?"
One day, the Master pointed to a rock in front of his hermitage and asked Xuefeng, "All the Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely contained within this.
Xuefeng said, "One must know that there are those who are not contained within it. The Master said, "A clumsy, lacquered barrel!"
One day, while traveling with Xuefeng at Longmian, there were two paths along the way. Xuefeng asked, "Which one is the road to Longmian?
The Master pointed it out with his staff. Xuefeng said, "Going east? Going west? The Master replied, "A miserable lacquer bucket!"
Xuefeng asked the Master, "Is there anyone here who can practice Zen? The Master took up his hoe and tossed it before him.
Xuefeng said, "If that is so, then I shall dig right here. The Master said, "You are a clumsy, lacquer-coated bucket."
Xuefeng asked, "What is it like when one is perfected by a single blow? The Master said, "Not a man of impulsive temperament.
Xuefeng asked, "What is it like when no single blow is required? The Master said, "An unbaked lacquer bucket."
Xuedou said: "In that case, although Xuefeng was once brought low, Touzi was a master of the forge.
At that time, had I been Xuefeng, when Touzi said, 'He is not a man of impulsive temper,' I would have simply told him:
'The tongs and hammer are in my hands. All you venerable monks, you should have been able to apply this to Touzi."
"What kind of words are these? If you can speak them, then you shall have spent your life in a state of radiant intensity, glorifying the eye of the school.
If you are merely vague and indistinct, I shall strike you once upon the crown of your head—do not say I did not warn you."
The Master was at Tóngchéng County. Because of this, Zhàozhōu asked him, "Are you not the Abbot of Tóuzǐ Hermitage?
The Master replied, "I have come to receive an offering of tea and salt money. Zhàozhōu returned to the hermitage first and saw the Master returning with oil himself.
Zhàozhōu said, "I have long heard of Tóuzǐ; having arrived, I see only an oil-seller. The Master said, "You see only the oil-seller; you do not yet see [me]."
Zhaozhou asked, "What is Touzi? The Master held up a water jar and said, "Oil, oil.
Zhaozhou asked, "What is it like when one attains life within death? The Master said, "Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive by dawn."
Zhaozhou said, "I have long been white-throated; you are even blacker.
When Chan guest Juyong came to visit him, the Master said, "I, this old monk, have never had so much as a single word or half-sentence to hang on the lips or teeth of those from all quarters.
Why trouble yourself to see me? Juyong said, "If I do not offer three prostrations upon reaching here, I simply cannot bear it."
The Master said, "A renunciant should be thus without a memorial stone. He circumambulated the meditation seat once and departed.
The Master said, "Having eyes but no ears, sitting by the fire in the sixth month."
Xuedou said: "One must not let him go; as soon as he turns, seize him! Who would not resent this?
If you can leap out, you will undoubtedly be a true Chan practitioner."
Daguang Zhe said: "Although this monk is well-versed in the battlefields, he cannot help but encounter Touzi’s skillful breaking and crushing.
Why? If true gold is not forged in the furnace, how can its brilliance emerge with such thorough clarity?"
A monk asked, "What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies? The Master descended from his rope bed and stood there. The monk asked again, "How far apart are the ordinary person and the sage?
The Master likewise descended from his rope bed and stood there.
Xuedou said: "Everyone knows this koan thoroughly. If it were presented in such a manner, all the monks under heaven would become like Du Fu, merely reciting the words.
Does Xuedou have no point of excellence? Let me try to present it for the sake of the great assembly:
how far apart are the ordinary and the sage? Touzi descended from his meditation seat and stood there. What does this mean?"
This is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies. Touzi descended from his meditation seat and stood there.
Tell me, is this the same as what was raised previously, or is it different? If you say they are the same, I grant you, Elder, one eye.
If you say they are different and possess some extraordinary quality, I also grant you, Elder, one eye. Furthermore, let us open another path: the ordinary and the sage.
"How far apart are they? Please, Senior, offer a turning phrase. What is the 'Tamer of the Ten Bodies'?
Please, Senior, give one word in reply. Not only will you have visited and seen Touzi, but you will also know the excellence of Xuedou.
If you simply say, "He descended from his meditation seat and stood there," then cherish your eyebrows well!
A monk asked, "Is it true that all sounds are the voice of the Buddha? The Master said, "Yes. The monk said, "Master, do not mistake the sound of a boiling pot for a bell.
The Master then struck him. Again he asked, "Is it true that coarse words and subtle speech both return to the primary meaning?
The Master said, "Yes. The monk said, "May I call you a donkey? The Master then struck him.
A monk asked, "How is it when one enters nirvana without severing afflictions? The Master changed his expression and said, "This monk is well-suited to stir up karma and kill people."
Xitang Zang said, "Every household has its Avalokiteśvara.
Guoqing Ji said, "If someone were to ask this mountain monk, 'How is it when one enters nirvana without severing afflictions?
I would strike them across the face with my palm. Why? Because if you do not seize it when you see it, it will be a thousand miles away when you think of it."
A monk asked, "Vaguely it resembles the crescent moon; faintly it is like the three stars. Neither heaven nor earth can contain it—where does the Master perceive it?
The Master said, "What are you saying? The monk said, "I imagine that you have only the ripples on still water, but lack the waves that flood the heavens. The Master said, "Idle talk."
Xuedou said: "Touzi was an ancient Buddha; one cannot say he did not know. Yet, if one were to examine it closely, there is a vast distance between them as wide as heaven and earth.
As soon as [a question] was asked, he struck him with his voice."
A monk asked, "The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition. For what purpose does the Master appear in the world?
The Master replied, "Minister Yin has today opened the hall for this old monk."
There was an old woman who went up the mountain and said, "I have lost my cow at home; I beg the Master to divine its whereabouts for me. The Master called out to the woman, and she responded.
The Master said, "The cow is here."
A questioner asked, "How is it before the golden rooster has crowed? The Master said, "There is no such sound. The questioner asked, "How is it after it has crowed?
The Master said, "Each knows its own time."
Question: "What is it like when the moon is not yet full? The Master said, "Swallowing three or four. Question: "What is it like after it is full?
The Master said, "Vomiting up seven or eight."
Question: "What is it like when Bodhidharma has not yet arrived? The Master said: "Pervading heaven and pervading earth. Question: "What is it like after he has arrived?
The Master said: "It cannot be covered over."
Question: "What is 'insentient beings preaching the Dharma'? The Master said: "Do not speak ill. Question: "The lion is the king among beasts;

why is it swallowed by the six sense-objects? The Master said: "It does not act as a great being; it is free from self and others. Question: "I bring this raw jade to you, Master; I pray you polish it for me. The Master said: "It is not timber fit for a ridgepole. Question:

"Within the entire Tripitaka of the Buddhist teachings, is there still anything extraordinary? The Master said: "There is. Question: "What is it? The Master said: "The Great Way is not difficult; it simply avoids picking and choosing."

"Even 'special matters' do not exist. The Master said, "I have performed a single recitation of the entire Tripitaka. A questioner asked, "When you, Reverend, dwell on this mountain, what kind of realm do you experience?
The Master said, "A girl with twin-tailed hair has white strands among her locks. The questioner asked, "How old are you, Reverend? The Master said:
Spring breeze, and again spring breeze.
Zen Master Runu of Mount Daochang in Huzhou (Fanyi). A monk asked, "How can one ensure that the nature of hearing does not follow conditions?
The Master said, "Listen! The monk bowed. The Master said, "A deaf man singing a Hu song—how good or bad it is!"
"High and low are naturally unheard; yet how can it be said that the nature of hearing is perfectly intact? The Master said: "A stone stands from within the void;
fire burns within the water.
Chan Master Lingzun of Qingping in Ezhou (three instances). He asked Cuibei: "What is the Patriarch’s West?"
Dongmi said, "My intention in coming was this: I wished for you to wait until we were in a secluded place, and then I would explain it to you.

After a long silence, the Master said, "There is no one here. Please, Preceptor, speak. Dongmi led the Master into a bamboo grove. The Master spoke again, "There is still no one here. Please, Preceptor, speak.
Dongmi pointed to the bamboo and said, "This stalk—how can it be so long? That stalk—how can it be so short? At these words, the Master attained his realization.
Later, while residing at Qingping, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The former master went through mud and water for my sake; since then, I have not recognized good from evil.
A monk asked, "What is the Mahāyāna? The Master said, "A well-rope. [The monk] asked, "What is the Hīnayāna? The Master said, "Money."
Xuefeng asked, "What is that which is with outflows (sāsrava)? The Master said, "A bamboo fence. Xuefeng asked, "What is that which is without outflows (anāsrava)?
The Master said, "A wooden ladle. Xuefeng asked, "What is it when presented face-to-face? The Master said, "Hand it over to the head cook."
A monk asked, "What is Chan? The Master said, "A monkey climbing a tree, tail and head trailing together.
Chan Master Zhaoshan Guangren (1) addressed the assembly, saying: "Is there anyone who has not failed their lifelong eyes and ears enough to come forward with a question?
At that time, a monk stepped forth and prostrated. The Master said, "Let it be that you have failed me; but as for the great assembly, why is this so?"
He then returned to his quarters. Later, a monk requested instruction, saying: "When the Master ascended the seat, he said, 'As for those who have failed me, let them follow the assembly.
What was the meaning of this? The Master said: "At mealtime there is rice for you to eat; at night there is a bed for you to sleep on.
Why do you constantly press and harass me? The monk bowed. The Master said: "How painful! How painful! The monk said: "I beg [for your further instruction]."
The Master gave him instruction. The Master lowered his foot and said, "Stretching and contracting are left entirely to this old monk.
Chan Master Baiyun Yue of Jianzhou (Case 1): National Teacher Shao came to see the Master. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From north of the river.
The Master asked, "Did you come by boat or by land? He replied, "By boat. The Master asked, "Did you encounter any fish or turtles on the way? He replied, [He did not answer.]
He encountered him frequently. The Master asked, "What is it like when you encounter him? Shao gave a shout and said, "Withdraw your head! The Master then laughed heartily.
Heshang Mo-yuan of Xizhou, Dharma heir of Heshang Xing-kong of Jizhou (Case 1).
When Pingtian arrived, the Master rose from his seat. Pingtian seized him and said, "Open your mouth!"
[If you] lose it immediately; [if you] close your mouth, you lose it immediately. At this very moment, I ask the Master to speak. The Master covered his ears with his hands.
Tianfeng released his hand and said, "One step is easy; two steps are difficult. The Master said, "What such urgent haste is there?
Tianfeng said, "Were it not for the Master, one could not avoid being scrutinized by those in all quarters."
The Sixth Generation under Qingyuan:
Chan Master Yantou Quanhuo of Ezhou, Dharma Heir of Chan Master Deshan Xuanjian of Dingzhou (Total:
fourteen). A native of the Ke clan of Quanzhou, he first visited Deshan and held [the master’s staff].

While sitting on his meditation mat, the Master went up to the Dharma Hall to pay his respects. Deshan said, "What is this? The Master then gave a shout. Deshan asked, "Where does the old monk’s fault lie?
The Master replied, "A double case," and then descended to attend the assembly hall. Deshan remarked, "What a fine master! You are somewhat like a true wandering monk.
The next day, the Master went up again to inquire after him. Deshan said, "Are you not the one who was 'new' yesterday?"
Damo replied, "Yes. Xuefeng asked, "Where did you learn this pretense? Damo said, "I truly do not dare deceive myself.
Xuefeng said, "In the future, you must not let me down."
One day, as the Master was entering to pay his respects, he had only just stepped across the threshold when he asked, "Is this ordinary or is it sacred?
Shanshan gave a shout, and the Master prostrated himself. Upon hearing of this, Dongshan said, "If it were not for Master Huo, it would have been very difficult to handle. The Master remarked, "..."

This old fellow Dongshan did not recognize good from bad; he mistakenly applied names and phrases. Little did he know that at that time, I was both raising up with one hand and pressing down with the other.
Xuedou said: "Thus, under Deshan’s gate, things were like grass bowing before the wind; yet even so, he could not silence the mouths of the world.
At that time, as soon as [Dongshan] prostrated, Deshan struck him across the back with his staff.
This not only cut off Dongshan, but also seized hold of Old Huo. Do you understand? The General already possesses his own glorious reputation."
"Not being granted a fief as a marquis is also idleness. Jiaochong Guang said: "Do you know where these three great elders ended up?
Deshan collapsed with his whole body; Dongshan dragged through water and mud.

Had it not been for Yantou’s possession of the eye that penetrates all quarters, how could the merit of those who sweated like horses in battle have been revealed? But tell me, what is 'raising with one hand'?"
The place where a single hand grasps is both the sword that kills and the blade that gives life.
When the Master, together with Xuefeng and Qinshan, took leave of Deshan, Deshan asked, "Where are you going?
The Master said, "I am taking temporary leave of the Master to go down the mountain. Deshan asked, "What will you do after this? The Master said, "I shall not forget the Master. Deshan—
[Shishuang] Yun: "On what basis do you say such a thing? The Master said: "Have you not heard it said: 'If one's wisdom is equal to the teacher's, one lacks half the virtue;
only when one's wisdom exceeds that of the teacher is one fit for transmission'? [Shishuang] Yun: "So it is, so it is. Guard and uphold this well."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Now, regarding matters within the great fundamental principles of our school, one must recognize the 'phrase' (*ju*).

If you do not recognize the phrase, it will be difficult to form a true understanding of the teaching. What is the phrase? When there is no thought of anything at all, this is called the 'right phrase.
It is also called 'dwelling on the summit,' 'attaining stability,' 'vivid clarity,' 'alertness,' 'precise certainty,' and 'the time before the Buddha was born.'"

It is also called "attaining the ground," and it is also called "at such a time. By means of "at such a time," one equally shatters all that is right and wrong. As soon as it is "thus," it is no longer "thus"; it turns and rolls about.
If you cannot see through this, the moment you are pricked by another, your eyes will stare blankly, like a sheep that cannot be killed. Have you not seen the ancient say: "Sinking..."?
It is not good to be muddled. You must be able to turn it about before you can succeed. As soon as you touch it, it turns. Just as it is so, it is no longer so.
This phrase is struck down; that phrase is also struck down. It turns of itself, rolling on and on. It reveals itself of itself, nakedly before one’s eyes.
Satiated and full, one neither understands nor fails to understand; one does not even bite. It is said: "To withdraw from things is superior; to pursue things is inferior."
This is for those of inferior capacity; if even a slight emotion flickers up, one has already fallen to the ground. If it were the "biting pig and barking dog" eye, it would be blazing red.
If someone were to ask, "What is Chan?", you would tell them, "Shut your anus! Only then would there be some breath of life remaining.
Thus one immediately knows the depth and shallowness; it is stubborn and rigid. You must recognize this face of the wildcat. At such a time, do not intentionally strike it, nor do you measure it.
Among them, there is a certain kind of person who, upon encountering an object, does not know how to turn away; when pricked, they defecate uncontrollably.
As for those of this sort, even if you were to beat a hundred thousand million of them to death, there would be no sin.
It is a mistake. If it were one of true substance, he would spring up the moment he was touched, biting with the urgency of fire;
he would be like a porcupine, busily preening his quills before anyone has even touched him—how pitiful! As soon as someone brushes against him, he immediately becomes enraged and snaps at them.
What proximity is there? If you have not yet attained such a state of vast openness, calling this "relying on the phrase" is a mistake.
In practice, whenever there is something, it must be equally shattered. At such a time, not a single thing remains.
One comes to know with certainty that all the phrases learned from the beginning have been confined within the chest; what use are they?

It is not a matter of setting aside views and setting aside phrases, of not allowing them to enter from without nor letting them go out from within. By cutting off both ends, one naturally becomes luminous and clear. Not...
To be in opposition to a single thing is itself the Samādhi of Non-contention. Brothers, if you wish to understand it easily, simply grasp it clearly at the root.

When you are about to emerge but do not yet emerge, you must turn [the light back upon itself]. Once you have bitten through with a single mouthful, there is no need to seek the distance of its coming and going;
simply let go, and it will naturally reveal itself in its nakedness. There is no need for conceptualizing or grasping; it is beyond the reach of delusion.

It is a state of spiritual darkness. As soon as there is the slightest attachment, it becomes a habitual trap. The ancients called this the "disease of the garment clinging to the body"; it is the most difficult to cure.
When I was traveling on pilgrimage in the past, I studied under one or two venerable masters who instructed me only to maintain constant vigilance day and night.
I sat until my buttocks grew calluses and my mouth ran with saliva; at first, I was inside the belly of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
It is pitch black. You say you are sitting in meditation, guarding [the mind] at such a time, yet desire still remains.
Have you not heard it said: "To be without dependence and without desire is itself the Capable One (Śākyamuni)"? An ancient said:
"If one places poison in milk, it can kill even when it has become clarified butter (*sarpis*). This is not something you can acquire through study; this is not something you can go [attain]."
It abides at the bottom. It is not that which is within your own form. Do not mistake the gate and the doorway;

do not let yourself be deceived on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, ending up in a state of frantic turmoil to no avail. You must not engage in artificiality or fabricate wonders. Simply know how to put on your clothes and eat your food.
When defecating or urinating, attend to these matters as they arise; do not act with disorderly arrogance and falsely claim to be a "Wayman" (*dào zhě*).
You have but this single robe, yet you dare not take it out to dry for fear that others might see it and cause you to lose your reputation as a Wayman, seeking instead the praise of others.
To act in such a manner is not to practice from the heart. Brothers, you must also not trust those old, gnarled blocks on the meditation benches who simply squat and defecate on the floor.
I thought you were merely a person skilled at deception, creating a separate hell to cast me into; now I truly know that the ancient style is excellent. Have you not heard it said:
"What exists is non-existent, and what is non-existent exists"? When one presents [the matter] in such a way, one immediately knows its depth. This is the ancient standard.

A dot. A dot that opens the eyes of all Bodhisattvas. Second, toward the west, place a dot below: this is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of all Bodhisattvas.
Third, toward the zenith, place a dot below: this is the opening at the crown of the heads (*mūrdhadvāra*) of all Bodhisattvas.

A monk came from the assembly of Guanyin. With his hand, he drew a circle on the left and a circle on the right, and then drew a circle in the center—just as it was about to be completed, but not yet finished—the Master gave it a single flick with his hand. The monk had no reply, so the Master shouted him out.
As the monk was leaving, the Master called him back and asked, "Are you not from Guanyin in Hongzhou? He replied, "I am. The Master said, "Just..."

[The Master] asked, "Regarding the circular mark on the left side that just appeared—what is it? [The student] said, "It is the 'sentence of existence' (*yǒujù*). The Master said, "What about the circular mark on the left side?

[The student] said, "It is the 'sentence of non-existence' (*wújù*). The Master said, "And what about the circular mark in the center? [The student] said, "It is the 'sentence of neither existence nor non-existence' (*bùyǒubùwújù*).
The Master said, "But as for my doing this—what then? [The student] said, "It is like slicing through water with a knife. The Master then struck him.
He immediately chased him out.
When the Master saw Shushan approaching, he began to sleep soundly. Shushan stood before him; the Master paid him no heed.
Shushan struck the meditation seat once. The Master looked back and asked, "What are you doing? Shushan replied, "Master, please stop dozing off," and then departed.
"Go! The Master laughed heartily and said, "For thirty years I have been riding a horse, but today I have been thrown by a donkey.
A monk of Linji had once made a grand boast, saying, "If I were to see him, I would pluck out his beard. One day, that monk arrived.
He prostrated himself. As he was about to rise but had not yet risen, the Master took a corner of his patched robe and gave him a single sweep across his face.

The monk remained speechless; shedding tears, he departed. Another monk took his leave. The Master asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going into the mountains to pay my respects to Xuefeng. The Master said, "Snow..."

for only three copper coins, I bought a dredging net. I am passing my time just so, catching shrimp and clams. When the monk arrived at Xuefeng, Xuefeng asked, “Where have you come from?
He replied, “I have come from Yantou. Xuefeng asked, “What words or phrases did he speak? The monk recounted the previous conversation, and Xuefeng said:
"You poor ghost-child! You have attained such great joy.
A monk asked, "How is it when the three realms arise in competition? The Master said, "Sit down and shut them up. The monk said, "I do not understand what you mean, Master.
The Master said, "If you could move Mount Lu here, then I would tell you."
Question: "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said: "A small fish swallows a large fish. Question:
"In the midst of the vast dust of the world, how does one discern the host? The Master said: "A copper strainer filled to the brim with oil. Question:

"When you encounter a fierce tiger on the road, what then? The Master said: "Press! Question: "Without a teacher, is there still a way to manifest oneself? The Master said: "The ancient felt robe before the sound."

[The Master] laughed. He asked, "When a sharp sword cuts through the world, who is it that stands directly before the blade? The Master said, "Darkness. When the monk prepared to offer a reply, the Master said, "Dull-witted fellow!"
Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun of Fuzhou (total of forty-six cases), a native of the Zeng family of Quanzhou. After leaving the mountain ranges, the Master first visited Yanguan.
Thereafter, he went to Touzi three times and to Dongshan nine times, but his karmic conditions did not harmonize with them. He later studied under Deshan.
He then asked, "In the matter of the School of the Patriarchs (zōngchéng), does a student still have a share in it or not? As soon as he spoke, Master Shàn struck him with his staff.

At that moment, the Master felt as if the bottom had fallen out of a bucket. Shàn spoke to him again, saying, "In my school there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to anyone."
When Yantou heard this, he said, "Deshan’s backbone is as hard as iron.
Nevertheless, within the gate of proclaiming the Teaching, he is still slightly inferior.
Baofu asked Zhaqing, "As for Yantou appearing in the world, what words or phrases of his surpassed those of Deshan such that you speak in this way? Zhaqing replied, "You do not..."
Yantou said, "It is like a person learning archery; only after a long time does one hit the mark. Fuyuan asked, "What is it like after hitting the mark?
Yantou replied, "Stretch out, Master! Do you not recognize pain and itchiness? Fuyuan said, "Does the Master not merely cite this story?
Yantou replied, "Stretch out, Master! What kind of mental activity is that?"
Mingzhao said: "The great and small Zhaoqing were mistaken in their choice of words.
When the Master was at Dongshan, serving as the head cook, he was once washing rice when Dongshan asked: 'Are you washing away the sand to keep the rice, or washing away the rice to keep the sand?'"
The Master said, "The rice and the sand go away all at once. Dongshan asked, "What will the assembly eat? The Master turned the rice bowl upside down.
Deshan said, "According to you, this karmic connection should have belonged to Deshan."
Langya Jue said: "Xuefeng acting like this is much like abandoning a tree of sweet peaches to climb the mountain and pick sour pears.
Dongshan asked the Master, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Tiantai. Dongshan asked, "Did you see Zhiyi? The Master—
[Yunmen] said, "Yi-cun has a share in being struck with an iron staff.
Dongshan asked the Master, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "I have come from hewing a trough. Dongshan said, "How many blows of the axe did it take to complete it?
The Master said, "It was completed with a single blow of the axe. Dongshan said, "That is still a matter of this side; what about the matter of that side? The Master said:
He was completely at a loss for where to begin. Dongshan said, "That is still a matter of this side. What about the matter of that side?

Fenyang Shanzhao spoke on his behalf, saying, "I am already exhausted."

Yunmen asked, "Since you do not know him, how do you know he has no face? The Master had no reply.
Langya Huijue said: "Those with coarse minds miss it.

When the Master was serving as the head cook at Deshan, one day the meal was late. While the Master was drying his rice-cloth, he saw Deshan carrying his alms-bowl toward the front of the Dharma Hall.
The Master said, "Old fellow, the bell has not yet rung and the drum has not yet sounded; where are you going with this bowl?"
"Where have you been? Deshan then returned to his quarters. The Master related this to Yantou, who said, "Great as he is, Deshan does not understand the final word.
Upon hearing this, Deshan ordered his attendant to summon Yantou. Deshan asked, "Do you not approve of me, old monk?
Yantou subtly conveyed his meaning, and Deshan desisted. The next day, when Deshan ascended the hall, it was indeed different from his usual manner. Yantou...
Arriving before the Sangha Hall, he clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "I am truly glad that the old man at the head of the hall has realized the final word.
Hereafter, no one in the world will be able to do anything with him. Nevertheless, he added, "Even so, he shall only last for three years.
After three years, he indeed passed away.
Mingzhao spoke on behalf of Deshan, saying: "Tut! Tut! Nowhere to go! Nowhere to go! Xuedou said:

Yesterday is not the same as today. Do you all wish to understand the final phrase?

One day, the Master and Yantou arrived at Aoshan Inn and were detained by the snow. While the Master sat continuously in meditation, Yantou did nothing but strike [the air].

You have traveled on pilgrimage with that fellow Wensui, and everywhere you have been brought to ruin by him.
Now, elder brother, you do nothing but sleep. The Head gave a shout and said, "Go eat and sleep! Every day you are just like a local deity in a village of seven hamlets. He— [The Master].
