The Master said, "All who encounter it perish. [The monk] asked, "What of those who do not encounter it? The Master said, "They too must have their heads fall off.

[The monk] asked, "Since they do not encounter it, why does their head also fall off? The Master said, "Have you not heard it said: 'It can exhaust all things'? [The monk] asked, "After everything has been exhausted, what then?
The Master said, "Only then will you know that this sword exists."
A monk asked, "An ancient said, 'Throughout the entire earth, there is only this one person. I wonder, who is this person?
The Master said, "There cannot be a second moon. The monk asked, "What is the second moon?
The Master said, "I want you, my elder brother, to determine it for yourself. The monk asked, "What is the first moon? The Master said, "Dangerous."
Question: "The snow covers the thousand mountains; why then is the solitary peak not white? The Master said: "You must know that there is the 'extraordinary within the extraordinary.
Question: "What is the 'extraordinary within the extraordinary'? The Master said: "It does not fall within the colors of the various mountains."
A monk asked, "Regarding 'this very mind is Buddha,' I do not ask about that. How is it with 'neither mind nor Buddha'?

The Master said, "One need not deny the horns of a rabbit; one need not affirm the horns of an ox. A monk asked, "Throughout the twelve hours of the day, how does one maintain [the practice]? The Master said:
It is like being in a region where there is contagious poison; one must not let even a single drop of water touch another person. A question was asked:
"When a single ox drinks water and five horses do not neigh, what is the meaning? The Master said: "Cao Shan knows how to avoid the taste."
Chan Master Daoying of Yunju in Hongzhou (23rd in the lineage). A native of the Ren clan from Yutian in Youzhou, he went to visit Dongshan.
Dongshan asked, "What is your name? The Master replied, "Daoying. Dongshan said, "Tell me something beyond that.
The Master said, "If I were to speak of what is beyond, it would no longer be called Daoying. Dongshan remarked, "Your response is no different from when you were with me at Yunyan."
The Master then served diligently at the foot of the seat.
Dongshan asked the Master, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from treading the mountains. Dongshan said, "Which mountain is fit for dwelling?"
The Master said, "Which mountain is not fit for dwelling? Dongshan said, "If that is so, then the entire country has been occupied by you.
The Master said, "Not so. Dongshan said, "If that is so, then you have found a way of entry. The Master said, "There is no way.
Dongshan said, "If there is no way, how can you meet with this old monk? The Master said, "If there were a way, then..."
"The Master [Dongshan] was already separated from his previous life. Dong said, "In the future, even if a thousand or ten thousand people try, they will not be able to hold you back.
The Master asked Dongshan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Dong said, "Disciple, in the future when you have a thatched roof over your head and someone asks you, what will you say? The Master said, "I would say, 'Venerable Daoying commits a transgression.'"
The Master was weeding grass when he happened to kill a worm. Dongshan pointed to it and asked, "What about this? The Master said, "It did not die.
Dongshan asked, "When the Second Patriarch went to Ye-du, what then? The Master did not answer.

Later, after he had established his own monastery, a monk asked him, "When you were at Dongshan, Dongshan asked you about the worm; was it not the case that you had nothing to say? The Master said, "At that time, I did have something to say."
[The Master] spoke: "It is simply that there is no one to listen.
Dongshan asked the Master, "I have heard that Sita is in Japan, acting as the king of the country; is this true?
The Master said, "If it were Sita, he would not even become a Buddha, much less a king. Dongshan was thoroughly enlightened by this.

Dongshan asked, "In the case of a great icchantika who kills his father, kills his mother, sheds the blood of a Buddha, and breaks the harmony of the Sangha—wherein lies such various forms of filial piety and support?
The Master replied, "Only then can one truly practice filial piety. From this point on, Dongshan esteemed him as the leader within the meditation hall.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who attain it do not regard it as trivial; those who see it do not disdain its application; those who recognize it do not sigh in lamentation; those who understand it have no aversion to it.
If one descends from heaven, one is poor and cold; if one wells up from the earth, one is wealthy and noble.

It is easy to emerge from within the gate; it is difficult to exit from within the body. To move is to bury oneself ten thousand feet deep; to remain still is for sprouts to grow right where one stands."
A single word transcends all; it stands alone, surpassing its time. Words need not be many; if they are many, they serve no purpose. He addressed the assembly, saying:

"When there is nothing at all, one attains that which is beyond scheming. When speech has nothing to rely upon and action has nothing to depend on, when the mind has nothing to entrust itself to, one then reaches the state of being without fault.
To be among the multitude as if there were no multitude, and to be without the multitude as if one were in the multitude—is this not so?"

Free from affliction, his virtue transcends all categories of beings. He has shed all fetters; though thousands and tens of thousands may follow him, he does not regard the Way as something belonging to himself.
As an ancient said: "Realize the matter of that side, yet come to this side to practice.
What matter is there on that side? And how does one practice on this side? Therefore it is said: "If it exists, do not bring it here."
"There is nothing that can be taken away. As for that which is presently here, whose affair is it?
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Even if you were to master the peripheral matters of the Buddha-dharma, you would already have applied your minds in error."
The ancients did not see it this way. Even if one could explain how "heavenly flowers fall to the ground" or "the stubborn rock nods its head," it still does not concern one's own affairs;
what else is there to do but remain idle? To intend to take this finite body and mind and apply them toward the infinite—what connection can there be?
It is like trying to fit a square block into a round hole; how much confusion and difficulty! If there were no such matter, even if...

Your gathering of flowers and clustering of brocade is likewise of no use; you have not yet escaped the realm of conceptual consciousness. You must exhaust yourself right here before you can attain freedom from transgression and find the path of emergence.
If there is even a single hair’s breadth that has not been exhausted, you will be ensnared by worldly defilements;

how much more so if it is greater? To err by a mere hair's breadth is to commit a transgression as vast as a mountain. As the ancients said regarding the place of study: [the text here implies the necessity of total exhaustion].

Not mysterious at all; these are entirely mundane matters, things of the inner chambers that one cannot bear to let go of. All are leaks and outflows. Only when every single thing is completely exhausted can one be faultless.
When everything is understood point by point and everything is penetrated object by object, one is simply called a "person who has accomplished the task."
Ultimately, this cannot be called "noble. One should know that the path of nobility is distinct from this. Thus, the ancients said: "It is like two mirrors facing each other;
their radiance reflects one another, and there is no waxing or waning. Is this not the very same thing?"
This is still merely called a matter concerning the periphery of reflections. When the sun rises and illuminates the world until it is bright and clear, that is one half;

what do you call the other half? People nowadays have not yet recognized even the coarse and shallow matters at their own gates and thresholds—treating such things as if they were the affairs within the house—and how can they possibly succeed?
He addressed the assembly, saying: "When you speak or breathe forth words, there must be a source for them; do not treat them with indifference.
Whenever you ask about a matter, you must also discern what is good and what is bad; do not merely mimic superficial similarities. Therefore, it is commonly said:

'Do not take offense at our lack of similarity,' for I fear there are too many who study in mere imitation. First, do not bring such things forward; if brought forward, they will not be similar. An eighty-year-old man..."
When an elder enters the examination hall, his sincerity is no mere child’s play. If a single word errs, one is separated from home by ten thousand *li*.
To "knock the bones and beat the marrow" must have its underlying reason; speech must be like tongs, shears, hooks, and locks, continuous and uninterrupted, only then will it suffice.
To be enlightened in every instance and manifest in every object—this is what it means to attain the subtle. One who knows this will never act with casual disregard;
they may speak ten times, but nine times they will cease. Why is this so? It is because those who have attained [the truth] fear that there might be no benefit for others.
It is like a fan in the middle of winter: the white mold that forms on its surface simply falls away; it is not a matter of forced effort, but occurs spontaneously.
To clarify such a matter, one must be such a person. If one is such a person, what need is there to worry about such a matter?

Addressing the assembly, [the Master] cited an ancient saying: "Hell is not yet the true suffering; it is only when one fails to clarify the Great Matter beneath these patched robes that one truly suffers.
Since you have all entered this stream of practice, you have already eliminated nine-tenths of your faults; there is no need for further comparison.
If you apply even a little more mental effort, then this elder’s lifelong journey will not have been in vain, nor will you have brought shame upon the monastic community. As the ancients said:
If you wish to provide a guarantee for this matter, you must stand atop the highest peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor;
only then will you have some measure of life-force. If the Great Matter has not yet been resolved, you must first tread the profound path.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If there is even so much as a hair’s breadth that cannot be cast off, one is immediately burdened by worldly dust;

how much more so if it is greater than that? Have you not seen the common saying: 'The matter of ascending to heaven is cast away before the assembly; the matter of ten-fold perfection is discarded before the assembly'?"
When cast upon the ground, it makes the sound of gold. There is no need to turn one's head back to look at it; what other use would there be for it?
Therefore it is said: "The wise do not seek within words; those who have attained do not search amidst speech. This is not to be distinguished from ordinary people;
it is the path that brings all myriad entanglements to rest. Even for a moment, when one is not on this path, there is a reason for it. It is not merely a matter of evil.
Retinue. A virtuous retinue that cannot be found elsewhere. Where has it gone? It has gone throughout the entire body; it has gone home; it has gone to pay its respects;
it has gone out through the gate of all existence; it has gone beyond the cage. It has escaped the perils and is a peerless assembly.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Twenty years ago, when this old monk was staying at Sanfeng Hermitage, the Elder Xinghua of Weifeng came and asked:
'May I borrow a question for a moment to serve as a preliminary probe? At that time, my mental faculties were dull and I could not speak.
Yet, because he had brought forth such an extraordinary topic, I did not dare to fail him. He continued: "He..."
Xiangshang said, "I cannot answer this question; it would be better to bow and withdraw. Reflecting on this now, at that time he need not have even said, "Why bother?

Later, when the fundraising master (huazhu) arrived at Xinghua in Weifu, Xinghua asked him, "When you were staying at Sanfeng Hermitage, I asked you a question and you could not answer it. Have you been able to answer it yet? The Master—
He recounted the previous conversation. Huizang said, "For twenty years at Yunju, I could only say, 'Why bother? Xinghua, however, is not like that;
how can he compare to one who says, 'No need'?"
The Three Sages said: "Even those who have mastered the Way after twenty years at Yunju are still half a month's journey behind Xinghua.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "It is like a man who buys a hunting dog for three strings of cash; it only knows how to track down those with footprints and lingering scents.
But when it encounters a wild goat hanging from a horn, there is not even a scent left. A monk asked: "What about when the wild goat..."

"How is it when the sheep has not yet hung its horns? The Master said, "Six times six is thirty-six. [The monk] asked, "How is it after it has hung its horns? The Master said, "Six times six is thirty-six. The monk bowed. The Master asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Have you not heard it said: 'All traces are cut off'? The monk related this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "Your elder brother Yunju is still here. The monk [went back to Yunju]. The Master said, "Did you ask about my previous words? The monk replied, "I did. The Master said, "Did he say anything? The monk said, "He said, 'Your elder brother Yunju is still here. The Master laughed heartily. The monk asked, "Why did he say that? The Master said, "If you had asked me, I would have said the same thing. The monk asked, "What would you have said? The Master said, "I would have said, 'He has already been dead for three years. The monk asked, "Why did he say, 'Your elder brother Yunju is still here'? The Master said, "Because he was afraid you would go and ask Zhaozhou. The monk asked, "Why was he afraid I would go and ask Zhaozhou? The Master said, "Because Zhaozhou is a man of great capacity. The monk asked, "What does 'great capacity' mean? The Master said, "It means that even if you were to present him with ten thousand pounds of gold, he would not accept it; even if you were to offer him ten thousand ounces of silver, he would not take it. This is what is called 'great capacity. The monk asked, "What is meant by 'not accepting gold' and 'not taking silver'? The Master said, "It means that even if you were to give him the whole world, he would not look at it; even if you were to give him all the wealth of the three realms, he would not desire it. This is what is called 'great capacity. The monk asked, "What is meant by 'not looking' and 'not desiring'? The Master said, "It means that even if you were to show him the sun and moon, he would not see them; even if you were to show him the myriad phenomena, he would not perceive them. This is what is called 'great capacity. The monk asked, "What is meant by 'not seeing' and 'not perceiving'? The Master said, "It means that even if you were to bring forth the Buddhas of the three periods, he would not recognize them; even if you were to manifest the dharmas of the ten directions, he would not know them. This is what is called 'great capacity. The monk asked, "What is meant by 'not recognizing' and 'not knowing'? The Master said, "It means that even if you were to speak of the ultimate reality, he would not be moved; even if you were to discuss the profound mysteries, he would not be startled. This is what is called 'great capacity. The monk asked, "What is meant by 'not being moved' and 'not being startled'? The Master said, "It means that even if you were to strike him with a staff, he would not feel pain; even if you were to hit him with a fist, he would not feel anger. This is what is called 'great capacity. The monk asked, "What is meant by 'no pain' and 'no anger'? The Master said, "It means that even if you were to offer him the four continents, he would not be pleased; even if you were to deprive him of the eight treasures, he would not be sad. This is what is called 'great capacity. The monk asked, "What is meant by 'no pleasure' and 'no sadness'? The Master said, "It means that even if you were to praise him with a hundred eulogies, he would not be elated; even if you were to revile him with a thousand insults, he would not be dejected. This is what is called 'great capacity. The monk asked, "What is meant by 'no elation' and 'no dejection'? The Master said, "It means that even if you were to place him in the midst of the five desires, he would not be attached; even if you were to cast him into the three evil paths, he would not be afraid. This is what is called 'great capacity. The monk asked, "What is meant by 'no attachment' and 'no fear'? The monk said, "I have come specifically for this; the Master must also reveal [the truth]. The Master said, "If you have come specifically for this, I must..."
[The Master] spoke out: "I request you, Master, to strike me right now. The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Waiting for a rabbit by a stump; you are wasting your mental energy.
Chan Master Xiujing of Huayan in Jingzhao Prefecture (Four cases total). The Master asked Dongshan, "The student has not yet seen the principle."
[The student] said, "I have not yet been free from conceptual consciousness. Shan said, "Have you even seen the path of principle yet? [The student] said, "There is no path of principle.

A monk asked, "Since you are an elder, why were you born later? The Master said, "At three years old, one is a dragon or a phoenix of the state;
at a hundred years, one is an aged court official beneath the steps. The monk asked, "What is it like when a prince has not yet ascended the throne? The Master said:

[The questioner] said: "He was greedily immersed in the pleasures of the six palaces, unaware that his kingdom was falling into ruin. What was it like when he first ascended the throne as the Son of Heaven?

fallen flowers cannot climb back onto the branch.

It is not a family treasure. To mistake the shadow for the head is surely a great error.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "The stone ox frequently spits forth spring mist; the wooden horse's neighing fills the roads.
He asked, "How can one see one’s original face? The Master said, "There is no need to hang up a stone mirror; the sky has already dawned."
From the time of cockcrow, Chan Master Huanyu of Mount Shao in Luojing (total of four cases) met the patch-robed monk Zun at the foot of the mountain.
Zun asked, "Where does the road to Mount Shao lead? The Master pointed with his hand and said, "To where the crows are dark and indistinct."
As he was leaving, Xuanzun stepped forward, seized him, and said, “I have long heard of Mount Shao; is it not so? The Master said, “It is indeed so. But what business do you have, *ācārya*?
Xuanzun said, “I intend to pose a question. Will you answer me? The Master said, “I suspect you are no son of the Golden Tooth;
how could you possibly draw the bow to shoot Wei-chi? Xuanzun said, “The phoenix flies straight into the misty heights.”
"Go! Who fears a wild sparrow in the forest? The Master said, "The skin drum spread before the hall is for you to strike;
try to display your family style as an old monk. Zhenzun said, "A single phrase transcends the thousand sages; the pine and vines do not equal the lunar disc."
The Master said, "Even if you were to break through beyond the era of Wei-yin, you would still be half a month's journey behind Shao-shan.
Zun asked, "I do not understand; where does the fault lie? The Master said, "Such eloquent words are known only by people of this age.

Zun said, "If that is so, then true jade is distinct from within the mud, and one need not brush away the dust of myriad activities. The Master said, "Under the workshop of Lu Pan, such cleverness is merely a waste of ingenuity."
Zun said, "I am just like this; how about you, Master? The Master said, "A jade maiden at night casts her shuttle, weaving brocade in the western house.
Zun said, "Is this not your own family style, Master? The Master said, "A farmer fashions a jade water-clock;
it is not the work of a master craftsman. Zun said, "That was still literary talk. What is your [true] self, Master?"
Regarding the family tradition, the Master said: "With one's body spanning the universe, who is the person who emerges?

He further said: "The *ajari* has the spirit to pierce the heavens; this old monk has the scheme to enter the earth. The *ajari* swallows the vast ocean in a single gulp; this old monk carries Mount Sumeru on his back.
The *ajari* comes forward brandishing a sword; this old monk waits with a leveled spear. Speak quickly regarding the single path that leads upward!"
Shu Daozong said, "A bright mirror stands upon its pedestal; I ask the Master to reflect upon it. The Master said, "It does not reflect. Daozong asked, "Why does it not reflect?
The Master said, "There are no fish in shallow water; it is a vain labor to cast down the hook. Daozong was speechless. The Master then struck him.
The Master asked Baizhang Huaihai, "Are you not that talkative Baizhang Huaihai? He replied, "I dare not. The Master said, "How many mouths do you have? He replied, "My whole body is it.
The Master said, "When you attend to the two necessities—defecation and urination—where do you void them? He replied, "In the mouth of Shaoshi.
The Master said, "If there is a mouth of Shaoshi, then let it be so; but if there is no mouth of Shaoshi, where then?"
As he was about to defecate, he remained silent. The Master struck him.
Yunmen spoke on his behalf, saying, "This talk falls into the trap; let me give you thirty blows.
He said again, "I took you for a lion's cub," and he said yet again, "Today, Shaoshan has crumbled like ice melting away."
Xuedou spoke differently, saying: "From the beginning, I have harbored doubts about Shaoshan.
A monk asked, "In a place where right and wrong do not reach, is there still a phrase? The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is that phrase?"
The Master said, "A single sheet of solitary cloud reveals no ugliness.
Question: "What is the nature of all phenomena? The Master said, "Birds fly through the azure heavens; distant mountains are a deep, profound blue. Question:
"If that is so, then all phenomena have departed? The Master said, "I knew you would misunderstand in confusion."
Chan Master Niu-t’ou Wei of Fu-chou, Dharma heir of Chan Master Ta-t’ung of Tou-tzu in Shu-chou (Part II).
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not employ even a single bit of artifice.
The teachers of the world have mouths like flat carrying-poles. How will you all manage? It is truly not easy."
"Unless one knows by knowing, none others can know.
A monk asked, "What is the master’s house style? The Master said, "Rice from mountain fields and plain yellow pickled vegetables.
The monk asked, "What if a guest of high rank arrives? The Master said, "If you wish to eat, let it be as you please; if not," [let it be as you please].
He ate whatever was offered to him.
A monk asked Master Anzhou Jiuzhongshan (Fanyi), "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "It is simply you."
A questioner asked, "I have long heard of Mount Jiuzhong; upon arriving, I see only one peak. The Master said, "You see only one peak, yet you do not see the nine peaks.
The questioner asked, "What are the nine peaks? The Master replied, "The water is swift and the waves are coarse."
Chan Master Jùn of Guānyīn Yán in Tōngjīng (Case 1). When the Master arrived at Tóuzǐ, the Master asked, "Where did you stay last night?
The Master replied, "The Immovable Dharma-Field. Tóuzǐ said, "Since you say it is immovable, how did you manage to get here? The Master replied:
Arriving at this point, how could there be any movement? Ziqi esteemed him.
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Qingyuan and the dharma heir of Chan Master Yantou Quanhuo of Ezhou.
Chan Master Daoyuan of Luoshan in Fuzhou (total of twelve fascicles), a native of the Chen family from Changxi in his home province.

The Master visited Shishuang and asked, "What is it like when arising and ceasing never cease? Shishuang replied, "You must become like cold ashes and withered wood; you must go where a single thought lasts ten thousand years;
you must go where the lid covers the vessel; you must go where there is pure clarity and no spot. The Master did not find resonance with this, so he went again to visit Yantou.
Lilian asked a question. [Linji] gave a shout and said, "Who is it that starts this diminution? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.
When the Master first entered the monastery, he ascended the hall; as soon as he adjusted his robes and was about to sit, he said, "Take care," and immediately descended from the seat.
After a long while, he turned back and said, "Those who do not yet know—come forward. At that time, a monk just stepped out to pay his respects, and the Master said, "That is quite something!"
[Ku] bowed and rose, saying, "I, [Name], inquire of the Master. The Master then shouted and sent him out. A monk asked, "What is the extraordinary phrase?
The Master said, "What are you talking about? After a long pause, he said, "If one is a superior man, as soon as his foot crosses the threshold, he will understand.
If you wait for it to be presented directly before your face, you are still a dullard. Even with your mouth chattering, you will not be spared a single stroke of the mattock."
Do you understand? It is not Zen, it is not the Way, it is not the Buddha, and it is not the Dharma.
What is it? It is the spiritual blade of precious steel, ever manifest before one; it can both kill and give life. If you are to wield it, wield it as you please.
If you are to step forth and settle the matter, you must be such a man before you succeed. Only when every faculty accords with its function and every dharma is without flaw will you be ready.
The faculties act as host and guest to one another. Even so, you must by all means avoid taking this upon yourself.
Why? If you let out the cry of a jackal, I shall roar like a lion; if I let out the cry of a jackal, you too shall roar like a lion. If you roar like a lion...
I too let out a lion’s roar. At the moment of application, one must grasp the essential phrases with mastery. Thus it is said: "The phrase within the meaning;
the meaning within the phrase. The meaning does not abide within the phrase; the phrase does not abide within the meaning. Meaning and phrase are of different orders—how should one understand this?
The meaning can eradicate the phrase; the phrase can eradicate the meaning. When meaning and phrase race against one another, this is what is truly formidable. Meaning...
The phrases are obscure; the affairs of the sages are not understood. It is nothing but a "screwdriver with no hole. The ancients called such people "vulgar masters.
Those like this are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds—what use are they? Compared to this gate, they are of no account.

One must be such a person: with eyes fixed and piercing, as soon as they are touched, they turn and roll like a wheel. How could this be something you can fathom through clarity or turbidity, or define through the categories of ordinary or sage?
There are such people. When a superior man meets another, it is like the spark struck from flint, like the crackling of a tortoise shell—swift as the wind and quick-witted as lightning.
Be alert and keen; there is but one or half a person who can handle such a matter. Otherwise, one’s affairs will be ruined.
Words and phrases move beyond ten thousand billions; yet if you lower your head to study Chan, in the end it cannot be attained.
Therefore the Way says: "In this way it is easy; in another way it is difficult. It is also said: "In this way it is difficult;

in another way it is easy. How will you all handle this? You must be extremely careful, brothers. Now, when traveling on pilgrimage, you must bring your eyes with you; do not be deceived by such people.
It covers you over. It teaches you that you must go into a state of profound stillness; you must proceed with continuous persistence. Alas!
To be caught by such a thing as this, to be unjustly shackled—what end is there in sight? This is like a gourd floating on the water: can anyone press it down?
It is constantly manifest before you, flowing along, free and at ease; never has there been a single dharma capable of covering it.
One attains "It. There has never been a single dharma that can be understood as equal to attaining "It. As soon as one strikes it, it is revealed; as soon as one touches it, it rolls and turns.

Covering both sound and form, when unfolded, it flows everywhere without obstruction, constantly manifest before one. How could it be something dull and inert? When it emerges, there is nothing that is not it;
when it enters, every single thing returns to the source. It stands far beyond sound—how could it fall into [conceptual categories]?
Existence and non-existence. Therefore it is said: "The phrase before the sound is not transmitted except by the Sages; never having been approached, it is as if separated by a great trichiliocosm.
That single thought before the sound—everyone fully knows this. How do you understand this? It is commonly said: "There is a path before the sound; let it be clearly illuminated by you.
If it does not come after the phrase, you still lack half of it. If even a hair’s breadth is not exhausted, you remain as if separated [from it]."

The Iron Encircling Mountains—how extraordinary that we have met! With what shall we question one another? Generally speaking, in proclaiming the Teaching, one must understand the life-and-death of the present moment;

only when one can master the intent and phrasing of killing and giving life may one truly extol the "sword that kills" and the "sword that gives life. These are the critical points of the ancients and are likewise the essential pivot of the present day.
To crush demons and shatter attachments, they cannot be dispensed with. One must know that direct revelation and direct exposition are required.
It already exists; it is that which is truly capable of shattering [delusion], its great function unimpaired, and perfect penetration manifest before one, so that demons have no room to act.
If you have not yet attained this state, how can you manifest it clearly within all four modes of deportment?
Do you still see his face? Here, it is commonly said: "A single thought before one’s face is constant and uninterrupted. Can you all truly attain such a state?
There is nothing at all. If you have not yet truly clarified this, you must first stand forth nakedly by yourself, not as a neighbor to the myriad dharmas;
no dharma whatsoever can cover it over. Thus the ancients said: "Before one's eyes there is no dharma, yet the meaning lies before one's eyes.
It is not a dharma of the present moment; it is not that which reaches the ears or the eyes. First, you must attain the manifestation of fundamental wisdom.
The scenery of the local ground is constantly exposed in its nakedness; it is free and at ease, entering and exiting without obstruction.
Only then can one truly transcend time, such that even when dragons and spirits hold up flowers, there is no path for them to follow, and when externalists peek secretly, they see no trace.

This is not a matter of merely dissolving form; it is a true departure. Brothers, you must penetrate to the very top and to the very bottom before you will succeed. Do not merely dabble here and there, picking up a few fragments.

Phrases and sentences; inserting words wherever one goes; pointing east and marking west; citing the ancients and the present—those who act in such a manner, even if ten thousand were beaten to death, what fault would there be?
Tomorrow or the day after, they will forge the men and women of the household and beat your ghostly buttocks;
that day will surely come. Do you know? The profundity of the Zen school requires that you measure it against your own breast; coarse food is easily satiated, but fine food...
It is difficult to avoid hunger; the fundamental difference lies solely in one's own errors. To labor in vain for a single lifetime, with an empty stomach yet a haughty mind—whose fault is this?

To consume the words of others, to discriminate between right and wrong, and to occupy oneself only with one’s own长处 (long-chang, "longs" or "strengths")—this will ultimately lead nowhere. When there is nothing to do, take care of yourself.

"Yes. The Master said, "If you do not approve of Deshan, I shall not ask about him. But as for Dongshan, what deficiency does he have?
He remained silent for a long while and then said, "Dongshan is a fine Buddha; it is simply that he has no radiance. The Master then prostrated himself.
In the assembly of Baofu, a monk came and paid his respects, saying, "Baofu sends his greetings to the Master.

He will enter the capital this autumn to have an audience with the Great King and present forty questions for you to answer, Master. Should you fail to provide a fitting response to even a single one, do not say that he did not tell you.
The Master laughed heartily and said, "Teacher Chen has entered the path of Fujian; Hong and Tang [shall follow]."
At the bridgehead, he established a formidable camp. Not a single hair-tip star had yet appeared. You previously cited Chengzhou Zhan’s words:
"Old Teacher Chen has no such multitude of questions; he has only one sword. Beneath that sword lies the intent of manifesting in myriad forms, and there is also a way to emerge from it.
If you do not understand this clearly, you must surely meet your end. Just transmit the message in this manner. The monk returned.

He related this to Baofu. Baofu said, "At that time, I was merely joking with him. When autumn arrived and they went on their official visit, the Master specifically prepared a tea ceremony and invited Baofu;
however, Baofu did not go. Instead, he said to the monks, "I did indeed have some joking words at that time."
Fearing that the Master might question him further, the monk returned and reported the matter to the Master. The Master said, "Go back again and tell him:
'A fierce tiger never eats meat that has already been submitted. The monk went back once more to request his presence, and Fú eventually came. The Master did not mention the matter.
The Master was serving at Heishan. While he was conversing with the Senior Monk Qinggui, Qinggui said, "There is no one in the world who is number one;
even the great and small Moshan lose out to Daowu. The Master asked, "What words did he say that caused them to lose out?
Qinggui replied, "When Shishuang took his leave of Moshan, as he rose from his prostrations, Moshan said: 'A phrase, a non-phrase—like a vine leaning against a tree. What do you think of this?"
"What? asked Xuefeng. Without answering, Xuefeng returned to Daowu. Daowu asked, "Where have you come from? Xuefeng said, "From Mount Gui.
Daowu asked, "What words were spoken there? Xuefeng recounted the previous conversation. Daowu said, "You stay here and look after my hermitage for me; wait while I go to settle the score with you.
Daowu went to Mount Gui, arriving just as the Master was plastering a wall. Suddenly, he turned his head and saw Daowu standing behind him.
Shan said, "Venerable Dharma Master, for what reason have you come here? I replied, "I have not come for any other purpose.
I heard the Master asking various practitioners about 'the phrase' and 'no-phrase,' and whether it is like a vine leaning against a tree—is that so, or not? Muzhou said, "It is."
I said: "For instance, when the tree falls and the vines wither—how is it? Guishan threw down his mud tray and laughed heartily.
I pressed him down into the mud, yet he paid no heed at all. When I finished my point, I said: "Is this not Guishan? He loses to Daowu. The Master said:
"Thirty years from now, you will have a thatched roof over your head; you must avoid raising this [topic]."
When he clung to this talk, Guì was unwilling to yield, yet he proceeded to act as the patron for Dàwú. The Master seized him and brought him down to the ground, saying:
"I address the assembly: please each of you cease your clamor. Today, I and the Venerable Guì shall directly clear the injustice of Dàméi."
"You must listen closely," he said. [The monk] replied, "I know, I know," and immediately prostrated himself. The Master said, "Why did you not speak like this sooner?
Do you recognize Daowu? He was merely a man of substance at an inn, one who gathers horse dung."
The Venerable Wuzhen asked Yantou, "Dongshan’s Buddha is excellent, yet he has no light.
I wonder what deficiency Dongshan has that you say he lacks light? The Master called out, "Wuzhen! Wuzhen responded, "Yes? The Master said, "Quite right;
his Buddha is excellent, yet he has no light. Wuzhen asked, "Master, why do you divert my words? The Master said, "What?"
"This is the place where you were dismissed; speak quickly, speak quickly! When Zhen was unable to respond, the Master struck him thirty blows and expelled him from the monastery.
Later, Zhen recounted this to Zhaoqing. For an entire summer, Zhaoqing scolded and reviled him. At the end of the summer, Zhen came to see the Master himself and asked about this matter.
The Master then explained it clearly to him. Zhaoqing prostrated in repentance, saying, "I have indeed wrongly accused the Great Master."
The Master was departing from Quanzhou with a Dharma teacher. As they parted ways at the crossroads, the Master asked the Dharma teacher, "The Grand Tutor suddenly asks:
'Great Master, throughout the twelve periods of the day, what do you use to instruct your disciples? How would you respond? The teacher was speechless. The Master said, 'Simply say:

"Riding the tiger's head, one takes the tiger's tail"—this first phrase clarifies the fundamental principle. The Master then asked further, 'What if he were to suddenly offer a word in reply? This... [text continues].
"This is still the verbal teaching of a bodhisattva; it is the non-verbal teaching of a bodhisattva. Again, [the student] asked, "And how about this?
The Master remained silent. The Teacher then spoke on his behalf: "The sharp edge of the encounter is like a flash of lightning."
The Master was staying at Daling. A monk took his leave to go to Shushan. The Master said, "I have a letter to send to Shushan. Will you take it? The monk replied, "I would be honored.
The Master pointed his hand to the top of his head, then spread it out and said, "Can you handle this?

The monk had no reply. Later, when the monk arrived at Shushan, he raised this matter during the assembly in the hall. One monk asked, "Do you understand yet? The assembly had no reply. The monk [who had been with the Master] [also] had no reply.
He said, "The people of the world cannot do anything about the Great Ridge.
While the Master was at Heyoshan, he was seeing off his fellow practitioner, Elder Kū. As they were leaving the gate, the Master tossed his staff toward the space before him;
Kū had no reply. The Master said, "The stone ox guards the ancient path; a single horse does not have twin foals. A monk later recounted this story.
Shushan said: "The stone ox guards the ancient path; one horse gives birth to three tigers.
Zhaoqing asked the Master, "When someone asks Yantou, 'How does one distinguish the host amidst the dust? Yantou replied, 'A copper saucepan filled with oil. What is the meaning of this?
The Master called out, "Great Master! The Master responded, "Yes? The Master said, "A monkey enters the Way."
Later, a monk asked Mingzhao about this. Mingzhao said, "An arrow pierces the shadow of the red sun.
Zhaoqing asked, "Master Yantou said, 'In this way, in that way; not in this way, not in that way. What is the meaning of this?
The Master called out, "Great Master! Zhaoqing responded, "Yes. The Master said, "Both are bright, yet both are dark. Zhaoqing then paid his respects.
He departed. Three days later, he returned and asked, "The other day, I received the Master’s compassion, yet I simply could not see through it.
The Master said, "I have told you everything with full sincerity. Qing said, "The Master walks with a torch in hand.
The Master said, "If that is so, then ask according to where your doubt lies. Qing asked, "What is meant by 'both being bright and both being dark'? The Master said, "Together."
"Life is the same as death. Qing then paid his respects and departed. Later, a monk asked Changqing, "When it is said that life is the same as death, what is the case at such a time?
Qing replied, "Both sides should shut their dog mouths. The monk said, "Master, keep your mouth for eating rice.
That monk then asked the Master, "What is the case when life is the same but death is not? The Master said, "Like an ox without horns."
A monk asked, "What is it like when one shares both birth and death? The Master said, "Like a tiger with its horns. When the Master was about to pass away, he ascended the hall.
After a long silence, he extended his left hand; the administrative officials (zhishi) did not understand this.
He then ordered the monks to step back. The Master again extended his right hand; the officials then directed the monks on the western side to step back as well.
The Master then said, "To repay the Buddha's kindness, nothing surpasses maintaining one's resolve; to repay the King's kindness, nothing surpasses circulating the Great Teaching.
He laughed heartily and then passed away suddenly.
Chan Master Shiyuan of Ruiyan in Taizhou (fourth in the series), a native of the Xu family of Fuzhou, asked Yantou, “What is the fundamental principle of constancy?
Yantou said, “Movement. The Master asked, “What is it when there is movement? Yantou said, “It is not the fundamental principle of constancy.
The Master pondered deeply. Yantou said, “If you accept this, you have not yet shed the root-dust; if you do not accept it, you will sink forever into birth and death. The Master...
Upon these words, he attained sudden enlightenment.
When the Master arrived at Jia Shan, Jia Shan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Wo Long. Jia Shan asked, "When you came, had the dragon yet arisen?
The Master stepped forward and gazed at Jia Shan with his eyes. Jia Shan said, "This is like applying moxa to an old scar on a burn."
The Master said, "Why does the Abbot continue to suffer so? Shanshan then desisted.
Daopei Zhe said, "Although Ruiyan was fierce and imposing, he could not avoid being excluded by the pure waters of Jiaxi."
The Master asked Jia Shan, "In this way it is easy; not in this way it is difficult. 'In this way, in this way'—that is being alert and awake.
'Not in this way, not in this way'—that is dwelling in the realm of emptiness. 'In this way, not in this way'—I ask you, Master, speak quickly!
Jia Shan said, "I am deceiving you, O Venerable One. The Master then shouted, "This old monk! At what time [did you say that]?"
Jie then went out. Later, there was a monk who recounted this to Yantou. Yantou said, "How tragic!
You are carrying away my branch of the Buddha-dharma in such a manner."
The Master would habitually call out, "The Host," and then respond himself, saying, "Yes. He would further say, "Stay alert; do not let others deceive you in the future.
Later, a monk recounted this to Xuansha. Xuansha said, "In one sense, it is all playing with the spirit;
how extraordinary! He added, "Why did he not simply remain right there? The monk replied, "He has already passed away. Xuansha said, "Even now, is he still here?"
"Did you call me? [The Master] asked. "Do you respond?
The monk had no reply. Chan Master Xuánquán Yàn of Huáizhōu (Fàn Yī). A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "The three sons of the Zhang family.
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Mèng, Zhòng, and Jì."

Chan Master Xuan Sha Shibei of Fuzhou (39th in the lineage), Dharma heir of Chan Master Yicun of Xuefeng in Fuzhou. He was the son of the Xie family in his native prefecture. Initially, he visited Xuefeng;

later, wishing to travel extensively throughout the various regions to seek out and study under spiritual teachers, he took up his traveling bag and crossed the mountain ridges. There, his foot struck a stone, drawing blood.
In his pain, he was suddenly and sharply awakened, saying: "This body does not exist; from where does the pain come? He immediately returned to Xuefeng.
One day, Xuefeng called out to him, "Which one is the Bhikṣu Bei? The Master replied, "I would never dare to deceive people. One day, Xuefeng summoned him again.
"Preceptor Bei, why do you not go on a pilgrimage to study everywhere? The Master said, "Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven.

Feng approved of this. Later, upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he realized the mind-ground. From then on, his responses to situations were swift and nimble, and they accorded perfectly with the *Sūtras*.
Whenever Feng questioned him, he never shied away from taking responsibility for the task. Feng said, "Preceptor Bei, as for that..."
This visitor was indeed one who stood preeminent among the disciples of Xuefeng.
While the Master was attending upon Xuefeng, as they were walking together, Xuefeng pointed to the ground before him and said, "On this plot of land, one could build a seamless stupa.
The Master asked, "How high would it be? Xuefeng looked up and down. The Master said, "It would be the merit and reward of humans and devas."
"It is not that there is no *upādhyāya*. [Yet] the prediction received at Vulture Peak has not even been dreamed of. Feng asked, "What do you say?
The Master said, "Seven feet or eight feet.
Langya Jue remarked, "At Guoqing, the talent is noble; in a wealthy household, the child is pampered."
Xuefeng pointed to the brazier and said, “The Buddhas of the three periods turn the Great Dharma Wheel within the flames.
The Master said, “Lately, the royal decree has become somewhat strict. Xuefeng asked, “How so? The Master said, “No encroaching upon others' paths or seizing their markets is permitted.”
Yunmen said, "The flames preach the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods of time; the Buddhas of the three periods of time stand upon the ground and listen.
Huanglong Xin said, "Xuefeng and Yunmen vie with one another in their brilliance; when the fuel is exhausted, the fire is extinguished."
"Where do you go to listen? Do not linger sitting in the depths of the white clouds. Be most careful not to let cold ashes burn you to death.
Xuefeng said to the Master, "There is an elder named Nanji; when questioned, there is nothing he cannot answer. One.
The Master ordered him to visit the teacher [Zhaozhou]. The teacher asked, "An ancient said, 'In this matter, only I can know it. Elder, what do you say?
Jì replied, "One must know that there is one who does not seek to know. The teacher said, "That old fellow on the mountain has endured so much hardship for nothing!"
"What is it? The Master went up the mountain to inquire after Xuefeng. At that time, Taoyuan Fu was serving as the lay steward. Xuefeng said, "I have a mouse here;
he is currently down in the bathhouse. The Master said, "Wait, let me examine him for you, Reverend. When the Master reached the bathhouse, he saw Fu.
[Daowu] was drawing water. The Master called out to him, saying, "I wish to see you, newly arrived one. Huifeng said, "We have already met. The Master asked, "In what kalpa did we ever meet?
Huifeng said, "Do not nod off to sleep. The Master went up to the abbot's quarters and said to Xuefeng, "I have already identified him.
Xuefeng asked, "How did you identify him? The Master recounted the previous conversation. Xuefeng said, "You were robbed by a thief."
[He] understood.
Xuedou spoke differently, saying, "This thief is defeated. Miaoxi said, "Another one has been exposed.
When the Master was standing in attendance at Xuefeng, two monks passed by from below the steps. Xuefeng said, "These two men are fit to be the seed."
Caoshan said, "I do not act in this way. Feng asked, "And how would you act? Caoshan said, "Then you should give him twenty blows of the staff."
The Master [Zhaozhou] then cited Xuefeng, who said: "The world is one zhang wide; the ancient mirror is one zhang wide.
The world is one chi wide; the ancient mirror is one chi wide. The Master pointed to the brazier and asked, "Tell me, how wide is this brazier?
Xuefeng replied, "It is as wide as the ancient mirror. The Master said, "This old fellow has not yet even touched the ground."
The Eastern Envoy asked the monk, "Is it the ancient mirror that makes the brazier so wide, or is it the brazier that makes the ancient mirror so large?
Yunmen said, "Rancid rice and a clay tea kettle. Baoning Yong remarked to Xuefeng, "Had it not been for me, you would have been deluded by him."
Xuefeng arrived and said to the Master, "Recently there was a monk who came to pay his respects to me.
I struck him once with my staff. As the monk turned his head, I asked him, 'What is this? He immediately had a realization.
The Master said, "Teacher, do not mistakenly sustain people; you must first undergo my own examination. Later, the Master went up to Xuefeng, and indeed—
He saw the monk. The Master asked, "When the Abbot in the mountains saw you coming, brother, he gave you a blow with his staff and said, 'What is this?
Is it so? You replied, 'It is. Then the Master shook out his sleeves and departed. Feng asked the Master, "How was that monk?
The Master said, "That monk is wild. Feng asked, "In what way is he wild? The Master said, "He is wild and bare all around."
The Master sent a monk to deliver a letter to Xuefeng. When Xuefeng opened the seal, he saw only three sheets of blank paper. He presented them to the assembly, saying, "Do you understand?
After a long silence, he said, "Has it not been said that 'a gentleman shares the same breeze from a thousand li away'? The monk returned and reported this to the Master.
The Master said, "That old fellow on the mountain has missed it, and he does not even know it."
The Fifth Patriarch Jie said: "I thought the beard was red. Huanglong Nan said:
"Xuefeng was not without his points of excellence; yet, having been exposed by Xuansha, until this very day he has never produced a 'snow'."
Master Haishi said: "If one's wisdom is equal to the teacher's, it is inferior to the teacher by half a virtue; only when one's wisdom surpasses the teacher's is one fit for transmission.
However, there is still one more step lacking."
Kaishan Xian said: "Xuan Sha’s white paper—how can one deny that its literary brilliance is already manifest?
Since Xuefeng said, 'A thousand miles share the same breeze,' why did he not realize he had missed the mark? Have you not heard it said: 'When raising a child, do not let him grow too large'?"
He was a truly great master-thief.
When Xuefeng passed away, the Master served as the presiding mourner. On the three mornings following the funeral, he gathered the assembly for tea.
Before the spirit altar, the Master picked up a single cup and said, "When our late teacher was alive, that was one matter; but tell me, how would you speak now? If—
"If you can speak [it], then the former master is without fault; if you cannot speak it, then the fault lies with the former master. "Is there anyone who can speak it?
He asked this three times, but the assembly had no response. The Master smashed the bowl and returned to the monastery. Later, he questioned Zhongta.
"How do you understand this? Guishan asked. Baotuo replied, "What fault has my late teacher? Guishan then turned his back to the wall. Baotuo went out. Guishan called out, "Baotuo!
Baotuo turned his head. Guishan said, "How do you understand this? Baotuo turned his face to the wall. Guishan desisted.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Way of the Buddha is leisurely and vast; it has no fixed path. It is the gate of liberation that has no gate, the intent of the Way-man that has no intent.

It does not reside within the three periods of time, and thus it cannot be subject to rising or sinking. To establish it would deviate from the Truth; it does not belong to the realm of conditioned creation."
Movement gives rise to the root of birth and death; stillness causes one to sink into the realm of stupor and intoxication. When both movement and stillness are extinguished, one falls into a void;

when both movement and stillness are gathered together, one merely grasps at a vague, superficial Buddha-nature. You must directly face sensory objects and environments like a withered tree or cold ashes;
yet, in responding to the moment, you must not fail to act appropriately. Like a mirror reflecting all forms, its radiance remains undisturbed—like a bird... [the text ends].
Flying through space, it is not mixed with the nature of space; therefore, there are no reflections in the ten directions and no traces of movement in the three realms.
It does not fall into the mechanism of coming and going, nor does it abide in an intermediate state of mind. There is no sound of a drum within a bell, and no sound of a bell within a drum;
the bell and drum do not intersect one another. In every phrase there is no before or after, like a strong man extending his arm—relying on no external force. The Lion...
Wandering freely, he seeks no companion. The nine heavens are utterly free of obscuration; where is there any need for penetration? This single mass of radiance has never been dimmed.
If one reaches this state, the essence is profoundly still and perpetually lucid. Like the blazing sun, its brilliance is boundless; within the space of perfect enlightenment, it remains unshakable.
It devours and eclipses heaven and earth, shining forth in absolute transcendence. Now, as for those who have transcended the world, there is fundamentally no coming or going.
Names and forms have no substance; the Way is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). It is the natural state of reality, true as it is, not something to be attained through cultivation or realization.
It requires only emptiness and leisure, yet its functioning remains unclouded. It does not involve the mire of worldly dust. Within this, even a hair’s breadth cannot be fully described;

to do so would be to become a follower of the Demon King. Before and after a phrase—this is where the student finds difficulty. Therefore, one phrase that hits the mark renders the eighty thousand gates eternally [unified].

To sever birth and death: even if one attains a state like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night—remaining unimpaired by being struck and undispersed by touching the waves—it is still merely a matter on the shore of birth and death.

Where the Path-walker moves, it is like fire melting ice; once melted, it never becomes ice again. Once an arrow has left the bowstring, there is no power for it to return. Therefore, it cannot be ensnared.
Willingly abiding, they do not turn their heads when called. The ancient sages made no arrangements; to this day, there is no fixed location.

If one reaches this point, every step ascends the profound mystery; it belongs neither to the heterodox nor the orthodox. Consciousness cannot perceive it, and wisdom cannot know it. To stir is to lose the source;

to awaken is to become deluded regarding the ultimate intent. The two vehicles tremble with fear, and those on the ten stages are struck with terror. The path of speech is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity—

Extinction. Directly, one attains that Śākyamuni closed his door in Magadha, Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī, Subhūti proclaimed non-speaking to manifest the Way, and Śakra and Brahmā ceased listening as flowers rained down. If it is thus manifest before you, what more is there to doubt?
There is no place to settle; it transcends past, present, and future; it cannot be delimited; the paths of mind and thought are cut off, not because of...
Adorned from the beginning, it is truly pure; whether in movement, speech, or laughter, it is clear and manifest in every situation, lacking nothing at all.

People of the present age do not awaken to this underlying principle, but instead recklessly involve themselves in worldly affairs and sensory dust. Everywhere they become stained and attached; at every turn they are bound by fetters.

Even if they were to attain awakening, they would find the sensory realm to be chaotic and the names and forms to be unreal; they would then attempt to settle the mind and withdraw their thoughts, seeking to withdraw from all phenomena.
To return to emptiness, closing the eyes and hiding the pupils, yet for thoughts to eventually arise— though one gradually breaks them down,

and as soon as subtle conceptions are born, one immediately suppresses them— with such a view, one is simply an outsider who has fallen into nihilism, a walking corpse whose soul has not yet dispersed.
Vast and boundless, without perception or cognition; it is like plugging one's ears and stealing a bell—merely deceiving oneself. Here, to engage in discrimination is not the way;
nor is it a matter of hiding in side doors or back alleys. Every phrase is manifest before you; it cannot be deliberated upon and does not involve literary artifice.
Fundamentally transcending the realm of dust, it originally has no rank or position. Though we provisionally call this person a "renunciant," in the end, there is no trace.
Traces—such as True Suchness, ordinary beings and sages, or the hells and heavens—are merely expedient means for healing a mad son. Even empty space undergoes no alteration;
how could the Great Way have rising or sinking? To awaken is to move freely in all directions without departing from the fundamental limit. If you reach this point, [you will realize this].
Both ordinary beings and sages have no place to stand. If you direct your attention toward the words, you will drown and destroy yourself as a student.

If you run outward in pursuit, you will fall into the realm of Māra. As for the state of suchness, there is nothing to be arranged; it is just like a furnace of glowing embers that harbors not even a mosquito.
This principle is fundamentally level—what need is there for excavation or removal? A single movement or a raised brow is true understanding.

Liberation! The Way is not something achieved through forceful effort. If one’s mental calculations and constructions deviate from the truth, then upon reaching this point, one must not admit even a hair’s breadth of it;
for any deliberate application of the mind results in error. Thus, even if a thousand sages were to appear, they could not arrange a single word. [The Master] stood for a long time.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The true宗 (teaching) of the ancient Buddhas constantly manifests in accordance with things.

Its majestic application shines forth everywhere; its appearance and disappearance are equanimous, illuminating all heights and depths. Therefore, for the superior śramaṇa, the eye of the Way must take precedence.

Only by acceding to the fundamental and clarifying the mind can one reach ultimate realization. The myriad phenomena of the forested universe share a single source and a common origin. Vast and boundless, who could possibly discuss it?"
There is stagnation. Events from kalpas ago are all present before one's eyes; yet people of this age are distanced by time and separated by years, leading them to deviate from the true essence.

With deluded minds, they identify with external objects and have long turned their backs on the True Doctrine. Clinging to existence and stagnating in emptiness, they fail to encounter virtuous friends or good companions.

Relying solely on their own private interpretations, even when they engage in discussion, it results entirely in mere intellectual conjecture. When they finally reach the ground where principles are investigated, they are unable to discern [the truth].
How much more so for one's own life, where one has never yet sought to grasp or pull anything out? As for the former sages and ancient worthies, they knew the proper time for themselves;

they disciplined themselves and yielded credit to others, dwelling in mountain huts and rocky caves. An ancient worthy said: "If the mind retains the measure of the sage, one still falls into the dust of dharmas."

If what you have seen is not yet forgotten, it will still result in leakage. One cannot say that by observing the fasts and precepts, sitting for long periods without lying down, dwelling the mind in contemplation of emptiness, or concentrating the spirit to enter meditative absorption, one shall immediately depart [from birth and death]. What connection could there be? This is merely the way of the non-Buddhists of the Western Heavens.

They may enter the great samādhi of eighty thousand kalpas, concentrating their spirits in profound stillness; they close their eyes and hide their pupils, extinguishing the will and ceasing the intellect.
Yet, once the kalpas have elapsed, they cannot avoid the cycle of saṃsāra. This is because their eye of the Way is not clear and the root-source of birth and death remains unbroken.
For those who have left the home-life, it is not so; they must not be equated with the non-Buddhists. They must, indeed, possess true clarity and penetration.
Great seeing and knowing. It is able to penetrate to the same depth as all Buddhas. Quiescent illumination forgets cognition; it emptily contains the myriad phenomena.
Right now, where is there that is not you? Where is there that is not clear? Where is there that is not manifest? Why do you not understand it in this way?
If you lack this ground, how can you deal with the various leaks during your daily activities? They will all become [obstacles].
This is false. Which of these, then, is the place where you have gained strength throughout your life? If you have not yet achieved realization, you must act with urgency;
forget your meals and lose your sleep as if your head were on fire, as if you had lost your very life, and seek salvation through silent contemplation.
Relinquish worldly attachments and bring the mind and consciousness to rest; only then will there be a slight degree of intimacy.
If you do not do so, tomorrow or the day after, everything will be carried away by the activities of the discriminating intellect.

What freedom will you have then? Now, however, even these insentient things are more capable than you; they proclaim clearly that earth, wood, stone, and rock preach the Dharma, and this is most truly so. Only...
Only a few people are able to listen. If one hears this teaching, only then can one begin to deliberate. But tell me: how does one deliberate upon the Dharma spoken by the insentient?
Try to say it! One cannot say that there is no speaking and no discourse, nor that there is no seeing and no hearing.
Nor can it be said that he spoke of his own accord without being questioned, extolling the path he had practiced.
Without seeing Sudhana, he visited fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Finally, upon seeing Maitreya, in the mere twinkling of an eye, he entered the gate.
As soon as he had entered, the gate closed of its own accord. Within the multi-storied pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), he beheld hundreds of thousands of Buddhas who had sacrificed their bodies in the past.
The body he received was that of one who had encountered fifty-three virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Within the pavilion, they all appeared simultaneously to serve as witnesses for him, and Sudhana’s doubts were instantly stilled. Generally speaking, if one possesses this true realization beneath the three rafters of a humble dwelling, one may then deliberate upon it;
thus, within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, one is identical to all Buddhas.
In the Pure Land, what further fear can there be of birth and death? Moreover, who knows that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely devoid of substantial reality?

Even at the assembly on Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa heard this directly, yet it was like speaking of the moon. An ancient worthy said: "Do not deliberate upon good or evil"—this is like pointing at the moon.
This extends even to the stages of practice and liberation of the Three Vehicles, the *nirvāṇa* of Bodhisattvas, and the [realization of] the Sages.
Virtue and the fruits of sagehood are both like flowers in the sky or the horns of a rabbit; they do not perceive the Way. Yet, when one returns to observe the world, it is like a dream-event.
Conditioned mental phenomena cannot be relied upon; over the long course of years, they provide no benefit at all.

It is simply because one has contravened the Truth and abandoned the Source, becoming weary of ordinary emotions and turning the mind away from the Holy Path—forming such views and cognitions that one does not transcend the limitations of others.
As for this measure: you cannot cast off the five aggregates; you do not yet see the Way that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. If you merely intend to move forward, how can you realize it? Only when you have penetrated through to the core will you know it.

If you have not yet investigated it thoroughly, you should know that it is all empty talk—this Dharma which is difficult for the world to believe. Only those with great capacity can clearly comprehend it. Now...
If one can thoroughly penetrate this life, it will be the same for ten thousand kalpas. As the ancient masters said: "One must resolve this very life;
who could endure the remaining calamities for eternal kalpas? Be careful.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "To serve as a patriarch and master is truly not easy. I have employed such expedient means to assist you, yet you are still unable to grasp it.
If I were to speak solely of the fundamental vehicle of the school, where else would you even find a foothold?
Therefore, among the hundreds of thousands of followers on Vulture Peak, only Kāśyapa heard it directly. Tell me, what is this matter that Kāśyapa heard directly?"
One cannot say that the World-Honored One did not speak what he spoke, nor that Kāśyapa did not hear what he heard; only then could one depart.
Furthermore, as for saying that I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and have entrusted it to Mahākāśyapa, my way of speaking is like talking about the moon.
When Caoqi held up his whisk, it was like pointing at the moon. Therefore it is said: "In the land of the Great Tang, regarding the matters of the School of the Patriarchs, there has never been..."
There is one person who raises the cry. Even if there were only one person to raise the cry, all the people in the entire world would lose their lives;
like iron hammers without holes, they would simultaneously have their sharp points blunted and their tongues tied.

Fortunately, having encountered me—who does not begrudge my own body or life—you may follow along with your delusions and upside-down views, for only then will there be a place to extend your inquiry. If it were not so, where else would you go to meet me?
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The World-Honored One said, 'I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, which I entrust to Mahākāśyapa.
This is like speaking of the moon. Caoqi [Huineng] held up his whisk; this is like pointing at the moon. At that time, Gushan stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "Where is the moon?
The Master said, "This fellow is seeking the moon right from me!"
Xuedou said: "Xuansha and Gushan were like two generals deploying a million-man army, yet they merely threw tiles and pebbles at one another to strike.
If there is a monk who can discern this, you should know that the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye has been entrusted to him."

The Master ascended the hall. When the assembly had gathered, he took up his staff and drove them down. He then turned back and looked at his attendant, saying, "Today I have produced a solution that was perilous;
it was like being shot into hell by an arrow. The attendant said, "I am glad the Master has returned to human form once more."
Cuiyan Zhi said: "Whether great or small, Xuansha neither reached the village in front nor arrived at the shop behind.
But how would you say it? Speak the single path by which one emerges."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Everywhere it is said that one should 'welcome things and benefit beings. But suppose three kinds of sick people were to come—how would you welcome them?
For the one suffering from blindness, if you raise the mallet or hold up the whisk, he still cannot see.

For the one suffering from deafness, if you employ the samādhi of speech, he still does not understand. For the one suffering from muteness, if you try to make him speak, he cannot speak. So, how will you welcome them?"
"If you cannot receive me, then the Buddha-dharma has no spiritual efficacy. At that time, Dizang came forward and said, "I have eyes and ears;
how will you receive me, Master? The Master said, "How shameful! and then returned to his quarters.
