Shān asked, "What is the reality beneath the paper-cloth? The Master said, "Once the single robe is hung upon the body, all phenomena are entirely as they are."
Mount Yun said, "What is the function beneath the paper robe? The Master stepped forward, responded with an assent, and then stood there and took it off.

Mount Yun said, "You only know how to go like that; you do not yet know how to come back like that. The Master suddenly opened his eyes and asked, "When the single, spiritual true nature does not rely on a womb, what is it like?
Mount Yun said, "That is not yet wondrous. The Master asked, "What is wondrous? Mount Yun—

He said, "Not borrowed, not lent. The Master then said, "I take my leave," and sat down until he passed away. Thereupon, Shanshan composed a verse which says: "The nature of awakening is perfectly luminous, a formless body;
Do not forcibly create intimacy or estrangement within knowing and seeing. When thoughts differ, one is obscured from the profound essence; When the mind deviates, it does not neighbor the Way.
Sentimental attachments cause the myriad dharmas to sink into the foreground; The many ends of discerning consciousness lose the original truth. Thus it is..."
Fully understanding within a single phrase, one clearly realizes that the person of old was without affairs.
Hanshan, while the assembly of monks were roasting eggplants, took a skewer of eggplant and struck one monk on the back.
When the monk turned his head, Hanshan held up the skewer and asked, "What is this? The monk replied, "This madman! Hanshan then [turned to] those nearby...
The monk said, "Tell me: how much salt and vinegar did this monk waste?
Hanshan once encountered Zhaozhou while traveling to Tiantai. Seeing the tracks of an ox, Hanshan asked Zhaozhou, "Upādhyāya, do you recognize this ox?
Zhaozhou replied, "I do not. Hanshan pointed to the ox tracks and said, "These are five hundred arhats."
Youshan was traveling through the mountains when Guizhou asked him, "Since you are an Arhat, why did you turn into an ox?
Youshan said, "Heaven! Heaven! Guizhou laughed loudly and said, "Why [do you say that]? Youshan said, "Heaven! Heaven!
Guizhou said, "This fellow truly possesses the bearing of a great man."
One day, Shide was sweeping the ground. The Abbot asked him, "Your name is Shide; it was Fenggan who picked you up and brought you here.
What, after all, is your name? What is your surname? Shide set down his broom and stood with his hands joined in reverence.
The Abbot asked again, and Shide picked up his broom, swept the ground, and departed. Hanshan beat his breast and cried out, "Heaven! Heaven!"
Shide said, "What are you doing? Shanshan said, "Have you not heard it said: 'When a member of the eastern family dies, the members of the western family offer their condolences'?
The two of us shall perform a dance, and then we shall depart laughing and weeping."
Shide saw the assembly gathered at Guoqing Temple for the fortnightly recitation of the precepts. Shide clapped his hands and said, "You all huddle together making mental calculations;
what is the point of that? The *vina* (chant leader) rebuked him. Shide said, "Virtuous ones, wait! To be free from anger is itself the precept;
a pure mind is itself the renunciation of the household life. I am already in harmony with you; all dharmas are without difference."
The Military Commissioner of Qiantang was serving as a local commander on the border. Whenever he questioned a monk and found him to his liking, he would invite him to stay the night.
One day, two monks arrived. The commissioner asked, "Where have you come from? They replied, "From the place of Master Mada (Mazu) in Jiangxi.

The commissioner asked, "What sayings or teachings does he have? The first monk said, "The very mind is Buddha. Upon hearing this, the commissioner immediately dismissed him with a bow. He then questioned the second monk, who said:
"It is neither mind nor Buddha. He then had the messenger also bow and leave.
Later, while Langzhong Xu Shi of Hongzhou was conversing with the two masters Shanglan Pu and Letan Cheng, Cheng said, "I have heard that you, Langzhong, once said:
'Sitting through the night on the Cloud-Linked Stone; planting pines in the rain during spring. How did you answer Dongshan at that time?"
"What kind of talk is this? Xue said, "Today the court is dismissed. Cheng asked, "I have heard it said that this is the story of how the Great Sage of Sizhou appeared in Yangzhou;
is this true or not? Xue said, "Have another cup of tea brought. Cheng said, "His reputation is well-earned."
Xuefeng said, "It turns out he was one who could maintain his own ground. Xuedou continued, "The Master will return to the mountain soon.
Chengyuan said, "Today you were seen through by Shanglan. Shanglan then gave a shout. Chengyuan said, "It must be you who can do this. Xuedou said, "There is no help for it;
the boat is being wrecked, so smash the scoop!"
Director Xu entered Shanglan Monastery and asked the Head Seat, "How old are you? The Seat replied, "Sixty-eight. Xu asked, "How many years of *śrāmaṇera* seniority do you have?
The Seat replied, "Forty-seven summer retreats. Xu asked, "How many summer retreats has the Holy Monk attained? The Seat replied, "He received the precepts simultaneously with empty space.
Xu struck the head of the wooden board and said, "I, your subordinate official, eat rice; I am not like the Head Seat, who eats too much salt."
Emperor Taizong of the Great Song asked a monk, "What sutra are you studying? The monk replied, "The *Benevolent Kings Sutra*.
The Emperor said, "Since this is my own sutra, why is it in your hands? The monk was unable to respond.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "Heaven has no favorites; it assists only those with virtue.
When the Emperor visited the Kaiyuan Pagoda, he asked a monk, "Who are you? The monk replied, "I am the pagoda master. The Emperor said, "This is my pagoda.
Why do you act as its master? The monk was speechless.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "The entire nation knows this.
Once, when a monk was having an audience with the Emperor, the Emperor asked, "Monk, from where do you come? The monk replied, "From the Sleeping Clouds Hermitage on Mount Lu.
The Emperor said, "If you are in such deep seclusion among the sleeping clouds that you do not attend court, why have you come here? The monk was speechless.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "It is difficult to escape the ultimate transformation.
Regarding the Emperor’s dream, a divine being informed him, saying: "I request Your Majesty to give rise to the bodhicitta.
At the morning audience, the Emperor summoned his attendants and asked, "How does one give rise to the bodhicitta? None of them could provide an answer.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf, saying: "Truly, this is rarely heard of in antiquity or the present.
A monk went to have an audience with the Emperor and said, "Your Majesty, do you still remember this humble monk? The Emperor replied, "Where did we meet?"
[The Emperor] said, "It has been from our parting at Mount Ling until this very day. The Emperor asked, "What proof do you have? The monk had no reply.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf, saying, "I, this poor monk, came specifically for this purpose."
The Emperor, upon hearing the monk’s report, ordered the Tripitaka to be burned and requested that it be granted anew by imperial decree. The Emperor asked, "In the past, Mokṣala did not burn it;
why then do you burn it now? The monk was unable to reply.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "Your Majesty has not forgotten the entrustment.
There was once an anonymous venerable master who did not speak with the monks for an entire summer. A monk sighed and said, "I am simply like this..."
"Ma! This summer has passed in vain. I did not dare hope for the Master to preach the Dharma, but it would have been enough simply to hear the two characters of the 'True Cause' (zhengyin).
Upon hearing this, the old master said, "Disciple, do not speak so hastily. As for the True Cause, there is not even a single character.
Having finished speaking, he struck his teeth with his tongue and said, "Just now, I spoke without reason; it was improper to say such a thing. An old master living in an adjacent wall heard this.
[The Master] said, "What a fine pot of soup! It has been defiled by a single mouse dropping.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf, saying, "In whose household are there not one or two such things?"

Long ago, there was an elderly master who lived in a hermitage. He wrote the character for "mind" (心) above his door, he wrote the character for "mind" on his window, and he wrote the character for "mind" on his wall.
Fayan said: "On the door, simply write the character for 'door'; on the window, simply write the character for 'window';
on the wall, simply write the character for 'wall'. Xuange said: "On the door, do not write the character for 'door';
on the window, do not write the character for 'window'; on the wall, do not write the character for 'wall'."

In the past, there were two hermitage masters living in separate huts. They did not see one another for ten days, and when they suddenly met, the master of the upper hut asked the master of the lower hut, "It has been a long time since we last saw each other; where have you been?
The master of the lower hut replied, "I have been in my hut constructing a seamless stupa. The master of the upper hut said, "I also wish to construct one. May I borrow your stupa from you?"
[The guest] showed him the model. The abbot of the hermitage said, "Why did you not tell me sooner? It has just been borrowed by someone.
Fayan said, "Now tell me: did he borrow the model, or did he not borrow the model?"
Long ago, there was an elder who said: "The Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years to seek out those with whom he could find resonance.
If you understand it in this way, you will have a day when you must eat iron rods. Another elder said: "The Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years; how can you not feel shame?
If you understand it in this way, you must buy straw sandals and travel on foot for another thirty years."
Langya Huijue said: "Since that is not so, tell me: what was the meaning of the Patriarch’s wall-gazing? After a long silence, he said:
"If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata."

In the past, there was an elderly master who kept a young attendant, yet neither of them knew the proper rules of conduct. One day, a wandering monk arrived and instructed the boy in the rituals of etiquette.
Later that evening, seeing the elderly master returning from outside, the boy went forward to offer his greetings. The master was astonished and suspicious.
He then asked the boy, "Who taught you? The boy replied, "A certain senior monk (shangzuo) in the hall.
The old master summoned that monk and questioned him: "Senior monk, you travel among the households; what kind of mental conduct is this?
This boy has been raised here for two or three years and is naturally quite endearing. Who taught you to corrupt him? Pack your things quickly and leave!"
He departed. At twilight, as the rain poured down, he was driven out.
Fayan said, "The ancients were like this; they revealed a little of their family style, which is truly strange. But tell me, what was their intention?"
Once there was a practitioner who followed a Dharma Master into a Buddha hall. The practitioner spat toward the Buddha, and the Dharma Master said, "Practitioner, you lack propriety;
why do you spit at the Buddha? The practitioner replied, "I thought this was not a place where there is a Buddha, so I spat at it for my own sake."
The Dharma Master had no reply.
Yangshan spoke on his behalf: "Just spit at the practitioner and wait for him to say something;
then you can say to him, 'Give me back my state of non-practice!'"

Long ago, there was a monk who arrived at Caoxi. At that time, the monk in charge of the robes and bowl held up the robes and said, "These are the ones that could not be lifted at the head of Mount Dayu.
The visiting monk asked, "Why are they now in the hands of the Senior Monk? The monk in charge had no reply.
Yunmen said, "Neither of them understood. He also said, "I thought you were a lion cub.
Once, there was a monk traveling to Fuguan who encountered a salt seller on the road. The monk asked, "Where does the road to Fuguan lead?
The old man remained silent for a long while. The monk asked again, and the old man said, "Are you deaf? The monk replied, "Are you speaking to me?"
"What do you say? The old man said, "I told you the way to turn the boat over. The monk asked, "Old man, do you not understand Zen? The old man replied, "Do not say that I understand Zen;
I have exhausted all of the Buddha-dharma as well. The monk said, "Try to explain it to me. The old man lifted up his salt basket.
The monk said, "It is difficult. The old man asked, "What do you call this? The monk said, "Salt. The old man asked, "What connection does that have [to my question]?
The monk asked, "And what do you call it? The old man replied, "I cannot tell you again that it is salt."
Long ago, there was an old woman who supported a hermit for twenty years. She regularly sent a young girl of eighteen to serve him with meals.
One day, she ordered the girl to embrace the hermit firmly and asked, "At this very moment, what is it? The hermit replied:
"A withered tree leaning against a cold cliff—throughout the three winters there has been no warmth.
When the woman reported this to the old woman, she said, "For twenty years, I have supported nothing but a worldly fellow. She then sent her away and burned down the hut.
Once there was a monk who went to visit Mihu. On the road, he encountered an old woman living in a hermitage.
The monk asked, "Do you have any kinsmen? She replied, "I do. The monk asked, "Where are they? She said, "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth; whether grass or trees—all are my kinsmen.
The monk said, "Are you not coming as a nun (śramaṇerī)? She asked, "What is it that you see in me? The monk said, [nothing].
The laywoman said, "You cannot be a monk. The monk said, "Lady, do not confuse and muddle the Buddha-dharma.
The laywoman said, "I am not confusing the Buddha-dharma. The monk said, "If you act like this, is that not confusing the Buddha-dharma? The laywoman said, [silently].
"You are a man; I am a woman. How could we have ever been confused?

Long ago, when Nanquan was serving as the kitchen steward, he prepared two portions of food and went to the garden to entertain the head gardener. At the time of the meal, as he was unfolding his alms bowl—"
Suddenly, a "Buddha-remembering" bird began to sing. The head gardener struck his pillow once; the bird sang again, so he struck it once more.
When the singing finally ceased, the head gardener asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The head gardener struck the pillow one final time.
Under the assembly of the Abbot of Yanguan, there was a monk serving as an administrator who saw a ghost messenger come to pursue him.
The monk said, "I am currently occupied with my duties as an administrator and have had no leisure to practice; I beg you to grant me seven days. Is this possible?

The messenger replied, "I must report this to the King. If he permits it, you may come after seven days; otherwise, I shall return in an instant. Having spoken, the messenger vanished. After seven days had passed, the monk returned to search for him.
That monk was completely unfindable. Later, another monk asked a monk, "When you suddenly find him, how will you deal with him? The monk had no reply.
Dongshan said, "He has been found by him.

Long ago, there was a monk at Mount Gui who went down the mountain seeking a place to stay. He happened to spend the night at the home of a lay practitioner. The practitioner asked, "Where are you going, Venerable Sir?
He replied, "I am looking for a place to stay. The practitioner wrote the character for "Buddha" (佛) and asked, "What kind of character is this?"
When the man said, "The character 'Buddha' (Fo)," he called his wife over and asked, "What character is this? His wife replied, "The character 'Buddha'.
The man said, "The senior monk and my humble wife have the same understanding; how could he possibly remain [in the monastery]? Thereupon, the monk returned to Mount Muzhou.
Once there was a monk who went to visit Cuiyan. Finding that Cuiyan was not present, he went down to see the administrative official.
The official asked, "Have you seen the Master yet? He replied, "Not yet. The official pointed to a dog and said, "If you wish to see the Master, simply prostrate yourself before this dog.
The monk was speechless. Later, when Cuiyan returned, he heard of this and said, "How could one have avoided this?"
Thus he remained silent.
Yunmen said, "If you wish to examine the master, first examine the disciple.
Miaoxi said, "At that time, had I been this monk, I would have prostrated once to the dog."
Once there was an old woman who entered Zhaozhou’s monks’ hall and said, "The masters and monks in this hall are all born of me;
there is only one great child who commits the five heinous crimes and is unfilial. As soon as Zhaozhou looked toward her, the old woman departed.
Once there was a Daoist practitioner who sat with his back turned toward the Buddha. A monk asked him, "Practitioner of the Way, do not turn your back on the Buddha.
The Daoist replied, "Virtuous One, the fundamental teaching states that the Buddha-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Where, then, am I instructed to sit?
The monk was speechless.
Long ago, there was a monk who returned from the dead and said: "In the underworld, I saw Kṣitigarbha, who asked me, 'Throughout your life, what kind of practice have you cultivated?
I replied, 'I recited the Lotus Sūtra. Kṣitigarbha said, 'Stop, stop! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. The monk had no reply."
Once there was a monk who asked an elder master, "When a lion seizes an elephant, it employs its full strength; when it seizes a rabbit, it likewise employs its full strength.
I wonder, what kind of strength does it employ in both cases? The elder replied, "The strength of non-deception."

Once, there was a donor who entered a monastery to distribute "money according to seniority" to the assembly of monks. The administrator said, "Place one portion before the Holy Monk (the Buddha image).
The donor asked, "How old is the Holy Monk? The monks had no answer.
Fayan said in his stead: "One knows it when the heart's expectation is fulfilled.
Once there was an old master who did not go to the hall. When the attendant came to invite him to the hall, the master said, "Today I am at the manor, having eaten my fill of oil-cakes.
The attendant said, "The Master has never gone out. The master said, "Just go and ask him."
Just as the head of the manor was about to leave, he suddenly saw the head monk returning. The headman thanked the monk for coming to the manor to eat oil-cakes (*youti*).
Miaoxi’s verse says: The monk did not attend the hall; The headman thanks him for his visit.
Once a single character enters the gate of officialdom, Even a nine-ox cart cannot get out.
Long ago, there was a monk living in a hermitage in Guangnan. By chance, the Great King went out hunting, and his attendants reported, "The master of the hermitage, the Great King is coming;
please rise. The master said, "Not only would I not rise for the Great King, but even if the Buddha were to come, I would not rise.
The King asked, "Is the Buddha not your teacher? The master replied, "He is. The King said, "If so, why do you not rise upon seeing your teacher? The monk had no reply.
Fayan said in his stead: "It is not yet sufficient to repay your kindness.
Long ago, there was an official who composed a "Treatise on the Non-existence of Ghosts. One night at midnight, as he was wielding his brush, he suddenly saw a ghost appear and say:
"You say there are no ghosts; what about me? The official was left speechless.
Wuzu Yan, in his place, simply made the beak of a magpie with his hand and said, "Gu-gu-ku.

Long ago, there was an old master who asked a presiding official (zuozhu): "Regarding the commentaries (*shuchao*) that explain the meaning [of the sutras], how do the detailed and concise versions compare?
The official replied, "The commentaries explain the sub-commentaries (*shu*); the sub-commentaries explain the sutras. The old master asked, "What do the sutras explain? The official was speechless.
Long ago, there was a monk traveling along a road who saw a fish dead in the water. He then asked, "The fish takes water as its life;
why has it died in the very water? No one could provide an answer.
Formerly, when people from the kingdom of Goryeo came to Qiantang and carved an image of Avalokiteśvara, they attempted to hoist it onto their ship, but it would not budge.

They subsequently requested that it be enshrined at Kaiyuan Temple in Mingzhou for offerings. Later, a monk asked: "The scripture says there is no land where he does not manifest his body; why was this [image] unable to move?"
He did not go to the kingdom of Koryo.
Changqing Ling said: "Although his manifestation is universal, the appearance perceived is partial.
In the past, there was a presiding master who constantly recited the name of Amitābha. A junior disciple called out to him, "Preceptor! The master turned his head; the junior...
The Master did not look back. This happened three or four times. The head monk scolded him. The junior monk said, "For how many years have you been calling him?
You may call him as you please, but as soon as I call him, he breaks out in a rage."
*The Essential Record of the Linked Lamp*,
Fascicle Twenty-nine and Fascicle Thirty.
Compiled by the monk Wuming, successor to the Patriarchs at Chongfu Chan Monastery in Quanzhou.
The Heart-King Inscription of Master Fu:
Contemplating the Empty King of the Mind— Subtle and wondrous, difficult to fathom; Formless and signless, Possessing great supernormal power.
It can extinguish a thousand calamities And accomplish ten thousand virtues. Although its essential nature is empty, It is able to bestow the Dharma rules.
When observed, it has no form; when called upon, it has sound. It acts as the general of the Great Dharma.
The flavor of salt in water, the glue and blue pigment within color—certainly they exist, yet their forms are not seen.
The mind-king is likewise: it dwells within the body, entering and exiting through the gateway of the face, responding to objects according to circumstances.
Sovereign and unimpeded, all that is done is accomplished. To realize the fundamental consciousness-mind is to see the Buddha through the consciousness-mind.
This mind is the Buddha; this Buddha is the mind. In every thought, the mind is the Buddha; the Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha.
If you wish to achieve success early, discipline yourself with the precepts; purify the precepts and purify the mind. The mind is itself the Buddha.
Apart from this mind-king, there is no other Buddha. If you wish to attain Buddhahood, do not defile yourself with a single thing.
Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and anger is real. Enter this Dharma-gate and, sitting upright, you shall attain Buddhahood.
Having reached the other shore, you will obtain the *pāramitās*. A true seeker of the Way should observe their own mind.
Know that the Buddha is within; do not seek him outwardly. Mind is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is itself the mind.
When the mind clearly recognizes the Buddha, one understands and knows the mind. Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no mind.
If one cannot fathom the non-duality of Buddha and mind, one will be incapable of anything. Clinging to emptiness and lingering in stillness, one drifts and sinks upon realizing this.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace through this mind; it is the Great Being who clarifies the mind who awakens to this profound resonance.
The nature of body and mind is wondrous and its function undergoes no change. Therefore, the wise let the mind rest in freedom;
do not speak of a "mind-king" that is empty and devoid of substantiality, yet which can cause the physical body to act either erroneously or correctly.
Neither existent nor non-existent, its appearance and concealment are indeterminate; the nature of mind transcends emptiness, yet it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely.
Therefore, I exhort you: take care to guard yourself with vigilance. Every moment of action leads once again to drifting and sinking.
The pure and luminous mind-intelligence is like the gold of the world; the treasury of Prajñā resides within both body and mind.
The Unconditioned Treasure of Dharma is neither shallow nor deep; all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas realize this original mind.
For those who encounter it through a karmic affinity, there is no past, future, or present.
— Master Zhigong’s *Song of the Twelve Hours*.
At dawn, the hour of Yin: within the frantic mechanism lies the person of the Way.
Having undergone diligent toil through immeasurable kalpas, yet lacking faith, one constantly grasps at the wish-fulfilling jewel as if clutching a mundane object;
thus one enters the ford of delusion. Were there even a hair’s breadth [of attachment], it would be but dust.
Do not dwell upon the old state that lacks characteristics; external knowledge is likewise not true.
When the sun rises at dawn, there is no need for artifice in its application.
Even if divine light illuminates existence and non-existence, the moment you give rise to a deliberate thought, you will be disturbed by demonic realms.

If you exert effort, you will never reach the end; day and night you are twisted by others and the self, so do not try to arrange things—just let them be as they are. When has affliction ever arisen from the mind-ground?
At the very moment of eating, ignorance is itself the body of Śākyamuni.
Sitting and reclining, one does not know that this is fundamentally the Way;
Thus one busily undergoes suffering and toil, recognizing sounds and forms, seeking out the distant and the near— This is merely being a person defiled by the world.
If you intend to seek the Buddha-way with the mind, Ask the empty sky, and only then will you emerge from the dust.
At the hour of Yuzhong (Yi), for those who have not yet attained realization,
even if they are taught extensively and reach a thorough understanding of the Patriarchs’ words, do not settle upon the meaning within the mind;
merely guarding the mysterious and devoid of texts, if you cling to this, it remains as before— not the truth.
If you momentarily accept this for yourself and do not pursue it further, you will not encounter the realm of demons throughout vast eons.
When the sun is at its zenith in the south, the priceless jewel within the body of the four elements is like a mirage or a flower in the sky;
if you refuse to cast it aside, your intentional cultivation will only become increasingly arduous.
Never deluded, do not seek enlightenment. Let the morning sun rise and set as many times as it may;
within the body of form lies the formless body. Upon the road of ignorance lies the path of non-arising.
Before midday, how could the mind-ground ever have attained the ultimate meaning?
The characters of other schools know no distinction between the distant and the near; do not exert effort to seek their underlying meaning.
Let them run free and unrestrained, without any taboos. Constantly present in the human world, they do not dwell in one place;
their functioning never departs from the midst of sound and form. Through kalpas, when have they ever been abandoned for even a moment?
The Hour of the Monkey (Shen), the Third Watch of the Afternoon: In studying the Way, one must first not loathe poverty.
Phenomenal forms are originally but provisional accumulations; Since the formless is what it is, why strive to establish a "true" reality?
To practice purification is merely to weary the spirit; Do not mistake ignorance for your neighbor.
Seeking nothing beneath words, there is no fixed place; For a brief moment, one is called a renunciant.
As the sun enters the hour of You (17–19 p.m.), illusory sounds will not last long.
If one does not even partake of the rare delicacies of dhyāna-joy, Who could possibly drink the wine of ignorance?
There is nothing to discard, and no object to guard; vast and free, it has never existed.
Even if you are widely learned and master the past and present, you are merely a madman wandering outside.
At dusk, the frantic one exerts his efforts, casting himself into a dark room.
Even if the mind were to penetrate immeasurable time, throughout kalpas, how could it ever differ from this very day?
If you attempt to deliberate upon it, you will instead chatter and fuss, only making the heart grow blacker than lacquer.
Day and night, it radiates light, illuminating both existence and non-existence; yet the deluded call this the "Pāramitā."
The hour of Ren-ding is Hai; though one may possess courageous diligence, it becomes indolence if not accompanied by even a hair’s breadth of the mind of cultivation and study.

Within the light of formlessness, one is eternally sovereign, transcending Śākyamuni and surpassing the ancestral generations; yet if there is even a speck of dust in the mind, it will once again create obstruction.
Reckless and dissolute, forever like one who is dazed and inert— The family of others naturally has those who understand.
At the hour of the midnight rat, when the mind abides in non-arising, that is birth-and-death;
Yet how could birth-and-death ever belong to existence or non-existence? When it is employed, it is employed without words or characters.
The Patriarch said: "External matters—recognize them as they arise, yet they are not there;
even if you search with deliberate intent, no trace remains. When the demons of birth and death come to test you, let them try;
at the hour of the rooster’s crow (1–3 a.m.), a single round light has long been shining."
Searching within and without, one finds nothing at all; In the midst of worldly activity, there is a total lack of head or hand. When the world is destroyed, it does not decay;
Listen to this one word for those who have not yet understood: Who is it that opens their mouth right now?
Master Zhigong’s Fourteen Points on the Non-duality of Bodhi and Affliction:
Sentient beings do not understand that they should cultivate the Way; instead, they merely wish to sever and eliminate afflictions.
Afflictions are originally empty and still; Seeking the Way further to find the Way is but a single thought. This very mind is it—why seek elsewhere?
The Great Way is clearly present before one’s eyes, yet deluded fools do not realize it.
The Buddha-nature is true and spontaneous, arising of itself; it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor created through cultivation.
Failing to recognize that the three poisons are empty and false, one falsely clings to them as they rise and fall, drifting through birth and old age.
What was lost in days past is not considered late; what is realized today is not considered early.
The man who realizes that upholding and violating are non-dual operates without hindrance;
he is not constrained by the rules of the precepts, for upholding and violating are fundamentally unborn. Only fools are bound by such prohibitions.
The actions of the wise are entirely empty; the śrāvakas encounter obstructions at every turn.
The great being’s physical eye is perfectly penetrating, whereas the divine eyes of the two vehicles are clouded with cataracts.
They falsely cling to existence and non-existence within space, failing to realize that form and mind are without obstruction.
Bodhisattvas dwell together with worldly people, yet they remain pure and untainted.

Worldly fools are greedily attached to nirvāṇa, whereas the wise realize that the reality-limit of birth and death is the nature of phenomena—empty and beyond verbal expression. This verse provides a brief summary of dependent origination.
A hundred-year-old child who lacks wisdom; a child who possesses wisdom is a Buddha of a hundred years.
Sentient beings and Buddhas are not two;
sentient beings and Buddhas are no different. Great wisdom is not distinct from folly.
Why seek jewels elsewhere? Within the field of the body, there is naturally the bright pearl.
The right path and the deviant path are not two; know that ordinary beings and sages share the same way.
Delusion and awakening are fundamentally without distinction; nirvana and birth-and-death are one and the same.
Ultimately, all conditions are empty and still; seeking only the purity and vacuity of mental conceptions, not a single dharma can be apprehended.
Spontaneously and serenely, one enters the state of non-remainder, where principle and phenomena are non-dual.
The mind-king is sovereign and carefree; the nature of phenomena is fundamentally free from the ten fetters.
Since everything is non-other than the Buddha-work, why need one restrain the thoughts through seated meditation?
Delusive thoughts are originally empty and still; there is no need to sever the pursuit of external conditions.
The wise have no mind to be attained; naturally there is neither contention nor clamor.
Not recognizing the unconditioned Great Way, when will one realize the profound mystery?
Buddhas and sentient beings are of one kind; sentient beings are themselves the World-Honored One.
Ordinary beings give rise to false discriminations, clinging to existence within non-existence;
deluded and rushing about, they fail to realize that greed, anger, and emptiness-quietude are one. Where is there that is not the gate of truth?
Stillness and turmoil are non-dual.
The śrāvakas weary of clamor and seek stillness, just as one might discard flour in search of bread;

yet the bread is nothing other than that very flour. Conditioned phenomena shift according to the person through a hundred variations, yet afflictions are themselves bodhi. Where there is no mind, there is no objective realm.
Birth-and-death is no different from nirvana; greed and anger are like flames and shadows.
The wise have no mind to seek a Buddha, while the foolish cling to the heterodox and the orthodox, laboring in vain throughout their lives and failing to behold the Tathāgata’s wondrous crown.
Thoroughly realizing that the nature of lust is empty, The cauldrons and furnace coals grow cold of their own accord.
Good and evil are non-dual;
my own body and mind are joyful, Tranquil and free, beyond both good and evil.
The Dharma-body is sovereign and without fixed direction; whatever meets the eye is none other than perfect enlightenment.
The six sense-objects are originally empty and still; ordinary people deludedly give rise to attachment.
Nirvana and birth-and-death are equally empty and level; in the four seas, who can say what is deep or shallow?
The unconditioned Great Way is spontaneous; there is no need to employ the mind to calculate or measure it.
The Bodhisattva is relaxed and naturally penetrating; whatever he does always contains wondrous enlightenment.
The Śrāvaka clings to the dharma and sits in meditation, like a silkworm spinning its own cocoon to bind itself.
The nature of phenomena is originally perfect and luminous; once the illness is cured, what need is there to cling to the medicine?
Fully realizing the equality of all phenomena, one dwells in a state of carefree purity and joy, where form and emptiness are non-dual.
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without blue or yellow;
sentient beings vainly compose treatises on self and other, and on cessation and contemplation. Their own minds are restless and deranged;
they do not recognize the wondrous principle of perfect penetration. When will they realize the true and eternal?
Being ill oneself yet unable to treat the ailment, one instead asks others to look at it from outside the medical prescriptions;
one deems this to be virtuous, yet within the heart one remains like a jackal or a wolf.
The fool fears hell, while the wise person sees no difference between it and heaven.
The mind never arises in response to objects; every step taken is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Buddhas and sentient beings are non-dual; it is sentient beings themselves who create separation.
If one wishes to eliminate the three poisons, one remains far removed from them yet cannot escape calamity.
The wise know that the mind is Buddha; the ignorant delight in going to the Western Land.
Birth and death are non-dual;
all worldly phenomena are like illusions, and birth and death are like lightning.
The Dharma-body is sovereign and perfectly penetrating; entering and exiting mountains and rivers without obstruction.
Inverted delusions are fundamentally empty; Prajñā is without confusion or disorder.
The three poisons are inherently liberated—what need is there to restrain the mind through dhyāna and contemplation?

It is only because the ignorant do not understand that they rely on the precepts for decisive judgment, failing to recognize the true suchness of quiescence; when will they ever reach the other shore?
The wise have no evil to sever; their functioning follows the mind, whether in gathering or dispersing.
The nature of phenomena is originally empty and still; It is not bound by birth and death.
If you wish to sever afflictions, This is merely an ignorant fool.
Afflictions are themselves bodhi; What need is there to seek meditation elsewhere?
In the ultimate reality, there is neither Buddha nor Māra; The essence of mind is formless and without division.
When the non-dual is severed, the Great Man acts with majestic dignity; He wanders at ease and freely, without hindrance.
Nothing can cause harm; it is as firm and solid as vajra.
It does not cling to the two extremes but abides in the Middle Way. It is transcendent, neither annihilated nor eternal.
Greed and anger for the five desires are themselves the Buddha; hell is no different from heaven.
Foolish people give rise to false discriminations, Wandering through birth and death in wild confusion;
The wise understand that form is without obstruction, While Śrāvakas are all filled with distress.
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally free from blemish, Yet sentient beings falsely cling to blue and yellow.
The Tathāgata guides and receives those who are deluded and ignorant;
he speaks of hells and heavens as being naturally present within the body of Maitreya. Why must one seek them elsewhere through deliberation?
To discard the true image of the Tathatā (Suchness) is for such a person to be truly insane.
Within the minds of the śrāvakas there is no understanding; they merely listen to and pursue words and phrases.

These words and phrases are not the true Path. Consequently, their strife increases, and within their hearts dwell vipers, pythons, and scorpions. As soon as one is bitten by them, one suffers injury.
If one does not understand how to extract the meaning from the text, when will one realize the True Constant?
One will die and enter the Avīci Hell, where the consciousness undergoes calamity and misfortune in vain;
for the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual.

The Dharma Master’s exposition of the Dharma is excellent; yet while his mind is not free from afflictions, he speaks of words and characters to transform others. Consequently, he further increases their birth, old age, and delusion.
Truth and falsehood are fundamentally non-dual, yet ordinary people discard the false in search of the Way.
The fourfold assembly gathers like clouds to listen to the discourse; from the high seat, the discussions flow in vast abundance.

The southern and northern seats contend with one another, and though the fourfold assembly speaks in praise, claiming it is excellent, their mouths may speak of nectar while their hearts remain as dry as ever.
Originally possessing not a single coin oneself, yet day and night counting another's treasures—
just like a foolish person lacking wisdom who casts away true gold to carry grass upon their back.
Without abandoning the three poisons within the mind, I do not know when one might attain the Way.
The Vinaya Master Jiebo (Unbinding Bonds) binds himself by upholding the precepts; While binding himself, he is also able to bind others.
Outwardly he displays dignified deportment and tranquil stillness, Yet within his heart it is like a surging, turbulent wave.
Without boarding the raft of the vessel of birth-and-death, how can one cross the river of craving?
Not understanding the true principle of the orthodox teaching, their words of false views are manifold.
Two bhikṣus having violated the precepts, went instead to question Upāli.
Upāli expounded the Vinaya and its precepts on offenses; meanwhile, in the chamber of the square-walled room, the layman Vimalakīrti increasingly ensnared the bhikṣus in his net.
Vimalakīrti then came forth to rebuke Upāli, who remained silent and without reply. Thus, the Dharma taught by the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) was beyond reproach.
Yet that nature of precepts is like space, existing neither within nor without this Sahā world;
though one may urge the removal of arising and ceasing, they are unwilling to comply. Suddenly awakening, one realizes it is identical to the realm of Śākyamuni, where illumination is non-dual.
The Chan Master’s essence is detached from ignorance; from where could afflictions arise?
Hell and heaven are of one and the same mark; Nirvana and birth-and-death are empty names.
There is nothing of greed or hatred to be severed, nor is there any Buddha-way to be realized.
Sentient beings and Buddhas are equal; the Self-Awakened One is ever-vigilant and unsullied by the six sense objects.
Every phrase uniquely accords with the Unborn Perfect Enlightenment;
through a single thought of profound understanding, the three periods of time are all serenely level.
Neither dharma nor vinaya, self-restrained; Transcending these four propositions and a hundred negations, one enters directly into perfect realization.
Like space, without action and without dependence, its functioning is unimpeded.
I now flow freely and with self-mastery, Envious of neither kings, dukes, ministers, nor officials.
The four seasons remain as steadfast as adamant; My former joy and mind are forever unchanged.
The Treasure of the Dharma is like Mount Sumeru, And wisdom is vaster than the rivers and seas.
Not led astray by the eight winds, Neither diligent nor indolent,
remaining natural and free from agitation or collapse; Relaxed and unhindered,
acting with sovereign ease even if a sword were placed upon one's head— I remain tranquil and do not concern myself with it.
Delusion and awakening are non-dual:
when deluded, one takes emptiness to be form; upon awakening, one takes form to be emptiness.
Delusion and awakening are fundamentally without distinction; form and emptiness are ultimately identical.
The fool calls south north; the wise person realizes there is no east or west.
If you seek the wondrous principle of the Tathāgata, it is always within a single thought.
A mirage is fundamentally not water; the thirsty deer chases it in frantic haste.
One's own self is false and unreal; Seeking emptiness within emptiness— The delusion of worldly people has reached its extreme, Like a dog barking at the roar of thunder.
—From the *Śraddhā-laghu-śāstra* (Mind Inscription on Faith) by the Third Patriarch, Master Can.
The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and all will be transparently clear.

A difference of even a hair’s breadth makes heaven and earth apart. If you wish for this to manifest before you, do not maintain notions of compliance or resistance, nor let favor and opposition contend;
these are the maladies of the mind. Failing to recognize the profound essence, your efforts at seeking stillness are merely labor in vain.
Perfectly identical to the great void, Without deficiency and without excess. It is precisely because of grasping and rejecting That things do not accord with reality.
Do not pursue what has conditions; Do not dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single kind of equanimity, All is naturally exhausted.
Cessation returns to movement; Cessation further intensifies movement. If one merely lingers on both sides, How can one know this "one kind"?

If one type is not penetrating, one fails at both ends. To dismiss existence and pursue non-existence, or to follow emptiness while turning one's back on emptiness—this leads to much talk and much thought, resulting in increasing disharmony.
When words are cut off and thoughts are extinguished, there is nowhere that does not penetrate;
returning to the root, one attains the essential meaning. Yet, if one follows after illumination, one loses the source. In a mere moment, it turns back again, surpassing the previous emptiness.
The preceding transformations of emptiness all arise from deluded views; do not seek the truth, but simply cease such views.
When these two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them. As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes distracted and loses the mind.
Because duality arises from unity, do not even cling to that unity. When the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
No fault, no law; no arising, no mind. The capacity can be extinguished by the object, and the object sinks along with the capacity.
The object arises from the capacity, and the capacity arises from the object. If you wish to know these two segments, they are originally one emptiness.
One emptiness encompasses both; together they contain the myriad phenomena. Seeing neither the refined nor the coarse, how could there be partiality?
The essence of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult. With narrow views and doubt, one becomes increasingly anxious and increasingly slow.
To grasp it is to lose its measure and inevitably enter a deviant path. To let it be of itself is natural; its essence has no coming or staying.

Let the nature act spontaneously and it accords with the Way; carefree and at ease, one is free from affliction. To bind the mind to thoughts is to deviate from the truth; sinking into dullness is not good.
Do not weary yourself with mental toil; why distinguish between the distant and the near? If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six sense-objects.
When the six sense-objects are not loathed, they are identical to perfect enlightenment. The wise act without contrivance; the ignorant bind themselves.
The Dharma has no differentiation, yet they give rise to false attachment. To employ the mind to direct the mind—is this not a great error?
Deluded beings are tossed between stillness and agitation; the enlightened find neither preference nor aversion.
All dualistic extremes arise simply from grasping at dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky; why labor to clutch at gain and loss, right and wrong? Let them all be cast aside at once.
If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord; if the mind does not diverge, the myriad dharmas are of one suchness.
The single suchness of the essence is profound; from the beginning, it forgets conditions. All phenomena are viewed as equal, returning to and merging with spontaneity.
Its cause is obliterated; it cannot be compared to anything. Where movement ceases, there is no movement; where movement stops, there is no stopping.
Since both are not established, how can "one" exist? Ultimately and exhaustively, it does not abide by any rules or patterns.
The mind accords with equality; all that is done comes to rest. Doubts are completely purified; right faith becomes straight and upright.
Nothing remains lingering; there is nothing to be remembered. Empty clarity illuminates itself spontaneously, without taxing the power of the mind.
This is a realm beyond deliberation, difficult for consciousness and emotion to fathom. It is the *tathatā* dharma-realm, where there is neither other nor self.
It requires urgent resonance; it is spoken of as non-duality alone. Where there is no duality, all are identical, encompassing everything without exception.

The wise of the ten directions all enter this school. This school is neither constricted nor extended: in a single thought-moment there are ten thousand years, yet there is neither being nor non-being.
It is right before one’s eyes throughout the ten directions. The smallest is identical to the great; boundaries are forgotten and severed.
The Great is ultimately one with the small; its boundaries and surface cannot be seen. Existence is itself non-existence; non-existence is itself existence.
If it were not thus, there would be no need for guarding. One is all, and all is one.
If one can simply be thus, why worry that completion will not be achieved? Faithful mind is non-dual; non-dual is faithful mind.
The path of language is cut off; it is neither past, future, nor present.
O Great Master Zhongjia Zhenjue, Song of Realizing the Way:
Have you not seen the man of the Way who has severed study and attained non-action? He does not eliminate delusive thoughts, nor does he seek the truth.
The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body, when fully realized, is not a single thing; It is the original source-nature, the natural, true Buddha.
The five aggregates are like floating clouds, coming and going in emptiness; The three poisons are like bubbles, vainly appearing and vanishing.
Realizing the true mark, there is no self or phenomena; In a single instant of cessation, even the karma of Avīci is extinguished.
If one uses false speech to deceive sentient beings, One will personally invite the punishment of having one's tongue plucked out for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
Sudden awakening is Tathāgata-dhyāna; The essence of the six perfections and myriad practices is perfected within it.
Within the dream, the six realms of existence are vividly clear; Upon awakening, all is empty, and not even a "great chiliocosm" remains.
There is neither sin nor merit, neither loss nor gain. Within this nature of quiescent extinction, do not seek or inquire.
Hitherto, the mirror of dust has never been polished; Today, you must clearly analyze it for yourself.
Who is without thought? Who is without birth? If there is truly no birth and no non-birth, call out to the wooden man at the mechanical gate and ask him.
Seeking Buddhahood through effort—when will it ever be accomplished?
Cast away the four elements; do not grasp at them. Within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow along with eating and drinking.
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and entirely empty; This is the Tathāgata’s definitive teaching on Great Perfect Enlightenment.

It manifests the True Vehicle. If there are those who refuse to accept it, I shall follow my own inclination and directly investigate the root, as sealed by the Buddha; I cannot pick at leaves or seek among branches."
The maṇi jewel, which people do not recognize, has been personally obtained within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Its six kinds of divine functions are both empty and non-empty; it is a single round radiance, neither form nor non-form.
It purifies the five eyes and attains the five powers—only through direct realization can its unfathomable nature be known.
Beholding one's form in a mirror is not difficult; But who can ever grasp the moon reflected in water?
Always walking alone, always pacing by myself, The realized ones travel together on the path to Nirvana.
Their tune is ancient and their spirit is pure, their wind naturally lofty; Though their countenance is haggard and their bones are firm, people pay them no heed.
The destitute Śākya son claims in speech that he is poor; yet in truth, while his body is poor, his Way is not poor.
Being poor, his body is always clad in coarse hempen rags; but as for the Way, his mind stores a priceless treasure.
This priceless treasure is inexhaustible in its use; to benefit all beings according to the occasion, he never begrudges it.
The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within the essence; The eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the mind-ground seal of the superior person.
With a single resolution, all is understood; Those of middling and inferior capacity, though much-learned, lack much faith.
Only by untying the stained robe from within one's own breast Can one truly know; who can boast of diligence while looking outward?
Let others slander me; let others be wrong. To burn fire toward heaven is but to exhaust oneself in vain.
Hearing this, it was as if I were drinking nectar; it melted away and I suddenly entered the inconceivable contemplation.
Evil words are indeed merit; they thus become my spiritual friends.
Not giving rise to enmity or kinship through slander or defamation, How could this not manifest the power of non-arising compassion and patience?
The principle is pervasive; the teaching is pervasive. With concentration and wisdom perfectly clear, one does not stagnate in emptiness.
It is not only I who have now attained realization alone; The essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical.
The Lion’s Roar, spoken with fearless confidence— Upon hearing it, the hundred beasts’ skulls split asunder;
Fragrant elephants flee in haste, their majesty lost; Heavenly dragons listen in silence, filled with joy.
Wandering rivers and seas, traversing mountains and plains, I seek teachers and inquire after the Way to practice Zen.
Since recognizing the path of Caoxi, one knows that birth and death are not interconnected;
walking is Chan, sitting is Chan—whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, the essence remains serene.
Even when encountering a sharp blade, one is ever at ease; even if given lethal poison, one remains unconcerned.
My Master met the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; Throughout many kalpas, he was once the Immortal of Forbearance.
How many times was he born? How many times did he die? In the long flow of birth and death, there was no fixed end.
Since attaining sudden enlightenment and realizing non-arising, What sorrow or joy can there be amidst all honors and insults?

Entering deep mountains, dwelling in an araṇya, amidst towering peaks and secluded depths beneath long pines, one idly sits in tranquility within the home of a wild monk. To dwell in quietude is truly elegant;
upon awakening, one realizes it without exerting effort— all conditioned phenomena are not like this.
Giving with attachment to signs produces the merit for rebirth in heaven; it is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void.
When its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down, bringing about an unfavorable rebirth in the next life.
How can this compare to the gate of the signless true reality, which transcends in a single leap, entering directly into the stage of the Tathāgata?

If you only attain the root, do not worry about the branches. Just as pure lapis lazuli contains a precious moon, if one can understand this wish-fulfilling jewel, then benefiting oneself and others will never be exhausted.
The river moon shines; the pines are stirred by the wind. Throughout the eternal night and the clear sky, what else is there to do?
The Buddha-nature is the pearl of precepts, the seal of the mind-ground; Mist, dew, clouds, and mists are the robes upon his body.

The dragon-subduing bowl and the tiger-unbinding staff, With twin-pronged golden rings jangling clearly— These are not for ostentatious display or empty ritual holding; They are the traces left by the Tathāgata’s own footsteps.
Not seeking the true, not severing the delusory, Thoroughly understanding that these two dharmas are empty,
signless, signless yet non-signless, empty yet non-empty— This is the Tathāgata’s true mark: the mirror of the mind is bright,
Reflecting without obstruction, vast and transparently clear, pervading the entire realm of saṃsāra.
Within the manifestation of the myriad phenomena, A single orb of light is neither inside nor outside.
It is vast and open emptiness; To reject cause and effect Is to bring about calamity and misfortune in a boundless expanse.
To abandon existence while clinging to emptiness is likewise a sickness— Like avoiding drowning only to leap into fire.
Abandoning the deluded mind and grasping at ultimate truth—this very mind of grasping and abandoning becomes crafty hypocrisy.
When practitioners do not understand this, they apply themselves to cultivation and instead recognize a thief as their own son.
They squander the wealth of the Dharma and extinguish their merit; all of this does not arise from anything other than this mind-consciousness.
Therefore, through the Chan gate, one brings the mind to its ultimate end;
By the power of sudden entry into the vision of non-arising, the Great Man wields the sword of wisdom— The blade of Prajñā with its adamantine flames.
Not only can it shatter the minds of externalists, It has long since struck down the courage of the heavenly Māras.

Thundering the Dharma-thunder, Beating the Dharma-drum, Spreading the clouds of compassion to sprinkle sweet dew— Dragons and elephants tread upon them, their moisture boundless; The three vehicles and five natures all awaken.
The snow-mountain fatness contains no impurities; Pure ghee alone emerges, which I constantly receive.
The single nature perfectly penetrates all natures; The single dharma universally contains all dharmas.
As the single moon universally appears in all waters, All moon-reflections in the waters are subsumed within that one moon.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my own nature; My nature is identical and united with that of the Tathāgata.
The first stage encompasses all stages; it is neither form nor mind, neither karma nor conduct.
In the snap of a finger, eighty thousand gates are perfectly realized; in a single instant, three great kalpas are extinguished.
Whether expressed through finite numbers or infinite enumerations—what connection have these have with my numinous awakening?
It cannot be disparaged; it cannot be praised. Its essence is like empty space, without shore or limit.
Without leaving its present location, it is eternally serene and still. If you seek it, you will know that it cannot be seen;
it cannot be grasped, nor can it be relinquished. Within this state where nothing can be attained, there is simply attainment as it is.
Silent when speaking, speaking when silent; The great gate of giving is open, unobstructed.
When someone asks me what school I follow, I reply: it is the power of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Whether right or wrong, people do not know; Moving against the current or with it, even the heavens cannot fathom it.
I have long practiced through many kalpas; this is no idle deception.
I raise the Dharma banner and establish the fundamental tenet—clearly, the Buddha’s command makes Caoxi the foremost.
Kāśyapa was the first to transmit the lamp; twenty-eight generations are recorded in the West.
The Dharma flowed eastward and entered this land; Bodhidharma was the First Patriarch.
The transmission of the robe through six generations became renowned throughout the world. As for those who later attained the Way, their number is beyond reckoning.
Truth cannot be established, for delusion is fundamentally empty. Both existence and non-existence are cast aside, yet even this "emptiness" is not truly empty.
The twenty gates of emptiness originally do not cling; the single nature is the Tathāgata’s body, inherently identical.
The mind is the root; phenomena are the dust. These two are like stains upon a mirror:
when the stains and grime are entirely removed, the light finally appears. When both mind and phenomena are extinguished, the nature is itself the truth.
Alas for the final dharma! In this degenerate age, sentient beings have meager merit and are difficult to discipline.
The Sage is far removed and false views run deep; demons are strong while the Dharma is weak, resulting in much resentment and harm.
Hearing speak of the Tathāgata’s gate of sudden teaching, they harbor resentment, wishing it were extinguished so that [their opposition] might be smashed like tiles.
The deed is formed in the mind; the calamity rests upon the body. There is no need for grievance or complaint, nor should one lay the blame on others.
If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
In a sandalwood forest there are no other trees; dense, deep, and profound, it is the dwelling place of the lion.
In the tranquil realm, amidst the forest, he wanders alone; The beasts and birds all flee far away.
O Lion Cub, with the multitude following behind, At three years of age, you can already let out a great roar.
If a wild jackal were to pursue the Dharma King, This century-old monster would merely open its mouth in vain.
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching transcends human sentiment; if there is doubt that cannot be resolved, one must struggle for it directly.
It is not that this mountain monk seeks to assert self and others; I fear that in practicing, one might fall into the pit of annihilationism or eternalism.
It is neither "not" nor "is," neither "is" nor "is not. To err by a hair’s breadth is to lose a thousand li.
This is the dragon girl who suddenly attained Buddhahood; This is not the same as Shanxing, who fell into ruin upon birth.
Since my youth, I have accumulated learning, And have also investigated commentaries and sought out sutras and treatises.
Distinguishing names and characteristics, I knew no rest; Entering the sea to count its sands, I only exhausted myself in vain.
Yet I was bitterly rebuked by the Tathāgata: "What benefit is there in calculating another's treasures?
From the start you have stumbled, realizing your journey was in vain; For many years you have lived in vain as a guest in the dust and wind.
Your spiritual nature is perverse, your understanding is mistaken, and you do not comprehend the Tathāgata’s perfect and sudden teaching."
The diligence of the two vehicles causes the mind of the Way to sink;
the cleverness of external paths lacks true wisdom and is likewise foolish and deluded. They are small and ignorant, giving rise to a false understanding based on an empty fist;
grasping at the finger as the moon, they labor in vain, falsely fabricating wonders within the phenomena of the faculties and their objects.
When not a single dharma is seen, one is then called the Tathāgata, the Sovereign Observer of Self;
at that moment, karmic obstacles are originally empty. If this is not yet realized, one must still repay past debts:
when hungry, one cannot eat the king’s banquet; when ill, how can one be cured by meeting the King of Physicians?
Practicing dhyāna amidst desire with the power of knowledge and vision, A lotus born from fire can never be destroyed.
Vīradatta committed grave offenses yet realized non-arising; He attained Buddhahood long ago and remains present even now.
With the Lion’s Roar, he speaks fearlessly; I deeply lament those who are ignorant, stubborn, and callous.
They know only that committing grave offenses obstructs Bodhi, yet they do not see the Tathāgata’s secret method for opening the way.
There were two bhikṣus who committed acts of lust and killing;
Upāli saw only the accumulation of karmic bonds like a firefly’s glow, while the Great Being Vimalakīrti instantly dispelled their doubts, just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow.
Inconceivable is the power of liberation; its wondrous function is as infinite as the sands of the Ganges.
To offer the four requisites, one would not dare decline the toil; even ten thousand taels of gold could not suffice.
To crush one’s bones and shatter one’s body would be insufficient as recompense. A single phrase, when clearly realized, transcends billions of worlds.
The King of Dharmas, most supreme, Realized by Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— I now understand this wish-fulfilling jewel.
Those who believe and accept it will all correspond with it;
They will see clearly: Not a single thing exists, Nor does a person exist, Nor does a Buddha exist.
The trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean; all sages and worthies are like lightning flashes.
Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one’s head, one’s perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom shall never be lost.
The sun may grow cold, the moon may grow hot, but no demons can destroy this true teaching.
An elephant carriage towering and grand advances in vain upon the road; who has seen a mantis able to block its tracks?
A great elephant does not roam the narrow paths of a rabbit; one of great awakening is not constrained by minor details.
Do not slander the vast heavens with your narrow perspective; before you have realized this, I shall now resolve it for you.
The Heart-Mind of the Great Immortal of the Land of Chu: East and West, it was secretly transmitted. People’s faculties are sharp or dull;
The Way has no North or South, nor Patriarchs. The numinous source is bright and pure; Its branches and streams flow on in obscurity.
The administrative official is fundamentally deluded; even to accord with principle is not awakening. In every gate and in all objects, there is mutual interpenetration and non-interpenetration.
When they interpenetrate, they further involve one another; otherwise, they abide in their respective positions.
Form originally has diverse substances and images; sound originally differs as pleasure or pain; darkness accords with words of superior, middling, and inferior.
The lines on clarity and turbidity are luminously clear: the natures of the four great elements naturally restore themselves.
Fire is hot, wind is mobile, water is moist, and earth is solid.
Eye and form, ear and sound, nose and fragrance, tongue and the salty or sour—yet within each and every phenomenon, they are distributed according to their roots and branches.
Root and branch must both return to the source; honor and humility employ their respective words.
When there is light within, one must not meet it with darkness; when there is darkness within, one must not encounter it with light.
Light and darkness face each other, like successive steps; all things possess their own inherent efficacy.
One should speak of function and locus; The reality of things lies in the meeting of lid and box. In principle, one should meet the point like the tips of two arrows;
When receiving words, one must grasp the source. Do not establish your own rules and regulations.

If you do not realize the Way upon seeing it before your eyes, how can you know the road while your feet move? Advancing forward is neither far nor near; Delusion creates a barrier as solid as mountains and rivers.
Respectfully addressed to those who investigate the Mystery: Do not let your time and light be spent in vain.
The Song of the Hermitage by Master Shitou:
I have built a thatched hut and possess no treasures; When the meal is finished, I leisurely seek the joy of sleep.
When first completed, I saw fresh thatch; after it was torn apart, I covered the hut with thatch again.
The hermit dwells forever; he belongs neither to the middle nor to the outside.
I do not dwell where worldly people dwell; I do not love what worldly people love.
Though the hermitage is small, it contains the entire Dharma-realm. The Elder of the Abbot’s Quarter understands this through his realization of the Supreme Vehicle;
bodhisattvas of superior capacity have no doubt. Those of middling or inferior capacity, upon hearing this, will surely feel strange, asking:
"Does this hermitage decay or not? Whether it decays or does not decay, the Master remains fundamentally present."
Not dwelling in the south, north, east, or west, With a foundation as firm as the finest pine trees beneath, Within a bright window, A jade palace and vermilion towers are no match for this place.
With patched robes covering one's head, all affairs come to rest; At such a time, the mountain monk understands nothing at all.
Dwelling in this hermitage, cease from conceptualizing and interpreting. Who would boast of setting up a shop to entice others to buy?
When the light returns and shines back upon itself, one immediately returns home. This vast and penetrating spiritual root is neither biased nor partial.
Having encountered the Patriarch and received his personal instruction, bind grass to make your hut and never give rise to thoughts of retreat.
Having cast aside a hundred years, one acts with total freedom; With a wave of the hand, one departs and incurs no blame.
Though there be a thousand kinds of words And ten thousand ways of explaining, It is simply to ensure that you remain forever undeluded.
If you wish to know the deathless person within the hermitage, How could they ever depart from this very sackcloth here?
The Inscription on the Cessation of Mind by the Monk Wuming (Wuming, a Right Reminder of the Sui Dynasty who abandoned his office to become a monk).

Within the Dharma-realm there is one who possesses the wish-fulfilling jewel; for a long time he has kept his person concealed, yet he inscribed upon his breast: "The ancient method of gathering the mind."
You are a human being. Be on guard! Be on guard! Do not seek excessive knowledge; do not harbor excessive anxieties. Much knowledge brings much entanglement; it is better to let the will rest.
Much anxiety leads to many failures; it is better to maintain the One. Excessive anxiety scatters the resolve; excessive knowledge agitates the mind.

An agitated mind gives rise to affliction; a scattered resolve obstructs the Way. Do not say, "What harm can there be? for the suffering is long-lasting. Do not say, "What is there to fear? for its calamities are vast.
The cauldron boils; not a drop of water ceases to fall. The four seas are about to overflow; not a speck of dust is brushed away. The five sacred peaks are about to be formed.
Guard the end by staying with the root; though small, do not treat it lightly. It governs your seven apertures and idles your six passions.
Do not gaze upon forms; do not listen to sounds. He who hears sounds is deaf; he who sees forms is blind. A single word or a single art is but a mosquito or gnat in the void. A single skill...
A single ability is like a solitary lamp beneath the sun; the talents and arts of the eminent and wise become obscured by folly.

They abandon simplicity and purity, becoming addicted to licentious beauty. It is easy to drive a horse, but the mind-monkey is difficult to restrain. When the spirit is exhausted by toil, the physical form will surely perish.

Erroneous conduct leads ultimately to delusion, and one remains forever mired in the long journey. Do not prize mere talent, for it causes one to grow increasingly dark and ignorant day by day. To boast of one's own clumsiness while envying the cleverness of others—such is their virtue.
Not expansive, it is called "thick conduct being thin. Such a state will swiftly collapse. Internally harboring arrogance and self-aggrandizement, one externally incurs resentment and hatred.
Whether spoken from the mouth or written by the hand, seeking the praise of others is most shameful. What the common folk call auspicious, the sages call a fault.
Pleasure and play are but momentary; sorrow and grief endure for a long time. Fearing the shadow and fearing the tracks, one goes further and further away. Sit upright.

Beneath the shade of trees, footprints vanish and shadows sink away. Loathing birth and fearing old age, one creates [karma] with every thought; yet if the workings of the mind are extinguished, the cycle of birth and death is forever severed.

There is neither death nor birth, no form and no name. A single path of empty stillness, where all things are leveled and equal. What is noble and what is base? What is disgraceful and what is honorable?
What is superior and what is inferior? What is heavy and what is light? It puts the clarity of the heavens to shame in its purity, and outshines the brilliance of the bright sun.
Preface by Ming’an: Tranquil upon the peaks of Mount Dai, like that city of gold, I respectfully present this to the worthy and wise. May this Way be beneficial and auspicious.
The Venerable Zhaozhou’s Song of the Twelve Hours:
The Cock Crows at the Hour of Chou (1–3 a.m.): Alas, seeing myself arise, I have become a source of leakage and folly.
Neither skirt nor tunic can be found; The form of the *kāṣāya* is but a faint trace.

The trousers have no waistband; The leggings have no opening. On his head, three or five pecks of green ash— He hoped to practice for the benefit and salvation of others, Who knew he would turn into such a wretched fellow?
At dawn, the hour of Yin: in this desolate village and ruined monastery, it is truly difficult to speak of.
There is not a single grain of rice for the morning and midday meals; one faces but empty windows and the dust of crevices.
Only sparrows chirp; no one is intimate. Sitting alone, I hear the falling leaves frequently.
Who says that leaving home severs love and hate? In deliberation, I am unaware as tears dampen my kerchief.
When the sun rises in the hour of Mao, Purity turns instead into affliction;
Conditioned merits are covered by the dust, And boundless fields have never been swept clean.

Furrowing their brows, many; satisfied at heart, few. I cannot bear this old Black Wang from the eastern village, who has not brought the ritual offerings. He lets his donkey eat the grass before my hall.
At mealtime, the smoke and fire are in vain as I look toward my neighbors.
The steamed bun was parted with last year; today I recall it and swallow my saliva in vain.
My recitation of the name is meager, and sighs of lamentation are frequent. Among a hundred households, there is not a single person of virtue;
those who come merely say they are seeking tea to drink. When they do not get tea, they depart while still grumbling.
At the hour of Youzhong (Yi): Having shaved my head, who would have known it would come to this?
Unprovoked, I was invited to serve as a village monk; humiliated and starving, I suffered as if I were about to die.
Hu Zhangsan and Hei Lisì never gave rise to even a fraction of respect.
Just now, arriving suddenly at the gate, I asked only for tea and paper.
At midday in the south, Tea and meals circulate without fixed measure;
Having gone from the south house to the north house, When one finally arrives at the north house, there is no need for excuses or omissions.
Bitter salt, barley vinegar, millet rice, and mustard greens—these offerings are truly no ordinary ones.
The Master’s resolve must be firm and steadfast;
before the sun has turned its course, this time shall not be wasted.
I have heard it said that once full, one forgets a hundred hungers; today, this old monk’s very body is such a one.
Not practicing Chan, not discussing doctrine, he spreads out a tattered mat and sleeps in the sun.
I suspect that even in the Tuṣita Heaven above, there is no such thing as having one's back scorched by the sun like this.
The hour of *shen* (the late afternoon): there are five people burning incense and prostrating;
three old women with goiters, a pair with faces as dark and coarse as sesame oil cakes—truly a rare sight!
O Vajra, there is no need to strain your muscles in vain.
May the silkworms and wheat ripen for me next year; Rāhula, give me a single coin.
When the sun enters the hour of You (the West), Beyond this desolation, what else is there to guard?
The wandering monk of the clouds and waters will surely vanish, But the novice monks visiting the temples shall remain forever.
Producing maxims that never reach the lips, He falsely continues the lineage of the Muni’s descendants.
A single staff, coarse and gnarled, Not only for climbing mountains, but also for beating dogs.
At the hour of dusk, the ninth watch, He sits alone in a solitary, empty, and dark room.
The mirage and the lamp-light are never encountered; before one’s eyes there is nothing but gold-lacquered bells, yet they are not heard.
Days are spent in vain, hearing only the shrill, clamorous scurrying of mice.
On what basis could one still have the heart-mind to contemplate and recite a *pāramitā*?
The hour of Ren-ding is Hai (9–11 p.m.). Who loves the bright moon before the gate?
As one goes inside, there is only worry about lying down; when departing, what clothes shall one wear and what shall cover oneself?
Liu Wei-na, Zhao Wu-jie—how strange it is that they speak of goodness with their mouths!
Let you, mountain monk, empty your bag; when questioned, you simply do not understand at all.
At this midnight hour, how could the mind and its objects ever find even a moment’s rest?
Among the world’s renunciant practitioners, how many can truly act as an abbot like me?
An earthen platform bed, Tattered reed mats, A pillow of aged elm wood, and not a single quilt.
The honored image does not burn aloeswood incense; From within the ashes, one hears only the scent of cow dung.
This is the "Verse on the Illumination of the Way" by Chan Master Luohan Chen.
The ultimate Way is profound and vast; it cannot be proclaimed through words. If proclaimed through words, it is not the essential meaning—who then would say it exists?

It is present everywhere; how could it be compared to true emptiness? If one were to establish a distinction of "true emptiness," then existence and non-existence would both appear within it like reflections in a mirror.
Though these appear, they do not harm its presence anywhere. Without harm and without location, what restriction or obstruction can there be?

If one does not rely on the accomplishment of effort, by what means can one accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)? If the nature of reality is not thus, both [effort and non-effort] become but mere lips and teeth.
To present it in this way causes the principle to lose its fundamental source. The source is not presented through conceptual intention;
if there is nothing to be seen or heard, then seeing and hearing are not liberated. Like the moon in water, if one is not clear regarding this, it turns instead into a superfluous teaching.
A single dharma has form, Obscuring your eyes; Because your eyes are not clear, The world appears rugged and vast.
My school is extraordinary: It is manifest and brilliant before one’s face. Both Buddhas and sentient beings All receive its power of grace.
It does not lie in bowing the head; It is difficult to attain through calculation. It shatters the gateway of the face, Encompassing heaven and earth.
Quickly you must realize it; cast off the roots and dust. How can one who does not understand yet prattle on about Master Chao-an Cha’s "Ten Mysterious Gates" and the Seal of Mind?
I ask: what color is the seal of the mind? Who dares to bestow and transmit this seal of the mind?
Through kalpas it remains ever-plain, without change of hue; to call it the "seal of the mind" is already a hollow word.
One must know that its essence is itself the nature of empty space, comparable to a lotus flower within a blazing furnace.
Do not say that "no-mind" is the Way; no-mind still leaves behind a further barrier.
The Patriarchal intent, the Patriarchal intent, is like space, yet it is not empty; how could the wondrous mechanism fall into the trap of existence or non-existence?
