The Three Sages of the Preliminary Stage do not yet understand this principle; how could the Ten Sages of the Holy Path reach this school?
A golden fish that has passed through the net still lingers in the water; a stone horse returning on its path emerges from the gauze cage.
I speak with earnest care of the meaning of the Westward Transmission; do not ask about the West or the East.
The profound mechanism is so remote that even the void kalpa cannot contain it; how could it ever be bound by the mechanisms of the mundane?
The wondrous essence is fundamentally without location; throughout the entire body, how could there be any further trace?
A single phrase, spiritually resonant, transcends the masses; It stands far beyond the Three Vehicles, requiring no cultivation.
Letting go there, beyond the thousand sages, The return journey is fit to be a fire-steering ox amidst the dust.
The turbid remains turbid; the clear remains clear. Enlightenment and afflictions are equal in emptiness.
Who says the Bian-tribe jade has no one to appraise it? I say the black pearl shines everywhere wherever it goes.
When all phenomena are extinguished, the whole body is revealed. The distinctions of the Three Vehicles are merely forced names.
A man of noble character naturally possesses a will that soars to the heavens; Do not walk where the Tathāgata has already trodden.
The Three Vehicles are expounded in their proper sequence, And these golden words have been proclaimed by the Tathāgatas of the three ages alike.
When he first taught that there is emptiness, all those who clung to existence were transformed; When he later refuted both emptiness and existence, the multitudes all abandoned their attachments.
The Dragon Palace was filled with treasuries of medical formulas and profound meanings; Yet at the final discourse beneath the *nyagrodha* tree, the principle was not yet fully revealed.
In the realm of True Purity, it takes but a single thought-moment; In Jambudvīpa, eight thousand years have already passed.
Having reached the source, do not leave midway to serve the King of Emptiness; Taking up your staff, you must return to your native land.
When clouds and waters part, do not remain behind; In the depths of the Snowy Mountains, I shall not forget you.
Alas, on the day he departed, his countenance was like jade; Yet when he returned, one sighs that his hair is like frost.
He cast off his hands and arrived home, unrecognized by his kin; Once more, as an offering to the honored hall, he returns to the source.
The task of returning to the root and restoring the source is already flawed; originally there is no abiding, so it is not called a "home.
Ten-thousand-year-old pines and paths are deeply buried under snow, and a range of peaks is further shrouded by clouds.
When host and guest are harmonious, it is entirely delusion; where ruler and subject unite, the very center is perverse.
How should one sing the tune of the "Song of Returning Home"? Before the Hall of the Bright Moon, the withered tree blooms;
The turning of the pivot within the City of Nirvana remains precarious; When meeting on the road, do not fix upon a set time.
Temporarily hanging up soiled robes, one claims they are the Buddha; Yet when dressed in precious regalia, who is it that is named?
A wooden man goes out at midnight wearing boots; A stone woman returns at dawn wearing a cap.
The moon in the empty expanse of the eternal green pool— Only after searching and grasping again and again will you finally know it.
Shifting his station,
he dons fur and antlers to enter the marketplace; Like an *utpala* flower blooming amidst fire,
he acts as rain and dew within the sea of afflictions, And becomes clouds and thunder upon the mountain of ignorance.
The boiling cauldrons and furnace coals are blown out by my teaching; the sword-trees and knife-mountains are made to crumble by my shout.
The golden lock of the profound pass cannot detain me; though I move among the various classes of beings, I remain in the single color of saṃsāra.
Before the withered tree at the crag, divergent paths abound; When travelers reach this point, they all falter.
The heron standing in the snow is not the same color as it appears; The bright moon among the reeds is not like what it seems.
When there is clarity, there is nothing to clarify; Even in the realm of the profoundest mystery, one must still apply a critique.
Eagerly sing this song of the profound mystery: Can the moonlight in the void be grasped?
Chan Master Fayan’s Verse on “The Three Realms are Mind Only”:
The three realms are mind only; All phenomena are consciousness only. Consciousness only is mind only— Sight is sound, and hearing is form.
Form does not reach the ear; how could sound touch the eye? The eye, form, ear, and sound—how are the myriad dharmas brought to completion?
If the myriad dharmas were not dependent on conditions, how could one contemplate them as being like illusions? As for the great earth, mountains, and rivers—who is firm and who undergoes change?
National Teacher Chengguan’s Response to the Imperial Prince on the Essentials of Mind.
The ultimate Way takes its root in the mind; the dharma of the mind takes its root in non-abiding. The essence of the non-abiding mind is a numinous awareness that is never obscured;
its nature and characteristics are quiescent, encompassing all virtuous functions and integrating both the internal and external. It is both profound and vast, neither existent nor empty.

Neither arising nor ceasing; without beginning and without end. One seeks it but cannot find it; one abandons it but cannot leave it behind. When one is deluded regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), confusion and suffering proliferate;
when one awakens to true nature, emptiness shines forth with vast clarity. Although it is said that "the mind itself is the Buddha," this is known only by those who have realized it.
Yet, if there is realization or knowing, the sun of wisdom sinks into the realm of existence. If there is no illumination...
Without awakening, the dark clouds obscure the gateway to the void. If not a single thought arises, then the boundaries of past and future are severed;

the essence of illumination stands alone, and both object and self are as they truly are. One directly reaches the source of the mind, where there is neither wisdom nor attainment, neither grasping nor rejecting.

There is neither opposition nor cultivation; yet delusion and awakening depend upon one another, and truth and falsehood stand in mutual relation. If one seeks truth by abandoning falsehood, it is like discarding a shadow while wearying the body.
If one realizes that falsehood is itself truth, it is as if shadows vanish while remaining within them. If one is mindless and forgets even this illumination, then all anxieties are cast aside.
If one allows spontaneous, tranquil awareness to arise, then all practices will emerge from it. Be expansive and let go of whether things come or stay; remain in stillness.

Discerning its source and flow, speech and silence do not lose their profound subtlety; movement and stillness do not depart from the Dharma-realm. When words cease, both knowing and stillness are forgotten;
when discussing contemplation, both stillness and knowing are illuminated simultaneously. To speak of realization is to show that it cannot be demonstrated to others;

to explain the principle is to say it cannot be understood without realization. Therefore, awakening to stillness means there is no stillness; true knowing means there is no knowing. Through this, knowing and stillness are non-dual.
With this single mind, one accords with the Middle Way in which emptiness and existence are fused as one. Without dwelling and without attachment, there is nothing to grasp and nothing to collect.
Both right and wrong are forgotten; subject and object are both severed. When even this severance is stilled, Prajñā manifests before one.

Prajñā does not newly arise outside of the mind; the nature of wisdom is inherently complete from the beginning. Yet, though fundamentally quiescent, it cannot manifest of itself; it truly arises through Prajñā.

The merit of this lies in the fact that Prajñā and the nature of wisdom are mutually constitutive through their reciprocal relationship; the primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the wisdom cultivated through practice (*ādikarmika-bhāvanā*) truly possess no dual substance.
When both are forgotten and one enters directly, then wondrous awakening is perfectly luminous. When the beginning and the end are encompassed and fused, then cause and effect penetrate one another.
Every thought-moment acts as a Buddha; there is not a single mind that is not the Buddha-mind. Everywhere one attains the Way; there is not a single speck of dust that is not...
It is not that there is no Buddha-land; thus, truth and falsehood, things and self, are fully encompassed by taking up any one of them.

Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are a seamless unity, their essence identical. Know this: in delusion, the person follows the phenomena, and as phenomena differ in myriad ways, people likewise differ.

In awakening, the phenomena follow the person; every person possesses the same single wisdom, thereby fusing all myriad objects. Words are exhausted and thought ceases—what fruit, what cause? The essence is fundamentally so.
It is silent and desolate. What is the same? What is different? Only by forgetting the self does one become empty and luminous;

as news and silence merge in profound harmony, it is like the reflection of the moon upon water—empty yet visible. Like a mindless mirror reflecting images, it illuminates while remaining eternally void.
The Verse by Master Daopan of Dingzhou on the "Phrase that Encompasses Heaven and Earth":
Heaven and earth together with the myriad phenomena, Hell and heaven— In every single thing, there is true seeing.
Every single application is unimpaired;
this phrase cuts off the myriad streams.
Though mountains and peaks may be piled up, they are all but dust and ashes. Yet you still attempt to discuss the profound and the subtle.
Ice melts and tiles crumble;

swept away by the waves, following the current—these are words of sharp eloquence and a clever tongue. High and low are all preserved without deficiency, just like medicine prescribed according to the ailment.
The examination of symptoms depends on the immediate occasion;
beyond these three phrases, it is for the person themselves to raise the cry. How could three phrases encompass everything? If there is a question as to what this matter is:
Nanyue and Tiantai both praise and censure:
gold dust is an obscuration in the eye; the pearl on one's own clothing is but a speck of dust upon the Dharma—how can one fail to value one's own spiritual nature?
Why do the Buddhas and Patriarchs distinguish between the near and the far?
Before the black bean has even sprouted, deliberation has already become madness; seek no further for meanings within words and phrases.
In vain they distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox across the Western Heaven,
and in vain they discuss the true intent; it is all because they have not yet attained clear discernment, merely guarding the ghost-caves of other mountains.
It cannot be avoided that this spiritual essence penetrates both guest and host;
from afar they hasten toward the wind of the Way, asking with clarity, "Tell us, tell us to desist. Though asked again and again, if one has not yet understood—
Extinguishing it further, he shakes his head;
raising it for recommendation, they deliberate, yet upon meeting, no brow is raised. You go east, and I likewise go west; crimson clouds pierce the azure void.
The white sun circles Mount Sumeru;

if you wish to rectify the guiding principles through deliberation, you must first let the great earth fall into ruin. Should anyone attempt to confront me, they will meet a sword that cleaves through the snow.
There is no avoiding the shattering of one's sharp edge;
let us deliberate according to reality:
when sleepy, close the eyes; when hungry, eat. Whether rising or sitting, there is ultimately no difference between them.
Those on the same path already know that words do not cause delusion; The worlds of the ten directions are viewed directly before one’s eyes.

Having thoroughly deliberated upon their application, they have been universally accessible everywhere from the beginning; Providing expedients according to the occasion is simply following the family style.
Raising the eyebrows, blinking the eyes, opening a single hand; holding the whisk, striking the mallet—these are for the purpose of exalting [the Dharma].
